nodes.name: Async Commit Applicability
nodes.content: Async commit returns after the first 2PC phase (single-Region writes collapse to 1PC), cutting commit latency materially; enabled by default on newly created v5.0+ clusters but not on upgraded ones, direct downgrade unsupported, external consistency only with tidb_guarantee_external_consistency=ON, and causal consistency (START TRANSACTION WITH CAUSAL CONSISTENCY) trades global ordering for one fewer network round trip.

nodes.name: Cop vs Root Task Concurrency
nodes.content: Cop tasks execute pushed-down work distributed on TiKV while root tasks run single-point on TiDB; they run concurrently in an upstream-downstream relationship (root pulls from cop), so plan tree IDs carry no execution order and cop parallelism is normal, not a defect.

nodes.name: Dashboard Serving PD Negotiation
nodes.content: With multiple PD instances only one negotiated PD serves TiDB Dashboard (not necessarily the leader); browsers are redirected automatically, and tiup cluster display <cluster> --dashboard reveals the serving endpoint — an unreachable dashboard on one PD node is expected, not a fault.

nodes.name: Database Time Formulas
nodes.content: The diagnostic-report time tree decomposes query time as get_token + parse + compile + execute; execute = wait_start_tso + TiDB-layer execution + KV request + KV_backoff; KV request splits into network (estimate as KV time minus tikv_grpc_message) and tikv_grpc_message, which divides into coprocessor (tikv_cop_wait + handle) and scheduler (latch wait, read processing, snapshot fetch, write); write time follows raft propose/append/commit/apply-wait/apply. Because Raft KV writes are batched, judge Raft metrics by P99/P999 rather than TOTAL_TIME.

nodes.name: Logical vs Physical Size Semantics
nodes.content: information_schema.tables.data_length is a logical per-row estimate excluding MVCC redundant versions, while TiKV store size is the physical SST bytes after compression - they legitimately differ when versions accumulate.

nodes.name: Disk Spill File Semantics and Encryption
nodes.content: When tidb_enable_tmp_storage_on_oom is ON and a query exceeds tidb_mem_quota_query, blocking operators spill intermediate results to temporary files that are deleted when the query ends; spilled-file-encryption-method (aes128-ctr or default plaintext) controls whether those spill files are encrypted, so sudden disk usage during memory-limited queries is normal spill traffic.

nodes.name: Estimated vs Actual Rows Semantics
nodes.content: estRows is the optimizer's pre-execution row estimate from statistics; actRows in EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the actual count. A persistent large gap indicates stale or unrepresentative statistics feeding the cost model.

nodes.name: EXPLAIN Column Semantics
nodes.content: EXPLAIN reports id, estRows, task (root on TiDB, cop[tikv] on TiKV, mpp[tiflash] on TiFlash), access object, and operator info. EXPLAIN ANALYZE additionally reports actRows, execution info (wall time including sub-operators, loops, cop_task detail), memory, and disk.

nodes.name: GC Safe Point Semantics
nodes.content: One elected GC leader triggers GC every 10 minutes by default and computes safe point = current time - gc life time (10 minutes default), capped below the start_ts of ongoing transactions; each round runs Resolve Locks (commit/rollback leftover Percolator locks), Delete Ranges (fast physical drop cleanup), then Do GC where TiKV nodes delete versions older than the safe point after the leader pushes it to PD (DISTRIBUTED mode)

nodes.name: Distributed Global Sort Flow
nodes.content: The distributed global-sort framework (used by IMPORT INTO and DDL backfill) scans and encodes data into locally sorted blocks uploaded to shared storage with per-segment statistics, then splits nearly equal key ranges into parallel subtasks that each sort and ingest into TiKV without overlap.

nodes.name: KV Key Encoding Semantics
nodes.content: Clustered primary keys encode row data as one KV pair keyed by the primary key; NONCLUSTERED tables store two pairs per row (_tidb_rowid -> row, PK -> rowid), costing an extra index write on insert and an extra index read on primary-key access. Clustering only applies to the PRIMARY KEY and must be chosen at CREATE TABLE; closely-spaced inserted PKs concentrate writes in one Region, and wide (>64-bit) PKs inflate row storage especially with many secondary indexes.

nodes.name: KV vs gRPC Duration Gap
nodes.content: Avg TiDB KV request duration minus avg TiKV gRPC duration covers network and client-side scheduling: normally under ~2 ms same datacenter and under ~5 ms cross-AZ; a much larger gap (tens of ms) indicates network or CPU overload on TiDB/TiKV rather than storage slowness.

nodes.name: Threshold Check Reference
nodes.content: Reference expectations used by the threshold-check rule: TSO wait under 50ms, token wait under 1ms, schema load under 1s, TiKV scheduler/rocksdb write durations in the tens-of-ms range, block cache hit ratios above 0.8-0.95, leader/region/store score imbalance under 5-20%, under 20000 Regions per store, and under 100 Regions in scheduling.

nodes.name: Query Latency Breakdown
nodes.content: Query duration decomposes into parse, compile, and execute; execute time is KV request time (Get/Prewrite/Commit gRPC) plus PD TSO wait, and on TiKV storage async write duration equals store plus apply duration while raft adds append/commit/apply log durations, so the slowest stage identifies the bottleneck layer

nodes.name: Lightning Progress Reporting Semantics
nodes.content: Lightning progress log lines refresh every 5 minutes by default; the final 'tidb lightning exit' line is printed regardless of success, so only the 'the whole procedure completed' marker confirms completion.

nodes.name: Lightning Worker Pool Semantics
nodes.content: lightning_idle_workers labels: io near the configured value is healthy while io near 0 means the disk is too slow; closed-engine near 0 means Lightning runs faster than the importer and may stall; table/index/region idles stay near 0 until the end of the process. lightning_apply_worker_seconds histograms show wait time to acquire each worker type.

nodes.name: Log Backup Checkpoint Semantics
nodes.content: Log backup gates GC at the global checkpoint ts (aggregated from per-TiKV local checkpoints reported to PD), and a snapshot backup instead holds back the TiDB GC safe point for its whole duration; in both cases a slow or stalled backup task blocks GC of MVCC versions

nodes.name: Metrics Query Granularity Semantics
nodes.content: Metrics-table queries call the Prometheus query_range API: step comes from tidb_metric_query_step and the $RANGE_DURATION in PromQL from tidb_metric_query_range_duration (default 60s); the minimum supported granularity is 30 seconds, so sub-30s metric resolution does not exist.

nodes.name: Monitoring Architecture Semantics
nodes.content: Prometheus pulls metrics from component HTTP status ports into Grafana panels, so metric migration needs no cluster restart, Pushgateway is not a single point anymore, and two independent Prometheus/Grafana sets can run to avoid a monitoring SPOF; panel expressions use counter rate over a window (e.g. rate[1m]), sum/group-by, and a default 15s resolution step. Prometheus pulls metrics from component HTTP status ports into Grafana panels, so metric migration needs no cluster restart, Pushgateway is not a single point anymore, and two independent Prometheus/Grafana sets can run to avoid a monitoring SPOF; panel expressions use counter rate over a window (e.g. rate[1m]), sum/group-by, and a default 15s resolution step. Grafana organizes dashboards per cluster into groups (Overview, PD, TiDB, TiKV-Details/Summary/Trouble-Shooting, TiFlash-Summary, TiCDC, Performance-Read/Write, Disk-Performance, Lightning, Binlog, Backup-Restore, Node_exporter).

nodes.name: Partitioned Raft KV Storage Engine
nodes.content: Partitioned Raft KV stores each Region's data in its own RocksDB instance instead of one shared instance, giving per-Region physical isolation, better write performance, faster scale-in/out, and support for larger write-heavy clusters with sufficient memory; still an experimental feature. Partitioned Raft KV stores each Region's data in its own RocksDB instance, giving per-Region physical isolation and better write performance for write-heavy clusters with sufficient memory. In its tuned mode expect different defaults: storage.block-cache.capacity drops to 30%, region-split-size defaults to 10GiB (1GiB with enable-region-bucket), so memory/region behavior differs markedly from the classic single-RocksDB engine.

nodes.name: PD metric push interval
nodes.content: PD pushes monitoring metric data to Prometheus every interval (default 15s), so PD-sourced time series have this sampling granularity and sub-interval spikes can be missed.

nodes.name: PD Scheduling Flow Semantics
nodes.content: PD scheduling has three steps: stores report store and region heartbeats (capacity, traffic, peer status), schedulers generate operators under safety constraints (no peers on down or low-space stores, no leader to pending peers), then operators execute stepwise with concurrency limits

nodes.name: Region Model Semantics
nodes.content: A Region is a left-closed key range of about 96 MiB by default; its replicas form a Raft group whose leader serves requests, and PD balances leaders and peers across stores via balance-leader/balance-region

nodes.name: Resource Control Token Bucket Semantics
nodes.content: TiDB flow-controls resource groups with distributed token buckets: each TiDB node's local token buckets resynchronize with the Global Admission Control on PD every 5 seconds, and Available RU of 0 means the group is pinned at its RU_PER_SEC rate and is being rate-limited

nodes.name: BR Restore Scheduling Pause Semantics
nodes.content: During restore BR asks PD to pause region scheduling, splits and scatters regions to match backup data, then TiKV rewrites table/index IDs and ingests SSTs; RegionNotFound and EpochNotMatch failures are retried, so transient region churn should not fail the restore

nodes.name: Request Unit (RU) Semantics
nodes.content: Request Units meter per-query resource consumption (CPU, IO, etc.); background activities also consume RUs, so RU-per-second can be non-zero while QPS is zero — treat RU as the true load signal when capacity or throttling is under diagnosis.

nodes.name: Stats Health and Auto-Analyze Semantics
nodes.content: SHOW STATS_HEALTHY reports a 0-100 health percentage (100 means estimates match current data); SHOW STATS_META exposes row_count vs modify_count. Auto-analyze triggers once a table or partition has at least 1000 rows and modify/total ratio exceeds tidb_auto_analyze_ratio (default 0.5) inside the configured time window; keep that ratio below the pseudo-estimate-ratio threshold (default 0.8) or the optimizer falls back to pseudo statistics.

nodes.name: Store/Instance Status Lifecycle
nodes.content: Dashboard instance status derives from PD scheduling state: Up, Down/Unreachable, Unknown, and for TiKV/TiFlash the scale-in states Leaving (data migrating out) = PD 'Offline' = TiUP 'Pending Offline', and Tombstone (migration complete). Leaving/Tombstone stores must not be restarted or destroyed while data migration is in progress.

nodes.name: TiCDC Pipeline Semantics
nodes.content: TiCDC is highly available through PD etcd and pulls KV change logs from TiKV via multiple Capture processes; each Capture pulls part of the log, sorts and merges it, and changefeeds then replicate to downstreams, so lag reflects capture scheduling, sort throughput, or sink speed; TiKV actively re-pushes change logs when a Capture detects a gap. TiFlash columnar replicas ride the same Raft group as learners, so their catch-up lag is Raft replication lag

nodes.name: TiCDC Checkpoint Timestamp Semantics
nodes.content: TiCDC replication status is described by ResolvedTS and CheckpointTS constrained as table ResolvedTS >= global ResolvedTS >= table CheckpointTS >= global CheckpointTS; the global CheckpointTS is the minimum across all Processors and tables, so a single lagging table or failed sink pins the whole changefeed's checkpoint while others stay current

nodes.name: TiCDC Service GC Safepoint TTL
nodes.content: TiCDC gc-ttl defaults to 24 hours: after a changefeed interruption or failure, GC will not delete the incremental data needed for resumption within this window; beyond it, resume becomes impossible and a fresh full+incremental run is required.

nodes.name: TiDB memory alarm ratio semantics
nodes.content: tidb_memory_usage_alarm_ratio (GLOBAL, dynamic, default 0.7) triggers the tidb-server memory alarm when usage exceeds ratio x tidb_server_memory_limit, or ratio x system memory if the limit is 0; values 0 or 1 disable the alarm, and tidb_memory_usage_alarm_keep_record_num bounds retained alarm records.

nodes.name: TiDB query metric semantics
nodes.content: TiDB panel Duration covers the full client request including commands like COM_PING/COM_SLEEP and all statements of a multi-query; QPS counts statements by type across instances; Failed Query OPM groups errors with module and code; Connection Idle Duration separates client-side slowness from database time; Internal SQL OPS counts internally generated statements (stats updates, global variable reads) that can dominate busy panels.

nodes.name: TiFlash Pipeline Execution Model
nodes.content: TiFlash's pipeline execution model splits a query at pipeline-breaker operators (e.g. aggregation) into a DAG of pipelines instantiated as fine-grained tasks on fixed CPU/IO/wait thread pools, reducing OS thread-scheduling overhead at high concurrency and enabling fine-grained TiFlash resource control; it is enabled automatically when TiFlash resource control is used.

nodes.name: TiFlash Write Amplification Semantics
nodes.content: TiFlash write amplification factor = (Read flow + Write flow) / total Write Throughput By Instance; File Descriptor denotes the DeltaTree stable layer and Page denotes the Pagestore delta change layer, so layer-split flows locate which layer drives IO.

nodes.name: TiKV Thread Pool Semantics
nodes.content: In the raft-kv storage engine the Raft log lives in raftdb (RocksDB), tuned by max-background-jobs (default 4) and max-sub-compactions; raftdb.wal-dir should never share a disk path with the data WAL, and separating Raft WAL onto its own disk improves write latency, while mechanical disks benefit from a compaction-readahead-size of at least 2 MiB. TiKV thread CPU is healthy only relative to its pool size: raftstore CPU below 80% of raftstore.store-pool-size, async apply below 90% of apply-pool-size, store writer below 90% of store-io-pool-size, gRPC poll below 80% of server.grpc-concurrency, and scheduler worker below 90% of storage.scheduler-worker-pool-size; exceeding these suggests enlarging the pool or finding the overload source. Normal-state error expectations: Server is busy and Channel full must be 0, and leader drop/missing or log-replication rejects indicate instability.

nodes.name: Transaction Limit Semantics
nodes.content: A transaction may hold locks at most max-txn-ttl (default 3600000 ms, extended to up to 24h for bulk DML) before its locks can be cleared by others; retryable optimistic transactions are capped at stmt-count-limit statements (default 5000) and error beyond it. These bounds shape bulk delete/import batching strategies.

nodes.name: TSO Timestamp Layout and Parsing
nodes.content: A TSO packs a 46-bit physical millisecond timestamp and an 18-bit always-advancing logical counter; parse it with TIDB_PARSE_TSO()/TIDB_PARSE_TSO_LOGICAL(), bitwise shifts in SQL, or `tiup ctl pd tso` to correlate a transaction's start_ts with wall-clock time when diagnosing TSO waits or lock conflicts.

nodes.name: Accidental Deletion Recovery Window
nodes.content: Mechanism: DROP TABLE and TRUNCATE TABLE leave recoverable metadata and data until GC reclaims them, whereas DELETE FROM only marks MVCC versions for deletion at GC, so the three statements have different recovery windows and mechanisms. Differential diagnosis: identify the statement type and the time of deletion, then check the remaining GC lifetime before choosing a method - an old deletion already passed by GC needs a backup restore instead. Repair family: use the built-in flashback/recover for dropped or truncated tables inside the GC window, read pre-GC MVCC versions for mistakenly deleted rows, or fall back to PITR from backup; avoid advancing GC safepoints or shortening GC lifetime while recovery is pending. Historical reads via the tidb_snapshot system variable recover any pre-deletion view while GC lifetime retains versions (raising tidb_gc_life_time keeps more versions at the cost of disk and scan overhead and must be reset afterwards); FLASHBACK DATABASE restores a dropped database within the GC safe point (check tikv_gc_safe_point in mysql.tidb) with optional rename, and FLASHBACK CLUSTER rolls back the whole cluster to a BackupTS-boundary, requiring SUPER privilege, a not-yet-GC safe point, and pausing log backup/TiCDC tasks and recreating changefeeds after schemas re-converge. FLASHBACK TABLE and RECOVER TABLE rebuild a dropped or truncated table from DDL history jobs plus snapshot reads recorded in mysql.gc_delete_range, fail with 'snapshot is older than GC safe point' once the window passed (find the DDL JOB ID via ADMIN SHOW DDL JOBS for RECOVER TABLE BY JOB), and like FLASHBACK DATABASE need binlog downstream checks - resume downstream replication with a full re-import of the table when replay fails.

nodes.name: Account Unlock Procedure
nodes.content: Mechanism: consecutive-failure counters reset on a successful login or on ALTER USER ... ACCOUNT UNLOCK; a temporarily locked account clears itself when the lock time elapses (evaluated at the next login attempt) or when explicitly unlocked, and changing FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS or PASSWORD_LOCK_TIME does not alter an already-active lock. Diagnosis: for a locked account, distinguish policy-triggered temporary lock from administrative ACCOUNT LOCK. Remedies: wait out PASSWORD_LOCK_TIME or run ALTER USER ... ACCOUNT UNLOCK, then adjust policy variables knowing they apply from the next cycle; risk of unlocking is that the underlying credential-stuffing source is still active.

nodes.name: Persisted ANALYZE Options
nodes.content: Mechanism: with tidb_analyze_version=2 and tidb_persist_analyze_options=ON, options from the latest ANALYZE (buckets, topn, samplerate, column choice) persist in mysql.analyze_options and silently govern later automatic analyses. Diagnosis: for unexpected stats quality, inspect the persisted row joined with information_schema.tables and SHOW COLUMN_STATS_USAGE to find predicate columns. Remedy: rerun ANALYZE with explicit desired options to overwrite, or disable persistence; stale persisted options are not cleared when the feature is toggled. Wide tables make full-column ANALYZE expensive; ANALYZE TABLE t COLUMNS a,b or PREDICATE COLUMNS (requires tidb_enable_column_tracking=ON, writes usage to mysql.column_stats_usage every ~300 s, v2 analyze only) collects just the WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY/GROUP BY columns plus indexed columns, and tidb_analyze_skip_column_types excludes noisy types. Warnings during ANALYZE also reveal auto-adjusted sample rates when stats_meta row counts disagree with PD counts.

nodes.name: Auto Increment Allocation Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB allocates AUTO_INCREMENT ids in batches per TiDB node, guaranteeing uniqueness and per-node monotonicity but not global sequentiality, so concurrently inserted rows can receive non-monotonic ids across instances. Diagnosis: when application logic assumes strictly ordered ids, confirm inserts span multiple TiDB nodes and that the gap pattern matches batch allocation rather than lost writes. Remedies: tolerate unordered ids, or centralize inserts, or use AUTO_RANDOM-style design only where ordering is truly unneeded; do not treat smaller later ids as data loss without diff evidence.

nodes.name: Auto-increment cache conflict runbook
nodes.content: AUTO_INCREMENT allocation is cached per TiDB (default AUTO_ID_CACHE 0 batches of 30000), so consecutive IDs across instances show large gaps; AUTO_ID_CACHE 1 provides the MySQL-compatible monotonic mode backed by a centralized allocator (v6.4+), but small gaps still occur after failover, rolling upgrades, and concurrent commits, and since v8.1.0 the allocator skips forceRebase on primary exit for faster restarts. ALTER TABLE cannot add the AUTO_INCREMENT attribute, can remove it only when tidb_allow_remove_auto_inc=true, needs FORCE to lower the counter, and lowering below MAX(column) causes duplicate-key errors because existing values are not skipped. Duplicate or jumping IDs after failover are therefore allocator semantics, not data corruption. AUTO_INCREMENT allocation is cached per TiDB (default AUTO_ID_CACHE 0 batches of 30000), so consecutive IDs across instances show large gaps; AUTO_ID_CACHE 1 provides the MySQL-compatible monotonic mode backed by a centralized allocator (v6.4+), but small gaps still occur after failover, rolling upgrades, and concurrent commits, and since v8.1.0 the allocator skips forceRebase on primary exit for faster restarts. SHOW TABLE t NEXT_ROW_ID exposes the live allocation position for _tidb_rowid, AUTO_INCREMENT, AUTO_RANDOM, and SEQUENCE columns, making cache effects directly observable. ALTER TABLE cannot add the AUTO_INCREMENT attribute, can remove it only when tidb_allow_remove_auto_inc=true, needs FORCE to lower the counter, and lowering below MAX(column) causes duplicate-key errors because existing values are not skipped.

nodes.name: AUTO_RANDOM Insert Handling
nodes.content: Mechanism: tables with an AUTO_RANDOM primary key reject INSERTs that specify that column with ERROR 8216; the session variable allow_auto_random_explicit_insert can lift the restriction. Diagnosis: on ERROR 8216, confirm the target column carries AUTO_RANDOM and whether the application can omit it. Remedies: prefer dropping the column from the INSERT and letting TiDB allocate values, since that preserves AUTO_RANDOM hotspot-spreading semantics; only set allow_auto_random_explicit_insert = true for workloads that genuinely must supply ids, accepting re-introduced hotspot and conflict risks.

nodes.name: Automatic Inspection Tables
nodes.content: The SQL diagnostics system exposes cluster topology (cluster_info), per-instance configuration (cluster_config), hardware, kernel parameters, and a cluster_log table that pushes filters down to instances (cheaper than grep); metrics_schema monitoring tables plus metrics_summary[_by_label] compare periods, and querying information_schema.inspection_result passively runs built-in diagnostic rules to surface known fault patterns. Start an investigation with inspection_result, then drill into inspection_summary for the affected module.

nodes.name: Backup SSE Key Handling
nodes.content: Mechanism: backups written to Azure Blob with a customer-provided AES256 server-side encryption key must present the identical key again at restore via --azblob.encryption-key, the encryption-key URI parameter (percent-encoded), or AZURE_ENCRYPTION_KEY. Diagnosis: a restore that fails decrypting or reading backup data indicates the key was absent or different from the one used at backup. Remedies: supply the correct key through any of the three channels; if the key is lost the backup is unrecoverable, so the only remedy is prevention through key custody outside ephemeral environments.

nodes.name: Backup Storage Credential Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: BR and TiKV authenticate to backup storage via URI keys, environment variables, shared credential files, IAM roles, or metadata servers; S3 operations additionally require privileges such as ListBucket, GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject, and AbortMultipartUpload (checkpoint and PiTR id-map subdirectories are written under the backup prefix). Diagnosis: when backup or restore fails with storage errors, match the error to the missing privilege or unresolved credential source. Remedies: supply access keys via URI/env/credential file, or attach an IAM role to the instance; for Azure SAS tokens percent-encode special characters; risk is that rotating credentials requires restarting TiKV to pick up env-based Azure AD variables.

nodes.name: Backup throughput runbook
nodes.content: Backup and restore ceilings are set by the backup network bandwidth and storage IOPS before TiDB itself becomes the bottleneck; TiKV needs about two additional CPU cores and performant disks for backup tasks, and the br node needs at least 8 cores/16 GiB. A backup that slows services or cannot reach expected throughput should be checked against these resource floors and RATE_LIMIT/ratelimit settings before deeper diagnosis. Backup and restore ceilings are set by the backup network bandwidth and storage IOPS before TiDB itself becomes the bottleneck; TiKV needs about two additional CPU cores and performant disks for backup tasks, and the br node needs at least 8 cores/16 GiB. Plan capacity from the reference rates of about 40 MB/s per TiKV for backup and 100 MB/s per TiKV for restore, prefer BR over Dumpling/mysqldump for terabyte-scale data, and check RATE_LIMIT/ratelimit settings when a backup slows services or misses throughput targets. Backup and restore ceilings are set by the backup network bandwidth and storage IOPS before TiDB itself becomes the bottleneck; TiKV needs about two additional CPU cores and performant disks for backup tasks, and the br node needs at least 8 cores/16 GiB. Plan capacity from reference rates of roughly 40 MB/s per TiKV for backup and 100 MB/s per TiKV for restore (other deployments report ~50 MB/s per TiKV), and expect backup/restore to be CPU-intensive enough to cost 10-50% of QPS/latency, so schedule off-peak and prefer BR over Dumpling/mysqldump at terabyte scale. Backup and restore ceilings are set by the backup network bandwidth and storage IOPS before TiDB itself becomes the bottleneck; TiKV needs about two additional CPU cores and performant disks for backup tasks, and the br node needs at least 8 cores/16 GiB. Plan capacity from reference rates of roughly 40 MB/s per TiKV for backup and 100 MB/s per TiKV for restore (other deployments report ~50 MB/s per TiKV), and expect backup/restore to be CPU-intensive enough to cost 10-50% of QPS/latency, so schedule off-peak and prefer BR over Dumpling/mysqldump at terabyte scale. Restores deliberately saturate TiKV CPU/disk/network, so target an empty cluster; for very large Region counts the default coarse-grained scattering (--granularity=coarse-grained) speeds restore about 3x, and --tikv-max-restore-concurrency (v8.0+) bounds downloads/ingest per node with a job queue of 32 * nodes * concurrency.

nodes.name: Backup Task Resource Impact
nodes.content: Backup threads default to MIN(CPU*0.5, 8) and BR auto-tune (enable-auto-tune, default on) throttles backup resource use when cluster utilization is high, so a slow backup under load can be auto-tune rather than a fault; diagnose backup slowness by comparing auto-tune state, thread counts, and sst-max-size-driven file splitting against observed throughput. BR auto-tune throttles backup resource use under high cluster utilization but has known blind spots: on write-heavy clusters it can enter a positive feedback loop (workload yields, auto-tune speeds backup up) — cap backup.num-threads manually; on hotspot nodes backup is over-throttled — evict the hotspot or disable auto-tune there; and its 1-minute refresh interval cannot track high traffic jitter — disable it. Backup CPU threads run near 100% of their pool, so thread count is the effective lever.

nodes.name: Bidirectional Replication Loop and DDL Discipline
nodes.content: Bidirectional TiDB Binlog replication prevents replication loops because Drainer stamps each replicated transaction with the _drainer_repl_mark table and filters marked events on the peer; both sides must configure the same channel_id. DDL cannot carry the mark, so DDL must replicate one-way only and must not run concurrently on both clusters or while DML is replicating, otherwise upstream and downstream schemas diverge and DML replication breaks. Bidirectional TiDB Binlog replication prevents replication loops because Drainer stamps each replicated transaction with the _drainer_repl_mark table and filters marked events on the peer; both sides must configure the same channel_id. DDL cannot carry the mark, so DDL must replicate one-way only and must not run concurrently on both clusters or while DML is replicating, otherwise upstream and downstream schemas diverge. In TiCDC-based BDR (v7.6+), DDLs split into replicable (CREATE TABLE, ADD COLUMN with default, ADD NON-UNIQUE INDEX, TTL changes...) and non-replicable (DROP/TRUNCATE TABLE, DROP COLUMN, ADD UNIQUE INDEX, RENAME, EXCHANGE/REORGANIZE PARTITION...); ADMIN SET BDR ROLE PRIMARY/SECONDARY enforces this and violations fail with Error 8263, while non-replicable DDLs need roles unset, writes quiesced, and manual execution on every cluster.

nodes.name: Binding From Historical Plan
nodes.content: Mechanism: CREATE BINDING FROM HISTORY USING PLAN DIGEST pins a past execution plan by its plan_digest from statements_summary (requires tidb_enable_stmt_summary); generated hints may be incomplete for TiFlash, three-way joins, or subqueries, in which case the creation warns, and original manual hints are preserved in the binding. Diagnosis: for a plan regression where the good plan recently existed, find its plan_digest in statements_summary and bind it directly. Remedies: create the binding, confirm with SHOW BINDINGS, and execute the statement then check @@LAST_PLAN_FROM_BINDING = 1; risk is that a stale pinned plan prevents the optimizer from adapting to data growth.

nodes.name: Binding Troubleshooting
nodes.content: Mechanism: a binding can miss the statement because the normalized digest differs, the binding is absent from an instance's LRU binding cache, or the bound plan is invalid for the current statement. Discrimination: SELECT @@last_plan_from_binding tells whether the last plan came from a binding; EXPLAIN format='verbose' plus SHOW WARNINGS prints the bindSQL actually used; SHOW BINDING_CACHE STATUS exposes cache usage versus quota. Fix family: recreate the binding from the exact statement text, drop stale bindings, or raise the binding cache memory quota; re-verify with last_plan_from_binding.

nodes.name: TiDB Binlog Alert Triage
nodes.content: Mechanism: binlog alerts are tiered - emergency binlog_pump_storage_error_count means Pump cannot write local storage; critical binlog_drainer_checkpoint_high_delay (lag >1 hour) and warning-level rules cover Pump WriteBinlog RPC p90 >1s, storage write p90 >1s, Pump free disk <20G, Drainer checkpoint unchanged for 1 minute, and Drainer execute duration p90 >10s. Diagnosis: high Drainer delay - compare Pump handle tso per node (pull side) against Drainer event rate and execute time (apply side); slow Pump writes point at disk latency/util; stalled checkpoint means check that all non-offline Pumps run; execute-time spikes during DDL can be ignored. Remedy family: fix the mapped layer - Pump disk or GC (gc_tso), pull-side Pump health, or apply-side worker-count/batch and downstream state.

nodes.name: Bidirectional Replication Loopback Control
nodes.content: Mechanism: Drainer bidirectional replication relies on loopback-control = true and an identical channel-id on both paths to recognize and skip echoed events; DDL must be replicated on exactly one direction (sync-ddl true on the DDL-source path, false on the other), and sync-mode SyncPartialColumn tolerates column differences while the checkpoint table must be ignored. Diagnosis: for duplicated or ping-ponged data, verify loopback-control/channel-id on both Drainer paths and that sync-ddl is one-way. Remedies: align channel-id and enable loopback marking, keep all DDL on the designated cluster, ignore tidb_binlog.checkpoint in the filter; risk is silent divergence if either path loses loopback marking, since every replicated row then re-enters the pipeline.

nodes.name: Binlog Upstream-Downstream Inconsistency Causes
nodes.content: Mechanism: silent replication divergence has a small cause set - some TiDB nodes have binlog disabled or entered 'ignore binlog' state (verify every node via the /info/all status interface); timestamp column values drift when Drainer's timezone (read from /etc/localtime, TZ unsupported) differs from the databases, or when TiDB's NULL timestamp default replicates to MySQL 5.7's current-time default (set explicit_defaults_for_timestamp=on upstream before enabling binlog); 'gen update sqls failed: row data is corruption' came from DML concurrent with DROP COLUMN (fixed v3.0.6) and a hung Drainer with frozen checkpoint was fixed in v3.0.4. Diagnosis: on reported inconsistency, first verify binlog status on all TiDB nodes, then compare timezone settings and timestamp defaults. Remedy family: enable binlog everywhere, align Drainer /etc/localtime with both databases, set explicit_defaults_for_timestamp before replication starts, and upgrade past the fixed versions; duplicate binlog writes across Pump nodes are safe because Drainer deduplicates by TSO.

nodes.name: Drainer Checkpoint and Rebuild Recovery
nodes.content: Mechanism: Drainer replicates from the checkpoint commit-ts (tidb_binlog.checkpoint for MySQL/TiDB sinks, a file for Kafka/file sinks) and falls back to configured initialCommitTs when the checkpoint is unreadable; a crashed Pump that cannot recover must be set offline with binlogctl, which forfeits its data and guarantees downstream divergence. Differential diagnosis: separate a healthy-checkpoint failure (redeploy Drainer elsewhere, offline the old one) from a lost checkpoint (recover the last commit-ts from downstream Kafka/file data), an ignore-error critical error (TiDB silently stops writing binlog - data already lost, rebuild required), and an abnormally exited Drainer whose relay log or consistency flag (consistent=false) allows in-place replay. Repair family: for divergence or binlog loss stop Drainer, clear downstream data including tidb_binlog.checkpoint, take a fresh full backup, restore it, and redeploy Drainer at initialCommitTs equal to the backup snapshot ts; patch gaps with Reparo over binlog files (start-tso = snapshot ts + 1, end-ts = 0), resuming an interrupted run by recording the last TSO as checkpoint-tso, one pass with safe-mode=true over the ambiguous window, then normal replication with stop-tso=0 and safe-mode=false. Pump nodes store binlogs locally and auto-purge anything older than their gc retention (default 7 days), so a drainer or checkpoint stalled beyond retention can no longer catch up incrementally and needs a re-snapshot.

nodes.name: TiDB Binlog Common Errors
nodes.content: Mechanism: frequent binlog-pipeline errors have mapped causes - Drainer-to-Kafka 'Message was too large' means big-transaction binlog exceeds Kafka limits (raise message.max.bytes/replica.fetch.max.bytes/fetch.message.max.bytes); Pump 'no space left on device' needs disk cleanup then restart, and a near-full Pump should first be checked against its gc_tso retention then fixed by shortening GC days or adding Pump nodes; Pump startup 'fail to notify all living drainer' means a Drainer marked online is actually dead - correct the state with binlogctl and restart Pump; gRPC ResourceExhausted on huge transactions is fixed by Pump max-message-size; Drainer sarama EOF is a Kafka version mismatch with syncer.to kafka-version. Diagnosis: follow the flow - check monitoring metrics, verify Pump/Drainer states with binlogctl, then search Pump/Drainer logs for ERROR/WARN. Remedy family: apply the mapped fix; a stuck-looking TiDB with 'listener stopped' on old versions is a binlog write failure, not a hang.

nodes.name: Binlog Write Failure: ignore-error Trade-off
nodes.content: Mechanism: when Pump/binary write fails, TiDB behavior depends on binlog.ignore-error - with true TiDB keeps serving but stops writing binlog (a silent replication gap, signaled by a rising tidb_server_critical_error_total metric), while with false the whole TiDB service stops on binlog write failure. Diagnosis: downstream Drainer lag or missing recent rows with a healthy TiDB implies ignore-error=true swallowed write failures - check the tidb_server_critical_error_total counter and TiDB logs around the gap window. Remedy family: decide availability vs replication completeness explicitly; with ignore-error=true treat a nonzero critical-error counter as data-loss risk for downstream consumers and repair by resyncing the gap from snapshot plus binlog.

nodes.name: Pump/Drainer Pipeline Unavailability
nodes.content: Mechanism: each TiDB with [binlog] enable=true pulls Pump lists from PD and writes binlog to every online Pump, so zero live Pumps blocks startup or breaks writes. Differential: check binlog flag with SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin' (0 means enabled), then compare SHOW PUMP STATUS / binlogctl pump state against actual processes. Remedies: (a) start or restart at least one Pump before TiDB; (b) if binlog is being retired, disable it consistently on every TiDB instance (a temporary instance without binlog must set run_ddl=false). Risks: inconsistent binlog enablement across TiDB instances causes upstream/downstream data inconsistency. Rolling upgrades must replace and restart Pump instances one by one so at least one Pump always accepts binlog, and the component boot order is PD -> TiKV -> Pump -> TiDB.

nodes.name: Drainer replication integrity runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: Drainer merges and sorts binlogs from all Pumps, converts them to SQL, and applies them downstream, recording applied commit-ts in the tidb_binlog checkpoint. Differential: compare @@sql_mode on both sides, inspect checkpoint progress, and test whether the failing statement is a downstream-unsupported DDL or a rename on ignored schemas. Remedies: (a) for an existing cluster, take a full backup, restore downstream, and start Drainer from the snapshot's initial-commit-ts; (b) align sql_mode; (c) configure skipping of the incompatible transaction and apply a compatible DDL manually downstream. Risks: skipping transactions permanently diverges the downstream; relay log is the guard for downstream consistency. The Drainer status endpoint reporting Synced=true (or inspecting the downstream tidb_binlog checkpoint) confirms old binlogs are fully applied before cutover or repair.

nodes.name: Drainer Slow Replication Causes
nodes.content: Mechanism: Drainer applies changes row-by-row to the downstream; replication slows when replicated tables lack primary/unique keys, when upstream runs frequent DDL, when the output disk is slow, or when worker-count is too low for the network distance (normal latency is seconds, roughly 3s off-peak). Diagnosis: compare the Drainer Event metric (rows applied per second by ddl/insert/delete/update) with SQL Query Time (downstream execution time) to separate apply-throughput problems from slow downstream SQL; Checkpoint TSO vs Pump Handle TSO and Pull Binlog QPS distinguish pull-side from apply-side slowness. Remedy family: add primary/unique keys to replicated tables, raise Drainer worker-count/batch (especially when downstream load is low), deploy Drainer close to the downstream for cross-DC replication, and quiet DDL churn during catch-up.

nodes.name: Stale binlog node state runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: Pump/Drainer report their state to PD periodically, and kill -9 or panic exits never update PD, so states go stale. Differential: run binlogctl -cmd pumps/drainers or SHOW PUMP/DRAINER STATUS and compare State/Update_Time with real processes; a Pump that exits citing an unreachable Drainer means a stale online Drainer. Remedies: (a) restart in order Drainer -> Pump -> TiDB; (b) correct the state with binlogctl offline-drainer / update-drainer / update-pump (or CHANGE PUMP/DRAINER TO NODE_STATE) before restart; (c) use pause-* for planned stops, offline-* only for permanent removal. Risks: update-* commands only rewrite PD state without notifying processes, so misuse interrupts replication or loses data; never use kill -9.

nodes.name: Choose the Binlog Failure Mode Consciously
nodes.content: Mechanism: with binlog enabled, ignore-error=false makes any Pump write failure halt the entire TiDB service, while ignore-error=true keeps serving but silently stops binlog writes and only increments tidb_server_critical_error_total. Differential: sudden TiDB unavailability with binlog errors points to Pump outage; downstream data loss without errors points to ignore-error=true. Remedies: restore Pump capacity and monitor the critical error counter; the choice between availability and downstream consistency is a business decision made in config, not a runtime fix. Risk: either side of the trade-off can mask a replication outage if not monitored.

nodes.name: Blue-Green / Cross-Cluster Cutover
nodes.content: Mechanism: the new cluster is built from a BR full backup, upgraded offline, then fed by forward TiCDC replication; switchability depends on GC lifetime covering the whole window and the changefeed checkpoint passing the frozen up-tso. Differential: compare checkpointTs against up-tso (BEGIN; SELECT TIDB_CURRENT_TSO(); ROLLBACK on the read-only old cluster), confirm incremental throughput exceeds peak write rate, and match new_collations_enabled_on_first_bootstrap between clusters or BR restore fails. Remedies: (a) raise tidb_gc_life_time before starting to cover backup + restore + upgrade + replication setup; (b) freeze traffic with ALTER USER ACCOUNT LOCK or SET GLOBAL tidb_super_read_only=ON plus TiDB restarts to clear lingering sessions; (c) verify data at up-tso/down-tso with sync-diff-inspector, pause the forward changefeed, restart new-cluster TiDB nodes to clear auto-increment caches, then build the reverse channel for rollback. Risks: an unrecoverable changefeed forces redo from a fresh full backup; raised GC lifetime costs storage and can affect query performance; TiCDC cannot replicate Sequence or TiFlash DDL and valid-index tables are required.

nodes.name: Backup storage layout discipline
nodes.content: BR writes through TiKV, so backups must go to shared storage (S3/GCS/Azure, or MinIO/NFS self-hosted); with non-shared storage each TiKV writes backup data locally, creating redundant collection problems. Organize snapshot and log backups under one cluster-scoped directory with dated snapshot subdirectories and a fixed log-backup directory, and prune historical data deliberately since BR has no built-in backup management.

nodes.name: Checkpoint backup resume
nodes.content: Interrupted snapshot backups can resume instead of restarting from scratch: br periodically persists backed-up key ranges to external storage as checkpoints and retries the differential. Preconditions and limits: br holds the backup GC safe point only for gcttl (default about one hour) so the retry must start before GC advances, and a system-killed br loses up to the last 30 seconds of checkpoint metadata, which is simply re-backed-up. The SQL BACKUP statement drives the BR engine in-TiDB: it needs BACKUP_ADMIN or SUPER, write access from both the executing TiDB and all TiKV nodes (local:// is barred under Security Enhanced Mode), blocks the session until the task finishes, supports SNAPSHOT/RATE_LIMIT/CONCURRENCY/CHECKSUM/LAST_BACKUP options, and only one backup or restore task may run cluster-wide - cancel a stuck one with KILL TIDB QUERY. Plan long-lived connections and serialize backup windows accordingly.

nodes.name: Encrypted Backup Restore Constraints
nodes.content: Mechanism: BR encrypts snapshot backups with a crypter method and key, and restore only succeeds when both decryption parameters match the backup exactly. Differential diagnosis: a decryption failure is distinguishable from storage or network failures because it occurs while reading backup files despite reachable storage. Repair family: re-run the restore with the correct --crypter.method and --crypter.key recorded with the backup; there is no recovery path for a lost key, so verify the key material before the next attempt rather than retrying blindly.

nodes.name: BR Full-plus-Incremental GC Discipline
nodes.content: Mechanism: BR full backup plus TiCDC incremental migration requires disabling GC (SET GLOBAL tidb_gc_enable=FALSE) before BACKUP so history data survives until the changefeed starts; the returned BackupTS marks both the end-of-full-data check and the changefeed --start-ts. After the changefeed is created, re-enable GC because TiCDC's GC safepoint only lets history data be removed once replicated. Diagnosis of failures: if backup/restore outlives TiCDC's default gc-ttl of 24 hours, the subsequent incremental task fails - check gc-ttl and elapsed time. Remedy families: adjust gc-ttl when starting TiCDC, run BACKUP with RATE_LIMIT during off-peak hours to avoid performance degradation, verify BR version compatibility between clusters, and validate consistency with sync-diff-inspector at the BackupTS snapshot.

nodes.name: BR Restore Error Families
nodes.content: Mechanism: BR restore failures cluster into families: Io(Os ...) system-call errors from the backup directory mount or filesystem; rpc Unavailable when cluster capacity is insufficient for restore concurrency; 'entry too large, max 6291456' when --ddl-batch-size sends schemas above the 6 MB job limit; and 'SST file not found' or 'could not read local://...: download sst failed' when backups on local storage are scattered across TiKV nodes that each need all SSTs. Diagnosis: classify the error text first, then confirm with cluster monitoring or TiKV logs. Remedies: fix mount/permissions or switch storage, scale out or reduce restore concurrency with RATE_LIMIT, set --ddl-batch-size to 128 or below, and keep backups on S3/GCS/Azure/NFS so every node reaches all files; risk is that collecting scattered local backups duplicates data and delays recovery.

nodes.name: BR Restore and Checksum Version Semantics
nodes.content: Remedy validity depends on version: since v7.1.0 BR checkpoint restore resumes an interrupted restore and keeps most progress, while older versions must restart the restore from scratch after any interruption. Since v8.1.2 full backups disable table-level checksum calculation by default, so post-restore data verification is no longer automatic - enable checksum explicitly when restore correctness must be proven. Diagnosis: check BR version and whether a checkpoint exists before choosing resume versus restart.

nodes.name: BR Storage URI and Credential Discipline
nodes.content: BR forwards its storage credentials to every TiKV by default (--send-credentials-to-tikv=true); in IAM-role environments each node has its own role, so credential forwarding must be disabled (-c=0 or SEND_CREDENTIALS_TO_TIKV = FALSE) or jobs fail with auth errors. Storage access failures are usually wrong URI parameters (scheme://bucket/prefix?access-key=...) or insufficient bucket permissions, and show up in BR/TiKV logs as storage initialization errors before any data moves.

nodes.name: Built-in Diagnostic Sweep
nodes.content: Mechanism: the inspection_result rules detect config or version drift between instances, high node load, module critical errors, and metric threshold violations, returning severity plus suggested follow-up SQL. Discrimination: use it as a first-pass sweep to narrow which component and rule family is abnormal before deep-diving dashboards; warning-level config/version findings often explain single-node anomalies. Fix family: align drifted config or versions, relieve loaded nodes, and follow the DETAILS pointers for threshold violations.

nodes.name: Bulk Update Batching Discipline
nodes.content: Mechanism: single huge DML transactions hit entry (6 MB) and total (100 MB) size limits, hold locks long (pessimistic) or invite write conflicts (optimistic), and pay full-commit Raft replication cost. Differential diagnosis: check the error text for entry vs total limits and confirm the change is a one-off bulk operation; loading data that fails while DDL runs indicates a concurrent schema change on the target table. Remedy families: (1) batch the change - DELETE ... LIMIT loops ending on affected rows 0 with a strong filter index or primary-key range, inserts of about 10 thousand rows per batch; (2) non-transactional BATCH ON <shard_column> LIMIT <n> DML, which splits into sequential batches - verify with DRY RUN, watch progress via SHOW PROCESSLIST ('job x/y'), and KILL TIDB to stop after the current batch; (3) raise txn-total-size-limit (max 10 GB) only with enough physical memory; (4) use IMPORT INTO/Lightning for bulk loads. Risks: non-transactional DML sacrifices atomicity and isolation - it requires no concurrent writes on the target data, idempotency or partial retry plans (especially with tidb_redact_log=1 and tidb_nontransactional_ignore_error=1), and never modify the shard column or use it as a join key, or rows may be written or modified multiple times.

nodes.name: CA Certificate Rotation Order
nodes.content: Mechanism: rotating a CA requires a combined CA certificate (new + old concatenated) deployed to both server and clients first, so both trust chains validate during the transition; only then are client and server key/certificate pairs reissued, and their subject/issuer fields must match the user's REQUIRE clauses; a TiDB restart is needed to load the combined CA. Diagnosis: for logins failing mid-rotation, determine which side still trusts only the old CA and whether the new certificate attributes satisfy REQUIRE ISSUER/SUBJECT. Remedies: follow the combined-CA order, restart TiDB once with the combined bundle, then replace leaf certificates; risk is a full outage window if the old CA is removed before all peers hold the combined bundle.

nodes.name: Cardinality Misestimation Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: the optimizer assumes column independence and uses hardcoded selectivity for string matches (like/rlike/regexp default 0.8), so correlated columns and fuzzy filters produce large estimation errors that drive wrong index or join choices. Diagnosis: compare estRows with actRows in EXPLAIN ANALYZE and identify correlated or string-match predicates. Fix family: create correlation extended statistics (ADD STATS_EXTENDED ... correlation, requires tidb_enable_extended_stats and a fresh ANALYZE), tune tidb_default_string_match_selectivity (0 enables TopN-based estimation with analyze version 2), or hint the correct plan. Risks: extended statistics change estimates cluster-wide and may flip other plans; verify with EXPLAIN.

nodes.name: Causal Consistency Ordering Anomaly
nodes.content: Mechanism: with START TRANSACTION WITH CAUSAL CONSISTENCY ONLY (effective only when async commit and one-phase commit are enabled), commits skip the PD timestamp so ordering is guaranteed only between transactions with a database-known causal relationship, e.g. lock or write intersection; lock-free reads create no causal edge. Diagnosis: when clients observe reads that violate expected commit ordering, check whether transactions use causal consistency, async commit, or 1pc, and whether the read pattern relies on ordering between independent transactions. Remedies: fall back to default linear consistency for transactions whose observers require global ordering, or establish a causal relationship through locked/written keys; risk is higher commit latency when PD timestamps are required.

nodes.name: Bidirectional Replication Limitations
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiCDC BDR supports one PRIMARY plus n SECONDARY clusters or role-less clusters with manual DDL, but mixed role assignments break correctness; clusters cannot detect write conflicts (application must guarantee disjoint keys), and cascading ring topologies are unsupported because one failure stalls the ring. Diagnosis: for duplicated or conflicting primary keys across BDR clusters, check AUTO_INCREMENT/AUTO_RANDOM overlap and role assignment. Remedies: partition id space with per-cluster auto_increment_increment/offset values, keep every cluster pairwise connected instead of cascading, and stop replication by inserting sentinel records, verifying both sides, then stopping changefeeds and running ADMIN UNSET BDR ROLE; risk is silent corruption if roles or id ranges are misconfigured while writes continue.

nodes.name: force-replicate Consistency Risk
nodes.content: Mechanism: changefeeds normally refuse tables without a valid index; force-replicate = true includes them, but such tables make INSERT/REPLACE non-reentrant while TiCDC only guarantees at-least-once delivery, so redundancy is expected after retries or resume. Diagnosis: for duplicated downstream rows, check whether affected tables lack a usable primary or unique key and whether force-replicate is enabled. Remedies: add an effective index such as an AUTO RANDOM primary key and re-create the changefeed, or deduplicate downstream with rebaseline tooling; risk is that keeping force-replicate accepts permanent duplicate-row exposure.

nodes.name: TiCDC Kafka Dispatcher Rules
nodes.content: TiCDC dispatches Kafka events by the first matching dispatcher rule: tables matching no matcher, or matching rules without a topic expression, fall back to the default topic in --sink-uri, and schema-level DDLs always go to the default topic. Topic expressions use {schema}/{table} placeholders (lowercase only, fewer than 1000 topics recommended), so consumers missing expected events should be traced to unmatched matchers or default-topic routing before suspecting replication lag.

nodes.name: Kafka Sink Latency Tuning
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiCDC-to-Kafka latency grows when broker or consumer size limits reject or throttle large messages, or when open-protocol batching (max-message-bytes, default 10 MB; max-batch-size, default 16 events) exceeds broker message.max.bytes and replica.fetch.max.bytes. Diagnosis: for rising sink latency, compare changefeed message size settings against Kafka server.properties and consumer fetch limits, and check whether the protocol batches rows (open-protocol) or sends per row (canal-json/avro). Remedies: raise Kafka message.max.bytes and replica.fetch.max.bytes to 1 GB and keep consumer fetch.message.max.bytes above them, or lower max-message-bytes/max-batch-size; risk is larger broker memory pressure when limits are raised.

nodes.name: Kafka Partition Dispatcher Selection
nodes.content: Mechanism: default/table dispatchers route each table to one partition, guaranteeing per-table order but capping throughput since adding consumers cannot speed a single partition; index-value, columns, and ts dispatchers spread rows over partitions for parallel consumption with order only within a partition, and ts additionally requires consumers to re-sort by commitTs because multiple changes of one row can land in different partitions. Diagnosis: for disordered consumers check the active dispatcher rule (first matching rule wins) and whether the downstream sorts by commitTs; changefeed errors naming a missing index or column mean the referenced index/columns do not exist. Remedies: switch throughput-bound tables to index-value or columns dispatchers, fix or replace dispatcher references that error, and keep dispatcher and partition keys out of the same rule; risk is cross-partition inconsistency if consumers do not implement commitTs ordering under ts.

nodes.name: Kafka Sink Resilience Setup
nodes.content: Mechanism: a changefeed sink URI listing only one broker breaks whenever that broker is down; listing multiple brokers keeps the changefeed connected through broker failures, and changefeed creation that never returns usually means the ctl host cannot reach the sink URI address. Diagnosis: for stalled changefeed creation or sink errors, test network connectivity from TiCDC to every broker in the URI and inspect changefeed state. Remedies: include all broker addresses in the sink URI, set partition-num/replication-factor/max-message-bytes to match the topic plan, and use per-table topics with index-value partition dispatch when consumers need per-table streams; risk is that a topic's partition count fixes ordering and scaling limits at creation time.

nodes.name: Pulsar Sink Configuration Faults
nodes.content: Mechanism: the Pulsar sink requires protocol = canal-json, scheme pulsar or pulsar+ssl for TLS, and authentication via token, basic credentials, OAuth2, or mTLS certificate paths; producers are cached per topic in an LRU of size pulsar-producer-cache-size (default 10240). Diagnosis: on changefeed errors against Pulsar, match the error to protocol support, missing or wrong TLS trust/key/certificate paths (client cert required when the server demands trusted client certs), or auth credential problems; replication lag with many topics suggests producer-cache eviction. Remedies: correct the sink URI and pulsar-config keys, raise pulsar-producer-cache-size when topic count exceeds the cache, and tune connection/operation/batching/send timeouts; risk is sink memory growth when caches and batching are enlarged.

nodes.name: Tune TiKV CDC Scan and Memory Quotas
nodes.content: Mechanism: changefeed catch-up scans are capped by incremental-scan-speed-limit (128 MiB/s) with 4 threads and 6 concurrent tasks, while old-value-cache-memory-quota and sink-memory-quota (each 512 MiB) bound memory; a queue beyond incremental-scan-concurrency-limit (10000) rejects new tasks. Differential: lag driven by scan caps vs sink stalls vs quota exhaustion. Remedies: raise scan speed or quotas when TiKV has I/O and memory headroom, or reduce upstream write rate. Risk: raising quotas shifts pressure onto TiKV memory and foreground I/O.

nodes.name: TiCDC Syncpoint Consistent Snapshot
nodes.content: Mechanism: with enable-sync-point on a changefeed, TiCDC periodically aligns upstream/downstream snapshots, writes their TSO pairs into tidb_cdc.syncpoint_v1, and advances tidb_external_ts on the downstream so readers with tidb_enable_external_ts_read = ON get transactionally consistent snapshots despite ongoing replication; ts-map rows are trimmed by sync-point-retention. Diagnosis: for verification jobs that see drifting data mid-replication, confirm syncpoint is enabled and pick a ts-map entry instead of comparing live data. Remedies: read the backup cluster through the external-ts snapshot, or per-task use the ts-map table when several changefeeds share a downstream (never enable the global external-ts read then); risk is stale reads by design, and retention deleting ts-map entries older than the verification window.

nodes.name: TiCDC Latency and Validation Version Semantics
nodes.content: Baseline TiCDC behavior shifts by version: v6.5.0 lowers cdc.min-ts-interval from 1s to 200ms (resolve-ts flush cadence, so older versions show structurally higher minimal latency); v7.1.0 optimizes replication of lossy DDLs on large tables and adds single-row checksum integrity validation for Kafka Avro changefeeds; v8.1.2 lets TiCDC with downstream SUPER privilege query async ADD INDEX DDL status, preventing repeated-DDL retry failures. Diagnosis: compare observed latency and retry patterns against the version's documented behavior before tuning.

nodes.name: Certificate REQUIRE Clause Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: CREATE/ALTER USER ... REQUIRE clauses make login verify that SSL is used and that the certificate issuer, subject, SAN, and cipher match the configured values; any mismatch yields ERROR 1045. Diagnosis: compare the failing user's REQUIRE clauses with the actual client certificate, and confirm the current connection's cipher and server SSL variables. Remedies: reissue a certificate carrying the required attributes, relax the REQUIRE clauses, or connect with a correct client certificate chain; risk is weakening authentication if REQUIRE checks are removed to restore access.

nodes.name: Certificate-Based Login Verification
nodes.content: TiDB certificate-based login validates the X.509 subject fields (CN, O, OU and friends) against the user's CREATE USER ... REQUIRE clause. Login failures with TLS enabled usually mean a subject mismatch, an untrusted or expired certificate, or a missing CA; reissue certificates signed by the cluster CA, align the REQUIRE subject definition, and verify chains with openssl verify before retrying. TiDB certificate-based login validates the X.509 subject fields (CN, O, OU and friends) against the user's CREATE USER ... REQUIRE clause; additionally policy-based access control can delegate time- or location-based validity to the key management server. Login failures with TLS enabled usually mean a subject mismatch, an untrusted or expired certificate, or a missing CA; reissue certificates signed by the cluster CA, align the REQUIRE subject definition, and verify chains with openssl verify before retrying.

nodes.name: Changefeed Failure Blocks GC Beyond gc-ttl
nodes.content: Changefeeds in Normal, Warning, or Failed state hold back upstream GC while their checkpoint is behind; a Failed changefeed keeps blocking for gc-ttl (24 hours default), after which GC advances past the checkpoint and the task hits ErrGCTTLExceeded/ErrSnapshotLostByGC and can never resume (a stopped changefeed blocks GC indefinitely). Distinguish by changefeed state and how long it has been failed versus upstream GC safe-point progress; fix family: repair the sink and resume within gc-ttl, or recreate the changefeed from a new snapshot; letting it lapse means a full re-copy. A changefeed start position (explicit TSO or timestamp) must lie within the GC safe point, otherwise creation fails and the snapshot has to be re-taken.

nodes.name: Changefeed Tables Without Unique Key
nodes.content: Mechanism: tables without a primary key or unique index have no unique identifier, so when duplicate events are replayed the changefeed downstream can end up inconsistent. Differential: inspect table definitions for a valid key and check which tables the changefeed reports as keyless. Remedies: (a) add a primary key or unique index before starting replication; (b) exclude the table from the changefeed with a table filter rule. Risks: replicating keyless tables as-is trades downstream consistency; excluding them silently drops the table from replication. Tables without a valid key (primary key or NOT NULL unique index) are hard to replicate consistently because downstream duplicate-event handling has no unique identifier; add a key or exclude the table with a filter rule like "!db.tbl" before starting the changefeed.

nodes.name: Changefeed lag runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: lag grows when the sink cannot consume peak upstream writes (data piles to TiCDC disk), when resumed changefeeds must scan TiKV history versions for minutes before progressing, when upstream long transactions block until max-txn-ttl rollback, and when DDL holds table progress until its commitTS; BR restore or Lightning physical import on replicated tables is incompatible and can stall replication or lose data. Differential diagnosis: read cdc cli changefeed list for state/checkpoint/error and compare checkpoint against the upstream TIDB_CURRENT_TSO (or tidb_cdc.syncpoint_v1 when Syncpoint is on); check TiCDC node disk usage and sink metrics to separate sink bottleneck from fetch bottleneck. Remedy families: (1) fix downstream sink throughput or scale TiCDC (enable-table-across-nodes for region-granular MQ sinks); (2) remove the changefeed, restore upstream and downstream consistently, then recreate with the backup timestamp as start-ts; (3) wait out catch-up scans or long transactions. Risks: recreating a changefeed with a wrong start-ts loses or duplicates events; keep start-ts above tikv_gc_safe_point or task creation fails. Changefeed lag alerts (documented trigger at 600 seconds) have three canonical causes to separate: upstream traffic growth that outgrows the changefeed specification (transient surges recover, sustained growth needs scale-up), downstream or network faults, and slow sink writes such as an RDS downstream missing indexes.

nodes.name: Changefeed Interruption Recovery
nodes.content: Mechanism: persistent downstream failure exhausts retries so the task stops; an incompatible downstream SQL blocks replication at a fixed ts; extreme cases restart the TiCDC service (FATAL logs); GC safepoint set by TiCDC protects post-checkpoint data within gc-ttl while stopped. Discrimination: changefeed list/query separates error from manually stopped via admin-job-type; checkpoint-ts locates the blocking transaction; exit error count and processor logs give the error stack. Fix family: resume after the downstream recovers, skip the offending transaction by adding its start-ts to ignore-txn-start-ts and resume, or upgrade to a version with the post-restart OOM fixed; check start-ts against the GC safepoint when creating tasks.

nodes.name: Charset and Collation Layering
nodes.content: Each database carries its own default charset/collation (visible via @@character_set_database and @@collation_database) and tables/columns can override them; mixed collations across layers change comparison and sort results and can make the same query return different orders or mismatch errors. Check SHOW CREATE TABLE plus the session charset when diagnosing unexpected comparison results, and align client, database, and table collations as the remedy. Each database carries its own default charset/collation (visible via @@character_set_database and @@collation_database) and tables/columns can override them; mixed collations across layers change comparison and sort results and can make the same query return different orders or mismatch errors. A classic post-upgrade failure is 'unsupported modify column charset utf8mb4 not match origin utf8' when tables created under an older default charset are altered under the newer utf8mb4 default — align column, table, and session charsets (or recreate the column with the original charset) before retrying the DDL. Each database carries its own default charset/collation (visible via @@character_set_database and @@collation_database) and tables/columns can override them; mixed collations across layers change comparison and sort results and can make the same query return different orders or mismatch errors. Classic failure modes: after upgrades, 'unsupported modify column charset utf8mb4 not match origin utf8' on tables created under an older default charset, and ERROR 1366 'incorrect utf8 value' once 4-byte validation (v2.1.2+) rejects surrogate pairs previously stored unchecked — align charsets or use session tidb_skip_utf8_check as a temporary bypass.

nodes.name: Clustered Index Design Tradeoffs
nodes.content: A clustered primary key stores rows in PK order, removing one network round-trip on inserts and one-to-many on PK lookups/ranges, but risks hotspots on sequential keys; non-clustered tables add a ROWID indirection with at least two IO steps per access. Choose CLUSTERED when PK-prefix grouping/range queries dominate and the key does not create write hotspots (one clustered index per table); diagnose wasted double lookups via IndexLookUp with large TableRowIDScan row counts in EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

nodes.name: Clustered Handle ODKU Consistency Repair
nodes.content: Mechanism: a clustered primary key is the physical row handle, so an ODKU auto-update that changes the handle but skips the changed-mark path desynchronizes secondary index entries; ERROR 8141 is an assertion failure and ERROR 8134 is an ADMIN CHECK TABLE mismatch. Differential diagnosis: reproduce with a nonclustered-PK control table, join the table definition and write history with the actual component version matrix (vulnerable vs fixed release across every TiDB/PD/TiKV instance), and check tidb_txn_assertion_level scope per endpoint and session, since changing the global level neither repairs existing rows nor proves the version. Repair family: stop the ODKU writer and preserve ADMIN CHECK output plus index snapshots first; if clustered records are canonical rebuild only the affected secondary indexes, otherwise reconstruct a replacement table from an append-only ledger and switch atomically - an assertion setting alone is never repair, and acceptance needs matching versions, clean ADMIN CHECK on forced primary and secondary paths, an authorized canary, and unchanged healthy neighbors.

nodes.name: Collation Framework Semantics
nodes.content: Before v4.0 TiDB treated all collations as binary (byte order, no PAD space handling), so case-insensitive duplicates that MySQL rejects were accepted and sorting differed; the new collation framework (gated by new_collations_enabled_on_first_bootstrap at first initialization, verified via SELECT VARIABLE_VALUE FROM mysql.tidb WHERE VARIABLE_NAME='new_collation_enabled') implements real case/accent-insensitive comparisons and PADDING behavior. Unexpected duplicate rows, wrong sort order, or join mismatches after migrating from MySQL should first check whether the cluster runs the new framework and whether the column collation is in the supported set (utf8(mb4)_general_ci/unicode_ci, utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci/bin, gbk_*).

nodes.name: Column Pruning Awareness
nodes.content: Mechanism: logical optimization prunes columns unused by downstream operators at the DataSource, so I/O scales with needed columns, not table width. Diagnosis: wide TableFullScan reads of narrow results suggest the read set or engine choice, not pruning, is the problem. Fix family: select only needed columns and route column-heavy analytical scans to TiFlash; pruning can be disabled only via the optimization-rule blocklist.

nodes.name: Component port probe failure
nodes.content: Blackbox probe alerts (probe_success == 0 for tidb/tikv/pd/tiflash/pump groups) mean the service port is unreachable: triage in order of host down, process gone, then network between monitor and instance; distinguish one-instance failures (host/process) from group-wide failures (network or deploy-wide outage) before restarting anything.

nodes.name: Component Timeout Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: 9001/9002/9012 indicate the PD/TiKV/TiFlash side did not answer within the RPC deadline, from overload, restart, network faults, or a slow busy PD disk (safepoint query timeout). Discrimination: correlate which component is named in the error, then compare that component's CPU, disk load, and restart history against the error timeline; ERROR 1105 Wire Error(InvalidEnumValue) instead signals a TiDB/TiKV version mismatch after partial upgrade; compare TiDB KV duration against TiKV gRPC duration to separate network latency or NIC saturation from component-side slowness; timeouts across many components point to network. Fix family: relieve the overloaded component, restore failed instances, repair network paths, or upgrade components consistently. When one TiKV degrades, client behavior decides cluster impact: since v8.0 unified health control (replica selector v2) steers requests away from unhealthy peers so a single bad node stops dominating latency; on versions without it, isolate by checking whether latency concentrates on one store before recycling connections everywhere. Also confirm the component finished initialization - servers were historically marked healthy before init completed, so a 'recovered' instance may still fail requests.

nodes.name: Component Mutual TLS Repair
nodes.content: Mechanism: inter-component TLS is cluster-wide (TiDB, TiKV, PD, TiFlash, TiCDC) with per-component certificate settings, Common Name caller verification such as cluster-verify-cn/cert-allowed-cn, and HTTPS control endpoints; control tools must then pass client certificates. Diagnosis: when components or ctl tools fail to connect, check whether the URL must be https, whether the client certificate is supplied, and whether the certificate CN is in the callee's allowed-CN list (PD accepts only one CN value). Remedies: reissue certificates with correct CN, align security config across components, and rely on per-connection certificate rereading or cloud-managed rotation instead of restarts; risk is that enabling TLS is all-or-nothing across components.

nodes.name: Remedy Connection Exhaustion
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB accepts unlimited connections by default (instance.max_connections / max_connections = 0); when a configured limit is hit, new connections are refused, and each connection holds session memory subject to tidb_mem_quota_query. Differential: distinguish a pool misconfiguration (steady climb to the limit) from a traffic spike or leaked sessions (SHOW PROCESSLIST reveals idle-in-transaction sessions). Remedies: raise the instance limit within memory budget, fix application pool sizing and leaks, and use resource control rather than connection caps to share capacity. Risk: removing limits lets session memory aggregate into TiDB OOM.

nodes.name: Connection Loss Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: connections die or are refused when server processes are down (panic, OOM, port conflict, file-descriptor exhaustion), when TiDB cannot reach PD/TiKV (Information schema out of date), when idle TCP is torn down by OS/proxy, or after a redeploy changed the cluster ID without restarting TiDB. Discrimination: component state and error/fatal/panic logs separate crashes from config/port issues; OOM records in system logs point to memory exhaustion; drops only after long idle point to TCP/proxy timeout; ERROR 1105 Wire Error(InvalidEnumValue) signals TiDB/TiKV version mismatch after partial upgrade. Fix family: restart failed components after fixing the crash/OOM root cause, free ports and raise descriptor limits, repair network paths, align keepalive/idle timeouts, and redeploy with consistent data plus a TiDB restart.

nodes.name: Connection Pool Tuning
nodes.content: Mechanism: connections are expensive to establish (TCP plus auth), so pools amortize them; pools too small serialize acquisition, pools too large waste TiDB memory and scheduling, and idle timeouts from TiDB (wait_timeout, 8h default) or intermediate proxies kill pooled connections, producing communications-link failures; connect/disconnect churn adds latency and TiDB resource cost. Diagnosis: connection count and idle-duration panels (in-txn vs not-in-txn), disconnections per second, and application pool monitors. Fix family: right-size maximum pool size and minimum idle, keep-alive probes below proxy/idle timeouts, cache prepared statement objects, and avoid short-connection patterns. Risks: oversized pools funnel load to few TiDB nodes; probes too frequent add pointless traffic.

nodes.name: Continuous Profiling Usage
nodes.content: Mechanism: Continuous Profiling collects CPU, heap, mutex, and goroutine profiles from TiDB, TiKV, PD (and TiFlash for CPU) continuously once enabled in the Dashboard, storing history as FlameGraph/DAG so non-reproducible stalls can be analyzed after the fact at measured overhead under 1%; it requires the NgMonitoring component and disables Manual Profiling while active. Diagnosis: for unexplained CPU saturation, memory growth, or process stalls, open the profiling window covering the incident and read the dominant functions per instance. Remedies: enable the feature with an appropriate retention duration for post-hoc analysis and download raw results for offline study; risk is additional disk usage for retained profiles.

nodes.name: Correlated Subquery Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: a correlated subquery re-executes for every outer row unless decorrelation rewrites it into a join; with few outer rows and an index on the correlated column, keeping Apply with index ranges can beat the single-pass join. Diagnosis: EXPLAIN - an Apply operator means not decorrelated; joins with range decided by the correlated equality mean per-row index lookups. Fix family: NO_DECORRELATE hint pinned with SPM for the few-outer-rows case, or let decorrelation happen for large outer sets; the decorrelate rule blocklist is a global lever. Risks: the rule blocklist affects every query, so prefer hint plus binding; decorrelation changes index usability and single-pass cost.

nodes.name: Cost-Based Physical Plan Choice
nodes.content: The optimizer picks the minimum-cost plan by multiplying estimated row counts by index/operator costs, so stale statistics or a cost model version change can flip the chosen index or join and regress latency. Distinguish by comparing EXPLAIN plans and statements summaries before and after the change; fix family: ANALYZE to refresh statistics, use hints or a plan baseline to pin the good plan, or revert the cost model version; risk is pinned plans going stale as data evolves

nodes.name: Cost Model Version Migration
nodes.content: Mechanism: Cost Model Version 2 estimates costs more accurately and picks engines (notably TiFlash) automatically, but switching versions can change many plans at once; new clusters default to version 2 while upgraded clusters keep the old model until tidb_cost_model_version is set. Diagnosis: after enabling version 2, a wave of plan changes is expected; validate regressions against the model switch before chasing statistics or hints. Remedies: bench representative workloads, then set tidb_cost_model_version = 2 to adopt it, keeping bindings for statements whose old plans were deliberately tuned; risk of upgrading without testing is broad plan churn under production traffic.

nodes.name: Cross-AZ Latency Amplification
nodes.content: Two-phase commit plus Raft majority replication means every write must reach at least two AZs and fetch TSO from the PD leader, so inter-AZ network latency is paid at least twice per write and reads suffer when Region/PD leaders sit far from the TiDB node; after an AZ loss, Raft re-election restores service within seconds to tens of seconds. Distinguish by correlating write latency with leader placement across AZs and network RTT rather than with load; fix family: concentrate TiDB traffic plus PD and Region leaders in the serving AZ (evict-leader/placement rules and PD leader priority) accepting single-AZ bandwidth limits, or keep the simple 3-AZ layout and budget the RTT.

nodes.name: Damaged SST Cleanup
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV panics on damaged SST files; tikv-ctl bad-ssts (run with the TiKV instance stopped) prints corruption details, SST meta, overlapping regions from PD, and suggested operations such as unsafe_remove_sst_file for the file and tombstone for affected regions. Diagnosis: correlate the panic log magic-number error with bad-ssts output to identify the file and overlapping regions. Remedies: follow the suggested operations to remove the file and mark regions tombstoned so replicas rebuild from other peers, then restart TiKV; risk is temporary data unavailability on affected regions until re-replication completes.

nodes.name: Dashboard Access Failure Modes
nodes.content: With multiple PD instances only one actually serves TiDB Dashboard, so hitting another PD redirects the browser - often to an internal address blocked by firewall or reverse proxy. Dashboard also listens only on the deployed IP, never 0.0.0.0, so dual-NIC hosts are unreachable via the second NIC. Fix by pointing access at the PD that hosts the dashboard and configuring the reverse proxy or firewall for it; a reverse proxy is the supported way to expose it on another NIC.
