With multiple PD instances only one actually serves TiDB Dashboard, so hitting another PD redirects the browser - often to an internal address blocked by firewall or reverse proxy; Dashboard also listens only on the deployed IP, never 0.0.0.0, so dual-NIC hosts are unreachable via the second NIC. The service can be disabled or re-negotiated with pd config dashboard-address none/auto; re-enabling may pick a different PD instance and loses locally stored dashboard data such as Key Visualize history, and tiup cluster display --dashboard reports the serving instance.

nodes.name: Dashboard Capacity Estimation for Resource Control
nodes.content: Before creating resource groups and quotas for resource isolation, estimate overall cluster capacity from the Resource Manager page; the Dashboard overview (QPS, execution time, statement types consuming most resources) grounds quota sizing. Dashboard runs embedded in PD without separate deployment, so PD availability affects console access.

nodes.name: Dashboard Health Check Semantics
nodes.content: Dashboard first-line signals: a changed Up Time means the component restarted and needs a cause; host resources above 80% call for scale-out; Region peer counts (down/miss/pending/oversized) may be briefly non-zero during scheduling but staying abnormal longer than about 30 minutes indicates a scheduling or availability problem; per-node KV request P99 skew points to hotspots or a slow node; TSO wait rises with network latency or TiDB/PD load; and a stale last-GC time signals GC backlog that bloats history. Slow queries above tidb_slow_log_threshold (default 300ms) feed the slow-query views, and since v6.5.0 the Performance Overview dashboard also carries TiFlash and CDC panels. Dashboard first-line signals: a changed Up Time means the component restarted and needs a cause; host resources above 80% call for scale-out; Region peer counts (down/miss/pending/oversized) may be briefly non-zero during scheduling but staying abnormal longer than about 30 minutes indicates a scheduling or availability problem; per-node KV request P99 skew points to hotspots or a slow node; TSO wait rises with network latency or TiDB/PD load; and a stale last-GC time signals GC backlog that bloats history. Dashboard login failures mean the root account is missing or password-protected differently, or PD/TiDB is unreachable rather than the UI being broken; since v6.5.0 the Performance Overview dashboard also carries TiFlash and CDC panels.

nodes.name: Dashboard Privilege Requirements
nodes.content: Mechanism: Dashboard sign-in requires PROCESS, SHOW DATABASES, CONFIG, and DASHBOARD_CLIENT; with Security Enhanced Mode the RESTRICTED_TABLES_ADMIN, RESTRICTED_STATUS_ADMIN, and RESTRICTED_VARIABLES_ADMIN privileges are additionally required, and UI configuration changes need SYSTEM_VARIABLES_ADMIN. Diagnosis: for sign-in failures, compare the account's grants (including roles actually active as default role) against this checklist. Remedies: grant the missing privileges or a prepared dashboard_access role set as default role, following least privilege instead of SUPER; risk of granting SUPER broadly is unintended destructive operations from the dashboard.

nodes.name: Dashboard Port Exposure Risk
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB Dashboard rides on the PD client port (2379), whose other PD API endpoints are unauthenticated and privileged, so exposing the port externally hands over cluster control; only the actual dashboard-serving PD instance responds, others redirect. Diagnosis: for audit or exposure review, identify which PD serves the dashboard via tiup cluster display --dashboard and enumerate what else listens on 2379. Remedies: firewall 2379 from untrusted networks, publish only the /dashboard prefix through an authenticated reverse proxy with TLS/mTLS, or use the Kubernetes independent-Pod deployment; risk is cluster-wide compromise if the whole PD client port is proxied.

nodes.name: Dashboard Behind Reverse Proxy
nodes.content: When TiDB Dashboard is accessed through a reverse proxy, PD dashboard.public-path-prefix must match the proxy's public URL path prefix, otherwise web resources fail to load; do not set it when no proxy is used. The enable-telemetry item is retained only for compatibility and has no effect since v8.1.0.

nodes.name: Data Inconsistency Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB validates row-versus-index consistency during transaction writes (assertion failures 8138-8141, handle or value mismatches) and via ADMIN CHECK (8003 count mismatch, 8134 value mismatch, 8223 missing index, 8133 index-count vs record-count). Discrimination: the error text names the table, index, handle, and both sides' values, so the inconsistent index and rows are directly identifiable. Fix family: stop writes to the affected table, confirm with ADMIN CHECK TABLE/INDEX, rebuild the affected index or restore from backup, freeze GC if instructed, and escalate persistent cases instead of forcing reads.

nodes.name: Data inconsistency runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB verifies write mutations and transaction assertions during commit; ADMIN CHECK reads both data and index directly, so its failures mean real corruption. Differential: check whether the error is tied to one SQL statement only (then an equivalent rewrite with different operators avoids the faulty path), map error codes 8138-8140 to the mutation checker and 8141 to assertion level. Remedies: (a) rewrite the offending SQL to an equivalent form; (b) urgently bypass with SET @@tidb_enable_mutation_checker=0 or SET @@tidb_txn_assertion_level=OFF; (c) repair genuinely inconsistent data by rebuilding the affected table from a verified backup after root-causing with support. Risks: disabling the checkers turns off verification for ALL statements and can propagate silent corruption; ADMIN CHECK failures are never bypassable because the data is already inconsistent.

nodes.name: Datetime Type Pitfalls
nodes.content: Mechanism: TIMESTAMP spans only 1970 through 2038-01-19 UTC, so earlier dates become zero on conversion while DATE/DATETIME accept them; DATETIME/TIMESTAMP keep fractional seconds only when fsp is declared and round otherwise; TIME-to-date conversions anchor to CURRENT_DATE so over-24h times shift the day, and two-digit years map 01-69 to 2001-2069 and 70-99 to 1970-1999 (with YEAR(4) numeral 00 becoming 0000). Diagnosis: for zero dates or shifted years, check the column type, fsp, and the literal's year format, remembering MIN/MAX misbehave on two-digit years. Remedies: store four-digit years and ranges within type limits, cast explicitly where precision matters, and migrate columns to DATETIME when pre-1970 or post-2038 dates must survive; risk is silent zero-value inserts under permissive sql_mode.

nodes.name: Database Time Analysis
nodes.content: Mechanism: database time is the sum of all SQL service time; user response time = service + queuing + coherency delay, and latency climbs sharply once utilization passes the knee (e.g. CPU queueing grows beyond ~65%). Diagnosis: compare average SQL latency with connection idle time (in-txn) to decide whether the bottleneck is inside TiDB; if inside, decompose DB time by SQL type, by get-token/parse/compile/execute, and by executor/TSO-wait/KV-request/retry; if outside, check app server, proxy, network, and client patterns (short connections, prepared-statement churn). Fix family: optimize the SQL class consuming most time, resolve hotspots, scale out when CPU/storage/IO run at limits. Risks: scaling out before removing hotspots wastes capacity; external bottlenecks misread as DB issues lead to wrong tuning.

nodes.name: Tune DDL Backfill to Protect Foreground Traffic
nodes.content: Mechanism: ADD INDEX reorg writes with tidb_ddl_reorg_worker_cnt (4) workers in batches of tidb_ddl_reorg_batch_size (256 rows); large batches under concurrent updates raise transaction conflicts, while DXF (tidb_enable_dist_task) spreads ADD INDEX and IMPORT INTO across TiDB nodes and Global Sort offloads sorting to cloud storage. Differential: distinguish conflict-driven DDL slowness (errors, retries) from TiKV write saturation. Remedies: shrink reorg batch size under conflict, keep batch large with tidb_ddl_enable_fast_reorg, lower reorg priority, or isolate backend tasks onto dedicated TiDB nodes via tidb_service_scope. Risk: bigger batches and higher priority increase TiKV write pressure; disable DXF before major upgrades to avoid index inconsistency. Before bulk loads, pre-split tables (PRE_SPLIT_REGIONS with AUTO_RANDOM or SHARD_ROW_ID_BITS, setting tidb_scatter_region=1 to wait for scattering) or use SPLIT REGION (timeout via tidb_wait_split_region_timeout, default 300s); writing before scattering completes hurts write performance, and PD may re-merge freshly split Regions unless merge is restrained.

nodes.name: DDL Compatibility Limits
nodes.content: CREATE TABLE parses but ignores index types (HASH/BTREE/RTREE) and ASC/DESC, rejects FULLTEXT use, defaults to a 3072-byte index length cap (max-index-length), and supports at most 4096 columns (1017 default). Unsupported partition types only raise 'Warning: Unsupported partition type ..., treat as normal table', so a table expected to be partitioned may silently be a normal table — check SHOW WARNINGS after DDL when pruning or syntax behaves unexpectedly.

nodes.name: Schema Limit DDL Failures
nodes.content: TiDB enforces max-index-length (default 3072 bytes), table-column-count-limit (default 1017) and index-limit (default 64) at DDL time; older TiDB rows or MySQL-sized schemas can exceed them on migration. Diagnose by measuring the actual index key length and column/index counts, then remediate by prefix indexes, dropping redundant indexes, splitting wide tables, or adjusting the config within its allowed range; risk: raising limits affects compatibility and memory footprint.

nodes.name: DDL Owner Failover
nodes.content: Only one TiDB node is DDL owner at a time, elected through etcd with a renewed term; if the owner goes down another TiDB takes over and pending DDL jobs wait for the election, so a cluster where all DDLs queue with no owner points to etcd or owner-term trouble rather than to the statements themselves. Distinguish with ADMIN SHOW DDL to see the owner and job queue; fix family: restore the failed TiDB node or etcd quorum

nodes.name: DDL reorg load diagnosis and tuning
nodes.content: Mechanism: ADD INDEX / column type change backfill competes with foreground traffic; if the cluster is also serving load, the reorg workers amplify read/write latency. Differential diagnosis: compare TiDB/TiKV read and write performance metrics and application response time before and after the write-reorg phase starts to confirm the DDL is the cause rather than query regressions. Remedy families: (1) lower tidb_ddl_reorg_worker_cnt and tidb_ddl_reorg_batch_size (both dynamic, take effect on the next transaction batch) and optionally tidb_ddl_reorg_priority to trade speed for less interference; (2) schedule heavy physical DDL in low-load windows; (3) issue multiple schema changes in one ALTER to reduce reorg rounds. Risks: too-small worker/batch values prolong index availability; tidb_ddl_error_count_limit bounds retries before the job fails, so persistent conflicts during backfill can cancel the DDL.

nodes.name: ADD INDEX Reorg Parameter Trade-offs
nodes.content: Mechanism: index backfill re-reads and rewrites the indexed column concurrently with business writes; when the workload updates the target column, larger tidb_ddl_reorg_worker_cnt and tidb_ddl_reorg_batch_size drive up TiKV_prewrite_latch_wait_duration, and with very large values the DDL job retries repeatedly on 'Write conflict, txnStartTS ... stale' (visible via ADMIN SHOW DDL), stretching ADD INDEX from tens of seconds to tens of minutes; read-only workloads are barely affected. Diagnosis: correlate Sysbench/client QPS drop timing with the running ADD INDEX, inspect TiKV prewrite latch wait and admin show ddl job retry counts. Repair family: keep reorg batch size moderate instead of maximizing it, reduce worker count when the target column is hotly updated, or schedule the DDL off-peak; on read-mostly tables larger parallelism shortens the DDL safely.

nodes.name: Reorg DDL Workload Impact
nodes.content: Physical (reorg) DDL such as ADD INDEX scans the whole table in TiKV and writes back new index data, consuming TiKV CPU/I/O plus TiDB CPU on the DDL owner or DXF-scheduled nodes, which can depress QPS and raise latency of concurrent DML. Distinguish by correlating degradation with a running DDL job via ADMIN SHOW DDL; fix family: schedule large reorg DDL off-peak or reduce DDL worker concurrency, risk is a longer total job duration. Reorg concurrency tuning is workload-dependent: raising tidb_ddl_reorg_worker_cnt and tidb_ddl_reorg_batch_size shortens the index build but depresses online TPS, and on a hot updated column it causes write conflicts and retries that can stall the DDL; read-mostly targets tolerate higher values. Online ADD INDEX backfills via the reorg phase whose speed is set by tidb_ddl_reorg_worker_cnt and tidb_ddl_reorg_batch_size; raising them (e.g. 16 workers/4096 batch) accelerates the DDL when the indexed columns are read-only, but on frequently updated columns larger settings multiply write conflicts and retries, stretching the DDL and hurting the online workload - lower them (e.g. 4/128) instead. Diagnose a slow or disruptive backfill by correlating reorg progress with conflicts on the target table. Online ADD INDEX backfills via the reorg phase whose speed is set by tidb_ddl_reorg_worker_cnt and tidb_ddl_reorg_batch_size; raising them (e.g. 16 workers/4096 batch) accelerates the DDL when the indexed columns are read-only, but on frequently updated columns larger settings multiply write conflicts and retries - lower them (e.g. 4/128) instead. ADD COLUMN is itself an online metadata change that blocks neither reads nor writes, so a slow schema change complaint usually points at index backfill or table size, not column adds.

nodes.name: Slow and Stuck DDL Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: DDL can be delayed by a slow commit of a preceding uncommitted DML in the same session, FIFO/dependency queuing (general vs Reorg queues, same-table serialization, concurrency limit), first-DDL owner election after startup, or TiDB losing contact with PD/TiKV. Discrimination: ADMIN SHOW DDL JOBS shows the waiting/stuck job; check the DDL owner (info endpoint or DDL META OPM) — no owner means election failure, owner present with a hung job means a stuck worker. Fix family: wait for election or re-trigger owner election, cancel and reissue the job, keep concurrent DDL low (retry from client on conflict), and repair TiDB-PD/TiKV connectivity.

nodes.name: DDL Stuck or Slow States
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB executes DDL jobs serially through an elected owner; job latency adds lease-based waits on top of backfill time, so Add Index duration scales with table rows and concurrent QPS while other DDLs take about a second. Differential diagnosis: run ADMIN SHOW DDL JOBS to see job state and owner; the first DDL after cluster start takes tens of seconds while the owner is elected; DDLs issued within roughly ten minutes after an unclean TiDB stop (kill -9 or PD communication loss) wait 2 * lease per state change; a load that fails with concurrent schema work suggests DDL ran against a table being loaded. Remedy families: (1) wait out lease-based delays once PD/TiDB communication is healthy; (2) cancel the job with ADMIN CANCEL DDL JOBS when it is wrongly issued; (3) serialize DDL work and schedule Add Index in low-load windows. Risks: cancelling only works for jobs still queued or reorganizable; lowering the lease speeds DDL but weakens schema-change safety in production.

nodes.name: Deadlock Diagnosis and Mitigation
nodes.content: Mechanism: transaction A waits on a lock held by B while B directly or indirectly waits on A's lock, so TiDB rolls one side back with a deadlock error. Discrimination: information_schema.deadlocks shows the waiting chain and the involved statements; if the blocking lock belongs to the currently executing statement the deadlock is retryable and only 'single statement deadlock, retry statement' appears in the log. Fix family: enforce consistent lock ordering, shrink transactions, add bounded application retries, or enable collection of retryable deadlocks to size the problem.

nodes.name: Foreign Key and Constraint Checking Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: deferring unique checks skips pessimistic locks for throughput, so conflicts surface late as 1062/9007/8147 and TiDB rolls back the whole transaction. Differential diagnosis: check whether tidb_constraint_check_in_place_pessimistic is OFF on the session; parse the 1062 message to find which index actually conflicts when several tables share index names, because the error may be raised by a later statement than the offending write; distinguish from pure application duplicate inserts by the LazyUniquenessCheck reason string. Remedy families: (1) set tidb_constraint_check_in_place_pessimistic=ON (default) to check eagerly; (2) add application-side retry with backoff for 9007/8147 rollbacks; (3) redesign access patterns to avoid concurrent inserts of the same unique key. Risks: eager checks add lock contention; 'Pessimistic lock not found' after forced rollback means deferred checking does not fit the workload.

nodes.name: Deployment config gotchas
nodes.content: Config edits not taking effect have component-specific mechanics: TiKV does not read a toml unless --config is set (binary deploys), PD reads its configuration file only at first bootstrap and afterwards must be changed through pd-ctl, and dashboards missing metrics are often monitor/cluster clock skew rather than missing data; the slow-query boundary is tidb_slow_log_threshold (300ms default) written into the TiDB log or a separate slow log file. Deployment-time choices that cannot be flipped later or that silently change behavior: TiFlash coupled vs disaggregated (S3, Compute/Write nodes) architectures are mutually exclusive and set only at deployment (v7.0+), systemd resource_control caps bind for the component lifetime until topology reload, and init-time settings like initialize-sql-file run once with unchecked privilege. Recheck these first when post-deployment behavior contradicts expectations.

nodes.name: Derived TopN/Limit Pushdown
nodes.content: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) row filters can be pushed to TiKV as a partition Limit when tidb_opt_derive_topn is on AND the partition column is a prefix of a clustered primary key; otherwise the window materializes all rows on TiDB. A slow top-n-per-group query should be checked for those two preconditions before rewriting the SQL.

nodes.name: Disaggregated TiFlash Activation
nodes.content: Mechanism: disaggregated TiFlash requires nodes configured as tiflash_write or tiflash_compute via flash.disaggregated_mode with storage.s3 settings (credentials may come from S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID/S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY environment variables which take priority over config values), Compute Nodes need remote cache dir/capacity, and TiDB itself must set disaggregated-tiflash: true then be reloaded. Diagnosis: when queries cannot use disaggregated TiFlash, check the TiDB flag, node roles, and S3 endpoint/credential reachability. Remedies: apply the missing flag via cluster config edit and rolling reload of TiDB, fix S3 endpoints or keys, and scale Compute Nodes for query load; risk is that wrong S3 credentials or endpoint block Write Node startup entirely.

nodes.name: High Disk I/O Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: storage writes (Raft log and data RocksDB, compaction) saturate disks and back-pressure the write path. Discrimination: one node with high IO util indicates a read/write hotspot on that machine while most nodes high indicates cluster I/O load; append log duration (expect p99 under 50ms) versus apply log duration (p99 under 100ms) localizes raft-log versus data-db pressure; WAL Sync Duration max confirms slow disks; 'server is busy' plus TiKV_write_stall alerts tie errors to stalls. Fix family: scale disk throughput or switch to faster media, trade CPU for disk with higher compression per level, add max-sub-compactions to clear level-0 backlog, right-size raftstore/apply pools within CPU, and disperse write hotspots.

nodes.name: Disk space exhaustion runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV appends SST, WAL, and snapshot files until the volume fills; writes then fail, and PD protects remaining stores by refusing to schedule onto any same-label node below 20% free capacity, which also stalls balancing. Differential diagnosis: distinguish true data growth from MVCC/GC lag (space not released after DELETE) and from RocksDB space amplification; estimate per-table disk footprint with TIKV_REGION_STATUS sizes divided by METRICS_SCHEMA.store_size_amplification, and watch capacity skew across stores. Remedy families: (1) add nodes or enlarge disks; (2) delete or archive data and let GC/compaction reclaim space; (3) rebalance regions away from the full store. Risks: free-space thresholds silently stop replica migration, so a nearly-full replacement store cannot take replicas during node offline - fix capacity before maintenance.

nodes.name: Disk Stall Self-Healing
nodes.content: Since v6.4.0 TiKV state detection actively wakes leader election when a node suffers disk failure or stuck I/O, roughly halving cluster self-healing time; slow recovery after storage trouble should first be attributed to node-state detection latency rather than raft election bugs, and versions before 6.4 lack this acceleration so recovery-time comparisons must be version-aware.

nodes.name: Distinct Aggregate Pushdown
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiFlash cannot execute some distinct aggregates (such as sum distinct), so by default TiDB pulls all rows and computes distinct at the root, which is slow on huge tables; enabling tidb_opt_distinct_agg_push_down pushes a group-by-style distinct partial aggregate into TiFlash even though full pushdown still warns. Diagnosis: for slow count(distinct)/sum(distinct) over TiFlash scans, EXPLAIN ANALYZE and look for the root HashAgg consuming all rows. Remedies: set tidb_opt_distinct_agg_push_down = ON to offload the distinct step, or rewrite the query as a group-by plus outer aggregate; risk is higher TiFlash memory when distinct cardinality is very large.

nodes.name: Distributed Execution Framework Tasks
nodes.content: Since v8.1.0 the Distributed eXecution Framework (tidb_enable_dist_task) is ON by default, so ADD INDEX and IMPORT INTO run in parallel across multiple TiDB nodes instead of a single node, and scale near-linearly by adding TiDB nodes with tidb_service_scope set. A slow backfill or import should confirm whether DXF is enabled and how many nodes participate before tuning single-node concurrency.

nodes.name: Adding Tables to a Running DM Task
nodes.content: Mechanism: adding tables mid-task is stage-dependent - Dump stage cannot resume with new tables (restart with new config), Load stage must not merge tasks with divergent binlog positions, and Sync stage continues incrementally from the existing checkpoint without full-importing the new table. Diagnosis: new tables empty downstream after adding them in Sync stage is expected until a separate full import is done; the procedure rewinds the global checkpoint (rows with id=source-id, is_global=1 in {task-name}_syncer_checkpoint) to the minimum of the task checkpoint-T and the new table's export position-S. Remedy family: stop-task, set binlog_name/binlog_pos to the smaller position, set syncers safe-mode=true for reentrant replay, start-task, and restore safe-mode once syncerBinlog passes the larger position; prefer separate tasks because this is error-prone.

nodes.name: DM Binlog Event Filter Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM binlog event filters match upstream events by schema-pattern/table-pattern plus event names (including incompatible-DDL classes like drop/truncate/rename, precision decreases) or SQL regex; actions are Do (allowlist - non-matching events dropped), Ignore (blocklist), and Error (pauses the task with an error). When multiple rules match one table, Ignore outranks Error and Error outranks Do (in v1-style configs Ignore outranks Do). Configuring filters at the source level as well as task level cuts downstream binlog work and relay storage, but in shard-merge the source-level and task-level rules must agree or the task can starve waiting for filtered increments. Diagnosis: downstream missing objects or changes means an Ignore/Do rule swallowed them; a task halted on a specific upstream DDL means an Error rule matched; long stalled incremental replication in shard merge means source/task filter rules mismatch. Remedy family: route dangerous DDL to Error for explicit handling rather than Ignore (silent divergence) and keep source and task filter rules aligned; filter changes require a task config update and resume.

nodes.name: DM Upstream Binlog Purged
nodes.content: Incremental DM replication fails when the upstream has already purged the binlog or GTID range the task needs, classically after a long full-export phase; the relay log feature stages binlog on DM-worker local disk to survive upstream purging and to share one upstream pull connection across tasks, at the cost of extra disk I/O and CPU that adds replication latency. Distinguish by the task error naming a missing binlog file or GTID versus slow progress; fix family: enable relay log before long full phases, set relay-binlog-gtid/name to a valid retained position, or re-run the full import, risk is duplicated import work and higher upstream load.

nodes.name: DM Block-Allow-List Filtering Order
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM block-allow-list decides what replicates via do-dbs/ignore-dbs first, then do-tables/ignore-tables (wildcards, or ~-prefixed regex); when do-dbs is non-empty any schema outside it is filtered before table rules are even consulted (and configuring both do-dbs and ignore-dbs means only do-dbs takes effect; likewise do-tables over ignore-tables), and DDL statements are judged by the explicitly qualified database name first, falling back to the USE database. Diagnosis: missing downstream tables or unexpected replicated tables - walk the schema-level then table-level decision order for the exact table; DM follows MySQL ROW-format semantics and only supports ROW binlog. Remedy family: correct the patterns (watch wildcard vs regex syntax) and re-verify replication; prerequisite is ROW-format upstream binlog.

nodes.name: DM Checkpoint and Safe Mode Semantics
nodes.content: For incremental DM tasks the effective start point is the downstream checkpoint if present, else the task meta binlog position/GTID, else the upstream latest position - misreading this ordering causes duplicate or missing increments. Safe mode converts INSERT to REPLACE and UPDATE to DELETE+REPLACE so DMLs can be re-applied idempotently; DM auto-enables it during the first minute after start or resume, and it should be enabled explicitly when re-replicating data already covered by a full migration that was not a consistent snapshot. GTID mode (enable-gtid) is required when upstream switches master automatically, and dmctl check-task should pass before start-task to catch configuration errors early.

nodes.name: DM Common Error Codes and Causes
nodes.content: Mechanism: recurring DM failures map to stable codes - 10002 bad connection (request not sent) and 10003 invalid connection (request partly sent; causes: network failure, TiDB restart, TiKV busy) both auto-retry on current versions; 20010 password decrypt failure (dmctl-encrypted mismatch); 26002 precheck cannot reach database (privilege/network from DM-master); 32001 mydumper 'argument list too long' (pass --regex via extra-args); 38008 gRPC between DM components (identify the pair via class). Operationally: dmctl timeouts despite a reachable master are usually https_proxy/http_proxy hijacking; DM-master restart failing with 'member already bootstrapped' means a relative data-dir moved etcd state; start-relay errors on 2.0.2-2.0.6 need stop-relay/start-relay or an upgrade; 'Unknown character set' during load means a TiDB-unsupported charset - pre-create the schema; ERROR 1236 with purged GTIDs means upstream binlog purged or empty/wrong relay.meta GTID; a >4GB upstream binlog file overflows uint32 positions causing event-diff/checksum-mismatch errors. Diagnosis: correlate code and scope with query-status/query-error plus component logs. Remedy family: fix the mapped cause (credentials, privileges, proxy vars, absolute data-dir, relay restart/upgrade, pre-created schema, manual recovery for oversized binlog) then resume-task.

nodes.name: DM deployment and task planning
nodes.content: DM stalls trace back to planning as often as runtime faults: deploy 3 DM-masters for long-running replication (across AZs on cloud) and keep 1.5-2x idle DM-workers; split tasks by shard family or write pressure to contain blast radius, remembering split tasks only give eventual consistency. Full export takes a global FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK that briefly blocks upstream writes, so run it against a replica with enable-gtid enabled to allow master switches.

nodes.name: DM Downstream Session Compatibility Failures
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM applies downstream session settings and compatibility knobs - if sql_require_primary_key is ON, DM's own metadata tables without primary keys cannot be created and the task fails at creation; collation_compatible='strict' appends the upstream default collation to CREATE statements and errors when the downstream does not support it (loose passes SQL through unchanged); a manual session sql_mode overrides the value auto-fetched from TiDB. Diagnosis: task-creation failures on metadata table creation, or DDL errors about unsupported collations, map to these settings. Remedy family: set sql_require_primary_key OFF for migration, prefer collation_compatible loose unless strict consistency of default collations is required, and align sql_mode/tidb_skip_utf8_check with the downstream; prerequisite is checking the error surfaces against task session config.

nodes.name: DM migration error semantics
nodes.content: DM task errors map to distinct causes: "required binary log no longer exists" means upstream binlogs were purged (only fix is a new task; extend expire_logs_days and avoid manual PURGE BINARY LOGS), connect failures check source/target availability and connection limits, "driver: bad connection" points at the downstream TiDB, storage-shortage errors need TiKV capacity added, and Error 1273 for utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci means the upstream collation is unsupported downstream — pre-create the schema with a supported collation and restart the task.

nodes.name: DM Error System and Troubleshooting Flow
nodes.content: Mechanism: every DM error carries code (stable per error type), class (failing component: database, config, binlog-op, checkpoint, relay-unit, dump-unit, load-unit, sync-unit, dm-master, dm-worker, schema-tracker, scheduler, dmctl), scope (upstream/downstream/internal), and level (low user-input, medium config affecting new services, high - risks task interruption), plus a wrapped message and optional workaround and stack. Diagnosis: daily checks are query-status for task state and errors, the DM Grafana dashboard for metrics, then DM-master/DM-worker logs matching the class; the outermost wrapped message is the DM-side failure and the innermost the source. Remedy family: fix per the class then resume-task; when the task cannot be recovered, reset it - stop-task, purge the downstream data, and restart with a new task name or start-task --remove-meta.

nodes.name: DM Binlog Value (Expression) Filter
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM's binlog value filter evaluates SQL expressions over ROW-format binlog column values and drops the row change when an expression is TRUE - insert-value-expr matches WRITE_ROWS events, update-old/new-value-expr match UPDATE_ROWS old/new values (both together require both conditions), delete-value-expr matches DELETE_ROWS; schema/table are exact names (no wildcards), multiple referenced rules filter on ANY match, and TIMESTAMP expressions use the task timezone. Diagnosis: rows missing downstream that exist upstream - inspect expression-filters referenced by the source and evaluate the expressions against the changed rows. Remedy family: correct or remove the filter rule; note each extra rule adds per-row evaluation overhead that slows replication.

nodes.name: DM Failed DDL Replacement
nodes.content: Mechanism: an upstream DDL that TiDB cannot execute (such as ADD COLUMN with a UNIQUE constraint) interrupts the DM sync unit with an unsupported-DDL error; dmctl binlog replace substitutes equivalent DDL statements that TiDB accepts, for example splitting one statement into ADD COLUMN then ADD UNIQUE. Diagnosis: on a paused task, read query-status for the RawCause and identify the offending DDL text. Remedies: replace the DDL with an equivalent TiDB-compatible sequence and confirm the subtask returns to Running with synced true; risk of replacements is semantic drift if the replacement DDL is not truly equivalent to the upstream change.

nodes.name: DM Full Import Conflicts and Checksum
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM full import via Lightning physical mode resolves duplicates per on-duplicate-physical - 'none' resolves nothing (fastest but can leave inconsistent data), 'manual' removes all conflicting records into the ${meta-schema}_${name}.conflict_error_v1 table and pauses the task for human resolution; after import DM runs ADMIN CHECKSUM TABLE when checksum-physical='required', pausing the task on any mismatch, which means data was inconsistent or lost. Diagnosis: a task paused at the end of the full phase - query the conflict_error_v1 table for recorded conflicts and check whether the pause is a checksum failure. Remedy family: resolve recorded conflicts then resume-task into the incremental phase, or re-run the affected tables; keep checksum at 'required' (optional only warns and continues) and treat analyze as off since it only affects statistics.

nodes.name: DM Full Import Throughput
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM full-import speed is bounded by loader-thread concurrency on the target and by mydumper export parallelism (rows chunk size, threads), so an under-provisioned loader or dumper makes a full migration crawl. Diagnosis: read the DM-worker log marker 'all data files have been finished' with its cost time and compute throughput against source data size; compare loader-thread, rows, and threads settings with source read and target write capacity. Repair family: raise loader-thread and mydumper rows/threads within the limits of upstream disk, network, and downstream write capacity, re-testing after each change.

nodes.name: DM Incompatible DDL Pause
nodes.content: DM pauses a task when it meets DDL it cannot parse or replicate. For online schema change tools DM only recognizes default gh-ost/pt-osc ghost and trash table names; customized names need shadow-table-rules and trash-table-rules with online-ddl=true, otherwise temporary tables are replicated downstream as real tables. DM pauses a task when it meets DDL it cannot parse or replicate; the recovery choices are to skip the statement (binlog skip / handle-error skip) when keeping the old downstream schema is acceptable, or replace it with a downstream-compatible statement (binlog replace / handle-error replace) applied manually. For online schema change tools DM only recognizes default gh-ost/pt-osc ghost and trash table names; customized names need shadow-table-rules and trash-table-rules with online-ddl=true, otherwise temporary tables are replicated downstream as real tables. DM pauses a task when it meets DDL it cannot parse or replicate - including TiDB-unsupported object types such as FULLTEXT, HASH, or SPATIAL indexes; the recovery choices are to skip the statement (binlog skip / handle-error skip) when keeping the old downstream schema is acceptable, or replace it with a downstream-compatible statement (binlog replace / handle-error replace) applied manually. For online schema change tools DM only recognizes default gh-ost/pt-osc ghost and trash table names; customized names need shadow-table-rules and trash-table-rules with online-ddl=true, otherwise temporary tables are replicated downstream as real tables.

nodes.name: DM Incremental Start Position Gap
nodes.content: Mechanism: an incremental task starts from the downstream checkpoint if present, else the meta entry (binlog-name/pos or GTID), else silently from the latest upstream binlog position - skipping the whole binlog range between the full export snapshot and now; the Dumpling metadata file per output directory records the export binlog position that defines the intended start. Diagnosis: rows missing downstream after migration cutover - compare the dump metadata files' binlog positions with the task checkpoint and the intended start point; per-source meta is required when no checkpoint exists. Remedy family: set meta explicitly from the dump metadata, prefer binlog-gtid when upstream switches masters automatically, and enable safe mode when the incremental start precedes the full data so overlapping DML replays idempotently.

nodes.name: DM Major-Version Upgrade Preconditions
nodes.content: Mechanism: a DM major-version upgrade replaces metadata storage (checkpoints, shard DDL lock state, online DDL metadata) and the inter-component gRPC protocol, so v1.0.x metadata cannot be reused and all DM components including dmctl must run the same version. Preconditions: no task may be in full export/import or in shard-DDL or online-DDL coordination during the upgrade. Repair family: convert DM-Ansible inventory or DM-worker settings into v2.0+ source YAML (server-id, source-id, from host/port/user/password), reuse the task config (largely compatible), and with enable-gtid resolve the old binlog position to its GTID set by parsing binlog/relay logs before restarting the task.

nodes.name: MariaDB Source Compatibility for DM
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM replicates standard MySQL/MariaDB ROW binlog only - MariaDB needs binlog_annotate_row_events=OFF and log_bin_compress=OFF plus SUPER or BINLOG MONITOR privileges (DM cannot check MariaDB privileges, so precheck needs ignore-checking-items replication_privilege); cloud RDS variants have quirks (Alibaba RDS writes hidden primary-key columns into binlog of PK-less tables; Huawei RDS does not allow direct binlog reads); block-allow-list regexes accept only Go re2 syntax (no (?!) non-capturing groups); multi-DDL statements are split best-effort, so one DDL per statement is safer; view DDL and view DML are not replicated at all. Diagnosis: precheck refusals, binlog decode errors, silently missing view changes, or unexpected hidden columns point at these boundaries. Remedy family: align upstream binlog settings, use a standard-binlog-compatible source, restrict to re2 patterns, split multi-DDL statements upstream, and manage views manually; prerequisite is ROW-format binlog.

nodes.name: DM Monitoring Panels and Alert Thresholds
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM-worker exposes the DM-task Grafana dashboard whose operational alerts encode failure deadlines - subtask Paused >20 minutes (task state), pending sharding DDL >1 hour or any shard DDL error (critical), DM-worker offline >1 hour, relay log disk remaining <10G, relay log corruption (emergency), failure to read binlog from master or write relay log (immediate, critical), master-to-relay binlog file gap >1 sustained 10 minutes, and dump/load unit exits (immediate, critical). Progress panels (dump/load/checksum percentage, binlog file gap between master and syncer, shard lock resolving) localize where a stalled task sits. Diagnosis: match the firing alert to the unit - relay gaps point at upstream pull, load/checksum progress at the full-import phase, task state and operation-error counters at subtask lifecycle failures. Remedy family: treat critical alerts as interruption warnings, inspect the named unit's logs and query-status, and free relay disk or fix upstream pull before the gap widens.

nodes.name: DM Online DDL Tool Handling (gh-ost/pt-osc)
nodes.content: Mechanism: with online-ddl enabled DM classifies gh-ost tables (ghost _*_gho, trash _*_ghc/_*_del) and pt-osc tables (ghost _*_new, trash _*_old plus triggers) and replicates only the final renamed schema change, recording ghost DDL state in dm_meta.{task_name}_onlineddl; the incremental checkpoint must start before the online-DDL binlog window or after it. Diagnosis: error 36046 'online ddls on ghost table' means the start position skipped the ALTER-ghost DDL while still inside the online-DDL window, so ghost state was never recorded; ghost/trash tables appearing downstream mean online-ddl is off. Remedy family: enable online-ddl (v2.0.5+), restart incremental replication from outside the DDL window, or as a workaround disable online-ddl and filter the ghost/trash tables via block-allow-list.ignore-tables so only the rename sequence replicates; only gh-ost and pt-osc are supported.

nodes.name: DM Optimistic Shard Mode Risks
nodes.content: Mechanism: in DM optimistic mode a sharding DDL is converted to a compatible statement and applied downstream immediately without blocking DML, but Type-2 DDL (column rename/type/default, index rename) applied in different orders across shards breaks the migration, and strict-optimistic-shard-mode interrupts the task directly. Diagnosis: on optimistic-mode errors, determine whether the DDL batch leaves shard schemas inconsistent and whether unsupported DDL (DROP TABLE/DATABASE, TRUNCATE, multi-table or TiDB-unsupported DDL, defaults using current_timestamp/rand()/uuid) was executed. Remedies: keep shard schemas consistent around each DDL batch, confine A/B tests to one shard and migrate only the final DDL to other shards, or fall back to pessimistic mode for guaranteed consistency; risk of optimistic mode is downstream data inconsistency if discipline slips.

nodes.name: DM Oversized Binlog Recovery
nodes.content: Mechanism: event verification and checkpoints store binlog positions as uint32, so positions past 4 GB in one binlog file overflow and corrupt event matching during relay pull or replication. Differential diagnosis: confirm the named upstream binlog file really exceeds 4 GB, separating the overflow from genuine checksum corruption and from plain connection errors. Repair family: for relay units stop the DM-worker, copy the upstream binlog into the relay directory, advance relay.meta to the next file (with its GTID when enable_gtid is set), and restart; for replication units stop-task, set binlog_name to the oversized file and binlog_pos to a completed valid position in both global and per-table dm_meta checkpoints, enable safe-mode for re-entrant writes, start-task, verify with query-status, and revert safe-mode after passing the file.

nodes.name: DM Replication Bottleneck Localization and Tuning
nodes.content: Mechanism: migration latency localizes by binlog file gaps - master-to-relay gap >1 pins the relay unit (check read-binlog duration against network, write-relay duration against disk; use local SSD), and when master-to-syncer grows, the relay-to-syncer gap splits relay-side from sync-side latency; in the sync unit, DML queue remain length per worker (q_0..q_7 modulo buckets) should be flat - skewed curves mean load imbalance - while transaction execution latency points at the downstream. Tuning knobs are per-unit and immutable after task creation (change requires stop-task, edit, re-create): mydumpers rows/threads enable intra-table parallel export (rows ignores chunk-filesize), loaders pool-size (default 16) for full import, syncers worker-count (default 16) and batch (default 100, keep <500); with high DM-to-downstream network latency raise worker-count and lower batch. Diagnosis: read gaps left-to-right, then the unit's duration metric; a large DML queue backlog with low downstream latency means raise concurrency. Remedy family: adjust the identified unit's knob and re-create the task; protect upstream by keeping dump threads moderate.

nodes.name: DM Sharded PK Conflict Remedies
nodes.content: Duplicate-entry failures during shard merge come from overlapping per-shard auto-increment ranges or business-key collisions; distinguish shard key (never conflicts), auto-increment PK (overlaps), and other unique keys (analyze by business logic). Fix families, all applied before full migration: demote the conflicting auto-increment PK to a normal index when a globally unique key exists (plus ignore-checking-items: ["auto_increment_ID"] to skip precheck), or rebuild the downstream table with a composite primary key that is globally unique; then re-run full+incremental and verify with query-status.

nodes.name: DM Precheck Items and Ignoring Rules
nodes.content: Upstream MySQL must satisfy a fixed precheck set before incremental replication: server_id > 0, binlog enabled with binlog_format=ROW and binlog_row_image=FULL, migrated schemas not excluded by binlog_do_db/binlog_ignore_db, and spare connection capacity under max_connections for the dump/load units. When a migration task fails precheck or stalls at start, walk this checklist against the actual upstream variables rather than restarting the task. Upstream MySQL must satisfy a fixed precheck set before incremental replication: server_id > 0, binlog enabled with binlog_format=ROW and binlog_row_image=FULL, migrated schemas not excluded by binlog_do_db/binlog_ignore_db, and spare connection capacity under max_connections. Failed items block the job, warnings can be consciously accepted after risk review, and a failed job is resumable after the fix — walk this checklist against actual upstream variables rather than restarting blindly.

nodes.name: DM Relay Log Control
nodes.content: DM relay log lets DM-worker hold upstream binlog locally; since v5.4.0 it is enabled by enable-relay in the source config and can be toggled dynamically with start-relay/stop-relay, while intermediate versions only accept the commands. Relay state matters when upstream purges binlog that incremental replication still needs: check relay status via dmctl query-status before assuming an interrupted task must be fully re-dumped.

nodes.name: DM Relay Log Purpose and Failover Risk
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM-worker can persist a local copy of upstream binlogs (relay log) so that incremental replication survives cases where full migration takes longer than upstream binlog retention (start position already archived) or where a long block would otherwise let upstream purge the needed logs. Diagnosis: incremental tasks failing to start because binlog was purged, or replication breaking with ERROR 1236 / checksum mismatch after a long stall, indicate the relay log was not enabled or its copy is incomplete. Remedy family: enable relay for large full-migration windows; on DM-worker failover the relay data does not move automatically - copy relay files to the promoted worker and fix its relay meta manually, or the HA promotion breaks replication.

nodes.name: DM Interruption and GTID Breakage Recovery
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM auto-retries transient invalid/bad-connection errors during incremental replication; a restart during full import (older DM) can break upstream-source to DM-worker bindings, and purged upstream binlogs with GTID auto-position raise ERROR 1236, while relay plus GTID against a MySQL secondary can show inconsecutive syncerBinlogGtid as a version-bound bug. Differential diagnosis: read query-status and separate auto-retryable connection errors from checkpoint/GTID breakage - syncerBinlogGtid inconsecutive with consecutive masterBinlogGtid indicates the known bug rather than real loss, whereas 1236 purged-binlog errors indicate the checkpoint points at removed logs. Repair family: stop-task/start-task when auto-retry is unavailable; for a broken full import clean downstream data and restart with start-task --remove-meta for small datasets, or import the dump with TiDB-Lightning local backend and switch the task to incremental at the dump metadata position for large ones; prevent purging with longer upstream log retention or enable-relay, and on the GTID bug continue from the subTaskStatus.sync syncerBinlog/syncerBinlogGtid values. DM continuous validation compares upstream binlog against downstream writes in real time, so suspected divergence can be confirmed with validator output (inconsistent rows, missing records) instead of full-table comparison.

nodes.name: DM Replication Lag
nodes.content: DM Sync replicates binlog through filter/route/compactor, then causality conflict detection groups conflicting rows for serial execution, so hot-row contention or a low worker-count caps concurrency; the checkpoint only advances to the earliest position across all workers every 30 seconds, so one slow worker freezes visible progress and after a resume the task re-executes recent events under safe-mode rewrite (INSERT to REPLACE) for idempotency. Distinguish by comparing per-worker lag and downstream TiDB CPU: high downstream CPU means raise concurrency only after capacity, a stalled single worker means find and fix the blocking statement; fix family: increase worker-count/batch, enable compactor and multiple-rows merge to cut write amplification, or resolve the stuck worker, risk is higher downstream write pressure.

nodes.name: Manage DM Safe Mode on Resume
nodes.content: Mechanism: when DM resumes from a checkpoint after an abnormal pause it cannot know which events already reached the downstream, so it auto-enables safe mode for 60 seconds (two 30s checkpoint intervals) or until passing safemode_exit_point; manual safe-mode=true in the syncer config covers a whole task. Differential: duplicated-key errors downstream right after a restart indicate replayed events that needed safe mode. Remedies: let automatic safe mode run, or enable it manually around planned resumes; keep checkpoint-flush-interval at defaults rather than shrinking the safe-mode window. Risk: long safe-mode stretches change DML semantics (idempotent rewrites) and mask genuine conflicts.

nodes.name: DM Safe Mode and Idempotent Re-apply
nodes.content: Mechanism: safe mode rewrites upstream INSERT into REPLACE and UPDATE into DELETE+REPLACE, so DML re-applies idempotently when the table has a primary key or unique index; DM automatically enters safe mode around task start/resume (about the first minute), after an abnormal pause, missing safemode_exit_point, unclean exit, or HA rescheduling (default ~60s; '0s' makes auto-entry an error). Risks of running it permanently: constant DELETE+REPLACE churn costs more than UPDATE; REPLACE silently overwrites conflicting rows, so shard-merge misconfiguration can lose large amounts of data with no error; and tables without PK/unique index still get duplicate rows because conflict detection has no key. Diagnosis: a stream of REPLACE statements downstream means safe mode is active - confirm via the 'change count ... new count' line in DM-worker logs; duplicate-entry errors right after resume point to a replay window without safe-mode coverage. Remedy family: rely on automatic safe mode or enable it temporarily; keep it permanent only when duplicate upstream keys exist and losing duplicate rows is acceptable.

nodes.name: DM Schema Tracker Mismatch Repair
nodes.content: Mechanism: during incremental replication DM keeps four schema views consistent - upstream now (U), the binlog event's historical schema (B), DM's internal schema tracker (I), and downstream TiDB (D); they diverge after downstream-side index changes or extra downstream columns, in optimistic shard-DDL mode, or when an incremental task seeds schema-I from the downstream. Diagnosis: replication errors like 'Column count doesn't match value count' or 'Schema/Column doesn't match' mean the schema views diverged - compare upstream, downstream, and the DM-cached schema (binlog-schema list). Remedy family: pause the task, update the internal schema to the correct table definition (binlog-schema update with --from-source or --from-target, --flush to persist into the checkpoint), or delete it so DM rebuilds from checkpoint table_info, optimistic-sharding meta, then the downstream table; for legitimately wider downstream tables use the more-columns migration pattern.

nodes.name: DM Encrypted Password Key Mismatch
nodes.content: Mechanism: since v8.0.0 DM dropped the fixed AES-256 key; encrypted passwords in source/task configs decrypt only when every DM-master uses the same secret-key-path file (64-character hex AES-256 key), and DM-worker must be rolled after DM-master. Diagnosis: sources or tasks failing with password decrypt errors after upgrade or key rotation point to a missing secret-key-path, nodes carrying different keys, or passwords encrypted with a mismatched dmctl version. Remedy family: set the identical secret-key-path on all DM-masters, rolling-restart DM-master then DM-worker, re-encrypt passwords with version-matched dmctl encrypt; avoid creating new configs during the rotation window.

nodes.name: DM Shard-Merge DDL Coordination Stall
nodes.content: In DM shard merge the pessimistic mode (default) pauses the whole sharding group when one shard runs a DDL: other DM-workers wait until every shard reaches the same schema, so replication delay grows and long waits risk upstream binlog being purged (mitigate with relay log). Optimistic mode keeps migrating during schema changes but stops the task on incompatible schema formats. Diagnosis: query-status showing unresolvedGroups/blockingDDLs or shard-ddl-lock on DM-master. Remedies: respect pessimistic restrictions (same-order DDL in all shards, no DROP DATABASE/TABLE or TRUNCATE TABLE which sync unit ignores, single-table single-rename RENAME limits); handle the lock manually only if the failure matches a documented abnormal scenario; otherwise redo the task by emptying downstream data and dm_meta then re-running full+incremental; isolate each sharding group in its own task so one lock cannot block everything.

nodes.name: DM Shard-DDL Lock Manual Unlock
nodes.content: Mechanism: in pessimistic shard-merge, a sharding DDL lock is released automatically once every source reaches it, but locks stay un-resolved when some sources are removed from the configuration mid-DDL or a source can never catch up. Diagnosis: query-status exposes unresolvedDDLLockID, blockingDDLs, and unresolvedGroups per source; dmctl shard-ddl-lock <task> shows the lock's ID, owner, DDLs, and the synced vs unsynced source lists - sources stuck in unsynced identify the blocker. Remedy family: prefer the clean path - stop-task, remove the departed source from the task config, start-task; only as a last resort use shard-ddl-lock unlock (pessimistic mode only), which makes the owner execute the DDL, makes all other workers skip it, and deletes the lock - pick --owner explicitly and --force-remove when the blocking source no longer exists, and only when you accept that unsynced sources will not apply that DDL.

nodes.name: Shard Merge Operational Discipline
nodes.content: Mechanism: with RDS upstreams, binlog table names can carry generated prefixes invisible to SQL clients, so table routing must match binlog names; DM cannot dynamically track created or dropped sharded tables, so schema changes require a stop-task/start-task window, and drops are safe only after DM's syncerBinlog passes the DROP TABLE's End_log_pos; concurrency (pool-size, worker-count) accumulates across DM-workers and can overload the downstream. Diagnosis: for missing tables or stalled merge, compare query-status syncerBinlog with upstream binlog positions and check downstream load. Remedies: follow the stop-change-start procedure around table creation/drops, fix route rules to binlog names, and lower per-worker concurrency when TiDB monitoring shows saturation; risk is data gaps if the task restarts before positions catch up.

nodes.name: DM Sharding DDL Conflict Recovery
nodes.content: Mechanism: optimistic mode replicates each shard DDL to the downstream immediately, so mutually incompatible schemas (same-name columns with different types, defaults, or generated expressions; same-name indexes with different keys) or drop-then-re-add DDL produces inconsistency DM only reports; in pessimistic mode a removed source leaves the shard-ddl-lock permanently unsynced. Differential diagnosis: compare each shard table schema and the reported error to identify the incompatible DDL, and check shard-ddl-lock unsynced members against the still-configured sources to separate a genuinely in-progress lock from a stale one. Repair family: in optimistic mode keep shard schemas compatible, roll back the offending DDL consistently, and fix the inconsistent downstream rows manually; for a stale lock manually unlock the DDL lock, stop-task, remove the offline source from the task configuration, start-task, and verify the downstream schema and data. A DDL lock can also reappear after unlocking when a DM-worker restart or network failure makes a non-owner skip the DDL and its checkpoint update fail, so re-confirm with shard-ddl-lock, unlock again, verify the lock is gone, and check query-status before resuming.

nodes.name: DM start-time And Safe Mode Semantics
nodes.content: dmctl start-task --start-time overrides both the config binlog position and the downstream checkpoint; when a checkpoint already exists DM forces safe mode until replication passes it, to prevent duplicated writes from rewinding. Resetting earlier can fail on schema mismatch with the current downstream schema; rewinding later silently skips binlog and leaves dirty data, and a start-time with no matching binlog errors as 'too late'. Choose start-time only with an explicit cutover reason and verify the checkpoint before restarting.

nodes.name: DM Subtask State Model
nodes.content: DM subtasks move New -> Running, switch to Paused on any error or pause-task, resume via resume-task, become Stopped via stop-task (cannot resume), and Finished only when a full-load subtask completes normally. Within query-status, sync reports masterBinlog versus syncerBinlog (lag), blockingDDLs and unresolvedGroups (sharding DDL waits), and RPS counters; note synced=false does not always mean real lag because the checkpoint is not refreshed in real time. Diagnosis and remediation therefore start from stage plus result fields, not from binlog equality alone.

nodes.name: DM Syncer Throughput vs Downstream Pressure
nodes.content: Mechanism: the DM syncer's worker-count (default 16) controls concurrent binlog apply threads and strongly affects downstream load, batch (default 100, keep under 500) sizes each apply transaction, while compact merges same-row statements and multiple-rows merges same-type statements into multi-row writes to cut statement count. Diagnosis: downstream write pressure, lock conflicts, or apply lag during incremental replication - check syncer worker-count/batch and whether multiple migration instances concurrently load into the same TiDB (reduce loader pool-size/syncer-thread accordingly). Remedy family: lower worker-count or batch to protect the downstream, enable compact/multiple-rows to reduce write amplification; per-instance *-thread settings override the shared processing-unit config.

nodes.name: DM Syncer Throughput Tuning
nodes.content: DM binlog replication throughput is governed by syncers worker-count and batch; when replication lag grows, raise worker-count first and adjust batch while watching query-status and the finished-sqls Grafana rate. Bound the increase by downstream write capacity - oversizing turns replication lag into downstream lock and conflict pressure.

nodes.name: DM Table Routing Failure Modes
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM table routes map upstream schema/table patterns to target-schema/target-table; a table may match only one route, schema-level routes are required to replicate CREATE/DROP SCHEMA, and shard-merge with extract-table/extract-schema/extract-source requires a pre-created merged table whose target-columns are the last columns and string-typed. Routing patterns use wildcards, not regex - 'table_pattern_[0-63]' matches only 0..6, so a mismatched route plus block-allow-list silently drops shard tables with no fatal error. Diagnosis: 'schema test doesn't exist' errors mean a missing schema-level route; multiple-rule-match errors mean overlapping patterns; missing source columns mean a malformed merged table; silently lost shard data means a route or block-allow-list pattern does not actually match the table name. Remedy family: add the schema route, disambiguate overlapping patterns, recreate the merged table with trailing string extract columns, and verify every shard table matches exactly one do/route pattern before restarting the task.

nodes.name: DM Migration Task Hang
nodes.content: DM-master coordinates migration via an etcd-elected leader and schedules tasks across DM-workers; when a worker fails and no idle standby worker exists, its tasks hang until a worker frees up, and full export/import phases have no checkpoint resumption so a reschedule restarts that phase. Fix family: reserve 20-50% standby workers, restore the failed worker, or recreate the task; risk is duplicated full-import work

nodes.name: DM Sharded Merge Verification
nodes.content: Mechanism: a DM all-mode task with shard-mode (pessimistic or optimistic) and route rules merges upstream sharding* tables into one target table, and correctness is verified by mutating upstream rows and diffing upstream against downstream. Diagnosis: when merged data is suspected wrong, run a sync-diff-inspector comparison scoped to the sharded tables and check DM task subtask states for paused error stages. Remedies: repair conflicting rows per the diff report, fix routing or block-allow-list mis-scoping that drops tables, and re-run the diff until clean; risk is that diffs taken mid-replication show transient mismatches, so quiesce or checkpoint-align before judging.

nodes.name: DM Mutual TLS Connection Repair
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM-master, DM-worker, and dmctl mutually authenticate with ssl-ca/ssl-cert/ssl-key plus cert-allowed-cn caller verification, so handshake failures come from wrong CN, missing client certificates, or stale certificate files. Diagnosis: when dmctl or DM-worker connections fail after TLS enablement, check certificate CN against cert-allowed-cn and confirm dmctl passes --ssl-ca/--ssl-cert/--ssl-key. Remedies: reissue certificates with matching CN, align configuration on both sides, and restart DM components after updating certificate files since reload happens on new connections or restart; risk is brief control-plane disconnection during restart.

nodes.name: DM upstream source configuration semantics
nodes.content: DM replication stalls or loses data can stem from upstream source config: enable-gtid and enable-relay must not both be true on DM v2.0.1 (risk of losing incremental data), relay log retention is bounded by the purge settings (interval/expires/remain-space), and binlog event filters (sql-pattern with action Ignore) silently skip matched DDL, which surfaces later as schema mismatch. Use dmctl-encrypted passwords and TLS security blocks; verify effective config with dmctl before restarts. Relay log purge strategy also bounds catch-up: automatic purge runs every purge.interval (3600s), removing relay logs older than purge.expires hours or when free disk drops below purge.remain-space GB, and active relay logs of a long All-mode full export can still be purged.

nodes.name: DM Upstream Master-Slave Switch
nodes.content: Mechanism: switching DM-worker to another MySQL instance in the same primary-secondary group requires GTID mode (enable-gtid: true) and a GTID-set precondition: the replication progress gtid-S (query-status syncerBinlogGtid) must contain the new instance's purged set gtid-P (gtid_purged) and be contained by its executed set gtid-E (gtid_executed) - otherwise the new instance lacks required binlog and migration must restart from re-deployment. Diagnosis: after an upstream crash or maintenance, replication errors naming unavailable binlog or a failed reconnect indicate a switch without GTID validation. Remedy family: two procedures only - via VIP: pause all tasks, repoint the VIP, resume-task (never repoint while running: concurrent reads of old and new instances corrupt replication); via address change: stop-task, operate-source stop the old source, edit and operate-source create the new address, start-task.

nodes.name: DM Continuous Validation Error Rows
nodes.content: Mechanism: DM continuous validation compares replicated rows and records inconsistencies as error rows without pausing the task; validation status reports validator binlog position, processed/pending rows, and new/ignored/resolved error counts, and show-error lists each error row's source and downstream data. Diagnosis: for suspected replication drift, read errorRowsStatus and dump error rows with dmctl validation show-error to see which rows differ. Remedies: fix the downstream data manually, then mark rows resolved with resolve-error, clear them with clear-error, or explicitly acknowledge with ignore-error; risk is that ignoring rows hides a widening divergence, since corrected data is not re-validated automatically.

nodes.name: DM Continuous Data Validation
nodes.content: Mechanism: the DM validator replays synced binlog events row-by-row (merging changes per table+PK), comparing downstream data in full mode or existence in fast mode; rows still failing after the retry window are marked error rows in the downstream meta database rather than failing the task. Diagnosis: inspect validation status and error rows before trusting a migration. Remedy: fix or re-sync the affected rows, and set the cutover point explicitly with dmctl validation update --cutover-binlog-pos/--cutover-binlog-gtid so validation covers up to the intended switch position.

nodes.name: DM Continuous Validation Semantics
nodes.content: DM continuous data validation compares replicated changed rows downstream during incremental migration (mode full compares values, fast only checks existence, none disables); a row that keeps failing is marked an error row after row-error-delay (default 30m). Use it to catch silent replication corruption that full-table diff tools cannot, but remember validation workers add downstream read load and only cover data written while validation is enabled.

nodes.name: DR Auto-Sync State Machine Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: DR Auto-Sync is PD-controlled with public replication-mode states sync, temporary async, and sync-recover, while Placement Rules bind label keys and domain values to replica roles and counts, where a learner is not a synchronous voter. Differential diagnosis: read the product replication-mode state and the Region-level contract as separate observations; correlate the rule bundle (role, count, label constraint, location labels) with current Store labels and Region peers - a PD Leader change or equal TSO text proves neither state nor convergence. Repair family: a role exchange needs an explicit business write boundary, a fence for the old writer, the documented synchronization state, and terminal placement/Region convergence; changing only a route or only the PD Leader is not an exchange. State switches are heartbeat-driven: when failed nodes exceed primary-replicas or dr-replicas for longer than wait-store-timeout, PD switches sync to async (native Raft majority), and on recovery passes through sync-recover, where PD records Region switching progress and only flips to sync once every Region finished two-AZ replication; losing most Voter replicas in the primary AZ during sync mode still allows RPO=0 recovery from the DR AZ, but requires manual professional-tool intervention.

nodes.name: DR Auto-Sync Mode Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: PD dr-auto-sync uses a label key to split primary and DR zones, keeps primary-replicas voters in the primary AZ and dr-replicas in the DR AZ, and switches to asynchronous replication after network trouble exceeds wait-store-timeout; returning to sync-recover waits wait-recover-timeout, and pause-region-split during async statuses protects the DR AZ from partial data loss while re-syncing. Diagnosis: query /pd/api/v1/replication_mode/status to see the current state and confirm label-key matches the placement rules. Remedies: fix network isolation, tune wait-store-timeout/wait-recover-timeout for the RPO/RTO balance, and enable pause-region-split during recovery; risk is that async mode accepts potential DR-AZ data loss on primary failure.

nodes.name: DR Auto-Sync State Flap
nodes.content: Two-AZ DR Auto-Sync deployments adaptively switch replication state between sync, async, and sync-recover; in async state the DR AZ is not synchronized, so failing over there loses recent commits, and sync-recover only gradually returns to label-based synchronous replication. Distinguish real AZ trouble from load-protection downgrades by checking PD replication state and connectivity history; fix family: restore AZ connectivity and let sync-recover finish, and verify the DR AZ checkpoint before any manual switchover; switching over during async loses data.

nodes.name: DR Replication External Storage
nodes.content: Mechanism: a primary-to-secondary DR setup first migrates full data, then TiCDC replicates incremental changes; br backup/restore and redo log shipping both read and write an external storage that must be reachable from every br, TiKV, and TiCDC node. Diagnosis: on backup or replication failures verify the S3-protocol URI parameters (endpoint, access-key, secret-access-key, bucket) and per-node connectivity; self-hosted deployments typically run MinIO over the S3 protocol (force-path-style=true) or mount NFS to br, TiKV, and TiCDC alike. Repair family: fix endpoint/credentials, pre-create buckets and directories, and keep the same storage visible to all three component types before retrying.

nodes.name: Multi-replica same-region DR placement
nodes.content: Regional DR with zero RPO relies on Raft majorities across AZs: a five-replica three-AZ layout keeps quorum when one AZ fails, PD replication.location-labels (e.g. Region,AZ hierarchy) drives replica placement, and locating Region leaders plus the PD leader in the primary region balances traffic across two AZs. Diagnose DR incidents by checking label-based distribution of peers and leaders rather than raw replica counts.

nodes.name: DR RPO and RTO Expectations
nodes.content: BR-based disaster recovery to independent DR storage expects an RPO of up to 5 minutes and an RTO between tens of minutes and a few hours (longer for very large databases), while block-storage-snapshot DR can cut recovery to about an hour. Use these budgets to judge whether a restore is abnormally slow or post-failover data loss exceeds expectation before investigating backup throughput or chain integrity.

nodes.name: DR Auto-Sync Joint State Timeout on Scale-Out
nodes.content: Mechanism: in DR Auto-Sync deployments, scaling out TiKV nodes can make the replica joint state transition time out, leaving replication state degraded even though the scale-out command succeeded; resolved-ts has also historically stalled for hours in corner cases, widening the stale-read window. Diagnosis: when replication state degrades right after a scale-out, look for joint-state timeout in TiKV/PD logs before suspecting the network or placement rules, and check resolved-ts progress for stalls. Repair family: retry the joint-state convergence (re-trigger placement/role exchange), keep scale-out operations small and supervised in DR deployments, and upgrade past affected versions where the corner cases are fixed.

nodes.name: Drainer OOM and Safe Mode
nodes.content: Mechanism: Drainer caches binlog items before applying downstream; one oversized upstream transaction can exhaust its memory, and non-idempotent SQL breaks re-replication into MySQL/TiDB. Diagnosis: Drainer OOM after a huge single transaction, or downstream duplicate/missing rows after restart. Remedy: lower cache-binlog-count to bound memory per item, enable safe-mode (INSERT becomes REPLACE, UPDATE splits into DELETE+REPLACE) for idempotent replay, and set initial-commit-ts when checkpoint state is absent.

nodes.name: Drainer Schema Load and Checkpoint Discipline
nodes.content: Mechanism: Drainer with load-schema-snapshot = true reads table schemas at the checkpoint TS, which fails once GC removes those historical versions; = false replays full DDL history instead. Multiple Drainer nodes sharing one checkpoint schema overwrite each other's progress. Diagnosis: on Drainer startup or replay errors, compare the checkpoint TS with the GC safe point and check whether several Drainers share a checkpoint schema. Remedies: deploy each Drainer with its own checkpoint schema, keep the checkpoint ahead of GC via service safepoints, and raise downstream read-timeout when long DDLs keep timing out; risk of load-schema-snapshot = false is heavy DDL replay cost on startup.

nodes.name: Dumpling Disk and Memory Failures
nodes.content: Dumpling's 'local disk space is insufficient' error or upstream memory exhaustion during table export typically comes from oversized result chunks when primary keys are unevenly distributed (for example with SHARD_ROW_ID_BITS) or when exporting partitioned tables. Remedies: use a newer Dumpling version, enable in-table concurrency splitting with -r (region-based on TiDB), cap single-file size with -F (256 MiB or less when the output feeds Lightning), and bound export threads with -t (each thread raises upstream memory; keep moderate). GC safepoint protection requires PD access; on Kubernetes or TiDB Cloud set GC time manually, and rely on tidb_snapshot for consistent snapshots instead of FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK.

nodes.name: GC Hold During Full Export
nodes.content: Mechanism: between full export and incremental replication start, history newer than the export snapshot must survive; Dumpling auto-adjusts the upstream GC service safepoint during export, but manual SET GLOBAL tidb_gc_enable=FALSE is still required because GC may resume immediately after Dumpling exits, GC-ing the binlog range the incremental task needs. The dump metadata file records the export TSO (BackupTS), which is both the changefeed --start-ts and the diff-inspector snapshot. Diagnosis: incremental tasks failing to start because the start timestamp was garbage-collected, or a diff check at a snapshot no longer readable - check tidb_gc_enable and the elapsed window. Remedy family: disable GC before export, record BackupTS from metadata, restart incremental replication at that exact TSO, and re-enable GC only after the changefeed exists (its service safepoint then protects needed history); disabling GC accumulates MVCC versions, so plan the window.

nodes.name: DXF background isolation runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: DXF binds a task to the tidb_service_scope of the submitting node and schedules only nodes with the same scope; scope changes take effect only for the next task. Differential: compare tidb_service_scope across TiDB nodes and check whether a background-scope node recently restarted or scaled in, pushing tasks onto empty-scope nodes. Remedies: (a) set background scope on two or more TiDB nodes so a single node failure does not spill tasks to front-end nodes (v7.4-v8.0 behavior); (b) assign a distinct scope to newly added nodes before they join; (c) accept that a running task keeps its original scope until it finishes. Risks: leaving scope empty lets internal tasks land on application-serving nodes during any background-node outage. TiKV-side background task management dynamically caps background CPU/IO below a threshold derived from foreground usage, but it requires per-instance cgroup quotas when components are collocated and is experimental.

nodes.name: Dynamic Config Application Scope
nodes.content: Mechanism: SHOW CONFIG inspects live TiDB/TiKV/PD settings; SET CONFIG updates TiDB, TiKV, and shared PD configuration online (PD persists to etcd, which prevails over the file), and tikv-ctl modify-tikv-config is an equivalent channel for TiKV items such as block cache or compaction rate limits. Differential: items not on the dynamic list (for example engine or listening addresses) require a config file edit plus instance restart. Remedies: prefer dynamic modification for quota/GC/compaction corrections; schedule restarts for static items after draining traffic. Risk: etcd-persisted PD settings silently diverge from topology config files, and a wrong dynamic value takes effect immediately cluster-wide. Static file changes flow through tiup cluster edit-config followed by tiup cluster reload, which redeploys files and restarts the affected components - plan rolling restarts off-peak instead of editing live configs by hand.

nodes.name: Encryption At Rest Key Management
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV encryption at rest activates when security.encryption.data-encryption-method is set to an AES-CTR or SM4-CTR value, which then requires a master key; TiKV rotates data keys on data-key-rotation-period (default 7 days), and rotation requires configuring both master-key and previous-master-key. Diagnosis: for a TiKV store failing to start after key changes, check which master key encrypted the file dictionary and whether the previous key is still configured. Remedies: restore access to the original master key, supply previous-master-key during rotation, and keep enable-file-dictionary-log compatible with the TiKV version; risk is permanent data loss if the master key is lost, since encrypted files are unrecoverable without it.

nodes.name: Encryption-at-Rest Key Availability
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV encryption at rest uses envelope encryption — a user-supplied master key (KMS CMK or 32-byte hex file) wraps weekly-rotated data keys that encrypt SST/WAL/MANIFEST files; if TiKV cannot reach the KMS CMK it fails to start or restart, and data encrypted with a lost key is unrecoverable. Diagnosis: on startup failure of an encrypted cluster, verify KMS connectivity/credentials and master-key file contents before other paths. Remedy: restore KMS access; prefer KMS keys in production and keep file-based keys only on tmpfs. TiKV encryption at rest uses envelope encryption — a user-supplied master key (KMS CMK or 32-byte hex file) wraps weekly-rotated data keys that encrypt SST/WAL/MANIFEST files; if TiKV cannot reach the KMS CMK it fails to start or restart, and data encrypted with a lost key is unrecoverable. Diagnosis: on startup failure of an encrypted cluster verify KMS connectivity/credentials and the Encryption initialized metric before other paths. Remedy: restore KMS access; prefer KMS keys in production and keep file-based keys only on tmpfs.

nodes.name: TiKV Master Key Rotation
nodes.content: Encryption-at-rest master key rotation is offline: set the new key in security.encryption.master-key, keep the old key in security.encryption.previous-master-key, and rolling-restart TiKV; during startup both keys must be reachable, afterwards only the new one. If the KMS or key file is inaccessible TiKV fails to start and existing data cannot be decrypted, so validate key availability and permissions before restarting.
