nodes.name: Encryption at Rest Throughput Cost
nodes.content: TiKV/TiFlash encrypt data files with AES or SM4 under a master key, and SM4 can degrade write throughput 50-80% (a large block-cache mitigates this to roughly 10%); an encrypted TiKV tracks files by absolute path, so changing data-dir or WAL paths breaks the node, and keys can leak through core dumps. Distinguish by correlating throughput/CPU drop with encryption enablement, algorithm choice, or master-key rotation; fix family: prefer AES, enlarge block-cache, disable core dumps, never change data paths while encryption is on, risk is the performance overhead itself.

nodes.name: Host Environment Precheck
nodes.content: Mechanism: host-level misconfigurations cause subtle cluster faults, so production validation covers OS version and CPU EPOLLEXCLUSIVE, system time skew (error above 500 ms) and ntpd, disabled swap and THP, kernel parameters (somaxconn 32768, vm.swappiness 0, fs.file-max 1000000, overcommit 0/1), file-descriptor limits, SELinux off, irqbalance on, ext4 mounted with nodelalloc,noatime, free ports, and optionally CPU cores >= 16, memory >= 32 GiB, and fio rand-read tests. Diagnosis: for unexplained latency jitter or instability on a node, replay the precheck items against that host. Remedies: fix the failing item (mount options need remount, SELinux disable needs reboot), and rerun tiup cluster check with -enable-cpu/-enable-mem/-enable-disk for the deeper checks; risk is that port checks fail spuriously on already-started clusters.

nodes.name: Expensive Query and Txn Log Thresholds
nodes.content: Mechanism: unlike slow logs printed after completion, the expensive query log prints statements still running whose execution time exceeds tidb_expensive_query_time_threshold (default 60s), and since v7.2.0 transactions uncommitted past tidb_expensive_txn_time_threshold (default 600s) are logged as expensive transactions; tidb_force_priority can bias statement priority but is superseded by resource control when enabled. Diagnosis: for a database suddenly loaded by runaway work, read expensive query logs to catch the offenders in-flight before they finish. Remedies: adjust thresholds to the workload, kill the logged sessions, and prefer resource groups with quotas and priorities over the legacy force-priority variable; risk is log volume growth with low thresholds.

nodes.name: EXPLAIN ANALYZE Operator Reading
nodes.content: Mechanism: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement and reports per-operator actual time, processed rows, RPC request counts, lock-conflict resolution duration, network latency, and RocksDB deleted-row scan plus cache hit rate; it also covers DML statements, and EXPLAIN FOR CONNECTION shows the same style of progress for in-flight SQL, while the slow log records the same execution details. Diagnosis: for a slow statement, compare actRows against estRows per operator and inspect RPC and lock timings to separate scan amplification, lock waits, and network cost. Remedies: add or fix indexes for over-scanning operators, resolve the blocking transaction for lock-heavy plans, and use the slow log to keep history; risk is that EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the statement, so avoid it for non-idempotent DML.

nodes.name: Expression pushdown blocklist recovery
nodes.content: Wrong query results can be caused by a buggy pushed-down expression computing on TiKV or TiFlash. Quick recovery: insert the function or operator into mysql.expr_pushdown_blacklist with the target store_type (tidb/tikv/tiflash), run ADMIN RELOAD expr_pushdown_blacklist (per TiDB instance only, repeat on all instances), and later remove the entry; risk: keeping compute in TiDB raises latency for that expression.

nodes.name: Expression Pushdown Control
nodes.content: mysql.expr_pushdown_blacklist disables pushdown of specific expressions to specific engines (one row per expression and engine label), and changes take effect only after ADMIN RELOAD expr_pushdown_blacklist; EXPLAIN confirms the effect as the Selection moves between cop[tikv] and root tasks. If an otherwise pushable filter suddenly executes at TiDB root and slows a scan, check for blocklist rows; conversely, expressions known to misbehave in storage can be blocked deliberately.

nodes.name: Extended Statistics Lifecycle
nodes.content: Mechanism: extended statistics (correlation between column pairs) refine optimizer estimates for correlated predicates; they require tidb_enable_extended_stats = ON, are collected at the next ANALYZE once registered via ALTER TABLE ADD STATS_EXTENDED, and each TiDB node caches mysql.stats_extended incrementally by version. Diagnosis: for stubborn misestimates on multi-column predicates, check whether a matching extended object exists and was analyzed. Remedies: register the column pair, re-run ANALYZE, and after any accidental direct edit of mysql.stats_extended run ADMIN RELOAD STATS_EXTENDED on every TiDB node to rebuild caches; risk of direct table edits is per-node cache divergence producing inconsistent plans.

nodes.name: Failover Fencing and Admission Evidence
nodes.content: Mechanism: a stopped SQL endpoint is not by itself an application fence; an unfenced old writer can resume and split the write path after promotion. Differential diagnosis: treat an accepted product request, a changed PD Leader, a healthy connection, or a short liveness result as intermediate observations only, and never treat a TSO comparison as an RPO proof - the acknowledged boundary, fence, terminal replication state, business truth, and canary are separate facts. Repair family: for an orderly exchange use the distributing router policy, drain to zero active connections, then submit the role exchange; for an outage apply and verify the route fence before promotion; bind a post-outage handoff record to public business invariants (marker count, amount total, checksum) plus the fence generation, and finish with a bounded surviving-endpoint write/read-back probe.

nodes.name: Failover Session Semantics and App Retry
nodes.content: Failover preserves committed data but can interrupt in-flight transactions: a failed TiDB node's transactions die while the gateway reroutes new work, and stateless gateways restart in another zone with brief connection disruption. Applications must implement retry logic for recoverable failures (transient connection errors, transaction aborts) rather than assuming connection-level transparency; RTO/RPO expectations should be set per HA architecture (zonal near-zero, regional hundreds of seconds downtime, both RPO 0 with log backup cadence).

nodes.name: Accelerated table creation
nodes.content: Bulk CREATE TABLE throughput is capped by the online DDL algorithm, which executes jobs only on the DDL owner; tidb_enable_fast_create_table lets simple CREATE TABLE jobs run on non-owner nodes (experimental), trading the owner bottleneck for tool limitations: TiCDC cannot replicate such tables and foreign keys are not allowed.

nodes.name: TiFlash FastScan Control
nodes.content: TiFlash FastScan trades some consistency guarantees for faster scans and is controlled per session by the tiflash_fastscan variable; the earlier ALTER TABLE ... SET TIFLASH MODE syntax is deprecated and v6.2.0 table-level settings become invalid after upgrading to v6.3.0. FastScan is off by default after upgrade to keep data consistency, so an unexpected analytics throughput change should check session-level tiflash_fastscan first.

nodes.name: TiFlash FastScan Semantics
nodes.content: tiflash_fastscan (session or global, default OFF) speeds TiFlash scans by skipping the Delta/Stable sort-merge that guarantees precision, so results may include old versions of the same primary key or deleted rows until compaction moves data older than the GC safe point out. Unexpected duplicate or stale rows from TiFlash queries are a FastScan signature - confirm the variable, then force compaction (ALTER TABLE ... COMPACT) or disable FastScan when exact results are required.

nodes.name: Fine Grained Shuffle Window Concurrency
nodes.content: Mechanism: window functions pushed to TiFlash execute serially per partition unless Fine Grained Shuffle is used; tiflash_fine_grained_shuffle_stream_count raises the stream count in the Exchange operators so window computation runs on more threads. Diagnosis: for slow window-function queries in MPP plans, check stream_count on the ExchangeSender/Receiver and Window operators. Remedies: raise tiflash_fine_grained_shuffle_stream_count at session level to trade more TiFlash resources for latency; risk is starving concurrent queries on the same TiFlash nodes.

nodes.name: Firewall Port Access For Cluster Nodes
nodes.content: Closed firewall ports stop read/write requests and data heartbeats between TiDB, TiKV and PD nodes. Remediation families: stop and disable firewalld when the network is already secure, switch the default zone to trusted, or add per-component services to the allowlist (TiDB 4000/10080, TiKV 20160/20180, PD 2379/2380, monitoring ports); risk: public-zone exposure of service ports, so prefer explicit allowlists in shared networks.

nodes.name: Flashback misoperation recovery runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB keeps MVCC versions until GC passes the safe point, so recent mis-writes can be undone without restoring backups via FLASHBACK CLUSTER or FLASHBACK DATABASE to a timestamp inside the GC window. Differential diagnosis: confirm the target timestamp is still older than the GC safe point but after the misoperation, and identify the blast radius (cluster, database, or table) before choosing the flashback level. Remedy families: (1) FLASHBACK to the pre-mistake timestamp; (2) PITR from BR backup plus log backup when the window has passed; (3) compensating DML for narrow errors. Risks: flashback rolls forward-valid writes back too, so quiesce application traffic first; once GC reclaims the versions, only backup-based recovery remains.

nodes.name: Follower Read mechanism
nodes.content: Follower Read serves reads from follower replicas without breaking linearizability: the follower obtains the latest Raft commit index from the leader via ReadIndex and waits until it is applied locally before reading. Load is spread round-robin; coprocessor request stickiness is per connection while point-query stickiness is per transaction, so mixed workloads may not spread as expected.

nodes.name: Offload Read Hotspots with Follower Read
nodes.content: Mechanism: tidb_replica_read routes reads away from the leader - follower, leader-and-follower, prefer-leader (avoids a slow leader), closest-replicas/closest-adaptive (zone-local reads gated by tidb_adaptive_closest_read_threshold), or learner; all modes keep strong consistency via ReadIndex at the cost of one extra network hop. Differential: distinguish a busy leader (cpu on one store) from a slow leader (prefer-leader case). Remedies: switch the variable at session or global scope and configure PD location-labels plus zone labels for closest modes. Risks: on v7.5 or earlier, explicit follower/learner modes error when no such replica exists, and wrong zone labels silently collapse closest modes to leader reads.

nodes.name: Full Scan Remediation by Indexing
nodes.content: Mechanism: predicates on non-indexed columns force a full scan whose cost grows with table size. Diagnosis: EXPLAIN shows TableFullScan with estRows near the table row count and the filter applied as a post-scan Selection; SHOW CREATE TABLE confirms the missing index. Fix family: add a secondary index on the filter columns (composite indexes follow the left-prefix rule, equality columns first; a covering index turns IndexLookUp into IndexReader and skips the table lookup), then re-run EXPLAIN to confirm IndexRangeScan. Risks: each index slows writes and consumes space, and low-distinctness columns rarely pay off; if an index is impossible, coprocessor cache or engine routing only mitigates.

nodes.name: Remedy GC Backlog and MVCC Version Accumulation
nodes.content: Mechanism: the GC safe point equals now minus tidb_gc_life_time (default 10m); long-running transactions block safe-point forwarding up to tidb_gc_max_wait_time (default 86400s), and a large life time (days to months) bloats storage and degrades range scans such as count(*). With GC in Compaction Filter, progress may lag and coprocessor scans degrade when next/prev calls far exceed processed_keys. Differential: distinguish GC lag (space not reclaimed) from real data growth. Remedies: verify tidb_gc_enable and life time, tune gc.auto-compaction redundant-row thresholds or region-compact thresholds, cap GC write impact with gc.max-write-bytes-per-sec. Risks: shortening life time breaks stale reads via tidb_snapshot; disabling GC degrades overall performance.

nodes.name: GC lifetime vs long-read runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: GC periodically removes MVCC versions older than tidb_gc_life_time (default 10m); any reader pinned to an older timestamp (tidb_snapshot session, stale read, export, flashback) fails once GC passes the safe point visible in mysql.tidb (tikv_gc_safe_point). Differential diagnosis: compare the requested timestamp/TSO against the current GC safe point, remember that long exports over 1 TB or tools without PD access cannot auto-adjust the safe point, and confirm the timestamps used come from PD time when node clocks skew. Remedy families: (1) temporarily raise GC life time (SET GLOBAL tidb_gc_life_time) before the operation and restore it afterwards; (2) let tools that can adjust the GC safe point automatically do so; (3) use stale read/tidb_snapshot with a timestamp inside the retention window. Risks: a longer life time accumulates MVCC versions, growing disk usage and slowing range scans, so always restore the original value; GC runs on a single elected TiDB node, so verify the setting took effect cluster-wide.

nodes.name: Global Kill Semantics
nodes.content: With enable-global-kill enabled (default), KILL and KILL TIDB from any instance are forwarded to the instance owning the connection, even through proxies, and Control+C can terminate a running query. Mechanism: 32-bit connection IDs make cross-instance kill unambiguous; when the cluster exceeds 2048 TiDB instances or one instance exceeds 1048576 connections the ID space auto-upgrades to 64-bit, after which Control+C no longer kills newly created connections. An apparently un-killable session should first be checked for ID-space upgrade or proxy stripping of KILL forwarding. With enable-global-kill enabled (default), KILL and KILL TIDB from any instance are forwarded to the instance owning the connection, even through proxies, and Control+C can terminate a running query; enumerate victims via INFORMATION_SCHEMA.CLUSTER_PROCESSLIST (SHOW PROCESSLIST shows only the connected instance and needs PROCESS privilege for other users' sessions) and since v6.2 KILL TIDB QUERY also terminates ongoing DDL jobs. Caveats: 32-bit connection IDs auto-upgrade to 64-bit beyond 2048 instances or 1M connections per instance, after which Control+C cannot kill new connections; without Global Kill, KILL only works with the explicit TIDB suffix and compatible-kill-query risks killing the wrong session behind a proxy.

nodes.name: Global Sort Capacity and Isolation
nodes.content: Mechanism: Global Sort is a DXF operator that externally sorts data (on supported cloud object storage) to stabilize IMPORT INTO and CREATE INDEX writes to TiKV; it is not used for query-result sorting. Diagnosis: when backend tasks OOM or degrade foreground traffic, check task status via DDL job inspection and TiDB memory trends. Remedies: dedicate TiDB nodes with ample CPU/memory by setting tidb_service_scope on them and submit DXF tasks there to isolate the workload; size Global Sort nodes generously (the documentation recommends at least 16 cores and 32 GiB) to avoid OOM; risk is added node cost and that Global Sort supports only specific cloud storage backends.

nodes.name: Goroutine Count Pressure
nodes.content: A TiDB or PD goroutine count above roughly 2000 signals excessive in-process concurrency that inflates request latency. Correlate rising goroutines with connection counts and incoming concurrency, then shed load or throttle client concurrency; confirm via the cluster diagnostic report or Grafana goroutine panels.

nodes.name: Graceful Shutdown Window Tuning
nodes.content: graceful-wait-before-shutdown gives clients time to disconnect and flips the TiDB HTTP status to failing so load balancers reroute traffic; the effective window is capped by systemd TimeoutStopSec (default 90s), TiUP --wait-timeout (default 120s) or Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30s). Restarts that drop client connections indicate the platform stop timeout is shorter than the configured grace period; align the platform timeout instead of raising only the TiDB setting.

nodes.name: Grafana Metric Reading Discipline
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB Grafana panels default to log2 Y-axes that visually compress latency spikes, PD dashboards show only the current leader's metrics, and legends default to Max/Current only. Diagnosis: when a latency regression is hard to see or a former PD leader's history is needed, switch the panel to linear scale and an auto baseline, add instance or sql_type dimensions by editing the query and legend format, enable shared crosshair/tooltip to correlate panels, and type the old leader's address:2379 manually to recover its history. Remedies: add Avg to legends for trend judgment on noisy metrics; risk of linear scale is noise on long trend windows, so switch per investigation.

nodes.name: HAProxy Load Balancing Failure Modes
nodes.content: Mechanism: HAProxy fronts TiDB with L4 load balancing (leastconn suits long SQL sessions); a backend is pulled after repeated failed health checks (fall count) and restored after rises, and global maxconn caps the proxy's concurrent connections. On the TiDB side, proxy-protocol.networks lists the sources allowed to speak PROXY protocol - once set, plain connections from those sources are denied, an empty value denies PROXY entirely, and '*' is risky and can break components that connect directly (e.g. TiDB Dashboard); proxy-protocol.fallbackable lets clients in the list connect without the header. Diagnosis: when clients see refusals, hangs, or uneven TiDB load, check the HAProxy stats page/socket for backend up/down flaps and connection saturation against maxconn; session idle timeouts (timeout client/server) also drop long-idle sessions; sudden connection denials indicate a PROXY-protocol configuration mismatch between proxy and TiDB. Remedy family: raise maxconn/nbthread, tune check intervals and rise/fall counts, lengthen idle timeouts, align send-proxy with proxy-protocol.networks (and fallbackable when mixed clients exist), and never use '*' casually.

nodes.name: Hash Partition Reorganization Cost
nodes.content: ADD PARTITION or COALESCE PARTITION on a Hash/Key partitioned table reorganizes by copying all data, so plan it like a bulk DDL and expect the warning that partition statistics are outdated (warning 1105) - run ANALYZE TABLE immediately after to avoid plan regressions. DROP PARTITION is unsupported for Hash/Key partitioning (use TRUNCATE PARTITION to clear data), and SHOW CREATE TABLE verifies the resulting layout. ADD PARTITION or COALESCE PARTITION on a Hash/Key partitioned table reorganizes by copying all data, so plan it like a bulk DDL and run ANALYZE TABLE after (warning 1105 flags outdated partition statistics); DROP PARTITION is unsupported for Hash/Key (use TRUNCATE PARTITION). RANGE INTERVAL partitioning (v6.3+) is syntax sugar that auto-expands to explicit RANGE partitions - boundaries shift with ALTER ... FIRST/LAST PARTITION LESS THAN while SHOW CREATE TABLE shows the expanded form.

nodes.name: Low CPU Utilization Under High Concurrency
nodes.content: Mechanism: client concurrency is high but TiDB/TiKV CPUs stay idle because the path is throttled elsewhere. Differential: compare single-TiDB pressure against proxied pressure to expose a proxy bottleneck (HAproxy nbproc/nbthread/cpu-map); TiKV total CPU low but a module hot means readpool/coprocessor/gRPC pool limits (check TiKV Thread CPU panel, raise module concurrency); NUMA hosts lose performance to cross-node memory access (deploy one TiDB per NUMA node with max-procs matching its cores).

nodes.name: Optimizer Hint Ineffective
nodes.content: Mechanism: hints can be stripped by old clients, lost when the database name is missing or ambiguous, ignored at wrong positions, or legally inapplicable (Projection/Selection on the IndexJoin probe side blocks INL_JOIN; hinted tables are not the inner pair under the current join order; NO_* hints or hash-join off exclude every join method, producing ERROR 1815). Discrimination: run EXPLAIN then SHOW WARNINGS - warning 1815 names the inapplicable hint; inspect the chosen operators to see what the optimizer did instead. Fix family: fix syntax, placement, and db qualification; add LEADING to set join order before INL_JOIN; enable the inner-multi-pattern variable for projection-heavy joins; remove conflicting NO_* hints or re-enable hash join.

nodes.name: Host Environment Preconditions
nodes.content: Mechanism: component startup and performance depend on host preconditions - SELinux must be disabled or permissive (check with getenforce; changing /etc/selinux/config to SELINUX=disabled requires a reboot to take effect), multi-instance hosts need NUMA binding via numactl to stop cross-instance CPU contention, and TiUP deployment assumes SSH mutual trust plus passwordless sudo for the deploy user. Diagnosis: on startup failures or unexplained CPU contention, check getenforce output, numactl availability, and per-host instance placement. Repair family: disable SELinux (reboot), install numactl cluster-wide (e.g. tiup cluster exec with --sudo) and bind instances to NUMA nodes.

nodes.name: Hot Region Scheduling Remediation
nodes.content: Mechanism: PD redistributes hot Regions from traffic analysis, but scheduling can lag load shifts, and a single un-splittable hot Region (e.g. one small table scanned intensively) cannot be balanced by movement alone. Diagnosis: compare PD hot-region metrics with TiKV CPU metrics; load skew visible despite normal region counts. Fix family: raise hot-region-schedule-limit, lower hot-region-cache-hits-threshold for sensitivity, manually split the hot Region, add a scatter-range-scheduler for the hot table, and relax merge limits when empty Regions accumulate. Risks: aggressive scheduling adds replica-migration I/O; some keys (split-region-on-table) need pd-ctl changes that are not dynamic.

nodes.name: Hotspot History Inspection
nodes.content: Mechanism: pd-ctl hot read/write/store lists currently hot regions and stores, while hot history <start_ms> <end_ms> plus optional filters (hot_region_type, region_id, store_id, peer_id, is_leader, is_learner) replays recorded hotspot records including hot_degree and flow bytes; pd-ctl health and label store show member health and store labels. Diagnosis: for uneven load, compare hot read versus hot write listings, then use hot history to correlate with past incidents or verify that balancing actually cooled a region. Remedies: confirm the hot region's table or index via its key range and apply splitting, placement, or caching remedies; risk is chasing transient hotspots that scheduling is already relieving.

nodes.name: Hotspot Key Encoding Analysis
nodes.content: Mechanism: row keys encode as tablePrefix_tableID_recordPrefix_rowID and index keys as tablePrefix_tableID_indexID_indexedColumnsValue, so data of a table is one contiguous range; sequential RowIDs (integer auto-increment primary keys or default row ids) and monotonically increasing index columns make every insert append to the same end Region, forming a write hotspot, while small hot ranges or read-only periodic reads can hotspot too. Discrimination: map the hot Region or key prefix to its table/index via the encoding rules and check whether the leading column is monotonic. Fix family: spread sequential keys (shuffled row ids or non-monotonic primary key design), avoid monotonically increasing leading index columns for append-heavy tables, and control Region merge behavior with table attributes for small hot tables.

nodes.name: Hotspot Heatmap Pattern Reading
nodes.content: Mechanism: traffic distribution over key ranges reveals hotspot classes. Differential: evenly mixed brightness is healthy; brightness alternating over time with even key spread means periodic scheduled jobs (verify peak resource headroom); a few thin bright lines mean concentrated hot Regions likely needing manual intervention; one bright sequential line means sequential writes/reads such as auto-increment inserts, imports, or full scans. Fix family: reshape the key or primary key to scatter Regions, exploit Region-based balancing, or move batch tasks off peak.

nodes.name: HTAP Engine Selection
nodes.content: HTAP keeps OLTP on the TiKV row engine and routes analytical queries to TiFlash columnar replicas that replicate via Multi-Raft Learner with strong consistency. Complex aggregation/join queries over large tables with low index selectivity are candidates for TiFlash, and hybrid workloads require isolation so OLAP load does not degrade OLTP latency; distinguish engine choice by reading EXPLAIN for TiFlash/MPP operators.

nodes.name: Hybrid Deployment Resource Isolation
nodes.content: In hybrid deployments with multiple TiDB/TiKV instances per host, instances share CPU, memory, and disks, so latency degradation can come from cross-instance contention rather than a single saturated resource; a host-level label (server.labels host plus PD replication.location-labels) is required or PD may place two of three Raft replicas on one machine. Differentiate by checking store labels and per-instance CPU/memory, then remediate with NUMA binding, unified readpool sizing (about cores*0.8 per TiKV instance), block-cache capacity per instance, raftstore.capacity per instance, and separate file systems for PD data. In hybrid deployments with multiple TiDB/TiKV instances per host, instances share CPU, memory, and disks, so latency degradation can come from cross-instance contention rather than a single saturated resource; a host-level label (server.labels host plus PD replication.location-labels) is required or PD may place two of three Raft replicas on one machine. Differentiate by checking store labels and per-instance CPU/memory, then remediate with NUMA binding, unified readpool sizing (about cores*0.8 per TiKV instance), block-cache capacity per instance, raftstore.capacity per instance, separate file systems for PD data, and hard limits on background work: rocksdb.max-background-jobs and max-sub-compactions lowered until write stall appears, rate-bytes-per-sec reserving foreground disk bandwidth, gc.max_write_bytes_per_sec (settable live via tikv-ctl modify-tikv-config) capping MVCC cleanup jitter, and performance.max-procs bounding Go runtime threads.

nodes.name: Hybrid Deployment Thread Pool Tuning
nodes.content: On hybrid (TiDB+TiKV+PD per node) machines, default TiKV thread pools sized for dedicated hosts cause QPS jitter from CPU contention; prefer stability by right-sizing readpool.unified.max-thread-count (about 80% of TiKV's expected cores), server.grpc-concurrency and storage.scheduler-worker-pool-size to observed 50-80% pool usage, and cap background work (gc.max-write-bytes-per-sec, rocksdb.max-background-jobs, rate limiter). Separate disks for PD and TiKV, then validate by monitoring gRPC/scheduler pool CPU panels under a representative load test.

nodes.name: Idle Transaction Timeout Behavior
nodes.content: Since v7.6.0 tidb_idle_transaction_timeout (default 0 = unlimited) terminates sessions that remain in a transactional state with no active requests beyond the configured duration; an unexpected value explains spurious connection drops that look like network failures. Diagnosis: compare the variable value and the application's transaction hold times; check last query info of affected sessions. Remedies: raise or reset the variable, or fix the application to not hold transactions idle.

nodes.name: Import conflict runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: physical import detects conflicts before or after encode via conflict.strategy (replace/error/empty), logical import adds ignore and maps empty to error; conflicts under replace/ignore are tolerated up to conflict.threshold and recorded in the downstream conflict_records table. Differential: compare table row count against unique-index count for silent divergence, inspect conflict_records for ignored rows, and note that a checksum failure with empty strategy proves undetected duplicates. Remedies: (a) pick a strategy deliberately - error for strict correctness, replace/ignore with threshold for dirty sources; (b) enable precheck-conflict-before-import when conflicts are at least ~1% of rows and local disk allows the extra encode pass; (c) for silent divergence, clean the target table and re-import with detection on. Risks: physical-mode conflict results can differ from SQL-based import; new-version detection is single-node only and incompatible with parallel import and disk-quota, so sharded imports must resolve cross-source key overlap before starting.

nodes.name: Prevent Import Disk Exhaustion
nodes.content: Mechanism: local-backend import materializes encoded key-value files on local disk; disk-quota defaults to unlimited (MaxInt64) and is enforced only at check-disk-quota intervals (60s default, each check briefly blocks import threads), so a large interval can overshoot the quota. Differential: distinguish Lightning host disk exhaustion from TiKV target disk growth. Remedies: set a real disk-quota with a small check interval, place sorted-kv-dir and checkpoint files on roomy high-endurance media, or switch to the logical (tidb) backend that streams SQL instead of local files; checkpoints (file or mysql driver) let the import resume instead of restarting. Risk: keeping checkpoints after success leaks source metadata, and mysql-driver checkpoints add load to the target cluster unless a separate database holds them.

nodes.name: Resolve Import Errors and Conflicts
nodes.content: 'Access denied to the source bucket' during import/backup means the storage credential lacks required object-store permissions — for S3 the reader needs s3:GetObject on objects plus s3:ListBucket and s3:GetBucketLocation on the bucket, with Resource ARNs matching the exact bucket/prefix. Check the IAM user policy or assumed role's trust and permission JSONs, fix Resource scoping, and re-run; a completed import showing zero rows means no files matched the URI naming, so fix names and re-import. 'Access denied to the source bucket' during import/backup means the storage credential lacks required object-store permissions — for S3 the reader needs s3:GetObject on objects plus s3:ListBucket and s3:GetBucketLocation on the bucket, with Resource ARNs matching the exact bucket/prefix. For local-disk or NFS backup targets, BR running even as root can hit 'Permission denied'/'No such file or directory' because TiKV (not br) writes the SST files: match the br and TiKV user UIDs (across machines for NFS) and verify permissions before restore, since the check may only fire when SST files are first read.

nodes.name: IMPORT INTO Tuning Options
nodes.content: IMPORT INTO runs at THREAD=50% of TiDB CPU by default (FROM SELECT defaults to 2) and sorts into the TiDB temp-dir up to DISK_QUOTA (80% of that disk), so slow or disk-full imports should be judged against these knobs plus MAX_WRITE_SPEED and SPLIT_FILE for large CSVs. For online clusters, DISABLE_TIKV_IMPORT_MODE and MAX_WRITE_SPEED bound interference with production traffic; CHECKSUM_TABLE=required (default) fails the import on checksum mismatch, DETACHED runs the job asynchronously, and CLOUD_STORAGE_URI/tidb_cloud_storage_uri route Global Sort KV data to S3 requiring full bucket permissions on all TiDB nodes.

nodes.name: IMPORT INTO vs TiDB Lightning selection
nodes.content: For imports whose capacity or disk footprint is the problem, switching the repair family is an option: IMPORT INTO runs as SQL on TiDB nodes, auto-splits into distributed sub-tasks, and with TiDB Global Sort avoids large local sort disks by using external storage that is cleaned after the import, with tidb_service_scope able to pin the task to dedicated TiDB nodes. TiDB Lightning instead needs separate servers, per-instance config files with manual file-range splitting, and local disks sized for sorting. Global Sort additionally requires the distributed task framework (tidb_enable_dist_task, ON by default since v8.1) and a valid tidb_cloud_storage_uri, or the IMPORT INTO CLOUD_STORAGE_URI option which takes precedence for that statement. Global sort yields non-overlapping KV ranges that TiKV writes directly without compaction, while parallel local-sorted imports overlap ranges (index-heavy worst) and trigger expensive compaction; IMPORT INTO also fails over tasks to surviving TiDB nodes automatically, whereas Lightning recovery is checkpoint-based and manual. IMPORT INTO sorts globally on external storage so TiKV receives non-overlapping KVs with no compaction storm, tolerates node failure by auto-transferring tasks, and needs no persistent local disks; TiDB Lightning's local sort overlaps data across instances, triggers resource-heavy TiKV compaction that degrades write stability, and requires manual checkpoint-based recovery after node loss. Choose IMPORT INTO for TiB-scale imports with external storage, Lightning for local-sort scenarios without such storage. IMPORT INTO sorts globally on external storage so TiKV receives non-overlapping KVs with no compaction storm, tolerates node failure by auto-transferring tasks, supports up to 16 concurrent tasks (v8.0), and needs no persistent local disks; TiDB Lightning's local sort overlaps data across instances, triggers resource-heavy TiKV compaction that degrades write stability, and requires manual checkpoint-based recovery after node loss. Choose IMPORT INTO for TiB-scale imports with external storage, Lightning for local-sort scenarios without such storage.

nodes.name: Import/Full-Migration Online Interference
nodes.content: Mechanism: import writes SST files directly and pauses PD scheduling on affected Regions; Checksum/Analyze afterwards adds scan load. Differential: correlate latency regression with a running tidb-lightning task and check pause-pd-scheduler-scope (table by default; global on pre-6.2 clusters or when set). Remedies: (a) keep default table-scope scheduling pause and reserve global scope for idle windows; (b) cap import write bandwidth with store-write-bwlimit; (c) lower tidb.distsql-scan-concurrency to shrink Checksum/Analyze impact; (d) schedule imports for low-traffic windows or move the job to a dedicated cluster since low-concurrency clients suffer the most. Risks: even with table scope, fast imports still degrade online latency; old clusters pause scheduling globally.

nodes.name: Physical import vs changefeed conflict
nodes.content: Physical-import jobs fail or are blocked on clusters with an active changefeed or Point-in-time Restore because physical import writes into TiKV without generating change logs, leaving those features blind to the new data. CSV imports also require empty target tables (stage into a temp table then INSERT SELECT), and throughput depends on file layout: split files around 256MB (100MiB compressed) with ascending zero-padded numeric suffixes and optional schema files in the storage path.

nodes.name: Import precheck runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: prechecks sample sources and cluster state so failures happen before data moves; the empty-Region threshold max(1000, 3x tables) and the disk estimate that includes index size are the two most surprising tripwires. Differential: read the specific failed check item, verify free space against source size plus index estimate plus local sorted-kv-dir, and check whether PITR or a changefeed is actually running. Remedies: (a) free or provision disk and compact empty Regions; (b) fix source schema or re-enable auto-slicing for large CSVs; (c) only when the imported tables provably need no log backup and no changefeed, set Lightning.check-requirements=false (or DISABLE_PRECHECK for IMPORT INTO) and rerun. Risks: bypassing the requirements check commits you to running a table-level snapshot backup after import, because physical-import data is invisible to log backup.

nodes.name: Import-CDC/PITR incompatibility runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: physical import bypasses the transactional write path, so log-backup streams miss the data and TiCDC throughput falls behind bulk ingest. Differential: check for active PITR tasks and changefeeds before import, and afterwards watch changefeed checkpoint lag. Remedies: (a) if imported tables need neither, pass the precheck bypass (Lightning.check-requirements=false or IMPORT INTO ... WITH DISABLE_PRECHECK) and take a table-level snapshot backup after import; (b) if tables need TiCDC replication, import the same data into the downstream separately instead of letting the changefeed chase the import; (c) keep log-backup tables out of physical-import scope. Risks: downstream re-import must preserve key overlap rules, and undiscovered changefeeds turn the bypass into silent divergence.

nodes.name: Import state cleanup runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: checkpoints record finished ranges so restarts resume, but any source or schema change between runs invalidates them; parallel imports additionally require per-instance unique sorted-kv-dir, checkpoint, log, and status-addr. Differential: determine whether the failed task used file or mysql checkpoints, whether sources changed since, and whether multiple instances shared paths or mixed backends. Remedies: (a) resume via checkpoint when inputs are unchanged; (b) otherwise fully destroy intermediate state - checkpoint-remove=all (or delete the checkpoint file), clear sorted-kv-dir, drop target tables, and DROP DATABASE lightning_metadata when checkpoints were hand-deleted; (c) enforce one backend type and per-instance unique paths for parallel runs. Risks: mixing physical and logical imports into the same cluster concurrently is unsupported; stale metadata silently breaks correctness of subsequent imports.

nodes.name: Incremental Restore Ordering Discipline
nodes.content: Mechanism: incremental backup restores updates in place, so applying it out of order or against a live writer conflicts with restored data. Differential diagnosis: confirm every backup earlier than LAST_BACKUP_TS is fully restored into the target cluster first, and separate restore-induced conflicts from application-side writes that continued during the restore window. Repair family: re-run the full restore before the incremental one, freeze application writes for the restore window, and retry the incremental segment; do not skip ordering to save time. For PITR the same discipline applies: the first initialization of a recovery cluster must include the snapshot (table-ID rewriting depends on it), replaying one log range twice produces inconsistent data, and multi-batch log restores must cover consecutive ranges with no gaps.

nodes.name: Incremental Migration Start Position
nodes.content: Mechanism: incremental-only migration starts from job-start time, a GTID set, or an explicit binlog file/position obtained with SHOW MASTER STATUS, and the start position is fixed once the job runs; a wrong position against a target that already holds data causes duplicate/conflicting rows and job failure. Diagnosis: on an incremental migration failing with conflicts, compare the configured position or GTID with the actual state of the target tables. Remedies: rebase the target data or restart the job from the correct position, accepting source-wins replacement where intended; risk is double-applied increments if the position is rewound without cleaning the target.

nodes.name: Index consistency repair runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: when replicas are lost, either row data or index entries may survive, so a table can hold index keys with no matching row (dangling) or rows with missing index entries. Differential diagnosis: run ADMIN CHECK TABLE/INDEX to identify the affected index and whether handles or values are missing, and correlate with recent disaster/recovery events. Remedy families: (1) ADMIN CLEANUP INDEX removes dangling index entries; (2) ADMIN RECOVER INDEX rebuilds missing index entries from row data; (3) for large tables, drop and rebuild the index instead of the single-threaded ADMIN path. Risks: ADMIN CLEANUP INDEX is not atomic (rerun until success if interrupted), runs single-threaded, and does not lock the table, so concurrent writes during cleanup can produce wrong results - quiesce writes first.

nodes.name: Index Merge AND Conditions
nodes.content: Mechanism: index merge natively auto-selects only for OR-combined filters; AND-combined index merge requires the USE_INDEX_MERGE hint, extending intersection access to arbitrary filter combinations. Diagnosis: for a query with several selective AND predicates each covered by a different index, check EXPLAIN for a single-index or full-scan plan. Remedies: add USE_INDEX_MERGE to force intersection of the candidate indexes, or build a composite index if the predicate pattern is stable; risk is that hinted index merges can misfire when selectivity estimates are wrong.

nodes.name: IndexMerge and Multi-Valued Index Access
nodes.content: IndexMerge combines per-index range scans with union (OR conditions) or intersection (AND conditions); each condition must itself be index-accessible, multi-valued indexes are reachable via MEMBER OF/JSON_CONTAINS/JSON_OVERLAPS predicates, and use_index_merge(t, idx1, idx2, ...) forces the plan. When OR/AND over json_member_of is not using the MVI, check each branch's index-eligibility and pseudo-stats before adding redundant indexes. IndexMerge combines per-index range scans with union (OR conditions) or intersection (AND conditions); each condition must itself be index-accessible, multi-valued indexes are reachable via MEMBER OF/JSON_CONTAINS/JSON_OVERLAPS predicates, and use_index_merge(t, idx1, idx2, ...) forces the plan. Semantic edges: multi-value json_contains joined by OR and json_overlaps joined by AND do NOT qualify (only single-value forms do). When OR/AND over json predicates is not using the MVI, check each branch's eligibility and pseudo-stats before adding redundant indexes.

nodes.name: Index Selection Mechanism and Control
nodes.content: The optimizer weighs index range scans plus table lookups: an IndexLookUp whose TableRowIDScan fetches millions of rows (visible as hundreds of extra cop tasks in EXPLAIN ANALYZE) is the signature that a covering index — one containing every WHERE and SELECT column — would eliminate the second lookup entirely; compare estRows vs actRows to spot misestimates driving the choice. The optimizer weighs index range scans plus table lookups; an IndexLookUp whose TableRowIDScan fetches millions of rows (hundreds of extra cop tasks in EXPLAIN ANALYZE) signals that a covering index would eliminate the second lookup, and SHOW INDEXES Visible=NO exposes invisible indexes that are silently skipped — a classic 'index exists but is not used' root cause. Compare estRows vs actRows to catch misestimates driving bad choices.

nodes.name: First-Boot initialize-sql-file Risk
nodes.content: initialize-sql-file runs once at first cluster bootstrap with unchecked highest privilege; if any statement in the script fails the TiDB cluster may fail to start. A bootstrap failure right after introducing the script should be diagnosed by validating the script SQL on a standalone instance first; keep privilege setup or user creation statements there minimal.

nodes.name: Internal Port Exposure Hygiene
nodes.content: TiDB components listen on privileged HTTP/status ports (TiDB 10080, TiKV 20180, PD 2379/2380, TiFlash 20292, TiCDC 8300, etc.) meant for internal communication only; exposing them publicly raises the attack surface. When internal RPC or monitoring suddenly fails, check whether firewall/network-policy changes blocked component ranges; the standard posture exposes only the SQL port 4000 and Grafana 9000 externally, with Dashboard served through a reverse proxy. TiDB components listen on privileged HTTP/status ports (TiDB 10080, TiKV 20180, PD 2379/2380, TiFlash 20292, TiCDC 8300, etc.) meant for internal communication only; exposing them publicly raises the attack surface, and the Dashboard shares TiDB SQL accounts so a passwordless root grants privileged SQL access through it. When internal RPC or monitoring suddenly fails, check whether firewall/network-policy changes blocked component ranges; the standard posture exposes only the SQL port 4000 and Grafana 9000 externally, protects Dashboard with a strong root password or a least-privileged SQL user behind SSO, and serves Dashboard through a reverse proxy.

nodes.name: JDBC Prepare and Batch Semantics
nodes.content: MySQL Connector/J preprocesses statements client-side by default, so without useServerPrepStmts=true the server never sees prepared statements and the plan cache stays cold; likewise addBatch/executeBatch still sends statements one-by-one unless rewriteBatchedStatements=true. When insert-heavy OLTP shows high compile overhead or network-bound low throughput despite batching, check these two connection parameters before tuning TiDB internals. MySQL Connector/J preprocesses statements client-side by default, so without useServerPrepStmts=true the server never sees prepared statements and the plan cache stays cold; likewise addBatch/executeBatch still sends statements one-by-one unless rewriteBatchedStatements=true, and plain multi-row INSERT VALUES lists beat repeated single-row statements. The maxPerformance config bundle (cachePrepStmts, useLocalSessionState, elideSetAutoCommits, etc.) trims per-statement round trips, so when insert-heavy OLTP shows high compile overhead or network-bound throughput, check these connection parameters before tuning TiDB internals. For huge result sets, streaming (FetchSize=Integer.MIN_VALUE) or cursor fetch (useCursorFetch=true) avoids client OOM, but a connection with an open streaming result rejects new statements ('No statements may be issued when any streaming result sets are open...') unless clobberStreamingResults=true silently closes it. The maxPerformance config bundle (cachePrepStmts, useLocalSessionState, elideSetAutoCommits, etc.) trims per-statement round trips, so check these connection parameters before tuning TiDB internals.

nodes.name: Fix Client Connection Lifecycle and JDBC Parameters
nodes.content: Mechanism: since v5.4 TiDB closes idle connections after wait_timeout (8h) and intermediate proxies cut idle connections sooner, producing "Communications link failure ... N milliseconds ago" errors (a very small N instead indicates a TiDB crash - check stderr); connection building is expensive so pools reuse connections, and uneven pool affinities skew load across TiDB nodes. Differential: large N points to idle timeouts, small N to server faults. Remedies: size pools around 4-10x app CPU cores, set maxLifetime below wait_timeout and graceful-wait-before-shutdown, keepalive below proxy idle timeout, enable test-before-use; for JDBC throughput set rewriteBatchedStatements=true (plus allowMultiQueries with useServerPrepStmts due to a driver bug), cachePrepStmts=true, useConfigs=maxPerformance to strip redundant session queries. Risk: rewritten multi-row statements grow toward packet and transaction size limits.

nodes.name: Prepared Statement Re-prepare Storm
nodes.content: Mechanism: Connector/J defaults to client-side prepare (useServerPrepStmts=false); even with useServerPrepStmts=true, statements re-prepare on every execution when cachePrepStmts=false, when SQL length exceeds prepStmtCacheSqlLimit (default 256), or when distinct statements exceed prepStmtCacheSize (default 25), wasting server prepare round-trips. Diagnosis: compare COM_STMT_PREPARE with COM_STMT_EXECUTE counts (CPS By Instance view) - prepare counts near execute counts, or many COM_STMT_CLOSE, indicate the client cache is not effective. Remedy family: enable cachePrepStmts and size prepStmtCacheSqlLimit/prepStmtCacheStmts to the real SQL length and variety; prerequisite is confirming via command-type metrics before changing URLs.

nodes.name: JDBC Streaming Result Set Behavior
nodes.content: Mechanism: JDBC by default buffers the whole result set in client memory; FetchSize=Integer.MIN_VALUE switches to streaming reads that keep the connection occupied until the ResultSet is finished or closed, and useCursorFetch=true with a positive FetchSize is the cursor alternative. Diagnosis: for clients OOM-ing on large results or connections/transactions held open for a long time, check whether huge result sets are fetched unstreamed; issuing another statement before closing an open streaming ResultSet errors out unless clobberStreamingResults=true (which discards the remaining stream). Remedy family: stream or cursor-fetch large results, keep streaming result sets short-lived, and ensure the streaming connection is not inside an idle transaction holding locks.

nodes.name: Join and Aggregation Control
nodes.content: Mechanism: join method (HashJoin/MergeJoin/IndexJoin), aggregation algorithm (hash vs stream), and MPP one/two-phase aggregation are cost-based choices; hash join spills its build side to disk when the query memory quota is exceeded, and runtime filters can cut hash join input early. Diagnosis: EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE - check chosen operators, memory and disk columns for spill, and join input cardinalities. Fix family: algorithm hints per query (HASH_AGG for speed, STREAM_AGG when memory is tight, MPP_*_AGG only in TiFlash MPP mode), tune query memory quota and join concurrency, enable runtime filters. Risks: hints ignore cost changes as data grows; raising memory quotas shifts pressure to the instance level.

nodes.name: Join Reorder Algorithms
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB's greedy join reorder sorts participating tables by row count and iteratively joins the pair with the smaller intermediate result set, so a bad row-count estimate directly produces a bad join order. Diagnosis: read the join order and estimated row counts in EXPLAIN and compare with actuals; fix via corrected statistics or join-order hints rather than assuming the algorithm is broken. Remedy family: refresh statistics, use leading_JOIN_ORDER/straight-join style hints, or restructure the query; prerequisite is confirming the plan is actually suboptimal.

nodes.name: tidb_auth_token Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: tidb_auth_token validates an RS256-signed JWT against a JWKS file that TiDB refreshes periodically, requiring sub equal to the username, iat not in the future or older than 15 minutes, exp not passed, iss matching REQUIRE TOKEN_ISSUER, and email matching the user ATTRIBUTE; the token travels via mysql_clear_password, so client-server TLS is mandatory. Diagnosis: decode the failing token, compare each claim with the CREATE USER definition, and confirm the JWKS path/refresh and TLS are working. Remedies: reissue a token with correct claims, update the user's TOKEN_ISSUER/email attributes to match the issuer, refresh JWKS, or enable TLS plus a cleartext-plugin-capable client; risk is that base64 header/payload are readable, so tokens must not carry secrets.

nodes.name: Kafka Private Link Advertised Listeners
nodes.content: Mechanism: when a changefeed reaches self-hosted Kafka through a private connection (Private Service Connect / port mapping), every broker needs an EXTERNAL listener plus an EXTERNAL advertised listener matching the pattern issued for the connection, so the load balancer can route each advertised port to the right broker; a mismatched or missing advertised listener makes clients bootstrap to the wrong broker and the changefeed cannot connect. Diagnosis: from the TiDB side reproduce bootstrap with kafka-broker-api-versions.sh and compare returned advertised endpoints against the required pattern; note that DisconnectException on advertised names is expected when testing from inside the Kafka network. Repair family: fix listeners/advertised.listeners/listener.security.protocol.map on each broker and restart brokers one by one.

nodes.name: Key-Range Batch Data Operations
nodes.content: Deep-OFFSET pagination re-sorts preceding rows on every page and degrades into a resource-heavy bulk job; instead compute page boundaries once with row_number() over the primary key (min/max id per 1000-row page) and run each DELETE/UPDATE as a key-range transaction (WHERE id BETWEEN start_key AND end_key). This keeps each statement bounded and index-ordered; the same slicing pattern suits backfills and purge jobs on single-field PK tables.

nodes.name: Key Visualizer Heatmap Reading
nodes.content: Mechanism: Key Visualizer renders per-region read/write bytes and keys over time as a heatmap; zooming changes region-compression granularity and the local hot basis, and brightness normalization means evenly loaded low-traffic areas can still glow bright. Diagnosis: to prove a hotspot, read bucket details for the bright key range, switch metrics between bytes and keys to separate big rows from many rows, and remember zoom changes redraw the picture rather than the workload. Remedies: combine heatmap evidence with pd-ctl hot data before splitting or moving tables, and enable collection in settings before the incident since history starts at enablement; risk is acting on brightness artifacts instead of absolute traffic.

nodes.name: Respond to TiKV Background Storage Errors
nodes.content: Mechanism: on recoverable RocksDB background errors, TiKV reports damaged SST peers to PD, which schedules the peers away and deletes the files; writes continue but reads of damaged ranges fail until recovery completes inside background-error-recovery-window (default 1h), after which TiKV panics. Remedies: rely on replica re-scheduling to restore redundancy and monitor Region health; restore from backup when many peers are damaged. Risk: replica count is temporarily reduced, so avoid further node loss during recovery. Under the partitioned-raft-kv storage engine, tikv-ctl recovery subcommands such as unsafe-recover and remove-fail-stores are unsupported (as is Titan), so recovery depends even more on replica re-scheduling.

nodes.name: TiKV Conflict Log Markers
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV logs distinguish conflict families - 'key is locked' means read-meets-uncommitted-write (sparse entries are benign; floods mean severe read-write conflict), 'write conflict' is optimistic write-write auto-retry (severe cases should move to pessimistic mode), 'TxnLockNotFound'/'PessimisticLockNotFound' mean a slow commit passed its TTL (about 3 seconds by default for transactions up to 0.25MB) and was rolled back, 'stale_epoch' follows Region split/merge or replica moves, and 'peer is not leader' is routing refresh or a leaderless Region. Discrimination: frequency and concentration per key or Region separate routine retries from real hotspots; pair with TiDB-side 'switch region peer' logs for send failures. Fix family: reduce hot-key contention or switch to pessimistic transactions for write-write conflicts, shorten slow transactions to stay within TTL, and investigate leaderless Regions separately.

nodes.name: Remedy TiKV Disk Space Pressure
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV reserves protection space (default 5 GiB, or the larger of it and 5% of disk capacity) and restricts writes when free space drops below it; space_placeholder_file is the last reclaim guard after exhaustion. Differential: separate data growth (Region count, GC backlog) from logs/WAL co-located on the volume. Remedies: expand the volume, remove obsolete logs, let GC and compaction reclaim space, or move WAL via wal-dir to a separate disk - never set reserve-space to 0, which disables protection. When several TiKV instances share one disk, set raftstore.capacity per instance so no store can consume the whole volume. Bound component log growth with log rotation settings (log.file max-size, max-backups, max-days) so logs do not consume the data volume.

nodes.name: KV RPC Index Strategy
nodes.content: Mechanism: because TiDB nodes cache no data, query cost is dominated by KV RPC count (Point_Get, Batch_Point_Get, coprocessor); composite indexes should order columns as equality/IS NULL/single-value IN first, sort columns next (enabling sort and limit pushdown), multi-value IN and range predicates after, and SELECT-list columns last for covering access, since multi-value IN before sort columns breaks ordered retrieval. Diagnosis: for slow queries count coprocessor requests per execution via EXPLAIN ANALYZE and audit index usage with information-schema index-usage tables. Remedies: redesign index column order per the guidelines, drop indexes unused per usage stats weighing write/read ratio, and avoid monotonically increasing index keys that create write hotspots; every extra index also slows writes and blocks single-phase commit optimization.

nodes.name: TiKV Write Stall and Busy Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV returns Server is Busy when scheduler, raftstore, or RocksDB write stalls back-pressure an excessive workload. Discrimination and fix family are elaborated by matching busy durations, write latency, and stall reasons on the affected store.

nodes.name: Remedy TiKV Write Throttle and Flow Control
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV flow control throttles at the scheduler layer when kvDB memtables exceed 5, L0 files exceed 20, or pending compaction bytes pass the 192 GiB soft / 1024 GiB hard limits, surfacing as ServerIsBusy; RocksDB-level write stall is disabled when flow control is on. Differential: separate compaction backlog (high pending compaction bytes, saturated disk_io) from quota-limiter delays and CPU starvation. Remedies: reduce write volume or batch size, increase compaction capacity (max-background-jobs, flush threads, compaction rate limiter), set storage.io-rate-limit max-bytes-per-sec to the disk optimal bandwidth, or relax flow-control thresholds - risk: raising thresholds increases read amplification and stall recovery time. On the TiDB side, tidb_txn_commit_batch_size (default 16384 bytes) batches commit requests; raising it past the TiKV raft-entry-max-size (8 MiB) makes commits fail outright.

nodes.name: Bulk Delete Batching
nodes.content: Non-transactional DML (BATCH ON <shard-column> LIMIT n DELETE FROM ...) splits one large DML into batched statements executed outside a single transaction; validate first with DRY RUN QUERY (the batch-dividing SELECT) and DRY RUN (first and last split statements) to confirm the affected range, index selectivity, and that later batches do not re-read rows written by earlier ones. Failures report the specific failed range in the error or log, so retrying is bounded; prefer integer or string shard columns and check TiDB's automatic column choice is not itself modified.

nodes.name: Latency Phase Breakdown
nodes.content: Mechanism: reads cost TSO wait plus index/table scan coprocessor time; writes split into execute (read+memory), pessimistic lock, and 2PC commit, with TiKV async write = propose + commit + apply wait + apply log. Diagnosis: per-stage fields in the slow query log and KV request vs TiKV gRPC duration gaps attribute time to network, TiKV processing, or TiDB scheduling. Fix family: reduce round trips and load on the slow phase (batching, plan cache for compile, network/replica placement, thread pools). Risks: each phase has distinct remedies, so fixing the wrong phase wastes effort and can regress.

nodes.name: SQL Layer Latency Decomposition
nodes.content: Mechanism: end-to-end duration decomposes into token wait, parse, compile or plan-cache lookup, TSO wait, and execution; histogram metrics average as sum/count. Read paths further split into point get, batch point get, and table/index scan coprocessor time. Discrimination: token-wait dominance means connection/token limits, compile time means plan cache misses, TSO wait means PD pressure, coprocessor time means storage-side scans. Fix family: address the dominant segment - raise token limits, improve plan reuse, check PD load, or optimize scans and indexes.

nodes.name: Transient versus Persistent Latency
nodes.content: Mechanism: latency faults split into transient spikes (plan flips, PD leader election or PD OOM, frequent TiKV leader drops) and persistent elevation (TiKV single-thread saturation such as one gRPC thread with too many Regions, raftstore or apply CPU above roughly 80%, overall CPU load, slow TiKV writes). Discrimination: classify the latency curve first - spikes that recover point to elections, restarts, or plan changes; sustained elevation points to thread or resource bottlenecks, checked on per-thread CPU panels. Fix family: for transient causes stabilize the failing component and reduce leader churn; for persistent bottlenecks reduce Region counts per store, scale out, or fix the slow write path.

nodes.name: Lightning Backend and Format Compatibility Errors
nodes.content: Mechanism: import startup and schema errors map to compatibility limits - 'rpc error: code = Unimplemented' on switch-mode means a component (e.g. TiFlash < v4.0.0-rc.2) lacks mode-switch support; Local backend requires TiDB >= v4.0.0 ('TiDB version too old') and nightly versions can bypass the check only via check-requirements=false at their own risk; 'unknown columns in header' means the CSV has no header row (set mydumper.csv header=false); 'Unknown character set' on schema creation means TiDB lacks that MySQL charset (pre-create the table with a supported charset); 'invalid compression type' means unsupported archives sit in the source directory (only gzip, official-format snappy, and zstd are accepted). Diagnosis: match the exact error string to the compatibility rule above. Remedy family: upgrade or switch backend, fix CSV header configuration, pre-create schemas, or remove unsupported compressed files from data-source-dir before restarting the import.

nodes.name: Lightning Backend and Progress Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: the local backend (default) writes sorted KV and imports SST directly, requiring the cluster to serve no other traffic and suitable around or above 1 TiB; the tidb backend runs SQL inserts online for smaller datasets. The local backend must have correct status-port and pd-addr (otherwise the import errors), an empty sorted-kv-dir larger than the dataset on dedicated flash storage separate from data-source-dir. Diagnosis: verify the 'the whole procedure completed' marker rather than process exit; progress log lines update every 5 minutes; Grafana dashboard and web interface show live progress. Remedy families: switch backend per data size and availability requirement, fix configuration errors reported at startup, and re-run from checkpoint after failures. Since v7.5.0 the IMPORT INTO statement exposes the same physical-import capability for CSV, SQL, and Parquet into empty tables without a separate Lightning deployment.

nodes.name: Lightning Checkpoint Identity and Resume
nodes.content: Mechanism: Lightning checkpoints are durable task state, reusable only when task identity, source file set/content, target schema, backend, checkpoint driver, and storage namespace all match, and admission evidence (generation, reservation token, renewed lease, fence) is current. Differential diagnosis: compare an immutable source manifest, SHOW CREATE TABLE schema identity, checkpoint storage tables, and Store admission state; a checkpoint merely existing does not prove reusability. Repair family: resume the original task only on full identity match; on mismatch, stop and report, or run a new task on a clean target - never delete or rewrite checkpoint state to force a match, and close the change only after row counts, aggregates, checksums, and table health agree. After an abnormal exit Lightning refuses checkpoints with unresolved errors: tidb-lightning-ctl offers --checkpoint-error-destroy (drop the table and reset the checkpoint, the safe default, including =all), --checkpoint-error-ignore (clear the error only when it is provably harmless; keep the final checksum enabled or data can be lost), --checkpoint-remove, and --checkpoint-dump for debugging; for parallel Lightning farms treat the checksum-wait error by waiting then restarting failed nodes, and re-import inaccurate tables everywhere with checkpoint-error-destroy plus the filter parameter.

nodes.name: Lightning Concurrency Tuning
nodes.content: Mechanism: physical import throughput scales first with Lightning host hardware (CPU and sorted-key-dir disk) and with parallel import across Lightning instances; the concurrency knobs (index-concurrency, table-concurrency, io-concurrency, region-concurrency defaulting to CPU cores) rarely help when changed, with rules like index-concurrency times files per table exceeding region-concurrency to keep CPU busy. Diagnosis: for an import underusing CPU, check engine pipeline counts versus region-concurrency and whether Lightning shares a host with other components. Remedies: upgrade CPU/sorted-key-dir storage, deploy Lightning standalone or lower region-concurrency when colocated, and add Lightning nodes for horizontal scaling; risk of cranking concurrency settings is engine pipeline pile-up rather than speedup.

nodes.name: Lightning conflict detection and resolution
nodes.content: Conflicting rows during physical import are handled by conflict detection strategies: remove records and drops conflicting rows for a consistent target while none is fastest but can leave inconsistent data (checksum is skipped whenever conflict detection is on, so verify separately). Old tikv-importer.duplicate-resolution is deprecated since v8.0 in favor of conflict.strategy (they cannot coexist); conflicted rows are inspected in lightning_task_info.conflict_error_v1 or the v2 conflict tables.

nodes.name: Lightning Conflict Strategy Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: the [conflict] strategy decides what happens on duplicate primary/unique keys - '' detects nothing in physical import (post-step errors) but maps to 'error' in logical import; 'error' terminates on first conflict; 'replace' keeps the latest row and records overwritten data in lightning_task_info.conflict_error_v2 / conflict_records (visible via conflict_view); 'ignore' keeps the old row (logical import only). precheck-conflict-before-import adds pre-import conflict detection (recommended when conflicts exceed ~1,000,000) and threshold (default 10000) caps handled conflicts - larger values degrade import performance. Diagnosis: import failing with duplicate-key errors or a post-import error step, or unexpectedly overwritten rows after 'replace' - inspect the conflict tables and the chosen strategy. Remedy family: pick the strategy deliberately (error for strict correctness, replace/ignore for deduplication with recorded evidence), enable precheck for conflict-heavy sources, and resolve recorded conflicts manually before cutover.

nodes.name: Lightning CSV Strict-Format Corruption Risk
nodes.content: Mechanism: Lightning parallelizes a single large CSV only when strict-format=true splits it into ~256 MiB chunks; this is valid only when the delimiter is empty and no field contains CR/LF, otherwise a multi-line field is split mid-value and corrupted rows can be imported without any error. CSV parsing is further governed by header mapping - with header=true and header-schema-match=true columns map by name, so a mismatched header with a false flag silently reverts to positional mapping and can shift data. Diagnosis: wrong or shifted field values downstream after CSV import, or single-file imports crawling at one thread, point at strict-format/header misconfiguration; also verify status-port and pd-addr are correct (required for the local backend) and sorted-kv-dir has more free space than the dataset. Remedy family: disable strict-format for non-strict CSV, split files offline, keep header names aligned with the target table, and note the local backend blocks target-cluster service during import while the tidb backend does not.

nodes.name: Lightning Error Table Audit
nodes.content: Mechanism: with max-error set, Lightning skips bad rows and finishes successfully while recording type-conversion failures in lightning_task_info.type_error_v1 and primary/unique-key conflicts in lightning_task_info.conflict_error_v1 (raw keys and row data included); conflict.strategy replace or remove decides duplicate handling, and strict sql-mode controls cast strictness. Diagnosis: after any import that tolerated errors, query both error tables and count them against source rows to prove completeness. Remedies: fix or drop offending source rows, re-import affected tables, or accept replacements deliberately; risk is treating a green import as complete while whole row groups were skipped.

nodes.name: Lightning Data File Recognition
nodes.content: Mechanism: Lightning only imports files matching its naming rules; a directory sweep that matches nothing completes without importing rows, and any unsupported compressed file (only gzip, snappy in official format, and zstd are supported; parquet re-compressed by another tool is not) makes the task error. Diagnosis: for an empty or failed import, verify file naming and compression against the source list and whether custom files need an [[mydumper.files]] pattern mapping regex groups to schema/table/type. Remedies: add [[mydumper.files]] patterns for custom layouts such as Aurora Parquet snapshots (schema file handled separately), move unsupported files out of the data directory, and split large compressed files since single-file streaming decompression cannot parallelize (keep under about 256 MiB uncompressed); risk is mis-mapped regex groups importing data into wrong tables.

nodes.name: Lightning Physical Import Capacity Planning
nodes.content: IMPORT INTO ... FROM FILE distributes sub-jobs across TiDB nodes only when tidb_enable_dist_task=ON and the files are on S3 or GCS; local files execute only on the TiDB node the session connects to, which is impossible through a proxy or load balancer. Compressed CSV/SQL is auto-detected by extension (.gz/.gzip, .zstd/.zst, .snappy - official Snappy only) but cannot be decompressed concurrently, so keep source files around or below 256 MiB uncompressed or import speed collapses on a single large archive. IMPORT INTO ... FROM FILE distributes sub-jobs across TiDB nodes only when tidb_enable_dist_task=ON and the files are on S3 or GCS; local files execute only on the connected TiDB node, which is impossible through a proxy or load balancer. Sub-jobs split by filename traversal order, so interleaved primary-key ranges or scattered index values make each sub-job's encoded KV ranges overlap and force continuous TiKV compaction that degrades speed and stability; Global Sort (CLOUD_STORAGE_URI option or tidb_cloud_storage_uri variable, S3-backed) sorts encoded KV externally before ingest to fix this, though with low overlap it adds a wait and can be slower, and it needs memory headroom under tidb_server_memory_limit to avoid GC thrash. Compressed CSV/SQL is auto-detected by extension (.gz, .zstd, official .snappy) but decompressed serially, so keep source files around or below 256 MiB uncompressed. IMPORT INTO maps file fields through an explicit column/user-variable list (skipping fields via variables), computes targets with SET expressions, and accepts FORMAT CSV/SQL/PARQUET; a field-count mismatch with the declared list is rejected. IMPORT INTO ... FROM FILE distributes sub-jobs across TiDB nodes only when tidb_enable_dist_task=ON and the files are on S3 or GCS; local files execute only on the connected TiDB node, which is impossible through a proxy or load balancer. Sub-jobs split by filename traversal order, so interleaved primary-key ranges or scattered index values make each sub-job's encoded KV ranges overlap and force continuous TiKV compaction; Global Sort (CLOUD_STORAGE_URI or tidb_cloud_storage_uri, S3-backed) sorts encoded KV externally to fix this, though with low overlap it can be slower, and it needs memory headroom under tidb_server_memory_limit. Compressed CSV/SQL is auto-detected by extension (.gz, .zstd, official .snappy) but decompressed serially, so keep source files around or below 256 MiB uncompressed. IMPORT INTO maps file fields through an explicit column/user-variable list (skipping fields via variables), computes targets with SET expressions, and accepts FORMAT CSV/SQL/PARQUET; a field-count mismatch with the declared list is rejected. IMPORT INTO ... FROM FILE distributes sub-jobs across TiDB nodes only when tidb_enable_dist_task=ON and the files are on S3 or GCS; local files execute only on the connected TiDB node, which is impossible through a proxy or load balancer. Sub-jobs split by filename traversal order, so interleaved primary-key ranges or scattered index values make each sub-job's encoded KV ranges overlap and force continuous TiKV compaction; Global Sort (CLOUD_STORAGE_URI or tidb_cloud_storage_uri, S3-backed) sorts encoded KV externally to fix this, though with low overlap it can be slower, needs memory headroom under tidb_server_memory_limit, and could stall outright when Region size exceeded 96 MiB until fixed in v8.1.2. Compressed CSV/SQL is auto-detected by extension (.gz, .zstd, official .snappy) but decompressed serially, so keep source files around or below 256 MiB uncompressed.

nodes.name: Lightning Physical Import Impact
nodes.content: Physical (local-backend) import switches TiKV into import mode, pauses region scheduling (scope configurable) and auto-compaction, and ingests sorted SSTs directly, so the cluster offers limited service during the import and a stalled phase blocks completion; afterwards it verifies checksums, rebuilds secondary indexes, and runs ANALYZE. Distinguish encoder/sort bottlenecks (lightning host disk/CPU) from TiKV ingest limits by which side shows utilization; fix family: add local NVMe for sorted-kv, tune worker/engine concurrency, or use logical (tidb-backend) mode for production-adjacent tables, risk being much lower speed and SQL-layer load.

nodes.name: Large-Scale Lightning Import Practices
nodes.content: Mechanism: physical-import throughput depends on source data ordered by primary key within files, minimal primary-key overlap across parallel Lightning instances, and secondary-index count (index size = index count x index size x rows); single instance suits up to ~10 TiB and parallel import beyond, and cluster compression ratio is unknowable in advance - import ~10% first to measure it, then size target storage as (data+index)xreplicas/compression-ratio plus ~20% reserve. Key knobs: region-concurrency, send-kv-size, disk-quota for local temp files, and GOMEMLIMIT to prevent Go heap OOM. Diagnosis: slow imports trace to unordered source data, index-heavy schemas, or disk saturation; checksum mismatch after import means inconsistent or lost data (or known conflict-detection interactions) - re-verify with ADMIN CHECKSUM and resolve before cutover. Remedy family: sort or split source files, drop and rebuild non-essential indexes after import, set disk-quota and GOMEMLIMIT before large runs, keep checkpoints enabled for resumability, and always stop Lightning without kill -9 so checkpoints stay consistent.

nodes.name: Lightning max-error Silent Row Skipping
nodes.content: Mechanism: Lightning's max-error tolerates up to N non-fatal row-level errors (parse/type errors), skipping the offending rows and continuing - skipped rows are written to tables in the task-info schema (default lightning_task_info); the default 0 stops at the first error. Diagnosis: post-import row-count shortfalls against the source point at a non-zero max-error silently dropping bad rows - compare source and target counts and query the task-info schema for the skipped records. Remedy family: keep max-error at 0 when completeness matters, or set it knowingly and always reconcile the skipped-row table afterward; parallel-import additionally requires empty target tables and an identical meta-schema-name on every Lightning instance or correctness is not guaranteed.

nodes.name: Lightning Import Monitoring Triage
nodes.content: Mechanism: Lightning exposes Prometheus metrics (status/pprof port) with Grafana panels whose worker-pool signals localize stalls - idle io-concurrency near 0 means the source disk is too slow, idle closed-engine near 0 means Lightning encodes faster than the importer can ingest (stall), and high chunk parser read-block, row-encode, or block-deliver durations all indicate slow or busy Lightning-local I/O; import speed briefly dropping to zero is normal backpressure. Verification discipline: 'tidb lightning exit' only means a normal process exit - success requires 'the whole procedure completed' at the end of tidb-lightning.log; progress lines update every ~5 minutes. Diagnosis: read Speed/Progress/Quota panels top-down - stalled import progress with a saturated quota panel names the bottleneck resource; the Failures panel lists per-table import errors and failure points. Remedy family: move sorted-kv-dir/data-source-dir to faster or separate disks, reduce region-concurrency pressure, or fix engine backlog (closed-engine) before resuming; monitor checksum progress to confirm post-import integrity.

nodes.name: Lightning Parallel Single-Table Import
nodes.content: Multiple TiDB Lightning instances can import one table in parallel by splitting source files via mydumper.files pattern rules (e.g. file ranges per instance, or dumpling --filesize/--where pre-split); tikv-importer.parallel-import must be true when instances write the same table, otherwise imports conflict. Source files on S3 use BR-compatible URI parameters. Risk: duplicate or conflicting KV if range boundaries overlap; verify non-overlapping file sets per instance.

nodes.name: Lightning Import With Placement Policies
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB Lightning is not compatible with Placement Rules in SQL - importing a dump whose CREATE PLACEMENT POLICY definitions reference a source topology either fails to create the policy on a differently-shaped target (error) or silently creates a policy with wrong placement semantics. Diagnosis: on import error or misplaced replicas, inspect the dump for placement policy statements and compare source/target TiKV+PD labels and regions. Remedy family: pre-create the labels and placement policy in the target cluster and apply it to the target table before import so the rule is transparent to Lightning; prerequisites are planned data distribution topology and configured TiKV/PD labels.

nodes.name: Lightning Region Split Stability
nodes.content: Since v7.1.0 Lightning exposes tikv-importer.region-split-batch-size (default 4096), region-split-concurrency (default CPU cores), region-check-backoff-limit (default 1800, 2s max interval, counter not raised when a Region comes online between retries), and pause-pd-scheduler-scope (table since v6.1.0, global only before v6.1.0; global is recommended for very large imports). Version-conditioned remedy: on old clusters the table-scoped scheduling pause is unavailable, so imports pause global scheduling and stall other workloads.
