nodes.name: Lightning Row Error Tolerance
nodes.content: By default lightning.max-error is 0: any row encoding error fails the import immediately. When set above 0, Lightning ignores bad rows and records them into lightning_task_info.type_error_v1 in the target TiDB, exiting only when the error count exceeds the configured threshold (syntax errors are not covered by this tolerance). Diagnosis: an import that 'succeeds' with fewer rows than expected should be checked by querying the type_error_v1 table for skipped rows. Remedies: fix the offending source rows and re-import, or keep max-error at 0 when completeness matters. The same remediation family applies to IMPORT INTO (GA since v7.5.0, integrating Lightning physical import for CSV/SQL/Parquet into empty tables): when invalid conversions terminate an import, drop the partially imported table, fix the schema file or source data types, and re-run the import.

nodes.name: Lightning Load Speed Bottlenecks
nodes.content: Mechanism: Lightning trades in-flight ACID for speed, guaranteeing consistency only after the whole import completes, so it fits new tables/indexes or truncate-and-reload flows; load throughput is bounded by host disk and cluster state, with TiClient Error, Backoff, and Thread CPU as the primary bottleneck indicators. Diagnosis: during slow imports, watch those three metrics plus host disk usage to find whether errors, retry backoff, or CPU saturation dominate. Remedies: relieve the binding resource (faster disks, more Lightning nodes, reduce conflict backoff by fixing duplicate keys) and reserve imports for scenarios tolerating the ACID window; risk is that import failures mid-run leave non-transactional partial data to clean up.

nodes.name: Lightning Table and Engine State Machine
nodes.content: Lightning exposes per-table phases pending -> written -> closed -> imported -> altered_auto_inc -> checksum -> analyzed -> completed with per-phase success/failure results, plus per-engine pending/written/closed/imported/completed and per-chunk states including failed. A stalled import should be localized to the phase whose failure counter grows: checksum or analyze phases fail independently of data delivery. Diagnosis: read the lightning_tables/lightning_engines/lightning_chunks counters (Grafana) and match the failing phase; remedies differ per phase (data conflict for checksum, KV delivery for import).

nodes.name: Lightning Import Diagnosis
nodes.content: For CSV imports Lightning recognizes only files named ${db}.${table}.csv (or zero-padded ascending numeric suffixes like ${db}.${table}.003.csv) searched recursively in the source dir, and takes schemas from ${db}-schema-create.sql and ${db}.${table}-schema.sql files (one DDL per file); if a table imports partially or stays empty, first verify naming, suffix ordering, and schema-file placement before suspecting engine or checkpoint problems. For CSV imports Lightning recognizes only files named ${db}.${table}.csv (or zero-padded ascending numeric suffixes like ${db}.${table}.003.csv) searched recursively in the source dir, and takes schemas from ${db}-schema-create.sql and ${db}.${table}-schema.sql files (one DDL per file); if a table imports partially or stays empty — or the console warns 'can't find the corresponding source files' / reports zero rows after completion — first verify naming, suffix ordering, and schema-file placement before suspecting engine or checkpoint problems. CSV imports only recognize files named ${db}.${table}.csv (zero-padded ascending suffixes for splits) plus schema files with one DDL each; strict-format imports must set a line terminator (mandatory from v6.5.10) because the splitter assumes record boundaries; 'can't find the corresponding source files' or zero rows after completion mean naming/URI mismatches, and the tidb.tls config values false/''/skip-verify/preferred are distinct from v8.1.0. Verify naming, terminators, and TLS settings before suspecting engine or checkpoint failures.

nodes.name: Cloud maintenance jitter runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: the hypervisor migrates the VM to another host, temporarily throttling CPU/memory so queries on that node slow down. Differential diagnosis: correlate latency spikes with cloud maintenance metadata events and check the spike is node-local while aggregate QPS stays normal, distinguishing it from workload-driven saturation. Remedy families: (1) deploy a metadata-watching script so TiDB pods are cordoned/deleted, TiKV leaders are evicted from the affected store, and the PD leader resigns before the event; (2) accept the transient jitter if SLOs tolerate it. Risks: pod eviction presumes an auto-scaling, TiDB-dedicated node pool, and leader eviction itself adds scheduling load.

nodes.name: Use Load-Based Split for Region Hotspots
nodes.content: Mechanism: Load Base Split flags hot Regions by byte rate (default 30 MiB/s, 100 MiB/s for Regions >= 4 GiB), QPS (3000 / 7000), or Region CPU ratio (0.25 / 0.75, scaled by region-split-size) so PD can split them. Differential: distinguish true key-level hotspots (split helps) from single-statement load that no split can spread. Remedies: verify split thresholds and region size settings; lowering thresholds splits earlier - risk: more Regions and heavier PD scheduling. Sustained load must persist for 10 seconds before a split; after splitting, PD MergeChecker skips the hot Regions so they are not immediately re-merged, and thresholds can be changed online with SET CONFIG tikv split.qps-threshold / split.byte-threshold / split.region-cpu-overload-threshold-ratio.

nodes.name: Local Latch Trade-off for Conflict-Free Batches
nodes.content: Mechanism: the TiDB txn-local-latches pre-identify write conflicts to cut transaction-commit retries, but they allocate many small objects; conflict-free batch tasks pay this memory for no benefit. Diagnosis: for high TiDB memory from small-object allocation in batch workloads, check whether latches are enabled and whether the workload actually produces write conflicts. Remedies: disable txn-local-latches for proven conflict-free batch tasks to reduce memory allocation; keep them enabled where conflicts are frequent, since disabling there raises commit retries against TiKV; risk is more write-conflict retries if the conflict assumption is wrong.

nodes.name: Resolve Lock Contention and Choose Transaction Mode
nodes.content: Mechanism: pessimistic mode is the default (tidb_txn_mode); TiKV waits per lock up to pessimistic-txn.wait-for-lock-timeout (1s), wakes one waiter after 20ms, and retries statements up to 256 times before erroring; pipelined and in-memory locking cut latency but can lose locks during TiKV failures, affecting apps that depend on lock semantics. Differential: separate true key contention (deadlocks visible in INFORMATION_SCHEMA.DEADLOCKS) from retry storms after component failures. Remedies: shorten transactions and spread hot keys, enable pessimistic-auto-commit to fold auto-commit writes into lock management, switch modes per session with BEGIN PESSIMISTIC/OPTIMISTIC, and disable pipelined/in-memory locks when correctness depends on them. Risks: optimistic auto-retry is removed since v8.0 (application must retry), pessimistic-auto-commit regresses bulk INSERT INTO SELECT workloads, and disabling pipelining adds lock latency.

nodes.name: Lock View Diagnosis Workflow
nodes.content: Mechanism: Lock View exposes pessimistic lock conflicts from two angles - aggregate DATA_LOCK_WAITS grouped by key to find the few hot keys queueing many transactions, or, given a blocked transaction's start_ts, join DATA_LOCK_WAITS with CLUSTER_TIDB_TRX and decode ALL_SQL_DIGESTS to reveal exactly which statements the blocker executed. Discrimination: many waits on one key indicate a hot-key contention problem; wide waits across keys point to long transactions or lock-order issues; DEADLOCKS rows give the cycle members and conflict keys. Fix family: redesign hot-key access, shorten or reorder blocking transactions, or kill the offending session; note Lock View tables may be read at slightly different times and show normalized SQL only.

nodes.name: Log Backup Checkpoint Stalls GC
nodes.content: A log backup task blocks GC for data newer than its checkpoint: each TiKV observer reports a local checkpoint, the coordinator derives the global checkpoint, and if any node or the target storage lags, old MVCC versions accumulate and disk usage grows. Distinguish by comparing global checkpoint progress against storage growth; fix family: restore the lagging observer or backup storage throughput, or stop the task cleanly; leaving it broken keeps GC blocked.

nodes.name: Log Backup Task Lifecycle
nodes.content: Mechanism: only one log backup task may run per cluster; br log start registers a long-running task that flushes change logs in small batches until manually stopped, and br log status reports state plus checkpoint[global] with its time gap; with IAM authorization the credentials flag must be disabled so TiKV uses roles instead of embedded keys. Diagnosis: for PiTR coverage doubts, read the task status gap and compare checkpoint against the target restore time. Remedies: restart or resume the task when the state is not NORMAL, monitor the gap as the real RPO, and schedule snapshot backups alongside to shorten restore replay; risk is a silently errored task widening the recovery gap until noticed.

nodes.name: Log Backup Task Recovery
nodes.content: Mechanism: a log backup task holds a PD service safepoint protecting its checkpoint; after a failure the task status shows ERROR, and br log resume continues from the last checkpoint only while the safe point data is still retained - once GC passed it, resume fails with ErrBackupGCSafepointExceeded. Differential diagnosis: read br log status and the GC service safepoint to separate a transient pause (checkpoint retained) from collected checkpoints; also distinguish feature-level unavailability, such as log backup turning unavailable under TiDB Lightning physical import mode. Repair family: resume with br log resume from the checkpoint when data survives, otherwise br log stop and recreate the task (relying on a fresh full snapshot for PITR); after br restore point, re-add TiFlash replicas explicitly (SET TIFLASH REPLICA, check information_schema.tiflash_replica progress); keep the log backup checkpoint inside the GC retention window by construction.

nodes.name: Log redaction semantics
nodes.content: If slow logs, error logs, or component logs show ? placeholders instead of literal values, log redaction is enabled (global.tidb_redact_log on TiDB, security.redact-info-log on TiKV/PD and both tiflash-server/tiflash-learner), not data corruption. Redaction protects user data but removes diagnostic detail; temporarily raising log verbosity does not bypass it.

nodes.name: Maintenance and GC Jitter
nodes.content: Mechanism: routine operations cause bounded jitter - PD leadership transfers add about 3 seconds of jitter, single-node (minority replica) failures jitter but preserve correctness under Raft majority, index creation backfills tables consuming heavy resources and conflicting with hot updated columns, and GC phases (scan_lock in Resolve Locks across all Regions, unsafe_destroy_range in Delete Ranges, per-leader Do GC) create observable request waves. Discrimination: correlate the jitter window with maintenance actions, DDL reorg jobs, or GC task panels and scan_lock request spikes. Fix family: schedule leadership switches and index builds off-peak, tune tidb_ddl_reorg_worker_cnt and tidb_ddl_reorg_batch_size down to limit impact (or up when headroom exists), and accept short GC-related waves or widen GC intervals knowingly.

nodes.name: Malformed Lock Bounded MVCC Recovery
nodes.content: Mechanism: GC is a phase sequence (Resolve Locks, Delete Ranges, Do GC); the lock CF value encodes start_ts, TTL, and async-commit min_commit_ts, and a lock with min_commit_ts <= start_ts or a missing default/write record is malformed rather than merely slow GC. Differential diagnosis: decode raw lock bytes per peer and correlate with the current safepoint and phase, separating legal pessimistic locks and long-running transactions that legitimately retain history, generic disk pressure or compaction, and a delayed later phase; bind scope by encoding the row key with the mem-comparable codec and selecting the single Region whose start_key <= key < end_key together with its complete current peer set. Repair family: only a version-pinned bounded recover-mvcc (read-only inspection on the exact Region and full peer set, then execution of the same unchanged scope, then independent re-scan for lock absence, Region health, legal-transaction liveness, and business truth) is supported - advancing the global safepoint, changing GC lifetime, deleting user data, restarting components, or killing legal transactions only masks the symptom.

nodes.name: Manual Profiling On-Demand
nodes.content: Mechanism: Dashboard Manual Profiling captures CPU, heap, mutex, and goroutine profiles for chosen TiDB, TiKV, PD, and TiFlash instances on demand for about 30 seconds, visualized as FlameGraph or DAG; it only covers problems happening now, and TiKV/TiFlash CPU profiling is unsupported on ARM while TiKV heap profiling needs a Perl dependency since v7.5. Diagnosis: for an ongoing hot CPU or stall, profile the suspect instances immediately and compare the hottest functions across instances. Remedies: use manual profiling for live incidents and switch to continuous profiling for historical analysis; risk is negligible but repeated profiling adds brief overhead.

nodes.name: MariaDB Migration Compatibility
nodes.content: MariaDB migration offers two paths - Dumpling+Lightning dump/restore (works for all versions, more downtime) or DM replication (version-restricted by the compatibility catalog) - and prechecks must cover MariaDB-specific features TiDB lacks: authentication plugins, system-versioned tables, sequences, CONNECT/Spider engines, RETURNING, UUID/INET4/INET6 columns and latin1_swedish_ci collations; system-versioning use cases map to AS OF TIMESTAMP stale reads.

nodes.name: Reduce Raftstore Pressure from Massive Regions
nodes.content: Mechanism: every Region generates Raft tick and heartbeat messages, so tens of thousands of Regions overload raftstore threads even when traffic is light. Differential: high raftstore CPU with low QPS indicates message overhead rather than workload. Remedies: keep hibernate-region enabled, let Region Merge consolidate small Regions (max-merge-region-size 20 MiB, max-merge-region-keys 200000, merge-schedule-limit 8), enlarge region size above the 96 MiB default on new deployments, modestly raise store-pool-size or grpc-raft-conn-num, or spread instances. Risk: raising raft-base-tick-interval also delays leader-failure detection, and oversized Regions slow scheduling.

nodes.name: Memory Quota and Spill Remediation
nodes.content: Mechanism: query-level memory quotas make oversized operators (hash join build, hash agg, sort) spill to disk or abort the query; TiFlash adds a per-node query quota with query-level spilling when a spill ratio is set. Diagnosis: memory and disk columns in EXPLAIN ANALYZE, OOM or memory-limit errors, and which operator spills. Fix family: size tidb_mem_quota_query and TiFlash tiflash_mem_quota_query_per_node with tiflash_query_spill_ratio, switch memory-hungry hash aggregation to stream aggregation, and use bulk DML for large writes. Risks: spilling trades latency for stability; quotas set too high convert query failures into instance OOM.

nodes.name: MEMORY_USAGE Table Investigation
nodes.content: To attribute memory pressure, query INFORMATION_SCHEMA.(CLUSTER_)MEMORY_USAGE for current instance memory and (CLUSTER_)MEMORY_USAGE_OPS_HISTORY for the latest 50 memory-control actions per instance; SHOW VARIABLES like tidb_mem_quota_query/tidb_server_memory_limit reveals current thresholds. tidb_memory_usage_alarm_ratio (default 0.7) sets the alarm threshold as ratio times tidb_server_memory_limit (or system memory when the limit is 0), and 0 or 1 disables the alarm. On TiKV, heap profiling (enable-heap-profiling with 512KiB sampling and thread-exclusive arena) attributes memory to threads when TiKV-side growth is suspected.

nodes.name: Metadata Lock Blocks DDL
nodes.content: Online DDL advances a table through None/DeleteOnly/WriteOnly/WriteReorg/Public states, and a state can change only after every TiDB node's transactions touching the table are less than two metadata versions behind, so one uncommitted transaction that read the old schema pins the version and stalls the DDL, with later DDLs queueing behind it. Distinguish from reorg slowness by the job waiting on state change plus existence of a long transaction on the table; fix family: commit or kill the blocking transaction; killing it discards its work.

nodes.name: Metadata lock runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: DML transactions take a metadata lock on first access to a table; a concurrent DDL must wait for old-metadata transactions to commit, which protects DML from 'Information schema is changed' errors but can stall the DDL behind a long transaction. Differential diagnosis: query mysql.tidb_mdl_view (needs PROCESS privilege) to list blocked DDL jobs with the blocking SESSION ID, TxnStart, and SQL_DIGESTS; a data-changing DDL under repeatable read can still surface ERROR 8028 'public column has changed' inside a transaction, which is different from a plain MDL wait. Remedy families: (1) wait for the blocking transaction to finish; (2) KILL the blocking session (Global Kill) to let the DDL proceed; (3) reschedule DDL off-peak and keep transactions short. Risks: killing loses the transaction's work; setting tidb_enable_metadata_lock=OFF shifts failures back onto DML as 8028 errors.

nodes.name: Metrics Schema Time Series Querying
nodes.content: metrics_schema monitoring tables turn Prometheus metrics into SQL rows, e.g. tidb_query_duration returns per-instance, per-sql_type quantile time series (including internal SQL), which fills the gap when slow logs lack historical coverage. Granularity is controlled by session variables tidb_metric_query_step and tidb_metric_query_range_duration, with 30 seconds as the minimum Prometheus granularity; DESC on such a query reveals the underlying PromQL.

nodes.name: Middleware Proxy Connection Pooling Trade-offs
nodes.content: Mechanism: third-party SQL proxies (e.g., ProxySQL) front TiDB with connection pooling, query caching, and query-rule filtering, keeping TiDB-side connection counts low for spiky applications. Diagnosis: when facing connection exhaustion or uniform extra latency, check whether traffic traverses a proxy layer; a standalone single proxy between app and TiDB is a scalability and fault-tolerance bottleneck and adds network-hop latency. Remedy family: move to a sidecar-style or highly available proxy deployment, or bypass the proxy; pooling config changes must match application concurrency.

nodes.name: Migration Capacity Planning
nodes.content: Mechanism: large MySQL-to-TiDB migrations fail or crawl when sized wrong: DM full import runs around 30-50 GiB/h while Lightning physical import reaches up to ~500 GiB/h; Lightning needs temp disk for the largest single table, and target TiKV needs roughly source size x replica count x 2 to cover indexes and RocksDB space amplification. Diagnosis: when import throughput collapses or disk fills, compare the tool in use against data volume and check per-schema sizes via information_schema.tables (DATA_LENGTH/INDEX_LENGTH). Remedies: switch to Lightning physical import for TiB-scale data, place Lightning on a dedicated host or cap region-concurrency near 75% of logical CPUs, provision 64+ GiB memory with CPU:memory above 1:2, and extend upstream binlog retention so incremental replication does not lose ground; risk is under-provisioned TiKV disk forcing a restart of the whole load.

nodes.name: Migration Collation And Binlog Compatibility
nodes.content: Replication or migration from MySQL 8.0 sources fails at table creation when the source default collation utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci is used, because TiDB does not support it; convert source or DDL collations to utf8mb4_bin or other supported values before cutover. Incremental replication additionally requires source binlog_format=ROW, and default RDS parameter groups (MIXED) must be replaced, which restarts the source. Replication or migration from MySQL 8.0 sources fails at table creation with Error 1273 when the source default collation utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci is used, because TiDB does not support it; pre-create schemas with supported collations or convert source collations to utf8mb4_bin before cutover. Incremental replication additionally requires source binlog_format=ROW and sufficient binlog retention (raise expire_logs_days, avoid manual purges), otherwise the task must be recreated; source-side max-connections exhaustion also presents as connect failures. Replication or migration from MySQL 8.0 sources fails at table creation with Error 1273 when the source default collation utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci is used, because TiDB supports only a small charset set (utf8mb4 default utf8mb4_bin, plus ascii/binary/gbk/latin1/utf8) - pre-create schemas with supported collations or convert sources before cutover. MariaDB sources add more checks: authentication plugins in mysql.user, system-versioned tables (use AS OF TIMESTAMP instead), sequences, CONNECT/Spider engines, RETURNING clause, UUID/INET types, and latin1_swedish_ci collations. Incremental replication requires source binlog_format=ROW and sufficient binlog retention, otherwise the task must be recreated.

nodes.name: Monitoring Config Persistence
nodes.content: Custom Prometheus rules, scrape settings, and Grafana dashboards must be declared in topology.yaml (rule_dir, additional_scrape_conf, dashboard_dir, config), because TiUP deploy/scale/reload overwrites files edited directly. Alertmanager behind a proxy is unreachable on its host address until listen_host is set to 0.0.0.0; confirm TiUP version supports these fields before relying on them.

nodes.name: Monitoring Metrics Not Reported
nodes.content: prometheus_not_found on overview panels means Prometheus is not deployed or an outdated deployment tool failed to register metrics addresses. Remediation: deploy Prometheus, upgrade the deployment tool, then re-run the cluster start command - it refreshes metric address reporting without disturbing running services. Distinguish from dashboard ACL problems by checking whether any metrics render at all.

nodes.name: Broadcast vs Shuffled Join Selection
nodes.content: Mechanism: MPP supports Broadcast Hash Join (build side broadcast via Broadcast exchange), Shuffled Hash Join and Aggregation (HashPartition exchange), Union All, TopN, and Limit; broadcast is chosen when the estimated build size or row count is under tidb_broadcast_join_threshold_size/count, or, with tidb_prefer_broadcast_join_by_exchange_data_size enabled, by whichever algorithm moves fewer network bytes (then the thresholds no longer apply). Diagnosis: for slow MPP joins, EXPLAIN and inspect ExchangeType: Broadcast versus HashPartition and the estimated build-side size. Remedies: tune the thresholds or enable exchange-size preference so small dimension tables broadcast and big joins shuffle; risk of forcing broadcast with a big build side is network and memory blow-up on every TiFlash node.

nodes.name: MPP Mode Capability Boundaries
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiFlash MPP distributes large joins across TiFlash nodes by redistributing join keys through Exchange operators and pushes aggregation down, cost-decided by TiDB; when a query uses constructs MPP cannot execute (historically partitioned tables, window functions, some collations or built-ins, reading from TiKV, spill, union, full outer join) the plan falls back to TiKV-side execution. Diagnosis: for analytic queries that unexpectedly lose MPP, EXPLAIN and look for missing mpp[tiflash] tasks and Exchange operators. Remedies: reshape queries away from unsupported constructs, keep statistics current so cost estimation picks MPP, and scale TiFlash nodes for data redistribution; risk is misreading a fallback caused by a single unsupported operator as a general TiFlash fault.

nodes.name: MPP Plan Reading
nodes.content: Mechanism: MPP plans slice queries into fragments whose boundaries are ExchangeSender operators; ExchangeType HashPartition marks shuffle-based aggregation or shuffle hash joins, Broadcast marks broadcast joins, and PassThrough returns data to TiDB, and MPP applies only to tables holding TiFlash replicas. Diagnosis: to verify MPP engaged, EXPLAIN the query and confirm ExchangeSender/ExchangeReceiver pairs under mpp or cop[tiflash] tasks, identifying each fragment's role from its exchange type. Remedies: zero out broadcast thresholds to force shuffle joins when diagnosing, add TiFlash replicas where plans show TiKV scans, and compare fragment row counts to find skew; risk is that a plan without exchange operators simply means the optimizer chose non-MPP execution rather than a fault.

nodes.name: MPP Runtime Filter
nodes.content: TiFlash MPP can push an IN-list runtime filter from the small hash-join build side to the large fact-table scan, skipping most row packs before they are read. Confirm via EXPLAIN ANALYZE operator info (runtime filter:N[IN] on the probe-side TableFullScan) and tiflash_scan total_scanned_rows before/after; best for fact-vs-dimension joins where the dimension side hits few values.

nodes.name: TiFlash Replica and MPP Selection Check
nodes.content: Mechanism: after ALTER TABLE ... SET TIFLASH REPLICA n, data is replicated asynchronously; the replica is usable only when information_schema.tiflash_replica shows AVAILABLE=1 (PROGRESS 0.0-1.0 tracks completion), and the optimizer then picks TiFlash by cost, emitting ExchangeSender/ExchangeReceiver operators in EXPLAIN ANALYZE when MPP mode is in effect. Diagnosis: for a slow analytical query, check replica availability/progress first, then read the plan for MPP operators and tiflash_scan metrics (scanned/skipped packs, threads) to see whether TiFlash was chosen and how the scan behaved. Repair family: wait for or repair replica availability, and force or encourage the TiFlash/MPP path with engine hints or optimizer settings when cost estimates mislead.

nodes.name: Restore MPP Selection for Analytical Queries
nodes.content: Mechanism: MPP runs only when tidb_allow_mpp is on and nothing blocks it - missing TiFlash replicas, unfinished replication, unsupported operators, or isolation-read engines excluding tiflash; tidb_enforce_mpp only removes cost consideration, not hard blocks, and EXPLAIN warnings name the blocker. Differential: compare plan operators (ExchangeReceiver) and warnings to distinguish replica lag from variable settings. Remedies: add replicas with ALTER TABLE SET TIFLASH REPLICA and wait for sync, fix allow/enforce flags per session or per instance (enforce-mpp config), and tune broadcast join thresholds (100 MiB / 10240 rows) for join distribution. Risk: forcing MPP cannot override hard blocks, and broadcast joins of oversized tables inflate network and memory. MPP access to partitioned tables requires dynamic pruning mode: with tidb_partition_prune_mode=static the plan degrades to a PartitionUnion of per-partition TiFlash batchCop scans and cross-partition MPP joins are not used. When MPP/TiFlash is expected but the plan runs on TiKV, check in order: TiFlash replica existence and availability, cost-based selection (force with READ_FROM_STORAGE hints to compare engines - beware TiKV result cache making reruns look faster), partition prune mode, aggregate pushdown toggle (tidb_opt_agg_push_down), and window-function stream settings (tiflash_fine_grained_shuffle_stream_count, seen as stream_count in EXPLAIN ANALYZE). TiFlash execution concurrency is tuned per session with tidb_max_tiflash_threads, observable as threads:N on tiflash_task operators.

nodes.name: Multi-Valued Index IndexMerge
nodes.content: Mechanism: multi-valued indexes on JSON path casts accelerate MEMBER OF (union IndexMerge), JSON_CONTAINS (intersection IndexMerge over each element), and JSON_OVERLAPS (union), including composite multi-valued indexes with leading/trailing scalar columns; without them these predicates fall to full scans. Predicates such as json_length comparisons cannot use the index and remain a Selection above the merge. Diagnosis: EXPLAIN the query to check whether an IndexMerge with IndexRangeScan children appears or whether the predicate degrades to a root Selection over TableFullScan. Remedies: create a CAST(... AS ... ARRAY) multi-valued index on the queried JSON path and hint use_index_merge when needed; risk is higher write amplification on JSON-heavy rows since each array element produces index entries.

nodes.name: Multi-Valued Index Hint Pitfalls
nodes.content: Mechanism: use_index hints on multi-valued indexes can fail with ERROR 1815 'Can't find a proper physical plan' for complex AND/OR member-of combinations while use_index_merge succeeds; plan cache caches member-of plans but skips plans where JSON_CONTAINS or JSON_OVERLAPS with immutable parameters would affect index selection, emitting a skip-plan-cache warning. Diagnosis: for errors or cache misses on JSON queries, switch hints between use_index and use_index_merge and read SHOW WARNINGS after execution. Remedies: prefer use_index_merge for multi-valued access, split predicates so cacheable member-of parts dominate, and accept cache misses where JSON functions must influence index choice; risk is plan instability across executions when hints are removed.

nodes.name: MVCC GC Backlog
nodes.content: MVCC keeps old row versions until GC clears them; the GC leader computes a safe point that never exceeds the start_ts of ongoing transactions, so long-running transactions (or anything holding the safe point back) let versions and delete-range data accumulate and disk usage grow while scans slow down. Distinguish by correlating disk growth with GC safe-point progress and listing long transactions; fix family: kill or bound long transactions, tune gc life time to the workload, and confirm the GC leader is alive; killing transactions discards their work and shrinking gc life time risks breaking long reads.

nodes.name: MyBatis Execution Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: #{} parameters become reusable prepared statements while ${} splices text, so each distinct value re-prepares a statement, floods TiDB's prepared-statement cache, and invites injection; Batch ExecutorType defers INSERT/UPDATE until commit or a SELECT, making writes look instant in-transaction but slow at commit; streaming large result sets needs fetchSize (Integer.MIN_VALUE for MySQL streaming) with Cursor or ResultHandler instead of materializing whole sets. Diagnosis: for prepared-statement cache growth or 'slow commit' reports, check mapper parameter styles and executor type before blaming the server. Remedies: standardize on #{}, use foreach multi-values inserts with rewriteBatchedStatements for batching, set ExecutorType deliberately, and stream big reads; risk of Batch mode is confusion during troubleshooting since per-statement timing shifts to commit time.

nodes.name: MySQL Compatibility Limits in Diagnosis
nodes.content: Behavior that differs from MySQL explains many false alarms: most performance-schema tables return empty (use Prometheus/Grafana metrics instead), optimizer_switch is read-only, ALGORITHM=INSTANT/INPLACE/COPY is only an assertion, and index types HASH|BTREE|RTREE|FULLTEXT are parsed and ignored. Single ALTER TABLE statements cannot touch the same column/index twice or multiple TiDB-specific objects (TIFLASH REPLICA, SHARD_ROW_ID_BITS, AUTO_ID_CACHE), unsupported type changes (e.g. DECIMAL to DATE) fail with 'Unsupported modify column', dropping a CLUSTERED primary key is unsupported, and partitioning quirks apply: LINEAR HASH/KEY are accepted but LINEAR is ignored (row distribution differs from MySQL when partition count is not a power of 2), NULL partition keys go to the lowest Range partition or hash to 0, and unsupported partition operations on a type are silently ignored with a warning. Behavior that differs from MySQL explains many false alarms: most performance-schema tables return empty (use Prometheus/Grafana metrics instead), optimizer_switch is read-only, ALGORITHM=INSTANT/INPLACE/COPY is only an assertion, and index types HASH|BTREE|RTREE|FULLTEXT are parsed and ignored. UPDATE evaluates SET expressions against original column values (MySQL uses the updated value within the same statement), and LOW_PRIORITY/HIGH_PRIORITY stop taking effect once resource control is enabled - use resource groups instead. Single ALTER TABLE statements cannot touch the same column/index twice or multiple TiDB-specific objects (TIFLASH REPLICA, SHARD_ROW_ID_BITS, AUTO_ID_CACHE), unsupported type changes (e.g. DECIMAL to DATE) fail with 'Unsupported modify column', dropping a CLUSTERED primary key is unsupported, and partitioning quirks apply: LINEAR HASH/KEY are accepted but LINEAR is ignored (row distribution differs when partition count is not a power of 2), NULL partition keys go to the lowest Range partition or hash to 0, and unsupported partition operations are silently ignored with a warning.

nodes.name: mysql Schema Diagnostic Tables
nodes.content: The mysql schema holds the diagnostic system tables: tidb_runaway_queries/watch/watch_done (runaway identification and watch lists, 7-day history), tidb_mdl_view (DDL blocked by metadata locks), tidb_ddl_job/tidb_ddl_reorg/tidb_ddl_history (running and finished DDL), tidb_global_task/tidb_background_subtask (_history) for DXF tasks, tidb_ttl_table_status/task/job_history for TTL jobs, gc_delete_range(_done) for GC delete ranges (self-managed only), stats_meta/analyze_jobs for statistics health, bind_info and plan_replayer_status/task for plan management, and request_unit_by_group for RU accounting. Query these before ad-hoc log grepping; avoid direct writes to system tables and prefer SQL statements, using FLUSH PRIVILEGES if direct grant-table edits are unavoidable.

nodes.name: Network Isolation Request Forwarding
nodes.content: During suspected network partition between TiDB and PD/TiKV, enable-forwarding lets requests be forwarded to the leader via followers, shrinking the service-unavailability window. Trade-off: when isolation cannot be distinguished from downtime, forwarding can misjudge and further reduce availability and performance, so it is only recommended for environments with known isolation risk; distinguish by checking whether the unreachable node recovers under probes.

nodes.name: Node Resource Pressure
nodes.content: Host-level CPU or memory saturation on a machine slows whichever TiDB/TiKV/PD process runs there, so diagnosis must separate component thread saturation from other tenants on the host. Distinguish by node_exporter CPU/load/memory panels versus component-internal thread metrics; fix family: scale out, isolate workloads across nodes (or NUMA binding in hybrid deployments), and move background tasks off-peak; risk is under-provisioning recurring under load growth. TiUP systemd resource_control (memory_limit, cpu_quota, io_read/write_bandwidth_max, limit_core) is enforced per instance, so instance-level CPU/memory/IO saturation can be a deployment-imposed cgroup limit rather than host capacity; compare observed usage against the configured limits.

nodes.name: Non-transactional DML usage and errors
nodes.content: Large DMLs can be split with BATCH ON <shard-column> LIMIT n non-transactional DML, but the internally rewritten statements may drop table aliases, so alias-qualified columns in WHERE fail with "Unknown column"; the shard column must be fully qualified and conditions on other tables moved into JOIN ON. Always preview the batch-dividing query and first/last batches with DRY RUN QUERY / DRY RUN before executing; a failed batch series leaves partial data that must be reconciled manually. Non-transactional DML rewrites statements in batches, so errors and semantics differ from plain DML: multi-table joins or table aliases raise Unknown column errors because rewritten WHERE clauses drop aliases (move join conditions into ON, avoid aliases, preview with DRY RUN QUERY/DRY RUN); batch sizes deviate from LIMIT when the shard column has duplicate values or concurrent writes race; ENUM/BIT/SET/JSON shard columns fail with restore errors (use integer or string shard columns); and results may diverge from the original statement because of concurrent writes, self-reading modifications, per-batch plan changes, or non-deterministic operations.

nodes.name: OLTP Client Interface Tuning
nodes.content: Mechanism: OLTP throughput depends heavily on the client interface: text-query traffic re-parses and misses the plan cache while prepared statements with client-side caching hit it, and RC read plus small-table caching further cut latency; measured effect is tens of percent latency reduction and large CPU savings on TiDB. Diagnosis: compare query duration, QPS, and TiDB CPU across applications to see which use prepared statements, using Top SQL and the Performance Overview database-time breakdown to locate whether the bottleneck is in TiDB. Remedies: enable server-side prepared statements with client statement caching (JDBC useServerPrepStmts/cachePrepStmts and adequate prepStmtCacheSqlLimit), adopt RC read and small table cache for point workloads, and profile with Top SQL and Continuous Profiling; risk is that prepared-statement benefits vanish when statement text varies.

nodes.name: Online Unsafe Recovery
nodes.content: Mechanism: Online Unsafe Recovery is a lossy PD-owned operation for Stores that are permanently damaged - it is not a normal drain and establishes no lossless RPO. Differential diagnosis: derive the full unrecoverable Store set from current PD Store state and Region peer evidence; a single Store named by an error is not the complete scope and healthy neighbors must stay outside it. Repair family: include every unrecoverable Store in the request, observe the asynchronous task to a terminal finished state without restarting affected Stores mid-recovery, wait for Region convergence, verify remaining peers and Store states, run ADMIN CHECK TABLE on affected data, and bound the unconfirmed write interval explicitly - a command exit status or one unchanged aggregate proves neither recovery nor zero data loss. Online Unsafe Recovery is a lossy PD-owned global task (pd-ctl unsafe remove-failed-stores) whose registration Success is not completion: wait for the terminal 'Unsafe recovery finished' across stages like collect report, force leader, demote failed voter, and create empty region, include every permanently failed Store and no healthy one, treat both record and secondary-index Regions as affected scope, capture the last confirmed commit boundary before stopping Stores so the unconfirmed write interval can be reported as observed RPO, and accept only after affected Regions regain leaders with three healthy peers, no residual peer on failed Stores, ADMIN CHECK TABLE plus INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES table-ID validation, unchanged protected truth, and restored scheduling settings. Prerequisites are that the offline stores really hold unavailable data and cannot auto-recover or restart; after the task finishes, repair damaged indexes by renaming the bad index to a lame-duck name, recreating it, and dropping the lame duck, remove unrecoverable stores by force scale-in plus prune (or PVC deletion on Kubernetes) to reach Tombstone, and query affected table IDs against INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES. Per-Region tikv-ctl diagnostics (bad-regions, region-properties showing raft last/commit/apply index gaps, remove-peer via pd-ctl operator, tombstone in local mode only) support the investigation, but the deprecated local tikv-ctl unsafe-recover remove-fail-stores and consistency-check (remote mode only, incompatible with TiDB GC) are not the supported path - Online Unsafe Recovery supersedes them.

nodes.name: Optimizer Rule Blocklist Remediation
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB optimization rules (join_reorder, topn_push_down, decorrelate, predicate_push_down, aggregation_push_down, partition_processor, etc.) can individually produce suboptimal plans for specific query shapes, and each rule has a fixed name. Diagnosis: identify the offending rule by comparing plans with/without the rewrite. Remedy: insert the rule name into mysql.opt_rule_blacklist (requires super privilege) and run ADMIN RELOAD OPT_RULE_BLACKLIST; reload only affects the TiDB node where it runs, so apply on every server, and delete the row to re-enable the rule.

nodes.name: Optimistic Read-Write Conflict
nodes.content: Mechanism: a read hits a key locked by a transaction between prewrite and commit, so the reader cannot tell committed from pending and backs off (txnLockFast retries from 10ms up to 3000ms each, 20s total). Discrimination: rising not_expired/resolve in Lock Resolve OPS and tikvLockFast in KV Backoff OPS indicate read-write conflicts; TiDB coprocessor logs show backoff_types with txnStartTS, and TiKV 'locked' error responses expose primary_lock, lock_ttl, and key. Fix family: conflicts retry automatically - reduce hot-key overlap, shrink transaction windows, or move the workload to pessimistic mode; decode the key to table/row id to find the contended object.

nodes.name: Optimizer Bad Plan Triage
nodes.content: Mechanism: the optimizer picks a plan whose operators do not match the predicates or index design. Diagnosis: CARTESIAN marks a product join costing left rows x right rows; check whether TableFullScan/IndexReader/IndexLookup/IndexFullScan are justified by the filters and index prefix. Fix families: correct the index, adjust join order, or fix expression pushdown blocklists. Unexpected full scans with index hints often mean the predicate class cannot use the index at all: multi-valued JSON indexes only serve IndexMerge when every OR/AND branch is index-accessible (json_overlaps/json_contains yes, json_length no, warning 1105 'IndexMerge is inapplicable'); otherwise the plan degrades to TableFullScan. Verify with EXPLAIN plus SHOW WARNINGS before blaming statistics, then rewrite the predicate or accept the scan. Unexpected full scans with index hints often mean the predicate class cannot use the index at all: multi-valued JSON indexes only serve IndexMerge when every OR/AND branch is index-accessible (json_overlaps/json_contains yes, json_length no, warning 1105 'IndexMerge is inapplicable'). The IN-subquery rewrite (tidb_opt_insubq_to_join_and_agg) turns IN (SELECT...) into GROUP BY + join - beneficial for small subqueries against large outer tables, harmful when the inner table is large and DISTINCT cannot be eliminated by a UNIQUE attribute, so disable it selectively. Verify all of these with EXPLAIN plus SHOW WARNINGS before blaming statistics. Unexpected full scans with index hints often mean the predicate class cannot use the index at all: multi-valued JSON indexes only serve IndexMerge when every branch is index-accessible (json_overlaps/json_contains/MEMBER OF yes, json_length no, warning 1105 'IndexMerge is inapplicable'), and deeply nested OR groups may not fully expand onto the index. The IN-subquery rewrite (tidb_opt_insubq_to_join_and_agg) helps for small subqueries against large outer tables but hurts when the inner table is large and DISTINCT cannot be eliminated by a UNIQUE attribute. Verify all of these with EXPLAIN plus SHOW WARNINGS before blaming statistics.

nodes.name: Oracle to TiDB Function Mapping Traps
nodes.content: Mechanism: Oracle idioms map to different TiDB functions with subtly different semantics - SUBSTRING position 0 returns an empty string (Oracle treats 0 like 1), TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH,...) returns an integer with swapped argument order versus MONTHS_BETWEEN, DATE_FORMAT/STR_TO_DATE format strings are case-sensitive, (+) outer-join syntax is unsupported (use LEFT/RIGHT JOIN), and NVL/NVL2/DECODE become IFNULL/IF/CASE WHEN. Diagnosis: on post-migration data or result mismatches, diff each migrated expression against this mapping table rather than suspecting the data first. Repair family: rewrite the offending expressions with the TiDB equivalents (CONCAT instead of ||, GROUP_CONCAT for LISTAGG, CHAR() for CHR(), NEXTVAL for sequences) and re-verify row-level results.

nodes.name: ORDER BY Index Design
nodes.content: ORDER BY ... LIMIT queries scan-and-sort (IndexLookUp feeding root TopN) when the filter index does not preserve the sort order - a composite index whose extra columns follow the filter prefix breaks id ordering even though the PK is implicitly appended. A slimmer index that ends where the PK order resumes restores keep order:true, replaces TopN with a Limit, and stops shipping non-matching rows to TiDB; verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE actRows on the IndexLookUp and ANALYZE the new index after creation.

nodes.name: Ordering Index Selection Tuning
nodes.content: For queries with ORDER BY ... LIMIT plus filters, the optimizer may pick the index satisfying the ordering (IndexFullScan keep order:true) instead of a selective filter index, making LIMIT 1 scans large data; tidb_opt_ordering_index_selectivity_threshold (0-1) makes it prefer a filter index whose selectivity is below the threshold. tidb_opt_prefer_range_scan=ON forces range scans over full table scans when estimates make full scans look cheap, and both take effect per session or via SET_VAR, verified by re-running EXPLAIN.

nodes.name: Verify Host OS and Storage Parameters
nodes.content: Mechanism: Transparent Huge Pages cause allocation latency spikes for sparse database memory access, non-noop I/O schedulers (deadline, cfq) add queuing delay on SSD/NVMe, dynamic CPU frequency scaling drops throughput mid-request, and data disks mounted without nodelalloc/noatime hurt write latency and fail deployment prechecks. Differential: attribute jitter that correlates with host, not with SQL shape or Region distribution. Remedies: set THP to never, use noop/none scheduler for SSD (none default on NVMe), fix the cpufreq governor to performance, and mount data disks as ext4 with nodelalloc and noatime; persist settings via kernel args, udev rules, and services. Risk: kernel-level changes need reboots or udev triggers to take effect and must be rolled out host by host.

nodes.name: OS Resource Tuning
nodes.content: Mechanism: OS defaults favor stability over database latency - CPU frequency scaling, THP compaction stalls, dirty-page flush bursts, and queueing I/O schedulers all add jitter visible as latency spikes without DB-internal cause. Diagnosis: run the 60-second Linux checklist (uptime, vmstat, mpstat, pidstat, iostat, sar, top), then perf or BCC tracing for deep dives. Fix family: performance CPU governor, NUMA binding, disable THP, lower dirty ratios on NVMe, noop scheduler for SSDs, NIC interrupt affinity. Risks: tuning one subsystem can degrade another; validate in a test environment before production.

nodes.name: Oversized Transaction
nodes.content: Distributed transactions use two-phase commit plus Raft replication, so a very large transaction commits slowly and stalls subsequent replication; TiDB caps a transaction at 5000 statements, 6 MB per KV entry and 10 GB total by default. Distinguish from lock contention by commit-duration metrics and transaction-too-large errors; fix family: split batches into smaller transactions or import via bulk tools, raising limits deliberately risks replication lag and memory pressure.

nodes.name: Paging Size and MPP Routing Variables
nodes.content: Mechanism: coprocessor paging batches rows per RPC (tidb_min_paging_size, default 128): too small inflates RPC counts while too large hurts IndexLookup-with-Limit, and raising it helps TiKV-only OLAP scans; after a TiFlash node (re)starts it serves no queries until tidb_mpp_store_fail_ttl (default 60s) elapses, and global statistics merge can run asynchronously (tidb_enable_async_merge_global_stats) to avoid OOM. Diagnosis: for OLAP scans over TiKV with high RPC counts, or MPP queries failing right after a TiFlash restart, inspect these variables. Remedies: raise paging sizes for pure-TiKV analytical workloads, accept or tune the TiFlash warm-up window, and enable async stats merging on large partitioned tables; risk of large paging size is latency spikes for short point queries sharing the instance.

nodes.name: Partition Global Statistics Refresh
nodes.content: Mechanism: dynamic partition pruning relies on table-level global statistics, which must be collected explicitly for partitioned tables. Diagnosis: for misestimated partitioned queries under dynamic pruning mode, check whether the table's global stats were ever analyzed. Remedies: enumerate partitioned tables via information_schema.PARTITIONS (TIDB_PARTITION_ID not null), generate ANALYZE TABLE ... statements in batch, and run them under tidb_partition_prune_mode = dynamic; risk is that analyze jobs on many partitions add background load, so batch them off-peak.

nodes.name: Partition Management Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: Range/List partitions support ADD/DROP/TRUNCATE/REORGANIZE PARTITION while Hash/Key changes (COALESCE, ADD) rebuild the whole table online; ADD PARTITION on Range requires strictly increasing VALUES LESS THAN or fails with ERROR 1493; EXCHANGE PARTITION swaps a partition with a non-partitioned table only when placement policies, TiFlash replica counts, and clustered-index type match, rows fit the partition definition, and neither BR nor Lightning is running, and TiCDC replicates it only when both tables have primary or unique keys. Diagnosis: for failed partition DDL, map the error to these preconditions. Remedies: adjust partition definitions or align table attributes before exchange, and schedule exchanges outside import/restore windows; risk of REORGANIZE and COALESCE is long-running rebuild load on large tables.

nodes.name: Partition Pruning Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: dynamic pruning (default since v6.3.0) needs table-level GlobalStats; before they exist TiDB silently falls back to static mode with per-partition stats and Union plans, and after switching static-to-dynamic no GlobalStats exist until an analyze runs (warning 8244 signals inconsistent partition stats). Differential: show stats_meta - a global row with fresh update_time means dynamic mode can engage. Remedies: ANALYZE the table or its partitions, then set tidb_partition_prune_mode=dynamic globally; session-level settings affect manual analyze and queries while auto-analyze follows the global value. Risk: enabling dynamic without fresh GlobalStats degrades plans as badly as stale stats.

nodes.name: Partition Reorganize Operations
nodes.content: ALTER TABLE ... REORGANIZE PARTITION splits, merges, or reshapes RANGE/LIST partitions online but physically rewrites rows between affected partitions, behaving like a backfill: long duration, region churn, and write amplification on the table. Plan scheme changes or boundary moves during low traffic, watch the DDL job progress, and remember hash/key partitions have separate constraints; overflow of new boundaries above an existing MAXVALUE partition requires reorganizing that partition too. ALTER TABLE ... REORGANIZE PARTITION splits, merges, or reshapes RANGE/LIST partitions online but physically rewrites rows between affected partitions like a backfill — plan for low traffic and watch DDL job progress. Structural guards apply: MODIFY COLUMN is unsupported on partitioned tables, renaming or dropping columns that partitions depend on is restricted, and hash/key partitions carry separate constraints.

nodes.name: Password Expiry and Locked Accounts
nodes.content: Passwords can be expired manually (ALTER USER ... PASSWORD EXPIRE) or by global/account-level expiry policies; an expired account must set a new password before login, and roles carry password_expired='Y' so they can never log in with empty passwords. When users report sudden authentication failures, check mysql.user (password_expired, account_locked) and remedy by resetting the password or adjusting/expiring-never policy with SUPER or CREATE USER privilege.

nodes.name: Password Policy Rejection and Lockout
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB validates plaintext passwords against the validate_password.* policy on CREATE/ALTER USER and SET PASSWORD (ERROR 1819), rejects passwords equal to the username or dictionary words, and its failed-login tracking can temporarily lock accounts after repeated wrong passwords. Diagnosis: for a rejected password change or a locked account, inspect validate_password variables and the failed-login lock counters. Remedies: set a policy-compliant password (hashed passwords bypass complexity checks), adjust policy variables globally for the environment, or wait out/use unlock for temporarily locked accounts; risk is weaker credentials if complexity checks are disabled.

nodes.name: PD Advertise URL Connectivity
nodes.content: Mechanism: PD listens on client-urls/peer-urls but clients and peers connect via advertise-client-urls/advertise-peer-urls; in Docker or NAT deployments the listened address (e.g. 0.0.0.0 or container IP) differs from the externally reachable host address. Diagnosis: when clients or PD peers cannot reach PD, compare each PD node's listened URLs with the address actually routable from the failing side. Remedy: set advertise URLs explicitly to host-reachable IP:port endpoints.

nodes.name: PD balance stall runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: PD schedules by store score and schedule-limit quotas, so balance can stall either because scores look equal or because operators cannot execute. Differential diagnosis: compare store scores first. If scores are close, look for hot regions, many empty/small regions needing merge, or heterogeneous stores (then adjust leader-weight/region-weight). If scores differ, check operator generation vs execution: when operators are generated but slow, raise leader-schedule-limit/region-schedule-limit and ease max-snapshot-count/max-pending-peer-count, stop competing tasks that share the quota (for example set enable-replace-offline-replica=false during balance), and check the Operator step duration metric - TransferLeader/RemovePeer/PromoteLearner should finish in milliseconds and snapshot steps (AddLearner/AddPeer) in tens of seconds, longer means TiKV or network pressure. When operators are not generated, check the scheduler was not removed or limited to 0, that no evict-leader-scheduler or label property blocks leaders, and that topology constraints (for example replica isolation across DCs with unequal store counts) allow global balance. Remedy families: raise limits, evict leaders manually via scheduler, adjust weights, free capacity. Risks: higher limits add snapshot I/O load; PD stops migrating regions to a same-label node with less than 20% available capacity - add nodes or delete data.

nodes.name: PD bottleneck runbook
nodes.content: PD leader saturation appears as very high PD CPU with rising TSO RPC and handle time at QPS far beyond a million and TSO requests above roughly 160k/s; remedies are lowering tso-update-physical-interval (e.g. 10ms), enabling client-side batching with tidb_tso_client_batch_max_wait_time (e.g. 2ms), and raising coprocessor.region-split-size (e.g. 256MB) to shrink Region heartbeat load - together these cut TSO request rate and PD CPU several-fold in published tests. PD leader saturation appears as very high PD CPU with rising TSO RPC and handle time at QPS far beyond a million and TSO requests above roughly 160k/s; remedies are lowering tso-update-physical-interval (e.g. 10ms), enabling client-side batching with tidb_tso_client_batch_max_wait_time (e.g. 2ms), and raising coprocessor.region-split-size (e.g. 256MB) to shrink Region heartbeat load - together these cut TSO request rate and PD CPU several-fold in published tests. The pending PD-heartbeat metric (available since v4.0.14) distinguishes slow PD threads from network trouble by counting heartbeats queued but not yet processed.

nodes.name: PD Election and OOM Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: PD leader changes come from disk I/O saturation on the PD node, TCP streaming losses between PD nodes, or system overload; elections stall on lease bugs or slow Region loading at startup; PD OOM historically came from the Regions API or unbounded gRPC during rolling upgrades. Discrimination: disk latency/load panels, 'lost the TCP streaming connection' and etcd round-trip for network, 'server is likely overloaded' for load, and 'regions cost' duration for Region-loading slowness. Fix family: separate PD from I/O-heavy neighbors or upgrade disks, repair inter-PD network, enable region storage to cut loading time, and upgrade past the fixed OOM bugs; verify TiDB-to-PD reachability when SQL times out.

nodes.name: PD etcd MVCC Space Exceeded
nodes.content: Before v6.0.0 TiCDC stored per-table changefeed metadata in PD's embedded etcd, whose default 1-hour MVCC compaction lets many-table changefeeds exhaust the quota and raise 'etcdserver: mvcc: database space exceeded', breaking PD writes cluster-wide. Diagnosis: correlate the error with PD disk usage and a large changefeed table count. Remedy: compact and clean etcd per etcd space-quota runbook, and upgrade TiCDC to >= v6.0.0 where metadata storage was redesigned.

nodes.name: PD Hardware Sensitivity
nodes.content: PD serves cluster metadata and allocates global timestamps, so slow PD disks or weak network stretch every operation cluster-wide; PD requires high-I/O SSD and bonded 10-gigabit NICs, TiKV requires SSD, and TiDB Binlog needs local disk sized to service volume and GC timing. When latency is uniformly inflated without a hot table, check PD disk I/O and clock stability first - Region count growth also raises PD CPU/memory needs.

nodes.name: PD Hotspot History Analysis
nodes.content: pd-ctl hot read/write/store shows current hot regions while hot history <start> <end> replays historical hotspot records with hot_region_type, hot_degree, flow_bytes, and query_rate filterable by region/store/peer/leader role. Use history to separate a transient traffic spike from a persistent imbalance that scheduling failed to resolve, and label store to check whether placement labels match the intended topology.

nodes.name: PD Label Misplacement
nodes.content: PD places replicas and leaders according to location-labels and placement constraints, so wrong store labels, over-broad reject-leader rules, or excessively large election timeout ticks leave regions without eligible leaders, co-locate replicas on one fault domain, or delay failover for minutes. Distinguish by regions-without-leader counts plus per-store label inspection versus actual node outages; fix family: correct labels/placement rules and keep election timeout ticks moderate; the risk of leaving it is silent HA loss where one machine failure drops quorum.

nodes.name: PD Leader Switch Slowness With Massive Regions
nodes.content: Mechanism: PD persists Region Meta for fast leader-failover recovery; at millions of Regions reading that metadata dominates the leader switch (tens of seconds). Diagnosis: correlate switch duration with Region count. Fix family: keep Region count bounded and ensure Region-metadata storage offloading is enabled rather than expanding etcd.

nodes.name: PD Metadata and Cluster Identity Recovery
nodes.content: Mechanism: losing the PD Raft majority stops ID allocation and TSO; a rebuilt PD generates a fresh cluster identity that surviving TiKV members reject, so a healthy control-plane endpoint must be distinguished from the original data-plane identity via PD/TiDB/TiKV logs, member and Store inventory, and PD data-directory evidence. Differential diagnosis: decide between a surviving-PD-node route (minority node, possibly outdated alloc_id/tso) and a full PD rebuild (all PD data lost, TiKV/TiDB data preserved); multiple cluster IDs in logs identify the old cluster. Repair family: either restart the surviving PD with --force-new-cluster and run pd-recover --from-old-member (alloc_id advances by a safe increment; TSO is not modified, so local clock must be past the failure time with NTP verified to avoid TSO rollback), or rebuild: read the cluster ID from component logs, take -alloc-id larger than the maximum allocated ID, deploy new PD, run pd-recover with that cluster-id; stop TiDB/TiKV/TiFlash first to prevent parameter interactions, keep old and new member identities distinct, preserve TiKV data, and reopen writes only after quorum plus Store/Region registration is validated. Separately from PD metadata, a lost deployment-tool meta file is restored from a tiup meta backup with tiup cluster meta restore, which overwrites the current meta file and should only run when the meta file is genuinely lost.

nodes.name: PD Metrics Reading
nodes.content: Mechanism: the PD dashboard exposes scheduler activity (balance leader/region events, replica/rule/merge checkers, filter source/target), gRPC command rates and P99 durations, etcd health (WAL fsync P99 under 1s, raft term/index), TSO handle and client receive times, TiDB request handling (P99 under 100ms), and region heartbeat QPS with error counts. Diagnosis: for scheduling stalls check balance events against filter-target/filter-source spikes; for TSO slowness check TSO handle time and etcd fsync; heartbeat errors indicate stores failing to report. Remedies: enable or rebalance schedulers, fix etcd disk latency, and investigate stores with heartbeat errors; risk is treating leader-only panel gaps as data loss when actually the PD leader changed.

nodes.name: PD microservice decomposition
nodes.content: When PD itself is the bottleneck (TSO long-tail jitter, scheduling-module failures taking down the cluster), microservice mode splits timestamp allocation (tso) and cluster scheduling into independently deployed primary-secondary services, and the scheduling service can be upgraded without restarting PD. Preconditions and risks: the feature is experimental; enabling or disabling the tso microservice requires a PD restart; it is incompatible with DR Auto-Sync and tidb_enable_tso_follower_proxy; scheduling primary/secondary switchover can leave scheduling unavailable up to peer-stale-state-check-interval when hibernate Regions exist; do not deploy microservices if PD is not the bottleneck.

nodes.name: PD operator scheduling metrics
nodes.content: Region scheduling health is read from PD operator metrics: creation vs finished counts per operator type, with timeout, replaced and canceled counts exposing stalls; operator and step finish durations show how long moves take, label distribution and region label isolation levels show placement balance, and store limit flow control caps per-store scheduling. Rising timeout/replaced counts with flat finished counts mean the schedule is not converging. Since v3.0 the store limit mechanism caps per-store operator speed and hot-region-schedule-limit caps hotspot scheduling, so stalled scheduling is checked against these flow-control settings first.

nodes.name: PD startup error runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: PD validates its etcd member list and encryption key files at startup, and most PD APIs only work after TiKV bootstraps the cluster. Differential diagnosis: 'TiKV cluster is not bootstrapped' on a new deployment just means TiKV has not started yet; 'etcd cluster ID mismatch' means --initial-cluster contains a member from another cluster; the encryption ErrEncryptionNewMasterKey error means the key file sits under /root, which is unsupported even with read permissions. Remedy families: start TiKV first for bootstrap errors, remove the wrong member from --initial-cluster and restart PD, or move the key file outside the root directory. Risks: member deletion is destructive, so verify which cluster each member belongs to before editing.

nodes.name: Mitigate PD TSO Unavailability Impact
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV caches TSO batches locally (causal-ts renew-interval 100ms); a PD leader failover still causes a short latency rise and about 15% QPS dip, and PD supplies at most 262144 TSOs per 50ms physical interval. Differential: distinguish TSO jitter (short, cluster-wide, synchronized with PD events) from store-level problems. Remedies: enlarge causal-ts alloc-ahead-buffer (e.g. 6s) and renew batch sizes together with a smaller PD tso-update-physical-interval (API V2), or enable pd.enable-forwarding to route around isolation - risk: forwarding misjudges failures and reduces availability, and oversized TSO batches drain the global TSO supply. Client-visible timeout storms can be tuned with tidb_backoff_weight, which scales the internal retry ceiling (base TSO timeout 15s times the weight); raise it on poor networks to absorb transient failures or lower it to fail fast. TiDB-side commit timeouts are bounded by tikv-client.commit-timeout (41s, required to exceed twice the Raft election timeout), so commit timeout errors during TiKV instability surface after that ceiling.

nodes.name: pd-worker Task Backlog
nodes.content: Mechanism: the single-threaded pd-worker reporting Region metadata piles up tasks under massive Regions or frequent leader changes, so routing updates lag. Differential: Worker pending tasks stay high in the TiKV panel; reads/writes proceed but PD scheduling becomes inaccurate and Region cache refreshes need extra round trips. Fix family: reduce Region churn/count and relieve the reporting path.

nodes.name: Background I/O Jitter Remediation
nodes.content: Scheduling, compaction, GC and TiFlash compression contend with foreground traffic and produce QPS/latency jitter even at moderate averages; remedy families: region-score-formula-version v2 plus sane store-limit to stop redundant balancing, enable-cross-table-merge to shrink empty-Region overhead, rate-limiter-auto-tuned for compaction I/O, gc.enable-compaction-filter to merge GC with compaction, and bg_task_io_rate_limit for TiFlash background tasks. Some flags were experimental when introduced - validate per version.

nodes.name: Performance Overview Analysis Method
nodes.content: The Performance Overview dashboard locates bottlenecks top-down: the database time overview shows whether user response time is spent in the database and which SQL type dominates the workload profile; the load profile section adds QPS, connection counts, command types, TSO/KV request rates and resource usage; the top-down latency breakdown splits query latency into connection idle ratio, execution phases, TSO/KV request latency and TiKV write latency. Use it to decide whether to tune the application, the optimizer, or storage before deeper analysis.

nodes.name: Pessimistic Lock Contention Remedies
nodes.content: Pessimistic DML persists row locks in TiKV during an Acquire Pessimistic Lock phase before 2PC, so contended rows block writers up to innodb_lock_wait_timeout (error 1205), cyclic waits are auto-resolved by killing one victim (error 1213), and NOWAIT fails fast (error 3572) while snapshot readers are never blocked; Point Get and Batch Point Get lock keys even when they match no rows. Distinguish from resource saturation by lock-wait errors and sessions stuck waiting on specific keys; fix family: shorten transactions, add indexes so locking predicates hit few rows, narrow locks with FOR UPDATE OF TABLES, kill the blocker, or tune the wait timeout; risks include more 1205 aborts under timeout shrinking.

nodes.name: Pessimistic Lock Error Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: pessimistic conflicts surface in three timeout forms - statement-level lock waits exceeding innodb_lock_wait_timeout return ERROR 1205, write-conflict re-locking retries bounded by pessimistic-txn.max-retry-count log 'retry limit reached', and transactions running past performance.max-txn-ttl (default one hour) hit 'TTL manager has timed out'; autocommit statements first try optimistic mode and switch to pessimistic on conflict. Discrimination: match the exact error to its knob, and use Lock View to identify the blocking transaction and hot keys. Fix family: restructure application access or shorten transactions, enable tidb_pessimistic_txn_fair_locking for high same-key concurrency (trading some throughput), raise the matching timeout only with justification, and split oversized transactions.

nodes.name: Pipeline Retries and EOF Errors
nodes.content: When import/export/replication components log many retries and EOF errors without other logical errors, the root cause is usually network degradation between nodes. Diagnosis: measure bandwidth and jitter between the affected nodes (for example iperf3 server/client runs); read_log on component logs confirms the retry pattern. Remedies: fix the network path with the provider, and only after connectivity is verified consider upgrading components.

nodes.name: Pipelined DML For Large Transactions
nodes.content: Standard transactions buffer every mutation in memory (red-black tree, O(N log N)) so multi-million-row DML hits TiDB memory limits and OOM; Pipelined DML (tidb_dml_type, v8.0+) streams writes instead - measured 2x faster with roughly half the peak TiDB memory and a smoother TiKV write flow. For bulk ETL-scale changes prefer pipelined DML, batched key-range transactions, or non-transactional DML depending on atomicity requirements.

nodes.name: PITR Chain and Log Reachability
nodes.content: Mechanism: PITR is a snapshot-plus-log chain; a point is recoverable only if a snapshot precedes it and log backup covers through it, where the global checkpoint (min of TiKV local checkpoints) is the cluster-wide continuity boundary. Differential diagnosis: compare snapshot BackupTS, log start boundary, global/log checkpoint, requested recovery point, retention window, and actual object inventory - a chain can look healthy while a segment is missing, corrupt, or out of retention, and a successful snapshot phase does not prove log-phase reachability. Repair family: pick a recovery point within the proven retained interval, restore the missing backup chain segment, or report that recovery cannot be proven; after a failed log restore, handle the paused-GC state with an explicit version-appropriate decision instead of silently changing GC or retention. A PITR restore point composes a prior snapshot (full-backup-storage) with log backup segments up to the restored timestamp, so retention cleanup that deletes snapshot data or truncates log backup segments (br log truncate --until) inside the recoverable window is itself a first-class cause of chain gaps. During log restore each TiKV worker downloads, rewrites table/index IDs, and applies KVs through raft, and BR retries ranges that fail with RegionNotFound or EpochNotMatch (for example a store down mid-restore) while unretryable ranges fail the task. Safe retention cleanup truncates only log backup earlier than the last full snapshot's end-version obtained via br validate decode. SQL-level RESTORE requires RESTORE_ADMIN or SUPER privilege and only one BACKUP/RESTORE task may run at a time, so a queued restore can masquerade as a hung one - check SHOW RESTORES for actual task state.

nodes.name: BR Checkpoint Restore Identity
nodes.content: Mechanism: BR checkpoint restore is version-scoped and bound to one request's upstream identity, snapshot BackupTS, log start-ts, restored-ts, and downstream target, plus target-side table identities and ID mapping. Differential diagnosis: if retry fails, check which identity component changed - upstream, backup, time range, target, or post-failure external DDL/data changes that blur restore-owned vs operator-owned state. Repair family: exact resume only when everything agrees; otherwise preserve the source and backup objects, retire the incompatible attempt through the restore control plane, make the old target unavailable for restore writes, and rerun on a newly isolated target - never delete checkpoint metadata, ID mappings, or log segments to force compatibility. Snapshot checkpoints persist restored key ranges with the target table ID, so recreating a table before retry changes its ID and bypasses the old checkpoint; log checkpoints address files by (log metadata name, file-metadata array offset, file offset) under a stable backup-to-restored-cluster ID mapping. Risks: GC is deliberately paused during log restore (gc.ratio-threshold set negative) and stays paused if br exits halfway, needing manual re-enable; a system-level kill loses up to the metadata flush interval of progress; and writing, deleting, or renaming tables mid-restore makes checkpoints ambiguous. Since v7.1.0 an interrupted recovery task resumes from its breakpoint by simply restarting it - deleting already restored data is never required. Restoring statistics before v7.6.0 loads them together with table info into memory, while later releases keep stats in a separate file restored per table, so memory pressure during restore is version-bound.

nodes.name: PITR Deployment Prerequisites
nodes.content: Mechanism: PiTR requires TiDB >= v6.2.0 with BR at exactly the cluster version, network reachability from BR to every PD and TiKV node, and identical BR/PD time zones, or backups and restores misbehave; backup storage must pre-grant S3 privileges (ListBucket/Get/Put/Delete/AbortMultipartUpload) and separate snapshot-${date} versus log-backup directories. Diagnosis: for backup or restore start failures, verify BR/TiDB version match, connectivity, time zone equality, and IAM permissions before deeper debugging. Remedies: install BR via tiup with the matching version, fix firewall paths, and structure the bucket by snapshot and log prefixes with a retention policy; risk of a time zone mismatch is restore-point confusion that shifts recovery objectives.

nodes.name: PITR restore throughput planning
nodes.content: PITR throughput baselines are roughly 2TiB/h snapshot and 30GiB/h log data per TiKV node, and br log truncate deletes about 600GB/h; restores slow down when many Regions with short flush intervals create many small files, raising per-batch overhead. Levers: TiKV import.num-threads, br pitr-concurrency, and moderately raising pitr-batch-size (16MiB default) / pitr-batch-count (8 default), whichever threshold hits first closes a batch.

nodes.name: Placement policy leader distribution
nodes.content: Placement policies control where Raft leaders sit: LEADER_CONSTRAINTS pins leaders to a region and availability still wins on failure (a new leader is elected elsewhere) unless the #evict-leader constraint marks that fallback region; PRIMARY_REGION with SCHEDULE=EVEN spreads followers for availability while MAJORITY_IN_PRIMARY keeps most followers in the primary for lower-latency commits but has no automatic failover when the primary region dies.

nodes.name: Placement Policy Diagnosis and Repair
nodes.content: Mechanism: FOLLOWERS=n means n followers plus the leader; PRIMARY_REGION/REGIONS/SCHEDULE cannot combine with CONSTRAINTS; placement changes are asynchronous PD scheduling where admission is not convergence, and binding follows database default < table < partition precedence with the keyword DEFAULT meaning inherit. Differential diagnosis: correlate information_schema.placement_policies, SHOW PLACEMENT states (PENDING/INPROGRESS/SCHEDULED), TABLES/PARTITIONS TIDB_PLACEMENT_POLICY_NAME bindings, Store labels, and Region peers, distinguishing a single-Store capacity mismatch from a service outage and checking partition overrides explicitly. Repair family: apply the smallest repair - reset only the target object bindings to DEFAULT (both table and partition if both explicit), never alter a shared policy definition, copy a neighbor's policy, or change PD scheduling to fake satisfaction, and close only after the exact target object converges with protected neighbors and business truth unchanged. Physically validate convergence by counting healthy voter peers, learner state, leader location, and fault-domain labels per target Region via TIKV_REGION_PEERS, TIKV_STORE_STATUS, and SHOW PLACEMENT LABELS, because a business query can stay successful while the migration is unsafe or incomplete.

nodes.name: Placement Policy Management
nodes.content: Mechanism: placement policies map replicas/leaders to stores by label constraints and are applied asynchronously, and inheritance means database defaults do not retroactively affect existing tables while table-level changes do propagate to partitions. Differential diagnosis: check SHOW PLACEMENT for scheduling progress, SHOW CREATE PLACEMENT POLICY and information_schema.placement_policies for definitions, tidb_placement_policy_name in information_schema.tables/partitions for attachments, and pd-ctl config placement-rules show for effective rules including global replica count (ALTER RANGE global / config set max-replicas, requiring TiKV instances >= replicas and reserve storage). Remedy families: (1) ALTER the policy or re-attach at table/partition level; (2) adjust rule groups or store labels/weights in pd-ctl; (3) for planned DR switchover, attach the secondary-region policy to user tables and shift PD leader_priority, then verify leader transfer on dashboards. Risks: PRIMARY_REGION/REGIONS/SCHEDULE cannot combine with CONSTRAINTS (error); improperly written rules can silently reduce replica counts and weaken high availability; policy changes reschedule snapshots, adding I/O load.

nodes.name: Placement Rule Bundle Operations
nodes.content: Mechanism: PD placement rules bind key ranges to replica counts, roles, and label constraints, organized in groups whose index and override flag decide precedence; table key ranges are obtained with tidb-ctl keyrange --encode. Diagnosis: for replicas violating expectations, fetch the rule bundle (rule-bundle get/load) and check which rule and group matches the target key range, remembering that DDL can change table IDs and invalidate rules. Remedies: edit counts, roles (e.g. follower-only zones), or label constraints and apply with rule-bundle set/save; use a high-index override group to force placement such as SSD migration or dedicated TiFlash learners; risk is that override rules shadow default replica rules and can leave ranges under-replicated if mis-scoped.

nodes.name: Placement Rules Switch Semantics
nodes.content: Placement Rules are enabled by default since v5.0; once multiple rules exist, PD ignores max-replicas, location-labels, and isolation-level, so replica-count or label problems must be fixed through the rules interface instead of the legacy replication config. Disabling placement rules reverts PD to those legacy settings while retaining all configured rules for re-enablement, which explains placement behavior flipping after a pd-ctl config placement-rules disable.

nodes.name: Execution Plan Bottleneck Reading
nodes.content: Mechanism: plans execute bottom-up but are read first-child-first top-down; blocking operators (TopN, HashAgg) materialize their full input, and memory/disk columns expose pressure. Diagnosis: scan execution info top-down for the first operator with high time, then compare actRows with estRows - a severe underestimation can make a HashJoin build an oversized table, get killed by memory control, or lock in a wrong join order. Fix family: refresh statistics first to restore estimates, add an index when a high-actRows TableFullScan dominates, then steer join order or method with hints or bindings.
