Risks: pinning a plan before fixing statistics freezes decisions on wrong estimates.

nodes.name: Plan Cache Diagnosis and Tuning
nodes.content: Mechanism: cached plans skip optimization, but misses come from unsupported statements (subqueries, TiFlash access, system views, Order By ?), StmtClose clearing the cache, schema/DDL or binding changes invalidating entries, or LRU and memory-guard eviction; cached plans also ignore statistics updates and can be suboptimal for skewed parameter values. Diagnosis: compare avg-hit plus avg-miss with StmtExecute, check @@last_plan_from_cache, watch compile-phase share of DB time, and the Plan Cache Memory Usage / Plan Num panels. Fix family: cache prepared objects client-side, set tidb_ignore_prepared_cache_close_stmt, size tidb_session_plan_cache_size and tidb_plan_cache_max_plan_size, or enable the non-prepared plan cache. Risks: per-plan memory (~100 KiB per session-plan) scales with sessions; a stale cached plan can regress specific parameter values.

nodes.name: Prepared Plan Cache Malfunction
nodes.content: With the (formerly experimental) prepared plan cache enabled, specific TiDB versions can surface invalid connection errors in applications and slow-query tooling. Verify by disabling the cache (tidb_enable_prepared_plan_cache=OFF) and re-testing; if errors stop, either stay with the cache off or upgrade to a version with the fix. Risk: disabling increases compile overhead for prepared statements.

nodes.name: Prepared Plan Cache Miss Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: prepared statement plans are not cached when the query pattern is uncacheable (subqueries) or parameters may change the plan (implicit type conversion), so each execution recompiles. Discrimination: SHOW WARNINGS after PREPARE/execute prints 'skip plan-cache: ...' with the exact reason. Fix family: rewrite uncacheable patterns or align parameter types with column types to restore caching; accept misses where rewriting is not possible and monitor compile time instead.

nodes.name: Non-prepared plan cache trade-off
nodes.content: The non-prepared plan cache speeds up generic TP workloads but adds matching/parameterization overhead that turns into a net loss when the hit rate is low. Verify candidates with EXPLAIN FORMAT=plan_cache (plain EXPLAIN never touches the cache) and read the skip reason from SHOW WARNINGS; watch the non-prepared hit and non-prepared-unsupported OPS panels and disable the feature when most queries are unsupported. Prepared-plan cache misses show their reason in SHOW WARNINGS after execution (v8.0+), so a plan-cache-heavy workload that regressed should first be checked for silent bypass - new predicate shapes, non-deterministic functions, or DDL invalidations - before assuming a bad cached plan; likewise Apply-operator concurrency blocking is named in SHOW WARNINGS.

nodes.name: Tune Plan Cache and Optimizer Variables for Compile Overhead
nodes.content: Mechanism: high CPU on compilation and unstable point-query latency come from plan cache misses (small tidb_session_plan_cache_size, prepared statements closed each execution) or disabled rule-based optimizations. Remedies: enlarge plan cache (default 100), enable non-prepared plan cache and tidb_ignore_prepared_cache_close_stmt, raise tidb_stats_load_sync_wait (default 100ms) so stats load before compilation, and enable targeted tidb_opt_fix_control entries per workload; baseline capture (tidb_capture_plan_baselines) depends on statement summary and evolves plans only inside its configured time window with per-task max time. Risk: fix controls and optimizer variables change plans cluster-wide - verify with EXPLAIN and canary instances before global rollout. Related optimizer switches: tidb_runtime_filter_mode OFF/LOCAL (GLOBAL unsupported) governs hash-join runtime filters, tidb_opt_enable_non_eval_scalar_subquery=ON stops EXPLAIN from executing slow scalar subqueries during online troubleshooting, and individual tidb_opt_fix_control entries isolate specific optimizer behavior changes after upgrades. When applications deallocate prepared statements after every execution, tidb_ignore_prepared_cache_close_stmt=ON keeps cached plans reusable; plan cache hit and miss OPS graphs verify the effect.

nodes.name: Plan Cache Skip Warnings
nodes.content: Mechanism: when the prepared plan cache refuses to cache a plan, TiDB emits a warning such as 'skip plan-cache: value may be converted to INT', because parameter type conversion could change the plan; the slow query log and Dashboard slow query page also carry a Warnings field since v6.6.0. Diagnosis: for queries that never hit plan cache, execute once and run SHOW WARNINGS to read the skip reason. Remedies: align parameter types with column types so plans become cacheable, or accept cache misses where conversion is required; risk of forcing types wrongly is implicit conversions that also break index usage.

nodes.name: Execution Plan Regression Detection
nodes.content: Mechanism: a previously fast statement class turns slow when its plan changes, usually after statistics drift or parameter range shifts. Discrimination: group cluster_slow_query by digest and count distinct plan_digest; entries with more than one plan indicate plan flips - fetch each plan via plan_digest and compare; also compare per-instance slow-query counts to separate node-specific effects. Fix family: refresh statistics, pin the good plan with a binding or hint, or constrain the query pattern; verify the plan stays stable across parameter ranges.

nodes.name: Plan Regression Remediation
nodes.content: Mechanism: the optimizer switches a statement class to a slower plan when statistics, data volume, or optimizer behavior changes (e.g. after upgrades). Diagnosis: compare per-statement latency in statements summary, EXPLAIN the regressed statement, and inspect existing bindings. Fix family: pin the good plan with CREATE GLOBAL BINDING / SQL Plan Management and baseline evolution, or use optimizer fix controls to suppress post-upgrade behavior changes; verify the new plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Risks: stale bindings outlive data distribution changes, so review and drop bindings that no longer help.

nodes.name: Plan Replayer Continuous Capture
nodes.content: Mechanism: PLAN REPLAYER CONTINUOUS CAPTURE, enabled via tidb_enable_plan_replayer_continuous_capture = ON, asynchronously saves a PLAN REPLAYER bundle (plan, statistics, and environment) for each SQL/plan digest exactly once, so on-site plan evidence exists even for intermittent regressions. Diagnosis: for plan regressions that vanished before inspection, list capture results for the statement digest and download the matching bundle. Remedies: keep capture ON during risky windows and analyze bundles offline or share them for replay; risk is extra storage for captured bundles on busy clusters.

nodes.name: Plan Replayer Load Reproduction
nodes.content: Mechanism: PLAN REPLAYER LOAD 'file.zip' restores a saved scene (session variables, bindings, table schemas, statistics) into another TiDB cluster so plans can be diagnosed offline; imported statistics get overwritten unless auto analyze is disabled first, and the mysql client needs --local-infile=true or the load errors 2068. Diagnosis: when reproducing a plan regression on a test cluster, verify after loading that stats_meta and the EXPLAIN output match the source. Remedies: disable tidb_enable_auto_analyze around the load, run the target statement, then compare plans; risk is contaminating a shared test cluster with production bindings and variables.

nodes.name: Post-Delete Space and Speed Behavior
nodes.content: Mechanism: DELETE removes rows but frees space only after compaction, while TRUNCATE/DROP free space at the next GC round (about 10 minutes by default); large deletes leave useless keys and empty regions that slow range scans until region merge and compaction finish. Diagnosis: after a mass delete, correlate slow queries with high MVCC/old-key reads and many small regions rather than assuming index loss. Remedies: run dos2volume-style compaction by letting GC and region merge proceed, or schedule deletes in batches; risk is that immediate re-import into the same keyspace still pays cleanup costs for a while.

nodes.name: Subquery Preprocessing and Rewrites
nodes.content: Uncorrelated subqueries default to semi join; special shapes are rewritten logically: < ALL / > ANY become MIN/MAX with explicit NULL-guarding (empty or NULL-bearing subqueries flip results), != ANY expands to a distinct-count form, and = ALL collapses to false when the subquery has more than one distinct value. When a rewritten subquery misbehaves, compare plans with the equivalent explicit aggregate formulation.

nodes.name: Primary-secondary cluster replication
nodes.content: A warm standby is built by seeding with BR snapshot and streaming TiCDC incremental into the secondary (TiDB or MySQL); when the primary fails, redo log replays to the last consistent point before promotion, giving eventual consistency between clusters. Diagnose standby incidents by checkpoint state and redo apply status rather than by comparing live row counts.

nodes.name: Privilege anomaly runbook
nodes.content: Privilege data lives in mysql.user, mysql.db, and mysql.tables_priv and is cached in TiDB memory at startup: GRANT/REVOKE/CREATE USER/DROP USER take effect immediately, but direct DML on those tables does not until FLUSH PRIVILEGES. Login identity is the first matching row of the sorted privilege tables (Host ranked before User), so overlapping host patterns can bind a login to an unexpected account and privilege set. Privilege data lives in mysql.user, mysql.db, and mysql.tables_priv and is cached in TiDB memory at startup: GRANT/REVOKE/CREATE USER/DROP USER take effect immediately, but direct DML on those tables does not until FLUSH PRIVILEGES. Login identity is the first matching row of the sorted privilege tables (Host ranked before User), so overlapping host patterns can bind a login to an unexpected account. Account lockout is account-level only: FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS with PASSWORD_LOCK_TIME locks an account after N consecutive wrong passwords (network failures and unknown users do not count, and high-concurrency logins get slower), while password_history/password_reuse_interval block reuse of recent passwords. Privilege data lives in mysql.user, mysql.db, and mysql.tables_priv and is cached in TiDB memory at startup: GRANT/REVOKE/CREATE USER/DROP USER take effect immediately, but direct DML on those tables does not until FLUSH PRIVILEGES - changing passwords with UPDATE mysql.user is the classic mistake and ALTER USER IDENTIFIED BY is the correct form. Login identity is the first matching row of the sorted privilege tables (Host ranked before User), so overlapping host patterns can bind a login to an unexpected account; login authentication uses MySQL-style SASL challenge-response. Account lockout is account-level only: FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS with PASSWORD_LOCK_TIME locks an account after N consecutive wrong passwords (network failures and unknown users do not count, and high-concurrency logins get slower), while password_history/password_reuse_interval block reuse of recent passwords.

nodes.name: Processlist Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: SHOW PROCESSLIST lists only sessions on the TiDB instance the client connected to (TiDB is a stateless multi-node SQL layer), shows session ids rather than OS pids, and its State column is not continuously updated because parallel statements occupy several states at once. Diagnosis: when hunting a stuck session, remember to check processlist on every TiDB instance or use the cluster-wide processlist view instead of assuming one node shows all sessions. Remedies: aggregate processlist across instances, then kill the offending session id on its own node; risk is concluding a transaction disappeared when it merely lives on another TiDB node.

nodes.name: Connection preservation runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: tiup cluster restart stops TiDB servers without rolling, so every session breaks; TiProxy migrates sessions only when all TiDB instances share the same session-token-signing cert and graceful-wait-before-shutdown exceeds the longest transaction. Differential: correlate drop time with restart/reload/upgrade events, compare session-token certs across TiDB instances, and compare graceful-wait-before-shutdown against the longest transaction duration from monitoring. Remedies: (a) use tiup cluster reload/upgrade (rolling) instead of restart for planned changes; (b) raise graceful-wait-before-shutdown above the longest transaction; (c) deploy at least two TiProxy instances behind an LB/VIP and pin the TiProxy version so cluster upgrades skip it; (d) if QPS plateaus while TiDB has headroom, treat proxy network bandwidth as the bottleneck and split into more, smaller TiProxy instances. Risks: a TiProxy upgrade inside a cluster upgrade disconnects clients; proxy restarts should be avoided because most config items support online change.

nodes.name: ProxySQL Query Rule Routing Pitfalls
nodes.content: Mechanism: ProxySQL query rules match in ascending rule_id order; a common split routes ^SELECT.*FOR UPDATE$ and writes to the writer hostgroup and other ^SELECT to a reader hostgroup, and transaction_persistent (default on) pins every statement of a transaction to the default hostgroup so transactions never straddle backends. Diagnosis: read-your-writes misses, missing rows, or lock errors through the proxy usually mean a rule mismatch - verify which hostgroup served the query (rule order, regex anchoring with ^/$) and whether the statement ran inside a transaction. Remedy family: correct rule ordering/regex, keep SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and writes on the writer hostgroup, rely on transaction_persistent for intra-transaction consistency; rules can also reroute or reject queries to shed overload.

nodes.name: QPS Jitter Comparison Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: a transient event (large batch writes, expensive queries, big analytical scans) steals capacity from normal traffic. Differential: compare the abnormal window against a normal baseline of equal length and rank max-diff items - surging coprocessor scans point to large analytical queries, high per-transaction written KV counts point to batch DML, rising leader-transfer counts mean scheduling coincided with the jitter; queries absent from the slow log still show up as expensive_query warnings or coprocessor load. Fix family: throttle or reshape the offending batch workload and reschedule it off peak.

nodes.name: Raft Engine IO Contention
nodes.content: TiKV write latency spikes when the Raft Engine (the WAL) shares a disk with KV RocksDB: every synchronous write batch calls fdatasync(), so the WAL device shows very high flushes/sec and queue depth competing with data I/O. Distinguish by comparing per-device flush rate and utilization; fix family: move raft-engine to a dedicated low-latency disk and enable log recycle, precondition is an available disk, risk is a brief latency blip during migration.

nodes.name: Raft Majority Commit and Geo-Distributed HA
nodes.content: TiKV replicates each write as a Raft log from the Leader to Followers and commits once a majority acknowledges, so availability under node failure depends on keeping a majority of replicas alive. Geo-distributed three-data-center deployments stay multi-active only when inter-DC network latency and stability are good (keep latency around 5 ms or lower).

nodes.name: Massive Region Raftstore Bottleneck
nodes.content: Mechanism: Raftstore polls every Region's message queue in a thread pool, so millions of Regions per store burn CPU on heartbeats and message polling; when Raft store CPU reaches about 85% of raftstore.store-pool-size the module becomes the bottleneck and propose wait duration climbs to hundreds of milliseconds, while commit log duration above 200-500 ms with fluctuation indicates heavy load, slow append, or network congestion. Diagnosis: read Thread-CPU Raft store CPU, Raft Propose propose wait duration (reference below 50-100 ms), and Raft IO commit log duration in the TiKV dashboard. Remedies: reduce Region count per store via region merge or higher split thresholds and cut per-Region message volume; risk is that raising pool sizes only masks the heartbeat overhead rather than removing it.

nodes.name: Raftstore Overload Diagnosis
nodes.content: Commit Log Duration spans copying raft logs to followers (thus usually the largest), Append Log Duration measures leader/follower log writes in Store threads, and Apply Log Duration measures log application in Apply threads; a Commit/Append spike with low Apply points at Store-side CPU or I/O limits, high network between TiKV nodes, or mis-sized pools. Remedies: adjust raftstore.store-pool-size / apply-pool-size moderately (oversizing also degrades), enable raft-engine for a lighter write path, or raftstore.store-io-pool-size for StoreWriter I/O; note these batch-level metrics do not map 1:1 to per-request Store/Apply durations.

nodes.name: RBAC Role Grant vs Enablement
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB RBAC (MySQL 8.0-like) stores roles in mysql.user and supports multi-level privilege inheritance, but granting a role to a user does not activate it - the role must be enabled separately before its privileges apply, so a user can hold correct grants yet still get access-denied. Diagnosis: compare SHOW GRANTS (granted) against the session's active roles to distinguish a missing grant from an unenabled role; granting or revoking roles itself requires SUPER (or the CREATE USER/CREATE ROLE privileges for role creation). Repair family: enable the role (session or default role setting) or adjust grants; keep role graph free of accidental self-grants even though relation loops are tolerated.

nodes.name: Engine Selection Hint Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: CBO decides between TiKV row storage and TiFlash columnar replicas by cost, and read_from_storage(tikv|tiflash[table]) overrides it per table; the hint needs the alias when a table has one, does not apply inside CTEs, and a mixed plan showing both cop[tiflash] and cop[tikv] means the query legitimately spans both engines. Diagnosis: when an analytical query unexpectedly scans TiKV (or a transactional one hits TiFlash), EXPLAIN and inspect the task column. Remedies: pin the engine with the hint using aliases, restructure CTE queries so the hint lands on real table references, and let CBO decide when statistics are healthy; risk of forcing TiFlash is freshness and resource limits of the columnar replica for latency-sensitive reads.

nodes.name: Read Hotspot Mitigation
nodes.content: Mechanism: reads concentrate on a single leader or Region (typically small tables under heavy access), queuing on one TiKV node while others idle. Diagnosis: Key Visualizer bright horizontal bands, coprocessor CPU skew across stores, and per-store QPS skew. Fix family: coprocessor cache for small-table hot reads, load-based replica read threshold to flee queued leaders, follower read or stale read where staleness is acceptable, cached tables, and TiKV in-memory engine when MVCC version accumulation slows hot reads. Risks: replica/stale reads trade freshness guarantees; caches only serve unchanged Regions.

nodes.name: Read versus Write Database Time Split
nodes.content: Mechanism: overall database time splits into SELECT (read) and write portions, telling whether slowness is a read or a write problem before deeper analysis. Discrimination: read-dominant time leads to top-SQL plan analysis of point-get and scan paths; write-dominant time leads to conflict checking (latch wait) then lock and commit duration analysis. Fix family: follow the corresponding read or write breakdown workflow instead of tuning blindly.

nodes.name: Cluster Read-Only Switch Semantics
nodes.content: tidb_super_read_only and tidb_restricted_read_only make the whole cluster eventually read-only: the change propagates asynchronously, so some servers stay writable briefly; since v6.2.0 the flag is also checked at commit, catching long-running autocommit writes; uncommitted read-only transactions commit, writes inside non-read-only transactions are rejected. tidb_restricted_read_only=ON forces super_read_only ON and blocks turning it off except for holders of RESTRICTED_REPLICA_WRITER_ADMIN. Diagnosis: SELECT @@global.tidb_super_read_only and @@global.tidb_restricted_read_only. Remedies: turn the switch OFF (needs SUPER or SYSTEM_VARIABLES_ADMIN) and verify propagation across all TiDB servers.

nodes.name: Region Failover and Switchover Discipline
nodes.content: Mechanism: DR paths trade RPO against RTO - replicas inside one cluster (or DR Auto-Sync) give zero-to-second-level RPO, TiCDC primary-secondary replication gives second-level RPO with redo logs buffering unapplied transactions, and BR/PITR restore gives minute-level RPO - and switchover means moving leaders or replication direction, not just restarting endpoints. Differential diagnosis: monitor both clusters and the changefeed checkpoint, record the target position with TIDB_CURRENT_TSO and compare against the replicated position before promoting, and separate planned switchover (drain, verify TSO >= Position) from disaster switchover (apply cdc redo to a transaction-consistent state). Repair family: for a two-region placement deployment stop the failed region and move user-table leaders by reattaching the secondary placement rule, checking leader distribution and labels via TIKV_STORE_STATUS; for TiCDC DR remove the old changefeed and rebuild the reverse one without start-ts after redo apply; after the primary region recovers, switch leaders back symmetrically, and if the primary is unrecoverable rebuild the whole DR pair from a fresh backup restore. After an unplanned failover the downstream may lag because TiCDC writes transactions concurrently; redo apply brings it to a transaction-consistent point, then rebuild reliability by restoring a full BR backup of the promoted cluster into a fresh primary and creating a new changefeed. TiCDC eventually consistent replication targets RTO <= 5 minutes and P95 RPO <= 10 seconds with redo logs on object storage or NFS. Keep the reverse replication link for an observation period (about a week of stable operation) before removing the reverse changefeed and deleting the old cluster; while retaining the old cluster raise tidb_gc_life_time so its versions survive, and restore the original value if kept long-term.

nodes.name: Region Count and Size Tuning
nodes.content: Mechanism: massive numbers of small Regions inflate raftstore, heartbeat, and scheduling overhead and pressure the PD leader with Region information requests, while oversized Regions slow scheduling and large-range scans. Diagnosis: Region inventory metrics, PD leader CPU under high Region-query concurrency, scan concurrency per query. Fix family: raise Region size within the recommended 48-256 MiB range, enable Hibernate Region or Region Merge for empty-Region accumulation, add buckets for concurrent scans of big Regions, and offload Region info requests with Active PD Follower. Risks: buckets and Active PD Follower are experimental; going beyond about 1 GiB per Region risks jitter and slow scheduling.

nodes.name: Region Read Progress Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: stale reads and DataIsNotReady errors occur when a region's safe_ts or resolved_ts stalls, usually because locks in the region's resolver block resolved-ts advancement. Diagnosis: find the offending region from Grafana Min Resolved TS Region / Min Safe TS Region panels or DataIsNotReady logs, then run tikv-ctl get-region-read-progress -r <region> --log [--min-start-ts <ts>] to dump safe_ts, resolved_ts, and the smallest lock start_ts blocking progress. Remedies: commit, roll back, or kill the blocking transaction once identified, and watch safe_ts resume; risk is killing transactions whose semantics the application still needs.

nodes.name: Region Size and Bucket Tuning
nodes.content: Excessive Region count overloads raftstore and PD scheduling; since v6.1.0 coprocessor.region-split-size can enlarge Regions to reduce their number, and bucket (sub-Range) concurrency keeps query parallelism on larger Regions while adapting hotspot Region sizes. Raft Engine is the default log storage since v6.1.0, cutting TiKV write IO and tail latency, so log-write stalls should first be attributed within Raft Engine metrics rather than RocksDB WAL.

nodes.name: Region split/merge control runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: hot tables concentrate traffic on few regions, so operators pre-split with SPLIT TABLE/PARTITION [INDEX] ... BETWEEN/REGIONS or BY values and scatter; but empty or newly-freed split regions are merged back by PD after the split-merge-interval (about one hour) unless the table or partition sets merge_option=deny via ALTER TABLE ... ATTRIBUTES. Differential diagnosis: check SHOW TABLE REGIONS / region topread/topwrite for concentration, and information_schema.attributes for existing merge_option settings; remember partition attributes override table attributes, and a partitioned table stays split per partition unless attributes are reset. Remedy families: (1) pre-split plus merge_option=deny for write hotspots on new tables; (2) keep manual read-hotspot splits with merge_option=deny after the hotspot passes; (3) allow/trigger Region Merge to clean up sparse regions after mass deletes. Risks: too many small regions raise PD heartbeat load; denying merge keeps empty regions consuming scheduling inventory.

nodes.name: Region Unavailable Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: a Raft group loses quorum or its leader so reads/writes on that Region fail; TiDB backoffs and retries internally (default threshold 20s) before surfacing ERROR 9005 to the client - 'TiKV server is busy' is flow control and may not count toward backoff. Discrimination: errors on a narrow key range mean few affected Regions (leader drop or restart); simultaneous OOM on multiple TiKV instances leaves Regions leaderless; co-located TiKV instances on one physical machine fail together when labels are misconfigured; 'epoch not match' after election means a lagging follower became leader. Fix family: wait for re-election, restore or restart failed TiKV instances, fix placement labels to spread replicas, reduce write pressure, and verify via error rate and per-store leader counts. Region membership changes (add and remove peer) were two steps before v5.0 and a crash mid-change made Regions unavailable; Raft Joint Consensus (enable-joint-consensus, default on) merges them so the intermediate state survives member failure.

nodes.name: Remote Troubleshooting Data Collection
nodes.content: Mechanism: when a cluster problem cannot be located locally, support escalation needs a complete, consistent diagnostic bundle rather than scattered manual captures; time-window collection (e.g. the two hours covering the incident) keeps bundles small, and air-gapped clusters use encrypted package upload. Diagnosis: use the diag client to collect logs, configs, metrics, and system info with one command, run its quick configuration health check to surface latent risks, and upload the bundle so remote support can reproduce the state. Remedy family: one-click collection replaces error-prone manual gathering; prerequisite is a TiUP/TiDB Operator deployment, credentials for SQL-level data, and optionally log redaction before collection.

nodes.name: Post-Replication Data Check
nodes.content: Mechanism: replication completeness is verified by comparing row data at consistent points; sync-diff-inspector can attach to a DM task via dm-addr plus dm-task name, automatically resolve upstream/downstream schema mapping after table routing, and export fix SQL for differing tables. Diagnosis: before cutover or when upstream/downstream row counts or samples diverge, run a data check over the routed target tables (check-thread-count sized to connection budget; check-struct-only for schema-only comparison). Remedy family: apply the exported fix SQL for confirmed diffs or re-sync the affected tables; prerequisite is a stable checkpoint or quiesced writes during comparison.

nodes.name: Resolved TS and Safe TS Stall
nodes.content: Mechanism: resolved-ts is computed from active transaction start-ts, so locks held by big prewrites or long-running transactions block its advance; a TiDB coordinator that crashes after prewrite leaves locks that TiDB resolves automatically. Differential: run tikv-ctl with --log or search TiDB/TiKV logs for the lock start_ts (a query over 60 seconds also prints an expensive_query log line containing txn_start_ts), fall back to information_schema.cluster_tidb_trx for active transactions, and SHOW PROCESSLIST for long statements; check network plus the Check Leader Duration panel when CheckLeader is suspected. Remedies: (a) fix application logic that holds transactions open; (b) prioritize killing or optimizing the slow query inside the transaction; (c) do nothing for orphaned locks from a crashed coordinator unless the problem persists. Risks: large-transaction locks hinder resolve-ts progress and therefore stale-read freshness for the whole cluster.

nodes.name: Resource Control Error Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: resource control rejects or terminates queries against group quotas and runaway rules. Discrimination: ERROR 8252 means quota exceeded (oversized transactions or too many concurrent transactions in one group); 8253/8254 mean the query matched a runaway/threshold or quarantine-watch rule; ERROR 8250 means the feature itself is disabled. Fix family: reduce transaction size or client concurrency, adjust the group quota or runaway watch rules, or enable tidb_enable_resource_control; each change trades isolation for throughput.

nodes.name: Resource Control Isolation Semantics
nodes.content: Since v7.1.0 resource groups bound users to RU quotas: when a group over-consumes under contention its sessions are limited to quota while other groups stay unaffected, and unused headroom is borrowed when the system is idle - so quota-induced latency is by design, not a fault. Diagnosis: check per-group usage and throttle metrics and the Resource Manager dashboard, and estimate capacity against actual workload. Remedies: raise the group quota, rebalance quotas, or bundle the throttle complaint with capacity planning instead of chasing phantom hardware bottlenecks.

nodes.name: Resource Control Setup
nodes.content: Mechanism: RU-based scheduling requires tidb_enable_resource_control ON plus TiKV resource-control.enabled true (both default since v7.0), and TiFlash enable_resource_control since v7.4; background task types (br, ddl, stats, lightning, background) are bound to the default group and drop to lowest priority under resource scarcity. Differential: without the TiKV switch only flow control works (not recommended), and throttle symptoms disappear entirely when the feature is off. Remedies: create resource groups with RU_PER_SEC and QUERY_LIMIT, mark background task types via ALTER RESOURCE GROUP default BACKGROUND, and tag sessions with tidb_request_source_type. Risk: mistuned RU quotas throttle legitimate foreground traffic, observable as resource_group_throttle events. When quota errors dominate, raise the PD resource-manager ltb-max-wait-duration (default 30s) or group RU; if PD network isolation loses both token buckets, degraded-mode-wait-duration (default 0s, disabled) can fall back to default group settings instead of failing requests. For backup interference, BR auto-tune (backup.enable-auto-tune, dynamically toggleable via tikv-ctl) limits backup threads when utilization is high - note it stays disabled by default on clusters upgraded from v5.3.x - and --ratelimit forces backup concurrency to 1.

nodes.name: Resource group throttling runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: users/sessions/statements bind to resource groups; unbound statements land in the default group (UNLIMITED, BURSTABLE), and groups without BURSTABLE are hard-capped at RU_PER_SEC when capacity is short. Differential: identify the bound group of the failing user/session/statement, check whether the group is BURSTABLE and its priority, and compare against cluster capacity from CALIBRATE RESOURCE. Remedies: (a) ALTER RESOURCE GROUP ... RU_PER_SEC (takes effect immediately) or add BURSTABLE/PRIORITY; (b) re-bind with ALTER USER (only affects new sessions), SET RESOURCE GROUP, or the RESOURCE_GROUP() hint; (c) rebind to the default group to unbind; (d) as an escape hatch disable resource control globally (SET GLOBAL tidb_enable_resource_control='OFF') plus TiKV resource-control.enabled=false and TiFlash enable_resource_control=false. Preconditions: creating or altering groups requires SUPER or RESOURCE_GROUP_ADMIN privilege. Risks: disabling resource control removes tenant isolation entirely; ALTER USER rebinding leaves existing sessions on the old group.

nodes.name: Restore Side Effects on Cluster State
nodes.content: Mechanism: an in-place restore overwrites the whole cluster including the mysql schema, so user credentials, permissions, and system variables revert to their backup-time state while existing connections are terminated and new ones blocked; restores exceeding the time limit are auto-canceled (in-place returns to Available, restore-to-new-cluster is deleted), and TiFlash replicas stay unavailable after restore until data is rebuilt. Diagnosis: after a restore, treat sudden login failures, changed privileges, or lost variable settings as restore reversion rather than attack or bug, and check replica readiness for analytics gaps. Repair family: re-apply post-backup credential/permission/variable changes, recreate TiFlash replicas, and rerun a canceled restore-to-new-cluster with support assistance for oversized datasets.

nodes.name: Post-Restore Missing Statistics
nodes.content: Mechanism: BR by default does not back up statistics (--ignore-stats=true), so a freshly restored cluster has empty statistics until auto-collection finishes and the optimizer produces poor plans. Diagnosis: check last_analyze_time / stats health on the restored tables. Remedy family: back up with br --ignore-stats=false and restore with --load-stats (default since v8.0), or LOAD STATS from exported JSON, or run ANALYZE TABLE manually; prerequisite is knowing the backup predates this option.

nodes.name: Restore Schema Creation Speedup
nodes.content: Mechanism: BR creates databases and tables before restoring data; with serial execution the TiDB DDL owner creates tables one by one and each schema-version change synchronizes to all DDL workers, which dominates restore time at tens of thousands of tables. Differential diagnosis: compare the TiDB and BR component versions - Batch Create Table needs both at v6.0.0 or later, otherwise BR silently falls back to serial execution, so distinguish a version-bound fallback from genuine scheduler or import slowness. Repair family: upgrade both TiDB and BR to a batch-capable release or keep the default --ddl-batch-size batching (setting it to 1 reverts to serial); verify via the restore success-summary speed and per-restore ranges. Throughput baseline is version-bound: about 100 MiB/s per TiKV for older BR releases, while coarse-grained Region scattering (GA and default from v8.0.0) plus batched schema creation and decoupled SST download/ingest reach roughly 1.2 GiB/s per TiKV, and --ratelimit caps per-TiKV restore speed, so compare the observed average-speed against the running BR version's expectation before chasing other causes.

nodes.name: Retryable Deadlock Behavior
nodes.content: Mechanism: in a deadlock cycle, if the lock blocking the other transaction is held by the currently executing statement, TiDB releases that pessimistic lock and retries the statement internally, so the client sees no error; otherwise the transaction is terminated with a deadlock error. Discrimination: 'single statement deadlock, retry statement' entries in the TiDB log indicate frequent transparent retries that cost performance; DEADLOCKS table by default excludes retryable cases. Fix family: reduce lock-cycle-prone access patterns (consistent lock ordering, smaller transactions); frequent retries call for application-side lock-order changes.

nodes.name: RocksDB Write Stall
nodes.content: TiKV's LSM engine blocks foreground writes (WriteStall) when L0 SST files accumulate faster than flush and compaction drain them, appearing as sudden sharp write-latency spikes with disk utilization pegged; L0 SSTs overlap in key range so reads must search them one by one. Distinguish by the WriteStall Reason metric on the RocksDB panel versus disk saturation from other tenants; fix family: raise the L0 slowdown/stop-write triggers, give compaction more background threads, or cut write amplification at the workload; raising thresholds trades read performance and delays backpressure.

nodes.name: Root Password Recovery Discipline
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB honors the skip-grant-table security option, which skips all authentication when starting and is restricted to the operating-system root user so local privilege is the only entry. Differential diagnosis: confirm it is an authentication loss rather than a network or port problem before entering the insecure mode window. Repair family: add skip-grant-table to the TiDB configuration, restart that tidb-server as OS root, reset the root password with SQL, remove the option and restart normally - the cluster is exposed to any local OS-root user during the window, so close it immediately and audit accounts afterwards.

nodes.name: RU Consumption History Audit
nodes.content: Mechanism: the mysql.request_unit_by_group system table stores daily total_ru per resource group, populated by a scheduled task at day end; zero-consumption days get no row and data is kept for up to 92 days. Diagnosis: for chargeback, quota disputes, or throttling investigations, aggregate total_ru by resource_group over the incident days to see which group consumed capacity. Remedies: adjust group quotas based on observed RU curves, and remember the table lags a day so use real-time metrics for live decisions; risk is treating missing rows as missing data when they simply mean zero consumption.

nodes.name: Manage Runaway Queries with QUERY_LIMIT and Watch Lists
nodes.content: Mechanism: resource group QUERY_LIMIT marks queries over EXEC_ELAPSED as runaway and applies DRYRUN, COOLDOWN, or KILL; the WATCH clause (EXACT, SIMILAR by SQL digest, PLAN by plan digest) quarantines matching queries immediately for the DURATION period. Differential: DRYRUN first to validate the threshold, then KILL for repeat offenders. Remedies: ALTER RESOURCE GROUP with QUERY_LIMIT, add QUERY WATCH entries, and remove stale items with QUERY WATCH REMOVE after checking INFORMATION_SCHEMA.RUNAWAY_WATCHES. Risks: SIMILAR and PLAN matches can quarantine legitimate work, watch items survive QUERY_LIMIT changes, and unbounded cartesian joins (allowed while cross-join is on) are a common runaway source.

nodes.name: Runtime Filter Absent on Large Hash Join
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB generates a Runtime Filter, a dynamic predicate built from hash-join build-side values, and pushes it into the probe-side Table Scan so non-matching rows are filtered before the join. Diagnosis: when a big fact-table join is slow, EXPLAIN the plan and check whether the probe-side TableFullScan shows a runtime filter and a sharply reduced row estimate; absence typically means the join is not an MPP hash join or the plan shape prevents filter generation. Remedies: enable MPP/TiFlash execution for the query, keep the join as hash join with the small table as build side, and rewrite predicates so the build side is highly selective; risk is that highly skewed build sides make the filter ineffective.

nodes.name: Online scaling runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiUP scale-out adds nodes without service interruption (config inherited from the cluster), while scale-in takes TiKV/TiFlash/Binlog offline asynchronously - the store must drain replicas and leaders until it reaches Tombstone before pruning. Differential diagnosis: a scale-in that appears stuck is usually snapshot/leader drain (check operator step duration and schedule limits) or a replacement candidate below 20% free capacity; a TiFlash scale-in with tables still holding more replicas than remaining nodes will leave tables under-replicated. Remedy families: (1) pre-adjust PD scheduling parameters before adding TiKV; (2) before removing TiFlash, lower per-table replicas (ALTER TABLE ... SET tiflash replica) and verify with information_schema.tiflash_replica; (3) for failed scale-ins, manually delete the store via pd-ctl store delete, wait for Tombstone, then prune the topology; (4) after PD membership changes, refresh cluster config and Prometheus, and never remove all pre-existing PD nodes at once - switch the PD leader to a new node first. Risks: removing stores or wiping PD data is destructive; removing the last PD that TiKV caches as leader list can stall the cluster.

nodes.name: Schema Version Change Errors
nodes.content: Mechanism: 'Information schema is changed' fires when a DML statement's schema version no longer matches (same-table DDL overlap, more than the delta-schema-count version changes during a long DML, schema reload failure from PD/TiKV disconnect, or first DDL right after restart); 'out of date' fires when schema cannot be loaded within the DDL lease, typically after the TiDB was killed mid-transaction or lost PD/TiKV connection. Discrimination: map the error to cause via ADMIN SHOW DDL for concurrent DDL, DML duration vs version-change count, and TiDB-PD/TiKV network health. Fix family: retry DML (most cases self-heal, metadata lock avoids most overlaps), shorten long transactions, and repair PD/TiKV connectivity.

nodes.name: Secondary Index Design Trade-offs
nodes.content: Mechanism: every secondary index adds a key-value write per insert, slows writes, consumes space, and enlarges optimizer search space; index access is two-phase (index scan to row IDs, then row fetch) unless the index covers the query columns or the table has an integer primary key usable directly as row ID; ordered index output uses serial scanning and reverse scans of ascending indexes run roughly 20% slower, worse with many MVCC versions. Diagnosis: for slow point/range queries, EXPLAIN to see whether the plan does IndexLookUp, covering index read, or full scan, and check the row-count volume behind the two-phase access. Remedies: build composite indexes with equality columns first, prefer covering indexes for hot projections, avoid reverse scans in frequently updated tables, and trim unused indexes; concurrency knobs (distsql scan, index lookup size/concurrency, serial scan concurrency) tune the parallel pipeline for OLAP-shaped reads.

nodes.name: Security baseline hardening
nodes.content: Unauthorized access on a fresh or long-running cluster usually traces to unset defaults: a new cluster root has an empty password, Grafana ships admin/admin, and the PD client port 2379 exposes Dashboard and other APIs. Fix family: set root and Grafana passwords at deploy time, enforce a password-complexity policy, run TiDB Dashboard with a least-privilege SQL user, and restrict 2379 to trusted networks (internal component traffic must keep reaching PD or the cluster breaks). Password lifetime policies add a lockout class: default_password_lifetime (0 disables) and per-account PASSWORD EXPIRE INTERVAL expire aged passwords at login, and TiUP safe start (--init) replaces the empty root password with a one-time generated password that cannot be retrieved again.

nodes.name: Selective Index Statistics
nodes.content: Mechanism: ANALYZE TABLE t INDEX [list] collects index statistics selectively; when tidb_analyze_version = 2 the command still collects the entire table including columns to keep statistics self-consistent. Diagnosis: for a newly added index whose stats are missing, run targeted index analyze instead of full-table analyze. Remedies: use index-scoped analyze to cut collection time, understanding version-2 semantics widen the scope; risk of relying on index-only stats is inconsistent table-level estimates under version 1.

nodes.name: Service Safepoint TTL Trade-off
nodes.content: Mechanism: a replication service (e.g. TiKV-CDC via gc-ttl, default 24 h) sets a service-level GC safepoint in PD whose TTL bounds how long replication tasks may stay suspended; while suspended, the cluster GC safepoint cannot advance, so obsolete versions accumulate; a longer TTL tolerates longer suspension but retains more stale data, a shorter one risks the service losing its replication position. Diagnosis: when disk usage grows without data growth or a changefeed cannot resume, check the service safepoint and its remaining TTL against the suspension duration. Repair family: resume or restart the replication task before the TTL expires, and size the TTL to the longest acceptable suspension versus tolerable version backlog.

nodes.name: Sharded-merge data verification
nodes.content: After a DM sharded merge, suspected data inconsistency is verified with sync-diff-inspector: route rules map upstream shard tables (wildcard schema/table patterns) to the merged downstream table, check-thread-count bounds the extra connections, and export-fix-sql produces repair SQL; small shard sets can be enumerated explicitly in Datasource config.

nodes.name: Slow or Failed Store Scheduling Handling
nodes.content: Mechanism: PD marks a failed store down after max-store-down-time (default 30 minutes) and rebalances its Region replicas; slow-store detection scores sampled requests 1-100 and at the threshold evicts leaders like evict-leader-scheduler, but slow I/O makes scheduling requests queue up and delays eviction. Differential diagnosis: decide recoverable versus unrecoverable - take an unrecoverable node offline immediately so PD replenishes replicas and data-loss risk drops, whereas a recoverable outage longer than the down-time window justifies temporarily raising max-store-down-time to avoid wasted replica replenishment; distinguish one slow store from cluster-wide I/O saturation before evicting. Repair family: add evict-slow-store-scheduler for slow-node handling, enable store-io-pool-size to prevent request accumulation from stalling leader eviction, or take the node offline for permanent failure; restore the temporary down-time setting once the node is back.

nodes.name: Slow Non-Operator Stages (TS and Region Lookup)
nodes.content: Mechanism: time goes to timestamp prefetch or Region routing instead of operators. Differential: Wait_TS close to Query_time indicates slow timestamp acquisition; regionMiss with large Cop_backoff_regionMiss/rpcPD totals indicates stale Region metadata forcing re-lookups from PD. Fixes target PD/TiKV health and Region metadata freshness rather than SQL tuning.

nodes.name: Slow Query Detail Reading
nodes.content: Mechanism: slow-query records expose the SQL text, execution plan (table/text/graph with component-colored operators), and tabs for basic info, per-stage time, coprocessor reads, and transaction key counts; the recorded SQL text is truncated by tidb_stmt_summary_max_sql_length, and per-stage durations can sum above wall time because stages run in parallel. Diagnosis: read the plan graph to locate the expensive operator and which engine (TiDB/TiKV/TiFlash) ran it, use the Time tab to split parse/optimize/compile versus execution, and the Coprocessor/Transaction tabs to attribute scan volume or write-key counts. Remedies: raise max_sql_length when long SQL is cut off, and compare plans of slow executions against the statements summary; risk is misreading cumulative stage time as wall-clock latency.

nodes.name: Slow Query Diagnosis Workflow
nodes.content: Mechanism: slow queries stem from optimizer issues (bad plan) or system issues (busy TiKV, slow TiDB operators, slow timestamp/Region stages), and a bad plan can masquerade as a system issue by saturating CPU. Diagnosis: find the slow query class via slow log or statement summary, locate the time-consuming stage with slow log fields or EXPLAIN ANALYZE, then check plan reasonableness before blaming capacity. Fixes follow the identified family: plan rewrite/indexing for optimizer issues, resource or configuration tuning for system issues.

nodes.name: Snapshot Backup Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: br backup full takes a cluster snapshot at the start time or an explicit --backupts (TSO or timestamp); if that snapshot's data is already GC'd the command errors out and exits; BR auto-registers backupTS as a PD safe point so GC holds still during backup, --ratelimit caps per-TiKV backup speed in MiB/s, and --log-file records progress. Diagnosis: for a backup that fails immediately, check whether --backupts predates the GC safe point; for slow backups compare --ratelimit with the intended window. Remedies: pick a snapshot inside the GC window or raise GC life time temporarily, and set ratelimit to balance backup speed against foreground load; risk is that holding the safe point too long accumulates MVCC versions that slow the cluster.

nodes.name: Space reclamation lag runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: MVCC keeps overwritten/deleted rows as old versions and GC is delayed (tidb_gc_life_time, default 10m) so concurrent transactions can read history; TRUNCATE/DROP reclaim only after GC, DELETE reclaims when RocksDB compaction rewrites data, and sparse deleted ranges degrade scans until Region Merge. Differential diagnosis: identify the operation type (DELETE vs TRUNCATE/DROP), check tidb_gc_life_time for artificial retention, and compare logical data_length against physical store size to estimate reclaimable MVCC garbage. Remedy families: (1) wait for GC/compaction and keep writing to trigger reuse; (2) enable/verify Region Merge for heavily-deleted ranges; (3) if space is urgent, plan node/disk changes instead of forcing GC. Risks: shortening GC life time risks long-running transactions and flashback windows; aggressive region merge settings can fight hotspot scheduling.

nodes.name: Spark JDBC Bulk Write Risks
nodes.content: Mechanism: Spark JDBC writes commit through TiDB transactions, so a default isolation level both hits 'ISOLATION LEVEL does not support' (TiDB supports REPEATABLE-READ only for this path) and builds huge single transactions that can OOM TiDB. Diagnosis: on TiDB OOM or isolation errors during Spark-based bulk loads, check the writer options - isolationLevel, rewriteBatchedStatements, batch size - and whether the source was repartitioned for balanced concurrency. Repair family: set isolationLevel to NONE, enable rewriteBatchedStatements=true with a moderate JDBC batch size, and repartition the DataFrame; TiSpark's own DataSource API writes keep ACID without this risk, and Spark SQL DELETE goes through tidb_catalog.

nodes.name: SPM Binding Management
nodes.content: Bindings can be created from historical plans (GA v6.6.0) on any node and dropped by statement or SQL digest; scope semantics matter when debugging: a SESSION binding shields the GLOBAL one even after it is dropped within the session, and DROP GLOBAL BINDING only marks the system-table row 'deleted' with cache cleanup on other TiDB nodes after ~100 bind-info-lease (about 300 s), so a binding can appear to linger. Verify effective bindings via SHOW BINDINGS and EXPLAIN before blaming the optimizer. Bindings can come from historical plans (GA v6.6.0), be dropped by statement or SQL digest, and since v7.6.0 be cross-database: enable tidb_opt_enable_fuzzy_binding and write FROM *.t to cover tenant-per-database schemas; matching precedence is SESSION standard > SESSION cross-db > GLOBAL standard > GLOBAL cross-db, a dropped SESSION binding still shields the GLOBAL one for the session's life, and DROP GLOBAL BINDING only marks rows 'deleted' with cache cleanup across nodes after ~100 bind-info-lease (~300 s).

nodes.name: SQL Digest Decoding
nodes.content: TIDB_DECODE_SQL_DIGESTS maps a JSON array of SQL digests back to normalized statement text by scanning statement summary tables (null for digests not seen recently), needs the PROCESS privilege, and carries high overhead because it queries per row without vectorization - decode small digest batches with stmtTruncateLength on busy clusters rather than whole TIDB_TRX tables. It turns digest-only records (slow logs, transactions, binding targets) into readable SQL.

nodes.name: SQL Mode GROUP BY Compatibility
nodes.content: TiDB enables ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY by default, so queries with non-aggregated columns outside GROUP BY fail with ERROR 1055 after migrating from permissive MySQL configurations - fix by adding columns to GROUP BY, wrapping in ANY_VALUE-style aggregation, or relaxing sql_mode deliberately. TiDB is otherwise more permissive than MySQL 5.7 on DISTINCT+ORDER BY and allows HAVING aliases, so exact behavior differs per construct.

nodes.name: SQL Mode Strictness Effects
nodes.content: sql_mode decides whether data-truncation or out-of-range values raise errors or only warnings: in non-strict mode TiDB inserts adjusted values (for example 0 for an overflow) and reports them only via SHOW WARNINGS. Unexpected stored values or silent data adjustments should be diagnosed by checking session/global sql_mode with SHOW VARIABLES and replaying the statement under SHOW WARNINGS before blaming application logic.

nodes.name: SQL Tuning Workflow
nodes.content: Mechanism: SQL tuning is an iterative loop - identify the statement class consuming the most resources, analyze its plan, then implement the fix. Diagnosis: statements summary groups queries by SQL digest (one digest can expose multiple execution plans), ranking by total and per-execution time. Fix family: rewrite the statement, add or modify indexes, refresh statistics, choose a better join type or storage engine, then verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and repeat until targets are met. Risks: tuning against one workload snapshot regresses as data volume and query mix evolve, so re-check after changes.

nodes.name: Batch Writer Statement Limit
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB transactions cap statement count (5000 by default, adjustable via stmt-count-limit); batch writers such as Sqoop multiply --batch statement groups into far more statements and fail with 'statement count N exceeds the transaction limitation'. Diagnosis: on BatchUpdateException with the statement-count text, compute the writer's statements-per-transaction against the limit. Remedies: reduce records per statement (for example -Dsqoop.export.records.per.statement=10) so each transaction stays under the cap, or raise the limit knowing memory use grows with transaction size; risk of raising the limit is OOM on huge transactions.

nodes.name: Stale Read Blocked by safe-ts
nodes.content: Stale Read serves queries from any peer whose safe-ts covers the read timestamp; safe-ts advances only when the leader's resolved-ts (which a resolver tracking LOCK CF entries holds back for uncommitted transactions) is applied on every peer, so a fault store, lagging peer, or long-running transaction stalls safe-ts and stale reads fail with stale-data errors while normal leader reads still work. Distinguish by checking which Regions' safe-ts/resolved-ts stopped advancing and whether those stores or transactions are stuck; fix family: restore the fault store, resolve or kill the long transaction, or fall back to current reads.

nodes.name: Stale Read for Local-Replica Reads
nodes.content: Mechanism: tidb_read_staleness pins session reads to the newest timestamp within N seconds (writes and interactive transactions still use latest data), while tidb_enable_external_ts_read plus tidb_external_ts reads a fixed timestamp and makes TiDB strictly read-only (ERROR 1836); TiKV resolved-ts advance-ts-interval bounds how fresh stale reads can get. Differential: verify session variables first, then global settings, before suspecting replication delay. Remedies: clear tidb_read_staleness (set "") or open a new session, disable tidb_enable_external_ts_read, and lower TiKV advance-ts-interval to reduce staleness latency. Risk: the staleness window must stay inside tidb_gc_life_time or history versions are purged; global external-ts read silently breaks all writes.

nodes.name: Stale Read Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: stale reads require resolved-ts and safe-ts to advance; long-running or long-lived transactions holding many locks, or delays in CheckLeader propagation, hold safe-ts back so stale reads miss and fall back. Discrimination: Stale Read hit/miss OPS panels show the trend, Resolved-TS panels (Max Resolved TS gap, Min Resolved TS Region) name the lagging Regions, RegionReadProgress/resolver state shows a huge lock count from one transaction, and 'locks with the minimum start_ts' log lines give its start_ts which correlates to the statement in TiDB logs. Fix family: find and shorten or split the blocking large transaction, resolve long-lived transactions, and check replication/CheckLeader health; safe-ts recovers once the blocker commits or is killed.

nodes.name: Stale Read Mechanisms
nodes.content: Stale Read serves queries from any replica at a chosen historical timestamp, trading real-time freshness for throughput: statement level AS OF TIMESTAMP with an exact timestamp is the recommended globally consistent form, a time range lets TiDB pick the newest unblocked timestamp on the replica, and session/global variants exist. It helps when strong-consistency reads concentrate load on leaders (small hot tables) or when geo-deployed ReadIndex checks add cross-center latency, but it must never be used where applications cannot tolerate non-real-time data.

nodes.name: Stale Region Info After PD Leader Switch
nodes.content: A TiKV defect (affecting v5.3.2 and v5.4.2, fixed in v5.3.3) stopped retrying Region heartbeats to PD after a PD leader switch or restart until reconnection, so that node's Region information went stale and SQL execution failed cluster-wide. The signature is continuous SQL errors beginning right after a PD leadership event; the workarounds are upgrading, or restarting the TiKV nodes whose heartbeats to PD stopped until no Region heartbeat is pending.

nodes.name: Statement Priority vs Resource Control
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB historically scheduled DML priority via LOW_PRIORITY/HIGH_PRIORITY/DELAYED, but with resource control (v6.6.0+) these PriorityOpt modifiers stop taking effect and scheduling is governed by resource-group quotas and priorities. Diagnosis: when background or interactive statements run at the wrong relative priority, check whether resource control is enabled before tuning the SQL modifiers - under resource control they are silent no-ops. Repair family: bind the sessions or users to appropriately sized resource groups (RU quotas and priorities) instead of per-statement priority keywords.

nodes.name: Use Statement Summary Without Eviction Blind Spots
nodes.content: Mechanism: statements_summary holds tidb_stmt_summary_max_stmt_count (default 3000) digests with refresh interval 1800s and history size 24; beyond the limit, least-recently-used digests are evicted into statements_summary_evicted, leaving holes in history, and in-memory summaries vanish on restart unless persistence is enabled. Remedies: compare statements_summary count against the limit and raise it by the evicted count, or enable tidb_stmt_summary_enable_persistent for restart survival. Risk: the trio of history size, max count, and max SQL length multiplies memory (roughly their product times 3), so oversized settings pressure TiDB memory.

nodes.name: Statistics Health Remediation
nodes.content: Mechanism: statistics drift after bulk writes, large deletes, or long gaps since the last analyze, so the optimizer mis-estimates and may flip plans (high risk after large deletions). Diagnosis: SHOW STATS_HEALTHY / STATS_META / STATS_HISTOGRAMS and stats:pseudo markers in EXPLAIN; a persistent estRows vs actRows gap in EXPLAIN ANALYZE confirms misestimation. Fix family: manual ANALYZE TABLE (optionally targeting indexes or bucket counts) or re-tuning auto-analyze; update statistics after large data changes. Risks: ANALYZE itself consumes I/O and CPU, so schedule it away from peak traffic.

nodes.name: Statistics Initialization Version Semantics
nodes.content: v7.1.0 introduced lite-init-stats (lightweight statistics initialization, experimental) and force-init-stats to control whether TiDB serves SQL before initialization completes; in v7.2.0 lite-init-stats became default true and force-init-stats default true, so post-restart plan regressions largely disappear - on older versions they are expected and the remedy is enabling force-init-stats or waiting for stats load. Diagnosis: correlate symptom onset with node restart time and stats-load completion; remediation depends on version defaults.

nodes.name: Statistics Loading Delay Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: large statistics (histograms, TopN, Count-Min Sketch) load asynchronously on demand, so statements optimized before loading completes use incomplete or pseudo statistics; right after a TiDB restart, queries can get suboptimal plans until initial statistics load. Diagnosis: round default-like selectivities in EXPLAIN and estimation gaps right after restarts or first touch of cold columns. Fix family: bounded synchronous loading (tidb_stats_load_sync_wait), tune lite-init-stats/force-init-stats for startup behavior, and review tidb_stats_load_pseudo_timeout. Risks: synchronous loading adds optimization latency; setting the pseudo timeout OFF makes statements error after the wait.

nodes.name: Statistics Lock Management
nodes.content: LOCK STATS freezes a table or partition's statistics so ANALYZE skips it (warning 'skip analyze locked table'), trading freshness for plan stability; SHOW STATS_LOCKED lists locked objects. Stale-but-locked statistics that regress plans are fixed by UNLOCK STATS followed by ANALYZE; also note ANALYZE warnings such as 'disable dynamic pruning due to no global stats' which explain missing global statistics on partitioned tables.

nodes.name: Statistics Locking
nodes.content: LOCK STATS [TABLE] [PARTITION p] pins statistics so ANALYZE silently skips the locked objects (visible as warnings), SHOW STATS_LOCKED lists pins, and UNLOCK STATS releases them; locked-stale stats keep bad plans alive after schema/data changes, so when ANALYZE does not improve a plan, check for locks before suspecting collection failures.

nodes.name: Maintain Statistics and Control ANALYZE Overhead
nodes.content: Mechanism: auto analyze triggers when modified rows exceed tidb_auto_analyze_ratio (0.5) within the tidb_auto_analyze_start_time/end_time window and requires tidb_enable_auto_analyze; manual ANALYZE total concurrency multiplies tidb_build_stats_concurrency by sampling plus partition concurrency. Differential: distinguish stale stats (bad plans on specific tables) from global resource saturation. Remedies: run manual ANALYZE for critical tables, widen the auto-analyze window or lower the ratio, and tune concurrency variables one at a time (partition, sampling, build) to bound overhead - risk: high concurrency loads TiDB and TiKV during business hours. Right after a TiDB restart the optimizer can run on pseudo statistics while initialization is pending (force-init-stats false on pre-v7.2 defaults), producing bad plans until init completes; with huge table counts, forcing init trades service start time for plan quality.

nodes.name: Statistics management runbook
nodes.content: Statistics can be deleted wholesale with DROP STATS when they are corrupt or misleading, after which plans run on pseudo statistics until ANALYZE or auto-collection rebuilds them, so use it as a deliberate reset rather than a routine fix.

nodes.name: Statistics After Partition Maintenance
nodes.content: Mechanism: partition maintenance has historically left statistics wrong - dropping, reorganizing, or truncating partitions did not update table statistics, converting a partitioned table kept its old statistics, TRUNCATE TABLE left stale statistics, and auto updates could fire outside the configured window - so plans degrade right after routine partition DDL. Diagnosis: when plans regress after partition DDL, check SHOW STATS_HEALTHY and last_analyze times for the table before blaming data changes. Repair family: ANALYZE the affected tables (or wait for a correct auto-analyze window) and verify plan regression disappears; keep the auto-analyze time window consistent with maintenance windows.

nodes.name: Stale Statistics Correction
nodes.content: Mechanism: after bulk data change the optimizer keeps old row estimates and may keep a suboptimal plan even though the plan shape looks unchanged. Discrimination: compare estRows with actRows in EXPLAIN ANALYZE; stats:pseudo means no statistics at all; SHOW STATS_HEALTHY quantifies staleness. Fix family: run ANALYZE TABLE on affected tables or rely on auto-analyze ratio; verify estimates converge before judging the plan itself.

nodes.name: Statistics Export and Import
nodes.content: Mechanism: table statistics export as JSON via the TiDB status-port HTTP endpoint /stats/dump/<db>/<table> (optionally at a past timestamp), and import with LOAD STATS 'file' from a client started with --local-infile=1. Diagnosis: when a test environment must reproduce production plans, export the source table's stats JSON and load it into the target. Remedies: transfer stats instead of copying data for plan-reproduction rigs, and verify versions match; risk is that stale imported stats mislead the optimizer in the target just as they would in production.

nodes.name: Statement Summary Capacity Truncation
nodes.content: Mechanism: the statements summary table keeps a bounded number of SQL fingerprints controlled by tidb_stmt_summary_max_stmt_count; when the limit is exceeded, less significant entries are evicted, so the statement under investigation can be missing from diagnostics. Diagnosis: if a known slow or faulty SQL is absent from cluster_statements_summary, check the capacity variable and the actual statement count. Remedies: raise tidb_stmt_summary_max_stmt_count so the workload's fingerprints fit; risk is higher memory held by the summary tables.

nodes.name: Statements Summary Persistence
nodes.content: Mechanism: statements summary data is memory-only before v6.6.0 and vanishes on TiDB restart; with persistence enabled, historical summaries are written to disk periodically and system table queries read from disk, so restarts no longer erase the evidence. Diagnosis: when post-restart statement history is empty, check whether persistence is enabled. Remedies: enable statements summary persistence so incident windows survive restarts, and combine with PLAN REPLAYER capture for plan-level evidence; risk is additional disk write load on busy clusters.

nodes.name: Storage Device Failure
nodes.content: A failing or read-only disk, or exhausted inodes, stops writes for the TiKV/PD/TiDB instance on that host, surfacing as write stalls, etcd fsync failures, or panic loops. Distinguish device failure from capacity pressure or filesystem corruption by SMART/LED, mount state, and df -i; fix family: evacuate replicas off the node first, then replace the disk or repair the filesystem and extend capacity; evacuating before failure protects data.

nodes.name: Store Down and Replica Rebuild
nodes.content: A TiKV store losing heartbeats goes Disconnect after 20 seconds and Down after max-store-down-time (30 minutes default), at which point PD starts replenishing every affected Region via snapshots, flooding network and disk and degrading service until replicas are rebuilt; a manually Offline store must drain all Regions to Tombstone and must not be power-cycled mid-drain or it can wedge if no target stores exist. Distinguish transient Disconnect (network, restart) from true Down by heartbeat timing before PD acts; fix family: restore connectivity or the process before the down threshold, control rebuild speed, or ensure free capacity for draining stores; rebuilding too fast starves foreground traffic.

nodes.name: Tune PD Store Limits and Scheduling Rates
nodes.content: Mechanism: PD store limit token buckets throttle add-peer/remove-peer consumption per store while leader/region/replica/hot-region schedule limits throttle operator generation; store-limit v2 auto-adjusts to TiKV snapshot capability and the true bottleneck becomes snap-io-max-bytes-per-sec. PD marks a store down after 30m without heartbeat and starts re-replication. Differential: stalled repair points to exhausted schedule limits or pending-peer caps; foreground IO interference points to snapshot floods. Remedies: raise store limit or max-snapshot-count/max-pending-peer-count temporarily for fast rebalance, keep replica-schedule-limit below region-schedule-limit, and restore conservative values afterwards. Risk: aggressive scheduling steals snapshot bandwidth and IOPS from foreground traffic.

nodes.name: sync-diff-inspector Output Interpretation
nodes.content: Mechanism: sync-diff-inspector streams structure and data comparison progress, writes checkpoints every 10 seconds for resumable runs, and produces summary.txt with per-table structure equality, DATA DIFF ROWS (+add/-delete), and UPCOUNT/DOWNCOUNT row totals; fix SQL lands in fix-on-<target-instance> using REPLACE for missing or altered rows and DELETE for redundant ones, each annotated with table and chunk range. Diagnosis: read summary.txt to scope the damage and open the per-chunk SQL files to review each fix before applying. Remedies: apply reviewed fix SQL during a quiet window and re-run the diff to confirm zero diffs; risk of blindly applying fixes is overwriting legitimate downstream-only writes in active replication.

nodes.name: Syncpoint Secondary Read Semantics
nodes.content: With enable-sync-point, TiCDC periodically writes tidb_external_ts on the secondary so sessions with tidb_enable_external_ts_read=ON read a transactionally consistent snapshot whose lag is bounded by sync-point-interval (default 10m, minimum 30s); Syncpoint needs SYSTEM_VARIABLES_ADMIN or SUPER and a secondary cluster must replicate from exactly one changefeed or transaction integrity is lost. Inconsistent or too-fresh secondary reads are usually the sync-point interval, missing privileges, or a second changefeed rather than replication failure.

nodes.name: Syncpoint snapshot-consistent validation
nodes.content: Replication correctness between TiDB clusters can be checked at aligned snapshots: with TiCDC enable-sync-point on, tidb_cdc.syncpoint_v1 stores ts-map pairs (upstream primary_ts, downstream secondary_ts) per changefeed, and sync-diff-inspector compares both sides with those snapshot TSOs. Preconditions: raise GC life (about 1 hour) so snapshot versions survive the check, and since v6.4.0 the changefeed needs SYSTEM_VARIABLES_ADMIN or SUPER to record syncpoints. Replication consistency is validated by pairing upstream and downstream snapshots from tidb_cdc.syncpoint_v1 (primary_ts/secondary_ts) and running a diff tool at those TSOs. The changefeed must have enable-sync-point=true and, since v6.4.0, SYSTEM_VARIABLES_ADMIN or SUPER privilege; temporarily extend TiKV GC life (e.g. 1 hour, restore afterwards) so snapshot history is not collected during the check, and identify the right ts-map rows by TiCDC cluster id plus changefeed id.

nodes.name: System Table Restore Compatibility
nodes.content: Mechanism: BR backs up mysql-schema system tables but restores only privilege and binding tables (and only with --with-sys-table, default on from v7.6.0), and pre-checks compatibility: same system tables, same column count, target column lengths not smaller, and target ENUM values a superset; mysql.stat_*, mysql.tidb, and mysql.global_variables are never restored. Differential diagnosis: separate a compatibility-check failure from a database-name mismatch (restore db only succeeds into the name recorded in backupmeta) and from post-restore binding anomalies caused by stale in-memory bindings. Repair family: restore to a same-version or schema-compatible cluster and same-name database, after restoring mysql.bind_info verify with SHOW GLOBAL BINDINGS, keep exactly one builtin_pseudo_sql_for_bind_lock row (delete extras), and run ADMIN RELOAD BINDINGS; statistics and system variables must be recovered by their own procedures instead. A 'cannot find rewrite rule' error during restore points at inconsistent target table structures or missing indexes rather than privilege-table incompatibility, and table filters decide which mysql-schema tables are restored at all.

nodes.name: Table Lock Disabled Behavior
nodes.content: When enable-table-lock is false (default) LOCK TABLES and UNLOCK TABLES take no effect and return a 'not supported' warning, so applications relying on table locks see unexpected concurrency; enabling it restores READ/WRITE/WRITE LOCAL coordination but the feature is experimental and not recommended for production. Distinguish from lock-not-taking-effect-due-to-autocommit by checking the warning text and the config value.

nodes.name: Temporary Table Shadowing
nodes.content: A session-local temporary table with the same name as an ordinary table hides the ordinary table for that session, so 'missing data' or 'wrong rows' reports traced to one session are often shadowing; temporary tables introduced before v5.3 persisted as ordinary tables after upgrade and silently occupy storage. Check SHOW FULL TABLES semantics per session and drop leftovers when diagnosing unexplained table data.

nodes.name: TiCDC Bidirectional Replication Start-TS
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiCDC bidirectional replication (bdr-mode = true) links two TiDB clusters with one changefeed each direction; replication only covers changes after each changefeed's --start-ts, which must be the respective cluster's TSO at a proven data-consistency point between the two clusters. Diagnosis: duplicated or missing rows after enabling BDR indicate a start-ts set before/after the verified consistency point, or a missing bdr-mode flag causing replication loops. Remedy family: re-derive the consistent TSO pair, recreate changefeeds with correct start-ts, and keep bdr-mode enabled so replicated writes are not re-replicated; initial data must be imported beforehand via export/import tools.

nodes.name: TiCDC Changefeed Stall
nodes.content: A changefeed's checkpoint advances only to the minimum across its tables and processors, so one stalled table (large transaction, DDL wait, unavailability of its owner Capture) or a failing sink pins the global checkpoint and lag grows even though most tables replicate fine; node or owner failures trigger re-election and table rescheduling, adding transient lag. Distinguish by per-table checkpoint comparison and sink error counters; fix family: resolve the blocking table or sink, let the cluster reschedule after Capture recovery, or recreate the changefeed from a valid checkpoint; risk is at-least-once duplicates downstream.

nodes.name: Changefeed State Semantics
nodes.content: Changefeed states carry remediation semantics: RUNNING means checkpoint-ts advances normally; WARNING means recoverable errors - the changefeed retries automatically and blocks GC while trying to reach RUNNING; FAILED means unrecoverable errors - resolve the cause and resume manually, which succeeds only if the needed incremental data is still within the GC TTL (default 24 hours); PAUSED/RESUMING/EDITING are operator-driven states. Diagnosis: query the changefeed list and state via cdc cli or OpenAPI, then read the error. Remedies: fix sink connectivity or config then resume; if data was GC'd, re-establish the full+incremental pipeline from a new snapshot instead of forcing a resume.

nodes.name: TiCDC cutover ordering
nodes.content: TiDB-to-TiDB incremental cutover is order-sensitive: record the backup timestamp (BackupTS) of the full export, create the changefeed with --start-ts equal to it, and keep tidb_gc_enable FALSE until the changefeed exists so GC cannot drop unreplicated history; afterwards re-enable GC and confirm with @@global.tidb_gc_enable. A start-ts newer than the backup point silently loses the writes between backup and start. The same flow also serves cluster splits, data-center relocation, and version upgrades, since TiDB-to-TiDB migration is the standard non-in-place cutover path.

nodes.name: TiCDC DDL Retry and Replay Boundary
nodes.content: Mechanism: when the sink cannot apply one event, ResolvedTS keeps advancing while CheckpointTS stays at the blocking event - a retry/ordering signal, not an event to skip. Differential diagnosis: the raw TiCDC log is the authoritative source for the failed event; keep the DDL error, table operation, and event commit timestamp together and deduplicate repeated log lines describing the same event before choosing a boundary. Repair family: make the downstream schema equivalent, then replay deliberately from the first timestamp after the isolated failed DDL event - starting from a later checkpoint can silently skip changes committed while the sink was retrying - and validate with checkpoint, resolved/source progress, and business rows rather than the recreate command's success response. A FLASHBACK DATABASE replicated to a downstream that cannot replay it breaks replication; the documented handling is to filter the database from the replication task and re-import its data in full. A failed downstream DDL stops the changefeed with checkpoint-ts equal to the DDL finish-ts: resume with cdc cli changefeed resume to retry it, or skip via ignore-txn-start-ts with the DDL start-ts found in the 'apply job' log entries - recreating the changefeed at checkpoint-ts+1 also skips the DML at that timestamp and is prohibited in production.

nodes.name: TiCDC DDL Replication Restrictions
nodes.content: TiCDC replicates only DDLs on its allow list; unlisted DDLs silently do not reach the downstream, so downstream schema divergence is an expected failure mode to check. RENAME TABLE is replicated only when the old name matches the filter; renaming into a filtered name from an unfiltered old name errors and exits replication, and name-swapping RENAME is unsupported. Asynchronous ADD INDEX/CREATE INDEX on a TiDB downstream can block the next same-table DDL in queueing state and repeat execution; since v8.1.2 TiCDC with downstream SUPER privilege polls ADMIN SHOW DDL JOBS and waits for index completion, trading latency for stability. Cross-database DDLs must name all databases explicitly, and the storage sink cannot handle DROP DATABASE.

nodes.name: TiCDC Unique-Key Swap Duplicate Entry
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB merges same-row DELETE+INSERT within one transaction into a single UPDATE row change; when the upstream pattern swaps unique key values between two rows (delete both, re-insert swapped), the replicated UPDATEs violate the downstream unique index partway through, surfacing as repeated CDC:ErrMySQLDuplicateEntryCDC errors. Diagnosis: frequent duplicate-entry errors on tables with unique secondary keys whose upstream workload swaps key values - inspect the conflicting statements in downstream logs. Remedy family: enable TiCDC sink safe mode via safe-mode=true in the sink-uri so UPDATEs execute as DELETE + REPLACE INTO, accepting that REPLACE overwrites conflicting rows; alternatively restructure the upstream pattern to avoid intra-transaction unique-key swaps.
