nodes.name: TiCDC Event Filter Pitfalls
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiCDC event filters ignore DML/DDL by matcher plus ignore-event, ignore-sql regex, or SQL value expressions; matcher includes the database name, so a '^drop' regex filters DROP DATABASE along with DROP TABLE, clustered-index UPDATEs arrive as DELETE+INSERT pairs that UPDATE-expression filters cannot match, and 'multi schema change' must be listed explicitly to filter combined ALTERs. Filtering a CREATE/DROP TABLE DDL does not stop subsequent DML in current versions (old versions did), but replicating DML for a table missing downstream, or schemas drifting between upstream and downstream, causes errors or undefined replication behavior. Diagnosis: on changefeed failure or missing/extra rows, review filter rules against the actual statements and compare upstream/downstream schemas. Remedy family: tighten ignore-sql patterns to the table level, keep schemas consistent when filtering DDL, and ensure every matcher table has the columns referenced by SQL-expression filters - if a later schema change removes such a column the task fails and needs a manual config change plus resume.

nodes.name: Joint TiCDC and GC Recovery
nodes.content: Mechanism: feed progress trouble and a stale service safepoint are independent chains - restoring the target capture does not release an abandoned PD owner, and removing the owner does not clear a target Region lock. Differential diagnosis: verify each chain separately (feed state and errors vs safepoint owners) since repair order can vary once product preconditions hold. Repair family: converge both chains, then close only after a final observation window shows feed health, ResolvedTS/CheckpointTS progress, lock absence on every observed peer, Region health, exact abandoned-feed removal with owner released to the gc_worker boundary, GC progress, and source/downstream business equality, while preserving healthy feeds, owners, and archives.

nodes.name: TiCDC gc-ttl Interruption Deadline
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiCDC holds the upstream GC safepoint at the replication progress, but only up to gc-ttl (default 24h); if a changefeed stays unavailable or interrupted longer, the task enters the failed state irrecoverably - PD's GC safe point resumes advancing and history beyond it is removed, so recovery requires a new full backup plus restart. Raising gc-ttl retains more MVCC versions (like raising tidb_gc_life_time), trading upstream storage for repair window. Diagnosis: a changefeed in failed state after a long outage, or checkpoint lag approaching gc-ttl during an incident - check changefeed state, checkpoint age, and PD GC safe point. Remedy family: restore the changefeed before gc-ttl elapses, temporarily raise gc-ttl for planned long maintenance (accepting MVCC growth), and monitor checkpoint lag plus sink throughput against write rate; once failed, re-seed from backup with start-ts at the backup TSO.

nodes.name: TiCDC Skips Table Without Valid Index
nodes.content: TiCDC replicates only tables with a valid index (primary key, or a unique index whose columns are all NOT NULL and non-virtual-generated), so a table without one is silently absent downstream instead of lagging. Distinguish from changefeed lag by the table missing entirely from the changefeed's table list; fix family: add a valid index to the table and let the changefeed pick it up; there is no workaround short of changing the schema.

nodes.name: TiCDC Kafka Sink Configuration Pitfalls
nodes.content: Mechanism: the Kafka sink URI encodes brokers, topic, protocol (canal-json/open-protocol/avro/debezium/simple), kafka-version, partition-num, max-message-bytes, and acks settings; changefeed creation fails when partition-num exceeds the actual partition count, sends fail when max-message-bytes exceeds broker limits, and produce errors appear when replication-factor is below the broker's min.insync.replicas. Diagnosis: match the configured kafka-version to the broker, check broker-side topic config and TiCDC logs for produce errors. Remedy: align version, partition count, message size, and acks/min.insync.replicas settings, then restart the changefeed.

nodes.name: TiCDC Kafka sink tuning
nodes.content: Kafka sink changefeed errors cluster around message size and connection hygiene: explicitly set max-message-bytes and partition-num (TiCDC auto-creates missing topics with them), a single row event larger than max-message-bytes fails the changefeed, and infrequent changes (>10 min silence) trigger broker idle timeouts seen as broken pipe errors, fixed by raising the Kafka connection idle timeout. Kafka auth failures need SASL params in sink-uri plus ACLs (Topic Create/Write/Describe, Cluster DescribeConfig) and enable-tls for encrypted brokers.

nodes.name: TiCDC oversized message handling
nodes.content: When an encoded row event exceeds the Kafka message limit, large-message-handle-option (handle-key-only or claim-check) sends only the handle key, marked by the onlyHandleKey extension field; consumers must fetch full rows from upstream via tidb_snapshot, and the cluster tidb_gc_life_time must be long enough or the snapshot version will already be GCed.

nodes.name: TiCDC Large Transaction Risks
nodes.content: Transactions above roughly 5 GB stress TiCDC: replication lag spikes, ErrBufferReachLimit errors appear when internal buffers fill, and OOM can hit TiCDC or the sink. Remedy family: set sink-uri transaction-atomicity=none (v6.2+) to split single-table transactions and cut latency/memory when atomicity is not required; otherwise recover by BR incremental backup from the changefeed checkpoint-ts (--lastbackupts), record the resulting BackupTS, restore incrementally, and recreate the changefeed from BackupTS.

nodes.name: TiCDC Multiple Changefeeds to One Downstream
nodes.content: A TiCDC secondary cluster must be fed by exactly one changefeed: running multiple changefeeds into the same downstream (or a second standby cluster alongside an existing one) breaks transaction integrity of the replicated data. Distinguish by listing changefeeds and their downstream targets and correlating integrity anomalies with overlapping sinks; fix family: collapse to a single changefeed per downstream or use bidirectional replication with region-scoped writes; prevention beats repair because already-applied duplicate streams cannot be undone.

nodes.name: TiCDC Pipeline Stage Triage
nodes.content: Mechanism: changefeed lag decomposes into resolved-ts lag (upstream TiDB to TiCDC pull) and checkpoint lag (TiCDC to downstream apply); healthy checkpoint lag is typically within about 10 seconds. Dataflow metrics trace the internal pipeline Puller -> Sorter -> Mounter -> Sink, where Sorter output throttles under Sink backpressure, Mounter slows on wide rows, and Sink flush rows/s below Puller output predicts growing latency. Persistent checkpoint-lag growth has a bounded cause set: insufficient TiCDC CPU/memory/disk, network interruption or bandwidth, upstream QPS beyond a single node's roughly 60K QPS ceiling, TiKV failing to advance min resolved ts under heavy writes, or slow downstream writes. For transaction sinks, Backend Flush Duration p999 should stay under about 500 ms and Full Flush minus Backend Flush is queueing time (fix with more task memory quota); redo-enabled tasks compare Redo write rows/s against Puller output; changefeed status codes map 0 Normal, 1 Error, 2 Failed, 3 Stopped, 4 Finished, -1 Unknown, and catch-up ETA is only indicative. Diagnosis: high resolved-ts lag means upstream pull or TiKV CDC issues; growing checkpoint lag with healthy resolved-ts means sink-side slowness - read the stage rates left-to-right for the first drop; rising lag with saturated TiCDC CPU means scale out nodes. Remedy family: relieve the first throttling stage (add TiCDC nodes or resources, fix network, increase sink concurrency or downstream capacity, allocate more memory quota) rather than restarting the changefeed.

nodes.name: TiCDC Progress Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: ResolvedTS is the source timestamp the capture has observed, CheckpointTS is what the sink durably committed; a restart clears a transient process failure but not underlying transaction locks or Region conditions. Differential diagnosis: compare progress over a bounded window against a healthy feed and business truth - advancing-but-behind is ordinary sink lag, while flat progress or a lagging checkpoint with sink capacity points to TiKV/MVCC locks or Region issues and needs source-region correlation. Repair family: wait out normal lag, restart the capture for transient failures, or resolve the specific Region lock on the full peer set via the version-compatible bounded product path; never infer recovery from one successful status call - recheck timestamp relation, error field, continued progress, and an independent data invariant. Known lag-increasing causes to check before assuming a fault: short-term TPS spikes, large or long transactions, upstream TiKV/TiCDC reload or upgrade, time-consuming DDL such as add index, and aggressive PD scheduling with frequent Region leader transfer, merge, or split.

nodes.name: TiCDC Pulsar Sink Authentication
nodes.content: Mechanism: a Pulsar sink authenticates via token, token-from-file, mTLS (requires pulsar+ssl:// sink URI plus certificate/private-key/trust-cert paths), or OAuth2 (only v7.5.1+/v8.0.0+); wrong mode, unreadable credential files, or a plain pulsar:// URI with an mTLS-only broker makes the changefeed fail at the sink. Diagnosis: read the changefeed error state and match it against the configured sink.pulsar-config entries; verify the URI scheme matches the auth mode and that all certificate/token paths are readable from every TiCDC node. Repair family: fix authentication-token / token-from-file / auth-tls-* / oauth2.* parameters, keeping issuer-url, audience, client-id, and scope consistent with the broker.

nodes.name: TiCDC Pulsar topic dispatch
nodes.content: Missing events in an expected Pulsar topic are usually dispatch routing: tables follow the first matching dispatcher rule, unmatched tables or matchers without a topic expression fall back to the default sink-uri topic, and database-level DDL always goes to the default topic; topic expressions use lowercase {schema}/{table} placeholders and totals above ~1000 topics are discouraged.

nodes.name: Pulsar Sink Connectivity and Topic Prerequisites
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiCDC never auto-creates Pulsar topics and needs ACL authorization plus network reachability, so a changefeed to Pulsar fails when topics are missing, the ACL lacks permissions, or VPC/firewall rules block broker access (VPC peering needs the cluster-region CIDR in inbound rules and DNS resolution enabled for broker hostnames; public-IP access is not recommended for production). Diagnosis: check changefeed error state for connect/authorization/topic-not-found errors, then verify topic naming matches the distribution mode (single topic, per-table <prefix><db><sep><table><suffix>, or per-database). Repair family: create topics manually or enable allowAutoTopicCreation on brokers, grant ACL permissions, and open the network path before recreating the changefeed.

nodes.name: TiCDC Delivery and Consistency Semantics
nodes.content: TiCDC replicates at-least-once: with safe-mode=true (default before v6.1.3) INSERT/UPDATE are rewritten to REPLACE INTO and DELETE+REPLACE INTO to absorb duplicates; since v6.1.3 safe-mode defaults to false and only events older than a startup ThresholdTs are converted, so unexpected REPLACE INTO downstream points to safe-mode or resume-after-restart behavior. For non-MySQL sinks, primary/unique-key UPDATE events are split into DELETE-then-INSERT by default (output-raw-change-event=false since v6.5.10/7.1.6/7.5.3/8.1.1); setting true makes the consumer responsible for ordering, and clustered-index primary-key updates are always split regardless. nodes.name: TiCDC Service Safepoint Owner Cleanup
nodes.content: Mechanism: changefeed processing registers a service-level GC safepoint with PD; owner identity, capture liveness, expiration, and the safe point value are separate facts, and a stale owner keeps pinning GC independent of the TiDB GC lifetime setting. Differential diagnosis: enumerate all service owners against the gc_worker boundary and the effective minimum, classifying active, healthy, backup, and abandoned scopes before touching anything. Repair family: stop the owning capture if running, remove the exact abandoned changefeed through the product-supported capture path, then verify the feed is gone and its owner is absent or advanced to at least the live gc_worker safe point; never delete all owners, advance a global safe point, change GC lifetime, or wait out a long TTL as a shortcut. The TiCDC owner holds the PD service safepoint at the smallest changefeed checkpoint-ts; if a task stays interrupted longer than gc-ttl (default 24h) it enters failed with ErrGCTTLExceeded and can never be resumed, at which point the safepoint stops being held and GC advances - recovery is fix-and-resume before the TTL, plus raising gc-ttl or (after impact evaluation) tidb_gc_life_time.

nodes.name: Sink Backpressure and Data Validation
nodes.content: Mechanism: table-bound hooks (triggers) on a business table consume downstream write capacity, stalling the sink while all control services stay healthy. Differential diagnosis: inspect every trigger with table, event, body, and observed latency - a trigger name alone is not a diagnosis key - and use a healthy neighboring table as counterfactual only after checking its rows and write behavior. Repair family: remove the slow hook on the affected table only, preserving the neighbor, its audit hook, and all source data; close recovery only after changefeed state, checkpoint/resolved progress, equivalent downstream DDL, complete business-row equality on both endpoints, and sink write capacity all agree.

nodes.name: TiCDC Sink Protocol Consumer Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiCDC MQ/storage sinks deliver At-Least-Once, so duplicate events can appear - with canal-json enable-tidb-extension=true consumers get _tidb.commitTs and TIDB_WATERMARK events and must ignore any event whose commitTs is below the received watermark; DDL events go to partition 0 and consumers dispatch on isDdl then type. The CSV sink rows carry an I/U/D op column, optional commit-ts (include-commit-ts), and with output-old-value=true an is-update flag distinguishing UPDATE-derived DELETE+INSERT pairs; in one CSV file commit-ts is non-decreasing and one table's transactions stay in one file. The Debezium protocol only emits Row Changed events, silently ignoring DDL and WATERMARK. Diagnosis: duplicated or out-of-order rows downstream, updates applied as delete+insert pairs, or missing schema changes point at consumer parsing or protocol parameter mistakes. Remedy family: enable commitTs/watermark fields, implement watermark-based dedup and op-type handling, and remember DDL is not delivered under Debezium so schema must be managed out of band.

nodes.name: TiCDC Sink Diagnosis
nodes.content: MySQL-sink apply throughput and stability are governed by sink URI parameters: worker-count (default 16, max 1024) for concurrency, max-txn-row (256) and batch-dml-enable for batching, 2m default read/write/dial timeouts, and time-zone alignment; apply-side stalls or errors should be checked against these before tuning TiCDC itself. The downstream user needs Select/Index/Insert/Update/Delete/Create/Drop/Alter/Create View (Super for replicated RECOVER TABLE, and RESTRICTED_REPLICA_WRITER_ADMIN when the downstream has tidb_restricted_read_only enabled); missing permissions surface as changefeed apply errors. MySQL-sink apply throughput and stability are governed by sink URI parameters: worker-count (default 16, max 1024) for concurrency, max-txn-row (256) and batch-dml-enable for batching, 2m default read/write/dial timeouts, and time-zone alignment; apply-side stalls or errors should be checked against these before tuning TiCDC itself. The downstream user needs Select/Index/Insert/Update/Delete/Create/Drop/Alter/Create View (Super for replicated RECOVER TABLE, and RESTRICTED_REPLICA_WRITER_ADMIN when the downstream has tidb_restricted_read_only enabled); missing permissions surface as changefeed apply errors. After upgrading to v6.5.2+, changefeeds using Avro on FLOAT columns need the Confluent Schema Registry compatibility policy set to None before the upgrade or the changefeed enters an error state on schema update, and sink.enable-partition-separator defaults to true (v6.5.2+) to prevent data loss when replicating partitioned tables to storage services.

nodes.name: TiCDC Sorter Backlog Disk Sizing
nodes.content: TiCDC accumulates large incremental backlogs when a changefeed is paused long or starts from an old timestamp; the old Unified Sorter spilled to data_dir to avoid OOM, while v6.0+ defaults to the in-memory DB Sorter and sort_engine should be left unconfigured. Size spill disk as allowed checkpoint lag times peak upstream write traffic (at least 500 GiB free historically) and note that mechanical or low-bandwidth storage cripples sorter performance - a changefeed that lags on weak disks is often storage-bound, not CPU-bound.

nodes.name: TiCDC Storage Sink Write Failures
nodes.content: Mechanism: a TiCDC storage sink (S3/GCS/Azure/NFS) writes change files governed by worker-count, flush-interval, and file-size; protocol is mandatory at changefeed creation (missing it raises CDC:ErrSinkUnknownProtocol), and cloud backends need credentials from the URI, environment variables, a shared credentials file, or IAM role, plus bucket permissions. Diagnosis: changefeed creation failing with ErrSinkUnknownProtocol means the protocol parameter is absent; a stalled checkpoint with upload errors in TiCDC logs indicates missing permissions (ListBucket/PutObject/GetObject, plus multipart-upload permissions when parallel file upload is enabled) or expired credentials. Remedy family: fix the sink-uri protocol, grant the minimum permission set for the configured upload concurrency, and verify credential chains; files flush on either flush-interval or file-size thresholds.

nodes.name: TiCDC Single Large Table Scaling
nodes.content: Mechanism: one TiCDC node replicates a whole table by default, so a single large or hot table saturates one node's CPU/memory while other nodes idle. Diagnosis: compare per-node resource use and check the table's region count via information_schema.tikv_region_status. Remedy: enable scheduler.enable-table-across-nodes with region-threshold/write-key-threshold to split one table's ranges across nodes (Kafka changefeeds only in v7.0.0); prerequisite is a table above the region or write-rate threshold.

nodes.name: TiCDC time zone chain
nodes.content: Wrong timestamp values downstream trace to the three time zones in the replication chain: upstream TiDB time zone, TiCDC server time zone (--tz, else TZ env, else machine default) used to convert timestamp columns, and the sink time-zone parameter. Keep them consistent; a mismatch converts rather than errors, so compare all three settings when replicated DML/DDL timestamps differ from source.

nodes.name: TiCDC Version Compatibility Traps
nodes.content: Mechanism: cdc cli must match the cluster version - operating a v4.0.x cluster with the v5.0.0-rc cli either wedges the cluster and stalls replication tasks (v4.0.8-) or silently enables old-value and unified sorter (v4.0.9+); sorter storage configuration moved across versions (changefeed sort-dir, then cdc server sort-dir defaulting to /tmp/cdc_sort, then data-dir defaulting to /tmp/cdc_data with the db sorter since v6.0.0), so an unconfigured directory on a small /tmp filesystem causes disk-space failures after upgrade; replicating global temporary tables to a downstream older than v5.3.0 raises table-definition errors. Diagnosis: changefeeds stuck after tooling changes, sorter I/O filling the root filesystem, or table-definition errors on temporary tables map to these boundaries. Remedy family: recreate changefeeds with the version-matched cdc cli (remove --force, restart -R cdc if stuck), configure data-dir/sorter.sort-dir explicitly at server level via TiUP before upgrading, and align downstream TiDB to at least v5.3.0 when global temporary tables are in scope.

nodes.name: Slow TiDB-Side Execution (Concurrency and Disk Spill)
nodes.content: TiDB-root execution slowness shows up as root-task operators over large cop data: aggregates with DISTINCT run single-threaded at TiDB unless tidb_opt_distinct_agg_push_down=ON lets TiKV/TiFlash compute them, and window functions shuffle and sort everything at root unless tidb_opt_derive_topn=ON derives a partition TopN that pushes down to TiKV when the PARTITION BY column is a prefix of the clustered primary key. EXPLAIN distinguishes these cases by operator placement (root vs cop[tikv]) before any memory or concurrency tuning.

nodes.name: TiDB Memory Control Remedies
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB tracks per-query memory against tidb_mem_quota_query (default 1073741824 bytes; SESSION|GLOBAL, dynamic; from v6.5.0 it bounds a whole session including its transactions) and instance memory against tidb_server_memory_limit (default 80% of system memory; dynamic; kills the largest running query but skips DDL and window/CTE statements). Diagnosis: distinguish quota breach (client error naming conn_id), instance-level cancellation ('Out Of Memory Quota!'), real process OOM (OS kill, estimate-inuse only half of RAM before crash), vs operator spilling. Remedies: set tidb_mem_oom_action to CANCEL to fail fast or LOG to continue; raise tidb_mem_quota_query for legitimate big queries; enable tidb_enable_tmp_storage_on_oom so Sort/MergeJoin/HashJoin/HashAgg spill to disk (log 'memory exceeds quota, spill to disk now'; HashAgg spill does not cover DISTINCT aggregates and adds latency plus tmp-storage-quota disk usage); lower tidb_server_memory_limit_gc_trigger eases GC pressure at most once per minute; for the v6.1.3-v6.5.0 pattern of OOM with estimate-inuse near half of memory, setting the GOMEMLIMIT environment variable and restarting tidb-server stabilizes Go heap growth. Risks: CANCEL breaks legitimate large statements; instance limit does not guarantee safety during startup or in hybrid deployments (it is per tidb-server instance).

nodes.name: TiDB OOM Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB memory exceeds the container/host limit and the process is killed, dropping all connections. Discrimination: OOM-killer records in system logs plus a fresh 'Welcome to TiDB' restart entry confirm OOM; 'expensive_query' (or 'memory exceeds quota') log lines point at candidate statements; typical patterns are HashJoin with a large inner table, oversized single UPDATE/DELETE, and many UNION-connected subqueries. Fix family: set per-query memory quota and let operators spill to disk, rewrite the offending statements or fix their plans, enable swap only as a buffer knowing large queries slow down, and right-size instance memory limits. Since v3.0.4 an executor exceeding tidb_mem_quota_query returns an Out Of Memory Quota error instead of dropping the connection, so client-side disconnect symptoms point elsewhere. TiDB instance memory blowups come from unbounded query memory, large transactions, and uncontrolled aggregate usage; remediation layers: per-query tidb_mem_quota_query (exceeding it errors or spills), the global tidb_server_memory_limit (v6.4+) which cancels the highest-memory SQL at the threshold and dumps diagnostic files, and INFORMATION_SCHEMA.MEMORY_USAGE / MEMORY_USAGE_OPS_HISTORY to see what the instance cancelled. Watch for range-building blowups from huge IN lists - tidb_opt_range_max_size makes the optimizer fall back to coarser ranges instead of OOMing.

nodes.name: TiDB Security Configuration Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB client TLS (ssl-ca/cert/key) makes client certificates optional to present but verified when shown; invalid certificate files let TiDB start without secure connections; tls-version sets the minimum protocol; disconnect-on-expired-password either drops sessions or restricts them to sandbox password reset; TiProxy session migration requires session-token-signing-cert/key identical on every TiDB node. Diagnosis: for TLS connection or session-migration failures, compare certificate paths and validity across nodes and check the effective TLS version. Remedies: distribute the same signing cert/key to all TiDB nodes, set tls-version to TLSv1.2+ since 1.0/1.1 are removed, or relax disconnect-on-expired-password to keep sessions in sandbox mode; risk is weaker security if certificate verification or SEM is disabled.

nodes.name: Migration tool selection
nodes.content: Import/copy failures often trace to wrong tool choice: DM alone fits full+incremental migration below ~1TiB, larger datasets use Dumpling export then Lightning physical import (TB-level, cluster offline to services during import) plus DM incremental, while Lightning logical import is slower but online and can target MySQL. TiDB-to-TiDB copies use BR backup/restore, TiDB-to-TiDB incremental uses TiCDC, and shard merges use DM with optional Lightning pre-load.

nodes.name: TiFlash Analytic Overload Tuning
nodes.content: TiFlash MPP slowness frequently traces to node saturation: per-instance CPU, memory and IO utilization approaching their ceiling (e.g. IO util near 90% or CPU near full core allocation) means the analytic workload has outgrown the TiFlash cluster. Confirm with the TiFlash resource panels, then choose between scaling TiFlash nodes, lowering analytic concurrency, or shedding queries back to TiKV row-store. TiFlash MPP slowness frequently traces to node saturation: per-instance CPU, memory and IO utilization approaching their ceiling means the analytic workload has outgrown the TiFlash cluster - scale nodes, lower analytic concurrency, or shed queries to TiKV. Thread overuse from per-task thread requests is mitigated by the pipeline execution model (tidb_enable_tiflash_pipeline_model, v7.2+), which centrally schedules threads; pre-v7.2 schema changes in a large database could also stall TiFlash reads while it re-replicated every table's schema, fixed by replicating only TiFlash-replica tables. TiFlash MPP slowness frequently traces to node saturation: per-instance CPU, memory and IO utilization approaching their ceiling means the analytic workload has outgrown the TiFlash cluster - scale nodes, lower analytic concurrency, or shed queries to TiKV; co-deployed TiKV+TiFlash must keep per-component resource reservations and separate disks. Thread overuse from per-task thread requests is mitigated by the pipeline execution model (tidb_enable_tiflash_pipeline_model, v7.2+); pre-v7.2 schema changes in a large database could stall TiFlash reads while it re-replicated every table's schema.

nodes.name: TiFlash Compact And Join Tuning
nodes.content: Heavy updates and deletes leave stale versions in TiFlash replicas, inflating disk use and scan cost; ALTER TABLE ... COMPACT [PARTITION ...] TIFLASH REPLICA rewrites physical data to reclaim space, run it during low-load windows since it rewrites column files. For MPP joins, tidb_broadcast_join_threshold_size/count decide Broadcast vs Shuffled Hash Join - raising them makes small-table joins broadcast instead of shuffle, visible as ExchangeType changes in EXPLAIN.

nodes.name: TiFlash corruption repair runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiFlash stores columnar replicas locally; corruption on one node invalidates only that node's copy and replicas are re-established by redeployment. Differential: confirm the failure is local to one TiFlash node and not a query/planner issue, and check remaining replica count still satisfies availability before taking the node down. Remedies: (a) take the corrupted TiFlash node down, delete its data directory, and redeploy the node so PD re-schedules learner peers onto it. Risks: do not wipe a node while it holds the only reachable replica; keep enough healthy nodes during repair.

nodes.name: TiFlash Disaggregated Cache Economics
nodes.content: Mechanism: in disaggregated TiFlash, Write Nodes convert Raft data to columnar format and upload to S3 while stateless Compute Nodes read hot data from Write Nodes and S3 through a local NVMe SSD cache. Diagnosis: for slow analytical queries, identify whether the working set is cold data not resident in the Compute-Node cache. Remedies: keep frequently queried hot data cached by sizing local SSD, elastically scale Compute Nodes for peak-and-valley workloads, and place latency-critical scans on cached data; risk is that first-touch cold reads pay remote-fetch latency and stopping Compute Nodes makes the data temporarily unqueryable.

nodes.name: TiFlash Encryption at Rest Semantics
nodes.content: TiFlash uses envelope encryption: a user-supplied master key (KMS or file) wraps data keys that rotate automatically (default weekly); enabling encryption or changing the method only guarantees encryption for newly written data. TiFlash has no online master-key rotation, so rotating requires configuring security.encryption.master-key plus previous-master-key and a rolling restart; a restart failure after rotation usually means the KMS key or endpoint is unreachable or the previous key was removed before all files were re-encrypted, and tikv-ctl can dump encryption metadata for verification.

nodes.name: TiFlash format rollback runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiFlash data written in a newer format (PageStorage V3, DTFile V3, newer RocksDB config) is unreadable by older binaries, and some upgrades forbid in-place downgrade entirely. Differential: check Grafana TiFlash-Summary > Storage Pool > Storage Pool Run Mode to see whether tables still run V2/V3/mixed, and confirm the node's binary version versus on-disk format. Remedies: (a) keep the node on the newer version and let compaction convert data; (b) after a v6.2 upgrade run ALTER TABLE ... COMPACT TIFLASH REPLICA per replica table then restart TiFlash to finish conversion; (c) for unavoidable downgrades, forcibly scale in the affected TiFlash node and let it re-replicate from TiKV, or use DTTool to rewrite DTFiles offline. Risks: re-replication trades cluster replica capacity during the window; avoid major-version jumps (upgrade through intermediate versions) and honor the stop-TiFlash-first rule for pre-5.3 sources.

nodes.name: TiFlash Index Build Progress
nodes.content: After bulk loads, freshly persisted data is indexed asynchronously and rows in the Delta layer stay unindexed until compaction, so queries are correct but slow until indexing finishes. Check INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TIFLASH_INDEXES (ROWS_STABLE_NOT_INDEXED reaching 0 means complete, ERROR_MESSAGE for failures) and ADMIN SHOW DDL JOBS row count; ALTER TABLE ... COMPACT forces Delta merge into the Stable layer to finish indexing.

nodes.name: TiFlash Query Failure Diagnosis
nodes.content: TiFlash columnar replicas are async Raft learners whose reads validate replication progress against the read timestamp, so a lagging, crashed, or re-syncing TiFlash node breaks MPP queries that chose it, and DTFile checksum failures make the node exit until its data is re-replicated; under high MPP concurrency the MinTSO scheduler's thread soft/hard limits can also reject or deadlock tasks. Distinguish replica unavailability from scheduler limits by node liveness and replica progress rather than query shape; fix family: restore the node, rebuild the table's TiFlash replica, or let the optimizer fall back to TiKV, accepting slower row-store performance.

nodes.name: TiFlash Raft Replication Lag
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiFlash applies TiKV data through raft log replication; high Raft Wait Index Duration (wait_index latency) or Raft Batch Read Index Duration means replication or TiKV interaction lags, caused by TiKV overload, TiFlash IO overload, or a network bottleneck between them; write amplification of the TiFlash layer is (read flow + write flow) / total write throughput. Diagnosis: compare the two raft metrics with TiFlash write/read flow split by stable (File Descriptor) and delta (Page) layers to see whether disks or the network saturate. Remedies: move TiFlash to higher-throughput local disks, reduce TiKV load, or add TiFlash nodes; risk is that cloud block storage sustains far lower throughput, so replication lag persists under heavy incremental writes.

nodes.name: TiFlash Replica Diagnosis
nodes.content: The optimizer picks TiFlash by cost in CBO mode; confirm with EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE showing cop[tiflash], and refresh statistics with ANALYZE if it is not selected. With only one TiFlash replica and its node down, CBO queries retry repeatedly and appear to hang; remedy by forcing TiKV via engine isolation (instance/session level, engine='tiflash'/'tikv') or a READ_FROM_STORAGE hint while the replica recovers. The optimizer picks TiFlash by cost in CBO mode; confirm with EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE showing cop[tiflash], and refresh statistics with ANALYZE (collect stats in advance for new tables) if it is not selected. With only one TiFlash replica and its node down, CBO queries retry repeatedly and appear to hang; remedy by forcing TiKV via engine isolation (instance/session level) or a READ_FROM_STORAGE hint while the replica recovers. Replica sync speed is double-throttled: per-instance snapshot write limit (server.snap-io-max-bytes-per-sec, default 100MiB/s on TiKV and raftstore-proxy on TiFlash, raisable live via SET CONFIG) and PD's global add-peer store limit (default ~30 regions/min, raised with pd-ctl store limit all engine tiflash 60 add-peer). Raise both progressively when spare CPU/IO exists; a stuck AVAILABLE=0 replica with progress frozen points at scheduling limits or an unhealthy TiFlash node rather than data volume.

nodes.name: TiFlash Replica Zone Placement
nodes.content: Mechanism: PD schedules TiFlash learner replicas according to the zone labels set on TiFlash nodes via learner_config server.labels and the replica count from ALTER TABLE ... SET TIFLASH REPLICA, enabling multi-AZ disaster recovery for the columnar layer. Diagnosis: verify distribution by joining information_schema.tikv_region_status, tikv_region_peers, and tikv_store_status filtered to stores labeled tiflash, per table or partition. Remedies: relabel TiFlash nodes with server.labels (avoid legacy flash.proxy.labels for special characters), adjust replica counts, and use tiflash_replica_read to steer reads across zones; do not configure TiFlash replicas with LOCATION LABELS since TiDB cannot parse multiple labels there.

nodes.name: TiFlash Restart Failure After Version Change
nodes.content: Since v6.3.0 TiFlash on Linux AMD64 requires CPUs with the AVX2 instruction set (ARM64 requires ARMv8 with crc32/asimd), so a TiFlash node that crashes or refuses to start after deployment or version change on older hardware is an instruction-set problem, verifiable by checking /proc/cpuinfo for avx2 before redeploying.

nodes.name: TiFlash scale-in unblock runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: PD will not move TiFlash learner peers away from leaving nodes while some table demands more replicas than the post-scale-in node count, and dropped tables' rules persist until their data meets GC conditions. Differential: run SELECT * FROM information_schema.tiflash_replica WHERE REPLICA_COUNT > <post_scale_in_nodes> and, when no replicas remain but removal still fails, check for recent DROP TABLE/DROP DATABASE on replica-carrying tables and list PD rules via the tiflash rules-group API. Remedies: (a) lower the affected tables' TiFlash replica count so it fits the remaining nodes; (b) wait for GC to clear stale rules, or manually DELETE each tiflash rule in PD before GC. Risks: manually removed rules are not restored by RECOVER TABLE, FLASHBACK TABLE, or FLASHBACK DATABASE - those tables lose TiFlash replicas. Related pitfalls: replicating over ~1,000 tables degrades PD scheduling, and replica settings left on system tables must be cleared before cluster upgrade; database-level ALTER DATABASE replication interrupted mid-run does not roll back completed operations.

nodes.name: TiFlash Slow Analysis Diagnosis
nodes.content: On multi-disk TiFlash nodes, storage.latest.dir and storage.main.dir split data by disk quality (v4.0.9+); on older versions path_realtime_mode writes all latest data to the first directory only, creating a per-disk hotspot, and the latest directory should hold roughly 10% of planned capacity. When TiFlash scans are slow, compare per-disk utilization and directory layout before blaming query plans. INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TIFLASH_TABLES.TOTAL_DELTA_ROWS (counting versions, not rows) shows how much data still sits un-compacted in the delta layer; 0 means the table is optimal, and ALTER TABLE ... COMPACT TIFLASH REPLICA moves delta data into stable segments, with a non-zero residue after compaction simply reflecting concurrent updates. On multi-disk TiFlash nodes, storage.latest.dir and storage.main.dir split data by disk quality (v4.0.9+); on older versions path_realtime_mode writes all latest data to the first directory only, creating a per-disk hotspot, so compare per-disk utilization before blaming query plans. On the Request Duration Overview, cop-dominant traffic means statements are not fully pushed down to TiFlash: large scans may be an intended cost-model choice, but cop floods on small data with missing indexes mean proper TiKV indexes should serve those reads instead; rising remote_read metrics point to replica or placement problems. INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TIFLASH_TABLES.TOTAL_DELTA_ROWS (counting versions, not rows) shows un-compacted delta data; 0 means optimal, and ALTER TABLE ... COMPACT TIFLASH REPLICA moves delta into stable segments. On multi-disk nodes, storage.latest.dir and storage.main.dir split data by disk quality (v4.0.9+); older versions' path_realtime_mode writes all latest data to the first directory only, creating a per-disk hotspot.

nodes.name: Control TiFlash Memory with Spill Thresholds
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiFlash spills hash join, hash aggregation, and TopN/Sort intermediate data once operator-level limits (tidb_max_bytes_before_tiflash_external_join/sort/group_by) or query-level memory ratios (v7.4+) are exceeded; unset thresholds let single analytical queries reach tens of GiB. Differential: attribute memory to operators via MemoryTracker peaks in TiFlash logs before choosing thresholds. Remedies: set operator or query-level spill thresholds sized to node memory, and use storage.io_rate_limit on TiFlash to protect disks shared with TiKV. Risk: spilling trades memory for disk I/O and longer runtimes; too-low thresholds degrade analytical latency.

nodes.name: TiFlash Workload Fit
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiFlash columnar storage with MPP fits large scans, heavy aggregation/joins, mixed OLTP+OLAP isolation, and SaaS multi-tenant arbitrary filtering where composite primary keys lead with tenant id and indexing hundreds of filterable columns is impractical; late materialization plus primary-key clustering gives efficient table range scans without per-column indexes. Diagnosis: when analytical queries dominate database time on TiKV with huge TableFullScan row counts, evaluate whether the tables have TiFlash replicas and whether the plan could run mpp[tiflash]. Remedies: add TiFlash replicas for the analytical tables and let cost-based selection or engine hints route the queries, keeping OLTP on TiKV; risk is duplicated storage cost and replication lag for hot analytic tables.

nodes.name: TiKV Block Cache Tuning
nodes.content: TiKV memory splits mainly into the shared block cache ([storage.block-cache] capacity, shared by all CFs since 3.0) and per-CF write buffers (write-buffer-size); an oversized cache plus buffers crowds out other components and contributes to TiKV OOM, while an undersized cache shows up as read amplification and latency growth on hot ranges. Diagnose memory pressure by checking configured cache capacity against actual TiKV RSS before blaming workload growth.

nodes.name: Leader Drop Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: leaders move when TiKV restarts (panic pulled up by systemd, killed by third party, OOM, hangs such as THP changes), when write stalls make heartbeats lapse, or under network isolation. Discrimination: panic entries and dmesg distinguish crash and external kills; server-is-busy on the errors panel ties re-election to write stalls; etcd round-trip and network monitoring expose isolation; after power-off, raft log errors such as unexpected raft log index or entries unavailable are expected with unreliable fsync (sync-log off, VMs) and need Region restore. Fix family: eliminate the crash or OOM root cause, relieve write stalls, repair network partitioning, and fix placement so one host failure cannot remove multiple replicas.

nodes.name: Diagnose TiKV Memory Consumers and OOM
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV memory is dominated by the shared block cache (default 45% of system memory on raft-kv, 30% on partitioned-raft-kv), memtables (write-buffer-limit default 20% of memory on partitioned-raft-kv), and thread pools; their sum must stay below host memory or TiKV is OOM-killed. Differential: heap profiling (enable-heap-profiling, 512KiB sampling, thread-exclusive arena) attributes usage to block cache growth vs memtable accumulation vs allocator fragmentation. Remedies: explicitly set storage.block-cache.capacity (mandatory when several TiKV share one host), cap write-buffer-limit, or add memory; risk: shrinking cache raises read I/O and latency. Raft Engine adds a memory limit defaulting to 15% of system memory, and PITR restore caps its memory with import.memory-use-ratio (default 0.3); include both when summing consumers. gRPC memory can also spike; grpc-memory-pool-quota caps it to avoid OOM at the cost of potential stalls, and coprocessor region buckets (region-bucket-size, default 50MiB) affect scan concurrency.

nodes.name: TiKV OOM runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV memory is dominated by the shared RocksDB block cache; large scans and complex queries add more, and co-located instances multiply the footprint. Differential diagnosis: check block-cache-size versus actual system memory and whether several TiKV instances share the host; OOM during large result-set queries points at query memory rather than cache settings. Remedy families: (1) lower block-cache-size (and write-buffer sizes) so instances fit in memory; (2) separate TiKV instances onto dedicated hosts; (3) cap query-side memory. Risks: shrinking the block cache raises read latency; raising it invites repeat OOM, so size for the sum of all instances on the host.

nodes.name: TiKV OOM Diagnosis
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV memory exceeds limits from an oversized block cache, coprocessor returning more data than gRPC can send, or other internal consumers. Discrimination: compare block cache size against the instance memory limit (default 45% of machine memory, which is wrong inside containers unless set explicitly); compare coprocessor response size with network outbound traffic to spot reply backlog. Fix family: set storage.block-cache.capacity to fit the real container quota, reduce large-scan result volumes and fix scan-heavy plans, and treat other-component growth as abnormal for escalation.

nodes.name: TiKV overload runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: when Raftstore threads or disk I/O saturate, TiKV returns busy errors that make the TiDB side back off (sleep up to seconds per retry), and slow Raft heartbeats cause frequent leader re-elections. Differential diagnosis: compare Raftstore CPU usage and disk I/O on the busy store; frequent leader switching with high Report failures points to network problems or a stuck original leader rather than local saturation; not_leader/stale_epoch TiClient errors are normally self-healing re-routing, but bursts correlate with leader churn; a single node failure is covered by Raft with leader re-election within 2 * lease (lease about 10 seconds). Remedy families: (1) add TiKV/TiDB capacity or shed load; (2) fix the underlying I/O or network bottleneck; (3) spread hot traffic (resource groups, hotspot remedies). Risks: sustained busy backoff amplifies client latency; repeatedly replacing disks without reducing write amplification reproduces the overload.

nodes.name: Tune TiKV Quota Limiter for Latency Jitter
nodes.content: Mechanism: foreground/background quota limiters softly cap CPU time and read/write bandwidth; requests over quota wait up to max-delay-duration (default 500ms), producing latency jitter and periodic slow queries while cpu stays below host capacity. Differential: distinguish quota waits (uniform small delays) from compaction stalls (disk_io) and Region hotspots. Remedies: raise the specific quota or reset to 0 (unlimited) on rich-resource hosts; on small instances set foreground-cpu-time around 1000-1500 millicpu per 4 cores instead. Risk: unlimited foreground on few-core hosts starves background work and destabilizes TiKV; background quota limiter is experimental.

nodes.name: TiKV Request Timeout Log Markers
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiDB logs encode TiKV request-path failures - coprocessor 'request outdated' after 60s queued at TiKV, region cache 'switch region peer' with context deadline exceeded (send-phase cancellation suggests send saturation when pending request counts exceed about 128; wait-phase points to the addressed TiKV), and 'inconsistent index' signals possible data-index corruption. Discrimination: split cancellations by phase and check the named TiKV's response time and PD/KV logs in the window. Fix family: relieve TiKV queue pressure from scan-heavy plans, inspect the specific TiKV for maintenance or faults, and for inconsistency run ADMIN CHECK TABLE, freeze GC, and escalate before further writes.

nodes.name: TiKV Scale-In Drain Semantics
nodes.content: Scale-in of TiKV (also TiFlash and TiDB Binlog) is asynchronous: TiUP marks the node Offline and returns immediately, PD then schedules its regions to peers, and only after draining does TiUP stop the service, clean data files and drop it from the topology. A node stuck in Offline for long means scheduling cannot satisfy replica rules (insufficient stores, placement labels, or down peers) rather than a hung TiUP; verify remaining replica capacity before scale-in because data files are destroyed once drained.

nodes.name: Slow TiKV Node Remediation
nodes.content: Mechanism: raftstore inspects component latency every inspect-interval (100ms); a high timeout ratio together with CPU above inspect-cpu-util-thd (0.4) marks the node slow, and SlowTrend tracks latency/QPS sensitivity. Differential: separate disk saturation (check kvdb disk via inspect-kvdb-interval) from thread-pool starvation and CPU exhaustion. Remedies: rebalance leaders or Regions away from the slow store, enlarge raftstore/apply/store-io thread pools (store-pool-size, apply-pool-size, store-io-pool-size) within CPU budget, or fix the underlying disk. Risk: bigger thread pools consume CPU and can worsen saturation; rolling restarts should respect min-pending-apply-region-count. Read-side ServerIsBusy instead indicates the unified read pool is saturated (max-tasks-per-worker 2000, pool default CPU*0.8); enlarge it only with confirmed CPU headroom because extra threads add context-switch overhead. At the PD level, scheduler add evict-leader-scheduler or evict-slow-store-scheduler drains leaders from the offending store, and scheduler pause/resume freezes balancing during maintenance windows.

nodes.name: TiKV-Side Slow Processing
nodes.content: Mechanism: cop[tikv] tasks dominate Query_time so the bottleneck is TiKV data processing. Differential: large Cop_wait Max_time on one address means a busy TiKV instance (confirm with that instance's CPU monitoring), while Total_keys greatly exceeding Processed_keys means too many outdated key versions must be cleaned during scans. Fixes: relieve the busy instance (capacity/scheduling) or reduce stale-version scan cost (GC/compaction health, scan range).

nodes.name: TiKV startup error runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV stores the cluster ID it learned from PD at initialization and re-checks it at every start; PD also remembers store addresses, so stale state on either side blocks startup. Differential diagnosis: cluster ID mismatch means TiKV's local data predates the current PD cluster (for example PD data was wiped and re-deployed); duplicated store address means the old store was not deleted from PD or --data-dir was changed or lost. Remedy families: point TiKV back at its original PD/data pair, or delete the stale store via pd-ctl store delete before restarting. Risks: deleting a registered store or wiping data is irreversible for that replica - confirm the old cluster is truly retired first.

nodes.name: TiKV Storage Metrics Reading
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV-Details panels expose RocksDB get/seek/write and WAL sync durations, compaction rate and pending bytes, block cache and memtable hit rates, read amplification, and write stall duration (normally zero); Raft Engine write duration breaks into wal/wait/apply; Titan adds blob file counts, live blob size, blob cache hits, and GC action metrics. Diagnosis: for write latency spikes check write stall duration and stall-condition changes first, then compaction pending bytes and WAL sync duration; low block cache hit or high read amplification points to scan-heavy reads. Remedies: relieve compaction backlog by throttling writes or scaling disks, tune cache sizing, and watch Titan blob GC when blob size grows; risk is misreading background compaction bursts as foreground faults.

nodes.name: TiKV Thread Pool Tuning
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiKV throughput is bounded by its thread pools - gRPC (network/deserialization), scheduler (transaction-to-KV conversion, where conflicts surface early), raftstore and StoreWriter (Raft log and RocksDB writes), and apply. Diagnosis: per-pool Thread CPU panels against targets: gRPC below 80% of pool size, scheduler 50-75%, raftstore below 60% without StoreWriter or below 80% with it. Fix family: size pools per CPU cores, enable StoreWriter only with spare CPU, and for write-heavy workloads also review storage-engine compaction, flow control, and Titan settings. Risks: enlarging raftstore/StoreWriter pools multiplies Raft log overhead onto other pools and disk; insufficient CPU turns the tuning into a regression.

nodes.name: TiKV Slow Write Path Analysis
nodes.content: Mechanism: write latency decomposes into scheduler command, latch wait, raft propose, append log, commit log, and apply log stages, each with distinct bottlenecks. Discrimination: scheduler command duration exceeding latch wait plus async write means scheduler CPU saturation; high append log duration with high WAL sync duration means slow disk; propose wait far above append log means raftstore pool too small or CPU shortage; apply log duration high with per-thread apply CPU hot spots a single Region or slow RocksDB writes; commit log duration high under write hotspot points to raft flow-control window. Fix family: enlarge the matching thread pool within CPU budget (store/apply pools 1-5), improve disk throughput, disperse write hotspots, or raise raft-max-inflight-msgs for hotspot commits.

nodes.name: Timeout Class Diagnosis (GC, Txn TTL, SQL Limits)
nodes.content: Mechanism: MVCC snapshots are reclaimed by GC, pessimistic transactions have a TTL, idle sessions hold locks, and read-only statements honor max_execution_time. Differential: 'GC life time is shorter than transaction duration' means a read outlived GC retention; long INSERT-SELECT rolled back means the transaction TTL was exceeded; hung sessions holding locks point to idle transactions; client setQueryTimeout not working points to missing global kill support. Fix families: temporarily raise GC retention (risk: extra MVCC versions degrade performance, revert promptly), split oversized transactions or raise the transaction TTL (risk: longer lock holding), terminate idle transactions via idle timeout, and set session-level max_execution_time/wait_timeout in connection strings. GC lifetime defaults to ten minutes; raising it trades error suppression for old-version pileup on heavy update/delete tables.

nodes.name: Temporal DDL Time Zone Semantics
nodes.content: Mechanism: temporal DDL interpretation is session-sensitive; a lower-bound TIMESTAMP default can pass upstream and fail downstream when the same displayed literal falls outside the downstream type's range under different time zones. Differential diagnosis: compare upstream DDL text and session time zone against downstream session and global time zones plus the downstream error, comparing the UTC instant and column contract rather than literal spelling. Repair family: probe with a connection-local time-zone setting, repair only the affected downstream object, verify column type/nullability/default via SHOW CREATE TABLE and INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS before resuming the feed, and never change a global time zone to make one DDL appear valid.

nodes.name: Time Zone Resolution and TIMESTAMP Behavior
nodes.content: Mechanism: time_zone defaults to SYSTEM, resolved from the TZ environment variable, then /etc/localtime, then UTC; the global variable seeds each session and only TIMESTAMP values are zone-converted (DATETIME/DATE/TIME are not), so wrong or shifting displayed times usually come from session/global time_zone or host TZ differences between TiDB nodes. Diagnosis: compare @@global.time_zone, @@session.time_zone, and @@global.system_time_zone. Remedy: set the session or global time_zone explicitly (offset or named zone) and keep node system time zones consistent.

nodes.name: TiProxy Connection Migration and Limits
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiProxy sits between clients and TiDB, migrates sessions between TiDB servers transparently when a server is taken offline (scale-in, rolling upgrade/restart) or when connection ratios exceed a threshold, and auto-discovers the TiDB list, so planned maintenance does not break client connections. On TiProxy's own shutdown, the HTTP port turns unhealthy while the SQL port still accepts new connections for graceful-wait-before-shutdown, then drains; after graceful-close-conn-timeout remaining connections are force-closed, so the drain timeout must exceed transaction lifetime or transactions are dropped. Diagnosis: for client connection errors, check whether the path uses TiProxy and whether the disconnecting TiDB went down as planned - migration only covers planned offline; unexpected TiDB failure still drops connections. Remedy family: keep TiProxy for connection persistence during rolling operations, size graceful-close-conn-timeout above the longest transaction, and reserve extra CPU headroom because its throughput is below HAProxy; use HAProxy/K8s LB when performance or cost dominates.

nodes.name: TiProxy Failure Triage
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiProxy failures cluster into connectivity (unsupported connector/auth plugin, no healthy TiDB, require-backend-tls certificates missing on either TiProxy or TiDB, TiDB older than v6.5.0, proxy-protocol wrongly enabled on TiDB while TiProxy already speaks it, or max-connections exceeded), failed connection migration (TiDB-side session-token-signing-cert/key and graceful-wait-before-shutdown misconfigured, or documented TiProxy limitations hit - check the supported-connector list first), unbalanced TiDB CPU (balancing is by connection count, not per-connection load), and added latency (decompose via Grafana: TiProxy latency, TiDB latency, backend network duration; TiProxy CPU above ~90% means saturation). The health endpoint /api/debug/health returns the config checksum while serving and errors when shutting down; the Disconnection OPM panel classifies every dropped connection by reason (client network break, handshake fail, auth fail, SQL error, proxy shutdown, malformed packet, get backend fail, backend network break, backend handshake fail), and Balance panels show per-backend connections, session migration rates/durations, and health-check cycle - a cycle over ~3 seconds means the backend list may refresh too slowly. Diagnosis: read client error strings and disconnection reasons first, then Grafana latency/CPU panels. Remedy family: fix certificate/proxy-protocol/max-connections configuration, align TiDB session-token settings to re-enable migration, scale out CPU-bound TiProxy, and treat load-based imbalance as expected behavior needing workload-side fixes.

nodes.name: TiSpark Access and Compatibility Boundaries
nodes.content: TiSpark reads TiKV directly and bypasses TiDB Server access control (own authentication exists since v2.5), and compatibility is not guaranteed with TiDB v7.0.0+ or Spark v3.4.0+. When Spark analytics against TiKV fails or degrades after an upgrade, first check the version pairing and Spark-side memory provisioning (reserve OS memory, roughly 32 GB executor/worker) before blaming TiDB health. TiSpark reads TiKV directly and bypasses TiDB Server access control (own authentication exists since v2.5), and compatibility is not guaranteed with TiDB v7.0.0+ or Spark v3.4.0+. Spark-side knobs change behavior: spark.tispark.isolation_read_engines=tiflash forces columnar reads and errors for tables without replicas, TLS needs both the TiKV-client and JDBC parts (TLSv1.2/1.3 only, JKS takes priority over X.509), timestamps follow -Duser.timezone rather than spark.sql.session.timeZone, and 'Failed to get database' ObjectStore warnings are benign Spark catalog noise.

nodes.name: TiSpark Deployment Prerequisites
nodes.content: TiSpark fails to start when JRE 8 is absent on its hosts; TiUP does not install JRE, so operators must install it or point the topology java_home parameter at an existing JRE path. Distinguish from network or config-template problems by checking java availability on TiSpark nodes first; note that TiSpark support in TiUP is deprecated, so new deployments should prefer native TiDB or alternatives.

nodes.name: Titan blob GC runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: with the Titan engine, values live in blob files that only shrink via blob GC (regular GC driven by discardable size after compactions, or Level Merge on the lowest levels), so space amplification persists until discardable-ratio thresholds trigger rewrites. Differential diagnosis: watch the Blob file count under TiKV-Details/Titan-kv and disk usage growth that logical data size cannot explain; check whether Titan was recently enabled or is being disabled. Remedy families: (1) let regular GC/compaction reclaim blob space (tune discardable-ratio; default 0.5 is safer when disk is tight, 1.0 saves GC bandwidth when space is ample); (2) to disable Titan set rocksdb.defaultcf.titan.blob-run-mode=fallback (avoid flipping rocksdb.titan.enabled off on older versions, which can crash TiKV); (3) optionally tikv-ctl compact-cluster --bottommost force for a full compaction. Risks: the fallback migration and full compaction consume heavy I/O/CPU and can degrade online performance substantially, and on a nearly full disk compaction can exhaust the remaining space - ensure headroom first.

nodes.name: Titan Enable and Disable Discipline
nodes.content: Mechanism: Titan (blob engine for wide-table/JSON write and point-query performance) is enabled by default since v7.6.0, but upgraded clusters keep their pre-upgrade RocksDB or Titan choice and prior min-blob-size; directly setting rocksdb.titan.enabled = false to disable Titan can crash TiKV on versions before v8.5.0. Diagnosis: for unexpected blob disk usage after an upgrade, check whether Titan state and min-blob-size were retained by the upgrade. Remedies: follow the documented staged disable procedure instead of flipping enabled = false, and set min-blob-size deliberately on new clusters; risk of mishandled disablement is TiKV crash or residual blob files.

nodes.name: Titan Level Merge Trade-offs
nodes.content: Mechanism: Titan stores values as blobs, and its default GC and compaction layout amplify disk usage and disturb foreground writes; the experimental level-merge option merges levels while keeping blob files, improving range-query performance, reducing Titan GC impact on writes, and lowering space amplification. Diagnosis: for TiKV disk growth or write latency with Titan enabled, check whether level-merge is on and how much GC churn is present in logs. Remedies: enable rocksdb.defaultcf.titan.level-merge to trade slightly higher write amplification (still below native RocksDB) for lower space use and steadier write latency; risk is experimental behavior, so validate under the production workload before rollout.

nodes.name: Titan min-blob-size Tuning
nodes.content: Mechanism: min-blob-size decides which values go into Titan blobs versus plain RocksDB; benchmarks show write- and point-read-heavy workloads benefit from small thresholds (around 1 KB) while scan-heavy workloads regress unless the threshold is at least about 16 KB, with heavy scans (like full exports) still about 10% slower on Titan; GC Range Merge rewrites blob files when sorted runs accumulate in a range, and scaled-in nodes start in RocksDB format before compaction converts them to Titan. Diagnosis: for write-boost but scan-degradation patterns with Titan enabled, compare the workload mix against the row width relative to min-blob-size. Remedies: set min-blob-size per workload (1 KB for write/point-read, 16 KB or higher for scan-heavy) and expect transient mixed-format behavior after scaling; risk is that the wrong threshold amplifies exactly the dominant workload's cost.

nodes.name: Titan enable/disable startup risk
nodes.content: Titan state changes are not freely reversible in place: disabling rocksdb.titan.enabled on an instance whose blob data directory is non-empty makes TiKV fail to start with "You have disabled titan when its data directory is not empty", requiring re-enable and the proper drain procedure. Since v7.6.0 Titan is on by default for new clusters (min-blob-size 32KiB) while upgraded clusters retain their pre-upgrade setting, so check per-instance config during startup failures.

nodes.name: TiUP No-sudo Deployment Preconditions
nodes.content: Mechanism: TiUP no-sudo mode runs components as systemd user instances, so deployment or startup fails when the user's systemd mode is not running (user@<uid>.service with XDG_RUNTIME_DIR set), linger is disabled so services die on logout, SSH authorized_keys permissions are wrong, or topology.yaml lacks systemd_mode: "user" with user-writable deploy_dir/data_dir. Diagnosis: check `systemctl --user` works as the deploy user, `loginctl show-user -p Linger` shows Linger=yes, and directory ownership; on CentOS only 8+ is supported. Repair family: set XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, start user@<uid>.service and enable-linger, fix authorized_keys ownership/600 mode, and chown the deploy/data directories to the deploy user.

nodes.name: TLS Certificate Login Diagnosis
nodes.content: With certificate authentication TiDB checks the client X.509 subject, issuer, SAN, and cipher against per-user REQUIRE clauses, so login can be rejected despite a correct password when the certificate does not match. On certificate replacement run ALTER INSTANCE RELOAD TLS to reload ssl-cert/ssl-key/ssl-ca without restart; new certificates apply only to connections established afterwards, and Ssl_server_not_before/Ssl_server_not_after status variables expose the validity window to catch expired certs.

nodes.name: TLS connection failure triage
nodes.content: Client TLS failures have asymmetric failure modes: with invalid ssl-cert/ssl-key the TiDB server still starts but TLS handshakes fail (confirm via the "mysql protocol server secure connection is enabled" INFO log at startup), while require_secure_transport or REQUIRE SSL users lock out non-TLS clients. MySQL 5.7+ clients attempt TLS by default and silently fall back, so check --ssl-mode on the client and the server ssl-ca chain when authentication fails.

nodes.name: High-Load SQL Triage
nodes.content: Top SQL and Continuous Profiling (both off by default) attribute CPU to SQL digests and code paths: in the documented seven-scenario OLTP comparison, the text Query interface (useServerPrepStmts=false) made Compile+Optimize consume over half of TiDB CPU and pushed per-connection driver housekeeping SQL (SELECT @@session.tx_isolation) to the top of Top SQL, while the Performance Overview dashboard showed compile dominating database time and zero plan-cache hits. High CPU with no matching business SQL therefore points at driver/plan-cache behavior before capacity changes.

nodes.name: TopN and Limit Pushdown Rules
nodes.content: Mechanism: ORDER BY plus LIMIT forms a TopN operator that TiDB pushes toward the data source to cut transferred rows: it can reach TiKV coprocessors, and into a Join's outer side only when the sort keys depend solely on outer-table columns; it cannot push below inner joins or outer-join inner sides or across multi-table sort expressions because results would change, and TopN degrades to a plain Limit when the sort key is the ordered primary key read with keep order. Diagnosis: for slow top-N queries, EXPLAIN and check whether a cop-layer TopN/Limit exists or the root operator consumes all join output. Remedies: rewrite sort keys to outer-table columns, index the sort column so keep-order scanning applies, or accept root-level TopN when semantics forbid pushdown; risk of forcing pushdown via rule overrides is wrong results.

nodes.name: Repair Topology Label and Placement Configuration
nodes.content: PD isolates replicas only from the labels TiKV/TiFlash actually report (server.labels in TiKV config or tiflash-learner.toml for the proxy, or --labels at startup) matched against replication.location-labels (e.g. zone,dc,rack,host); a missing replication.location-labels entry makes PD unable to spread replicas and deployment-time errors can occur. TiDB nodes can also carry [labels] with a zone entry so follower reads prefer same-zone replicas; when replicas co-locate after scale-out, verify labels on the new stores and PD's location-labels list before manual rescheduling. PD isolates replicas only from the labels TiKV/TiFlash actually report (server.labels in TiKV config or tiflash-learner.toml for the proxy, or --labels at startup) matched against replication.location-labels (e.g. zone,dc,rack,host); a missing replication.location-labels entry makes PD unable to spread replicas and deployment-time errors can occur. TiDB nodes can also carry [labels] with a zone entry so follower reads prefer same-zone replicas. Region replica count is independent of instance count: scaling to N TiKV instances still tolerates only one replica failure, and more instances without label isolation widens the blast radius, so plan layered labels (zone > az > rack > host, with a logical zone layer left room to grow) so future scale-outs do not force relabeling and rebalancing.

nodes.name: TSO Allocation Stall
nodes.content: The transaction model (Percolator-style two-phase commit) needs a monotonic timestamp for every transaction, and PD is the sole TSO allocator; PD leader loss or etcd quorum loss stalls timestamp allocation cluster-wide, so all TiDB nodes stop serving while TiKV still looks healthy. Distinguish from storage faults by the pattern of zero QPS everywhere plus PD leader/etcd alarms rather than TiKV errors; fix family: restore the PD leader or etcd quorum and verify TSO latency recovers; there is no application-side workaround.

nodes.name: TSO Batch Wait Remedy and Limits
nodes.content: tidb_tso_client_batch_max_wait_time (default 0, range 0-10 ms) makes the PD client batch more TSO requests per RPC to relieve a PD-leader CPU bottleneck. Distinguish the cause first: if TSO RPC latency is high for other reasons (typically network), increasing this value only adds latency and hurts QPS; keep the value as small as possible. Diagnosis: check PD leader CPU and network metrics alongside TSO wait. Remedies: raise the batch wait briefly for CPU-bound TSO pressure, or fix the network/add PD capacity.

nodes.name: TSO Wait Tuning
nodes.content: Mechanism: high-frequency small queries and transactions request timestamps from PD each time, making TSO wait a visible slice of execution time. Diagnosis: the SQL Execute Time Overview breakdown shows TSO wait share. Fix family: low-precision TSO reads (tidb_low_resolution_tso) when slight staleness is acceptable, and batch DML to cut per-statement timestamp requests. Risks: low-precision TSO reads possibly seconds-stale data, which is unacceptable for strict-consistency reads.

nodes.name: TTL backlog runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: per-table TTL jobs split into up to 64 region-based tasks dispatched across TiDB nodes; unsplittable tables (clustered index with non-int/non-binary-string primary key) run sequentially on a single node, and expired rows stay readable until the background job deletes them. Differential: compare TTL Insert Rows Per Hour against TTL Delete Rows Per Hour (sustained insert > delete means growth), check table TTL attributes and TTL_ENABLE, verify tidb_ttl_job_enable and the schedule window, and inspect mysql.tidb_ttl_job_history to see which job ran. Remedies: (a) re-enable TTL_ENABLE or the global job switch and widen the schedule window; (b) raise tidb_ttl_scan_worker_count or tidb_ttl_delete_worker_count based on whether scan workers sit in dispatch (delete-bound) or delete workers idle (scan-bound); (c) increase tidb_ttl_running_tasks for cluster-wide concurrency. Risks: too many TTL workers pressure TiDB CPU and TiKV disk; short-term insert>delete is not proof of backlog. Limitations: TTL cannot be set on temporary tables and TTL tables cannot be primary tables in foreign keys.

nodes.name: TTL interference runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: TTL tasks run distributedly across TiDB nodes and their worker pressure scales with tidb_ttl_scan_worker_count, tidb_ttl_delete_worker_count, and tidb_ttl_running_tasks. Differential: correlate latency regressions with mysql.tidb_ttl_job_history entries and TTL worker-time panels to confirm a TTL job was active at the same time. Remedies: (a) reduce the worker counts and tidb_ttl_running_tasks; (b) constrain tidb_ttl_job_schedule_window_start_time/end_time to off-peak hours; (c) set TTL_ENABLE='OFF' on the noisiest table or lower its TTL_JOB_INTERVAL frequency as trade-off. Risks: throttling TTL too hard recreates the deletion backlog, so re-check insert vs delete rates after the change.

nodes.name: Restore TTL Cleanup Throughput
nodes.content: Mechanism: TTL tables are cleaned by background jobs scheduled inside tidb_ttl_job_schedule_window_start/end_time (default the whole day), scanning in batches of tidb_ttl_scan_batch_size (500) with 4 scan and 4 delete workers per node; a disabled flag or narrow window silently stops cleanup. Differential: confirm the job state in TTL system tables before blaming delete failures. Remedies: re-enable tidb_ttl_job_enable, widen the schedule window, raise worker counts, and mark heavy TTL work as background task type under resource control. Risk: aggressive worker counts add delete I/O competing with foreground writes.

nodes.name: Two-AZ Replica Placement
nodes.content: Mechanism: cross-AZ replica placement combines replication.location-labels with per-store server.labels and placement rules that pin voter, follower, or learner counts to each AZ via label_constraints; rollback means restoring the backed-up default rule bundle. Diagnosis: when replicas concentrate in one AZ or DR quotas are unmet, dump the rule bundle and compare label constraints with store labels. Remedies: apply rules with rule-bundle save after backing up defaults, keep the DR Auto-Sync label-key consistent with the rules, and validate via region inventory; risk is degraded quorum if an AZ loses more replicas than the rules reserve.

nodes.name: Write conflict handling runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: optimistic transactions detect conflicts only at commit; conflicting keys abort the transaction, and DDL schema changes invalidate in-flight statements (8028). Differential diagnosis: classify the error code - 9007 write conflict means hot-row or key-range contention, 8028 means a concurrent DDL changed the table schema, 8002/8022 are retry-limited conflicts; correlate with statement summary or application SQL to find the contended table. Remedy families: (1) application-level retry with rollback and exponential backoff for codes 8002/8022/8028/9007 up to a max_retries bound; (2) switch hot-path transactions to pessimistic mode; (3) redesign schema or access patterns (queue tables, auto-increment hotspots) that cause frequent conflicts. Risks: unbounded retries amplify load and latency; persistent 9007 storms indicate a schema design problem that retries only mask.

nodes.name: Transaction Mode and DML Type Selection
nodes.content: Mechanism: pessimistic mode locks keys during execution and suits conflict-prone workloads; optimistic mode suits low-conflict multi-statement transactions; bulk DML reduces memory and overhead for large conflict-free writes but requires autocommit and pessimistic-auto-commit disabled. Diagnosis: conflict and retry rates against workload write patterns decide the mode. Fix family: switch tidb_txn_mode or tidb_dml_type per workload segment. Risks: optimistic mode pays at commit when conflicts appear; bulk DML weakens per-statement transactional semantics.

nodes.name: Transaction Size Limit Remediation
nodes.content: Mechanism: rows over txn-entry-size-limit (default 6 MiB, hard max 120 MiB) fail with entry too large, transactions over txn-total-size-limit (default 100 MiB, max 1 TiB) are rejected, and TiKV refuses writes above raft-entry-max-size (default 8 MiB); TiDB session memory scales 2-3x transaction size. Differential: entry errors implicate row width, total-size errors implicate batch design, TiKV refusals implicate raft-entry-max-size. Remedies: split large batches into smaller transactions, raise the limits (txn-entry-size-limit is dynamic since v7.6.0), or use bulk DML mode which bypasses txn-total-size-limit; keep txn-total-size-limit at most 1 GiB when Kafka consumes binlog. Risk: larger transactions shift pressure onto tidb_mem_quota_query and downstream consumers. For oversized legacy batch changes, non-transactional DML is the supported splitting path - deprecated batch-dml variables (tidb_batch_insert/delete/commit) can split work into non-atomic transactions and risk data corruption.

nodes.name: Unstable Result Set Discrimination
nodes.content: Mechanism: distributed parallel reads give no implicit row order, and NON-FULL GROUP BY leaves non-aggregated columns ambiguous, so multiple results satisfy the same SQL. Discrimination: classify the SQL pattern - missing ORDER BY, ORDER BY keys that are not unique, GROUP_CONCAT without an inner ORDER BY, SELECT * ... LIMIT N (which Region answers first varies), or SELECT columns not functionally dependent on GROUP BY columns. Fix families: (1) add explicit ORDER BY and extend keys until the combination is unique; (2) add ORDER BY inside GROUP_CONCAT; (3) make LIMIT queries deterministic by ordering; (4) enable ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY in sql_mode to surface ambiguous aggregations as ERROR 1055 - risk: previously accepted queries get rejected until rewritten.

nodes.name: Upgrade Control Plane Preparation
nodes.content: Mechanism: cluster upgrades fail when the control plane lags: TiUP and the cluster component should be at a recent version, offline deployments need the new server/toolkit mirrors merged (tiup mirror merge) before upgrading, and stale manifests after overwrite can break TiUP until cleared. Diagnosis: when tiup cluster operations error mid-upgrade, check tiup --version and whether manifests are stale. Remedies: upgrade tiup --self and tiup update cluster first, merge offline mirrors for air-gapped clusters, and rm -rf ~/.tiup/manifests/* if TiUP errors after overwrite; risk of skipping compatibility-change review is semantic breakage that only appears post-upgrade.

nodes.name: Upgrade DDL Precheck Discipline
nodes.content: Mechanism: upgrades are unsafe with in-flight schema changes because the DDL queue semantics change across versions, and leaders are evicted per node during rolling restart. Differential: ADMIN SHOW DDL for ongoing jobs, SHOW BACKUPS/RESTORES for running backup tasks, tiup cluster check --cluster for Region health, and verify server-version is set to the real (or empty) version before starting. Remedies: (a) wait or ADMIN CANCEL DDL, and finish backup/restore tasks before upgrading; (b) disable the DXF before a smooth upgrade so indexes added mid-upgrade cannot diverge from data; (c) raise --wait-timeout (e.g. via tiup update cluster --wait-timeout) when performance.force-init-stats lengthens startup, and --transfer-timeout when leader eviction needs longer; (d) use offline upgrade inside a maintenance window. Risks: no version downgrade exists after upgrade; pre-v7.1 sources must never run DDL during upgrade; avoid creating clustered-index tables while TiDB Binlog rolling updates are in progress.

nodes.name: Upgrade DDL risk runbook
nodes.content: Mechanism: DDL state machines interact with the upgrade path. Pre-v7.1.0 clusters must not upgrade with a DDL job running or run DDL mid-upgrade (undefined behavior); smooth upgrade (v7.1.0+ paths, or /upgrade/start+finish HTTP API) pauses user DDL during the upgrade instead. Additional gates: a canceling-state DDL cannot be paused, so the upgrade retries canceling and exits on failure; with versions before v8.1.0, disable DXF (tidb_enable_dist_task=OFF) and finish or cancel all distributed ADD INDEX and IMPORT INTO tasks first, otherwise ADD INDEX during upgrade risks index inconsistency; more than about 300 queued DDL jobs can exceed the TiUP upgrade timeout. Differential diagnosis: run ADMIN SHOW DDL before upgrading to find running or queued jobs; check whether DM/TiCDC will deliver DDL statements during the window. Remedy families: (1) wait, pause (ADMIN PAUSE DDL JOBS) or cancel jobs before upgrading; (2) schedule rolling updates off-peak with the minimum topology (TiDB x2, PD x3, TiKV x3) met and Drainer stopped; (3) use TiUP/Kubernetes upgrade paths rather than manual binaries. During upgrade, do not run DDL on system tables, ADMIN CANCEL DDL JOBS, imports, or BR (it can replicate paused DDL jobs that then stay stuck). Risks: ignoring these restrictions causes stuck jobs, blocked DM/TiCDC pipelines, or undefined behavior; upgrading below minimum topology removes failover headroom.

nodes.name: Upgrade Default Changes Affecting Diagnosis
nodes.content: Some post-upgrade symptoms come from identity and default changes rather than faults: security scanners reject the reported MySQL-compatible version string, which can be re-published via the server-version config (or tiup cluster edit-config plus reload -R tidb) - masking the real version, so cross-check the string when version-dependent behavior shifts. Review configuration and variable defaults that changed between versions before attributing new behavior to bugs.
